| Rules of engagement and authorisations | [Retention Period] | [Financial Entity Legal Name] | Confidential; preserve signed approvals and approved changes |
| Findings and remediation records | [Retention Period] | [Financial Entity Legal Name] | Confidential; maintain traceability from finding to remediation action and validation status |
| Closure meeting records | [Retention Period] | [Competent Authority Name / Financial Entity Legal Name] | Confidential; retain agreed actions, decisions, and open items |
| Communications with competent authority | [Retention Period] | [Competent Authority Name / Financial Entity Legal Name] | Confidential; retain formal correspondence and supervisory submissions |

Records must be:

- Stored in approved repositories with access limited to personnel with a documented need to know.
- Protected from unauthorised disclosure, alteration, deletion, or copying.
- Marked with the appropriate confidentiality classification.
- Transferred only through approved secure channels.
- Retained for the required period and disposed of securely when retention obligations expire.
- Made available to authorised supervisory, audit, legal, or governance stakeholders where there is a legitimate and approved need.

Where supporting evidence is held by testing providers or third-party ICT service providers, [Financial Entity Legal Name] must ensure that contractual and operational arrangements allow secure retention, controlled access, and timely provision of records when required.

Any suspected unauthorised access, disclosure, loss, or compromise of this attestation or related TLPT evidence must be escalated immediately through the applicable security incident and regulatory notification processes.

DORA-031.title: ICT Internal Audit Reports
DORA-031.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| ICT-AUD-RPT-[YYYY]-[NN] | 1.0 | Head of Internal Audit | [DD MMM YYYY] | DORA | Confidential - Internal Audit |

## Purpose

This report presents the results of the internal audit of the organisation’s Information and Communication Technology Risk Management Framework (ICT RMF). The audit assessed whether the ICT RMF is appropriately designed, implemented, operated, monitored, and improved to support the organisation’s operational resilience obligations.

The report is intended to provide the Management Body, Audit Committee, senior management, risk management function, compliance function, ICT function, and other authorised stakeholders with an independent view of:

- The adequacy of ICT governance and oversight arrangements.
- The effectiveness of ICT risk identification, assessment, treatment, monitoring, and reporting.
- The organisation’s preparedness to prevent, withstand, respond to, and recover from ICT-related disruptions.
- The maturity of controls supporting ICT security, business continuity, incident management, third-party ICT risk, change management, data protection, and resilience testing.
- Identified weaknesses, root causes, risk implications, and required corrective actions.

This report is prepared by competent internal auditors independent of the activities reviewed. Where specialist technical knowledge was required, the audit team used appropriately qualified subject matter experts while maintaining internal audit ownership of the audit conclusions.

## Reporting Period & Scope

### Reporting Period

This report covers the audit work performed during the following period:

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Audit planning start date | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| Fieldwork start date | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| Fieldwork completion date | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| Draft report issued | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| Management response received | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| Final report issued | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| Period of activity reviewed | [DD MMM YYYY] to [DD MMM YYYY] |

### Audit Scope

The audit reviewed the design and operating effectiveness of the ICT RMF across the organisation, including policies, governance structures, processes, control evidence, risk records, operational practices, monitoring activities, and management reporting.

The scope included the following areas:

| Scope Area | Included Activities |
|---|---|
| ICT governance and accountability | Management Body oversight, ICT risk ownership, committee reporting, escalation arrangements, and segregation of responsibilities |
| ICT risk management framework | Risk identification, assessment methodology, risk appetite, treatment planning, acceptance, monitoring, and reporting |
| ICT asset and information asset management | Asset inventory completeness, ownership, classification, criticality, and dependency mapping |
| ICT security controls | Identity and access management, privileged access, logging and monitoring, vulnerability management, endpoint security, network security, and secure configuration |
| ICT operations | Capacity, availability, performance monitoring, backup operations, job scheduling, operational procedures, and service management |
| Change and release management | Change approval, testing, segregation of duties, emergency change handling, and post-implementation review |
| Incident management | Detection, classification, escalation, response, communications, root cause analysis, lessons learned, and management reporting |
| Business continuity and disaster recovery | Business impact analysis, continuity planning, recovery objectives, disaster recovery arrangements, backup restoration, and testing evidence |
| Digital operational resilience testing | Testing strategy, penetration testing, scenario-based testing, remediation tracking, and retesting |
| ICT third-party risk management | Due diligence, contract requirements, ongoing monitoring, exit planning, subcontracting visibility, and concentration risk |
| Data protection and integrity | Data backup, restoration, encryption, retention, integrity controls, and secure disposal |
| Awareness and training | ICT risk awareness, role-based training, phishing exercises, and training completion monitoring |
| Metrics and reporting | Key risk indicators, key control indicators, audit trails, dashboards, exception reporting, and management action tracking |

### Business Areas and Systems Reviewed

The following functions and systems were included in the audit sample:

| Area / System | Owner | Criticality | Audit Coverage |
|---|---|---:|---|
| [Core Banking / Trading / Payments Platform] | [System Owner] | Critical | Governance, access, resilience, incident, change, third-party dependency |
| [Customer Portal / Mobile Application] | [System Owner] | High | Security controls, availability, change, monitoring, vulnerability management |
| [Identity and Access Management Platform] | [System Owner] | Critical | User lifecycle, privileged access, recertification, logging |
| [Security Monitoring Platform] | [System Owner] | High | Alert handling, escalation, coverage, evidence retention |
| [Cloud Hosting Environment] | [Service Owner] | Critical | Configuration, third-party oversight, resilience, backup, monitoring |
| [Enterprise Resource Planning System] | [System Owner] | Medium | Access, change, backup, operational monitoring |

### Scope Exclusions

The following areas were excluded from this audit and may be considered for future audit activity:

| Excluded Area | Reason for Exclusion | Future Coverage Consideration |
|---|---|---|
| [System / Process] | [Reason] | [Planned review date or dependency] |
| [Geographic location / subsidiary] | [Reason] | [Planned review date or dependency] |

### Audit Objectives

The audit objectives were to determine whether:

1. The ICT RMF is approved, documented, maintained, and embedded across relevant business and technology functions.
2. ICT risk governance provides clear accountability, effective challenge, timely escalation, and informed decision-making.
3. ICT risks are identified, assessed, treated, monitored, and reported consistently and in line with the organisation’s risk appetite.
4. ICT controls are proportionate to the criticality of systems, information assets, services, and third-party dependencies.
5. ICT-related incidents are detected, managed, escalated, reported, remediated, and used to drive control improvement.
6. Continuity and recovery arrangements are defined, tested, and capable of supporting critical or important functions.
7. ICT third-party arrangements are appropriately governed throughout the lifecycle.
8. Resilience testing is risk-based, realistic, documented, and followed by effective remediation.
9. Management information is accurate, complete, timely, and sufficiently detailed to support oversight by senior management and the Management Body.
10. Prior audit findings and agreed management actions have been implemented effectively.

## Executive Summary

### Overall Audit Opinion

**Overall rating: Needs Improvement**

The organisation has established the core components of an ICT Risk Management Framework and has made measurable progress in documenting policies, assigning responsibilities, and implementing key operational controls. The audit found that ICT risk management is recognised as a management priority, with regular reporting to senior governance forums and active involvement from the ICT, risk, compliance, and operational resilience functions.

However, the audit identified weaknesses in the consistency, completeness, and evidence quality of several key ICT risk management activities. In particular, the organisation should strengthen the linkage between critical business services, supporting ICT assets, third-party providers, risk assessments, resilience testing, and recovery plans. The current framework provides a foundation, but further work is required to demonstrate that it operates effectively across all critical and important functions.

The most significant issues relate to:

- Incomplete mapping of ICT assets and dependencies supporting critical or important functions.
- Inconsistent quality of ICT risk assessments and risk treatment plans.
- Gaps in privileged access review and recertification evidence.
- Insufficient validation of disaster recovery capabilities for selected critical systems.
- Incomplete third-party ICT risk monitoring and exit planning.
- Delayed closure of control remediation actions arising from incidents, resilience testing, and prior assurance work.

No evidence was identified of unmanaged severe ICT risk that would require immediate suspension of a critical service. However, several findings increase the likelihood that the organisation may be unable to demonstrate effective ICT resilience under regulatory, supervisory, customer, or internal challenge unless corrective action is completed promptly.

### Summary of Findings

| Rating | Number of Findings | Summary |
|---|---:|---|
| Critical | 0 | No critical findings identified. |
| High | 3 | Material control weaknesses requiring prompt senior management attention. |
| Medium | 6 | Control weaknesses requiring planned remediation and management oversight. |
| Low | 4 | Improvement opportunities with limited immediate risk impact. |
| Advisory | 3 | Observations to improve maturity, efficiency, or assurance quality. |

### High-Rated Findings

| Ref | Finding Title | Risk Area | Owner | Target Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F-01 | Incomplete mapping of critical ICT assets and dependencies | ICT governance and operational resilience | [Chief Information Officer] | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| F-02 | Disaster recovery evidence does not demonstrate recoverability of selected critical systems | Business continuity and disaster recovery | [Head of Infrastructure / Technology Resilience] | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| F-03 | Third-party ICT risk monitoring and exit plans are incomplete for critical providers | ICT third-party risk management | [Head of Procurement / Third-Party Risk] | [DD MMM YYYY] |

### Positive Observations

The audit identified several areas of effective practice:

- The organisation has approved an ICT risk management policy suite covering key domains such as access control, incident management, change management, vulnerability management, business continuity, and third-party risk.
- ICT risk is included in regular risk reporting to senior governance forums.
- A formal ICT incident management process is in place, including severity classification, escalation paths, and post-incident review requirements.
- Vulnerability scanning is performed regularly across the core infrastructure estate.
- Change records for sampled standard and normal changes generally included approval, testing evidence, and implementation notes.
- The Security Operations team demonstrated effective awareness of escalation procedures for high-priority alerts.
- Management has initiated a programme to improve operational resilience mapping and resilience testing.

### Overall Risk Implication

The current control environment reduces several important ICT risks but does not yet provide consistent, complete, and fully evidenced assurance that the organisation can maintain resilient operations across all critical or important functions during severe but plausible ICT disruption scenarios. The most important near-term management priority is to improve traceability between business services, ICT assets, third parties, risk assessments, recovery arrangements, and test evidence.

## Methodology

### Audit Approach

The audit was performed using a risk-based internal audit methodology. The audit team assessed both the design adequacy and operating effectiveness of controls. Testing was performed using a combination of document review, interviews, walkthroughs, sample-based control testing, data analysis, and review of management information.

The audit work was conducted in the following phases:

| Phase | Activities Performed |
|---|---|
| Planning | Defined audit objectives, confirmed scope, identified key stakeholders, reviewed prior reports, assessed inherent ICT risk areas, and prepared the audit work programme |
| Fieldwork | Conducted interviews, reviewed policies and procedures, tested selected controls, inspected records, assessed management reporting, and validated evidence |
| Analysis | Evaluated results, identified root causes, rated findings, assessed risk implications, and developed recommendations |
| Management validation | Discussed findings with control owners, confirmed factual accuracy, and obtained management responses |
| Reporting | Prepared the draft and final report, including agreed actions, owners, and target dates |
| Follow-up planning | Logged agreed actions for tracking through the internal audit issue management process |

### Evidence Reviewed

The audit team reviewed evidence including, but not limited to:

- ICT risk management policies, standards, and procedures.
- ICT risk registers and risk assessment records.
- Management Body and committee packs relating to ICT risk.
- ICT asset inventories and configuration management data.
- Business impact analyses and service dependency maps.
- Incident logs, post-incident reports, and root cause analysis records.
- Change management tickets and emergency change records.
- User access review evidence and privileged access records.
- Vulnerability scan reports and remediation trackers.
- Backup logs, restoration evidence, and disaster recovery test reports.
- Third-party due diligence files, service reports, contracts, risk assessments, and exit plans.
- Resilience testing plans, results, issues, and remediation records.
- Prior internal audit, external audit, compliance, and risk assurance reports.

### Interviews Conducted

| Role / Function | Interview Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Chief Information Officer] | ICT strategy, governance, risk ownership, investment priorities |
| [Chief Information Security Officer] | Security control environment, monitoring, incident response, vulnerability management |
| [Chief Risk Officer / Operational Risk Lead] | Risk appetite, ICT risk oversight, risk reporting, challenge process |
| [Head of Operational Resilience] | Critical function mapping, impact tolerances, scenario testing, remediation tracking |
| [Head of Infrastructure] | Availability, capacity, backup, recovery, network resilience |
| [Head of Applications] | Application ownership, change management, system lifecycle, technical debt |
| [Head of Procurement / Third-Party Risk] | ICT outsourcing, supplier due diligence, monitoring, exit planning |
| [Data Protection Officer / Privacy Lead] | Data security, breach handling, retention, confidentiality controls |
| [Service Desk Manager] | Incident handling, service request management, user provisioning |
| [Business Service Owners] | Business impact, service continuity, dependency validation |

### Sample Testing

The audit used judgemental sampling focused on higher-risk systems, critical processes, recent incidents, high-risk changes, privileged users, critical third parties, and resilience testing evidence.

| Test Area | Population | Sample Size | Basis of Selection |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Critical ICT assets | [Number] assets | [Number] | Criticality, business service dependency, hosting model |
| Privileged users | [Number] accounts | [Number] | Elevated access, administrator roles, shared platform coverage |
| User access reviews | [Number] reviews | [Number] | Critical systems, overdue reviews, high-risk roles |
| ICT incidents | [Number] incidents | [Number] | Severity, business impact, recurrence, closure status |
| Changes | [Number] changes | [Number] | Emergency changes, failed changes, critical systems |
| Vulnerabilities | [Number] open items | [Number] | Severity, age, internet exposure, compensating controls |
| Third-party providers | [Number] providers | [Number] | Criticality, outsourcing dependency, cloud concentration |
| Disaster recovery tests | [Number] tests | [Number] | Critical systems, failed tests, incomplete evidence |
| Risk assessments | [Number] records | [Number] | High residual risk, overdue review, critical service linkage |

### Rating Criteria

Findings were rated using the following internal audit criteria:

| Rating | Definition | Management Attention Required |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | A severe control failure that creates immediate risk to critical operations, legal obligations, customers, financial stability, or regulatory standing | Immediate executive action and urgent remediation |
| High | A material weakness that could significantly impair ICT resilience, security, recovery, or risk oversight if not remediated promptly | Senior management action with defined remediation plan |
| Medium | A control gap or inconsistent practice that increases risk but is not expected to cause immediate severe disruption | Timely management action and tracked remediation |
| Low | A minor deficiency, documentation gap, or isolated control weakness with limited risk impact | Local management action |
| Advisory | Improvement opportunity to enhance maturity, efficiency, consistency, or assurance quality | Management consideration |

### Limitations

The audit conclusions are based on the evidence made available during the audit period and the samples selected. Internal audit does not provide absolute assurance that all control weaknesses have been identified. Where management could not provide evidence, the audit team assessed the control as not demonstrably operating effectively.

### Finding F-01 - Incomplete Mapping of Critical ICT Assets and Dependencies

| Field | Detail |

| Rating | High |

| Status | Open |

#### Condition

The organisation has begun mapping critical or important business functions to supporting ICT systems, infrastructure, data flows, and third-party providers. However, the mapping is incomplete and inconsistently maintained across business areas.

The audit identified the following issues:

- Not all critical or important functions had documented end-to-end ICT dependency maps.
- Several dependency maps did not identify supporting infrastructure components, network dependencies, identity services, monitoring tools, or cloud services.
- Third-party dependencies were not consistently linked to the specific business functions and ICT assets they support.
- Asset criticality ratings in the ICT asset inventory did not always match business service criticality.
- Ownership fields were incomplete or outdated for selected assets.
- Evidence was not available to show periodic validation of dependency maps by both ICT and business owners.

#### Criteria

The organisation should maintain a current and accurate understanding of ICT assets, information assets, interdependencies, supporting infrastructure, third-party services, and business services. Dependency information should be sufficiently complete to support risk assessment, continuity planning, incident response, recovery prioritisation, testing, and management reporting.

#### Cause

The dependency mapping activity is being managed as a programme deliverable rather than a fully embedded ongoing control. Asset management, operational resilience, procurement, enterprise architecture, and service ownership data sources are not yet integrated or reconciled through a defined control process.

#### Risk Implication

Incomplete dependency mapping may result in:

- Inaccurate ICT risk assessments.
- Recovery plans that omit key technical dependencies.
- Ineffective resilience testing scenarios.
- Delayed incident response due to unclear ownership or dependency impact.
- Inadequate oversight of third-party concentration risk.
- Inability to demonstrate how critical or important functions are protected and recovered.

#### Evidence

- Review of [Number] critical service maps identified [Number] with missing infrastructure or third-party dependencies.
- Review of [Number] asset inventory records identified [Number] with incomplete ownership or criticality fields.
- Interviews with business service owners indicated inconsistent awareness of upstream and downstream ICT dependencies.
- No formal evidence was available showing periodic reconciliation between the asset inventory, service maps, and third-party register.

#### Recommendation

Management should implement a controlled dependency mapping process covering all critical or important functions. The process should define required data fields, ownership, update triggers, validation frequency, evidence retention, and reconciliation with ICT asset, third-party, business continuity, and risk records.

### Finding F-02 - Disaster Recovery Evidence Does Not Demonstrate Recoverability of Selected Critical Systems

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Rating | High |
| Risk Area | Business continuity and disaster recovery |
| Process Owner | [Head of Infrastructure / Technology Resilience] |
| Supporting Owners | [Application Owners], [Business Continuity Manager], [Business Service Owners] |
| Target Completion Date | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| Status | Open |

#### Condition

Disaster recovery arrangements are defined for critical systems; however, the audit could not confirm that all selected critical systems can be recovered within approved recovery objectives.

Weaknesses identified included:

- Disaster recovery test reports did not consistently record start time, recovery time achieved, data loss position, test scope, exclusions, defects, and business validation.
- Some tests were limited to technical failover checks and did not include application, data, interface, or business process validation.
- Recovery plans for selected systems did not include dependencies on identity services, network connectivity, batch processing, reporting tools, or external providers.
- Backup restoration testing was not performed for all selected critical systems within the reviewed period.
- Issues from prior recovery tests were not consistently tracked to closure.

#### Criteria

The organisation should maintain and test recovery arrangements for critical ICT systems in a way that demonstrates recoverability against approved business requirements. Testing should be documented, realistic, risk-based, independently reviewable, and followed by remediation of identified weaknesses.

#### Cause

Recovery testing is primarily coordinated by technical teams, with inconsistent participation from application owners and business service owners. The organisation does not yet use a standard test evidence template that requires confirmation of recovery objectives, business validation, dependencies, defects, and lessons learned.

#### Risk Implication

The organisation may be unable to demonstrate that selected critical systems can be recovered within business-approved timeframes and data loss limits. In a severe ICT disruption, this may result in prolonged service outage, customer harm, financial loss, operational disruption, regulatory scrutiny, and reputational damage.

#### Evidence

- Review of [Number] disaster recovery tests identified [Number] with incomplete evidence of achieved recovery time.
- [Number] test reports did not evidence business owner validation.
- [Number] critical systems had recovery plans that omitted key technical dependencies.
- [Number] prior test defects remained open beyond agreed target dates.

#### Recommendation

Management should strengthen disaster recovery governance, test design, evidence requirements, and defect remediation. Recovery testing should validate end-to-end service recovery, not only infrastructure availability.

#### Management Action Plan

| Action | Owner | Due Date | Success Criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| Implement a standard disaster recovery test plan and results template | [Head of Technology Resilience] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Template approved and used for all new tests |
| Re-perform recovery testing for selected critical systems where evidence was incomplete | [Application Owners] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Test reports demonstrate recovery time, recovery point, business validation, and defect tracking |
| Update recovery plans to include infrastructure, identity, network, data, third-party, and business process dependencies | [Head of Infrastructure] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Recovery plans updated and approved |
| Establish monthly reporting of recovery test defects and overdue remediation actions | [Business Continuity Manager] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Monthly report issued to resilience governance forum |

#### Condition

The organisation maintains a register of ICT third-party providers and performs due diligence during onboarding. However, ongoing monitoring and exit planning for critical ICT providers require improvement.

The audit identified the following:

- Criticality assessments were not consistently documented for all ICT providers.
- Service performance and resilience reporting was not retained consistently.
- Provider incident notification and escalation contacts were not current for all sampled providers.
- Exit plans were incomplete or not tested for selected critical providers.
- Subcontractor visibility was limited for selected cloud and managed service providers.
- Concentration risk analysis was not sufficiently developed to show aggregate exposure to individual providers, regions, platforms, or service models.

#### Criteria

The organisation should manage ICT third-party risk throughout the full provider lifecycle. This includes due diligence, contractual safeguards, ongoing monitoring, incident communication, resilience assurance, subcontractor oversight, concentration risk assessment, and credible exit planning for providers supporting critical or important functions.

#### Cause

Third-party ICT risk responsibilities are distributed across procurement, legal, ICT, business service owners, and risk management. The operating model does not yet provide consistent evidence that all lifecycle controls are performed for each critical provider.

#### Risk Implication

Inadequate third-party monitoring and exit planning may result in delayed response to provider disruption, unclear contractual recourse, unmanaged subcontractor exposure, concentration risk, extended service outage, and inability to transition services within acceptable timeframes.

#### Recommendation

Management should implement a consistent lifecycle control framework for critical ICT third parties, supported by a complete register, assigned owners, minimum evidence standards, periodic reviews, and risk-based monitoring.

## Analysis

### Control Environment Maturity

The ICT RMF is at a developing-to-established maturity level. Core policies and governance structures exist, and key ICT control domains are operational. However, evidence quality and consistency vary across teams. The organisation should focus on embedding repeatable controls, improving traceability, strengthening ownership, and consolidating reporting.

| Domain | Design Assessment | Operating Effectiveness | Maturity View |
|---|---|---|---|
| ICT governance | Partially effective | Partially effective | Established foundation; reporting and accountability require refinement |
| ICT risk assessment | Partially effective | Partially effective | Method exists; quality and consistency require improvement |
| Asset and dependency management | Partially effective | Needs improvement | Material gaps in completeness and validation |
| Identity and access management | Generally effective | Partially effective | Core controls exist; privileged review evidence needs strengthening |
| Vulnerability management | Generally effective | Partially effective | Scanning routine; remediation governance requires improvement |
| Change management | Generally effective | Partially effective | Standard changes controlled; emergency change evidence inconsistent |
| Incident management | Generally effective | Partially effective | Process works; lessons learned closure requires strengthening |
| Business continuity and recovery | Partially effective | Needs improvement | Recovery documentation exists; test evidence insufficient for selected systems |
| Third-party ICT risk | Partially effective | Needs improvement | Onboarding stronger than ongoing monitoring and exit planning |
| Resilience testing | Partially effective | Partially effective | Programme developing; scenario design and remediation tracking need maturity |
| Metrics and reporting | Partially effective | Partially effective | Reporting frequent but not sufficiently risk-based or forward-looking |

### Root Cause Themes

The audit identified several recurring root causes across findings:

1. **Fragmented ownership**
 - ICT risk activities are distributed across multiple functions without always having clear end-to-end accountability.

2. **Manual evidence management**
 - Several controls rely on manual evidence capture, local storage, spreadsheets, and informal follow-up.

3. **Programme dependency**
 - Some important capabilities are being developed through transformation initiatives but are not yet embedded as business-as-usual controls.

4. **Inconsistent data linkage**
 - Asset inventories, dependency maps, risk registers, third-party registers, incident records, and resilience test results are not fully integrated.

5. **Limited control quality assurance**
 - Control performance is often reported, but independent quality review of underlying evidence is inconsistent.

6. **Action tracking discipline**
 - Remediation actions from audits, incidents, tests, vulnerabilities, and third-party reviews are not always consolidated into a single management view.

### Risk Appetite Alignment

The organisation has defined ICT risk appetite statements; however, operational metrics do not yet consistently demonstrate whether exposure remains within appetite. Some metrics are activity-based, such as number of changes or incidents, rather than risk-based, such as overdue high-risk vulnerabilities affecting critical systems or recovery test failures linked to critical services.

Management should ensure ICT risk appetite is supported by measurable thresholds, escalation triggers, and board-level reporting that enables timely challenge and decision-making.

### Overall Conclusion

The organisation has taken meaningful steps to establish its ICT RMF and support digital operational resilience. The framework is directionally aligned with expected good practice and contains the key domains needed to manage ICT risk.

The framework is not yet fully mature. The main gaps are not the absence of policies but the completeness, consistency, integration, and evidencing of control operation. The organisation should prioritise remediation of high-rated findings, particularly dependency mapping, disaster recovery validation, and third-party ICT risk monitoring. These areas are foundational to demonstrating that critical or important functions can remain resilient during ICT disruption.

### Remediation Governance

Management should oversee remediation through a formal issue management process. At a minimum:

- Each action must have a named accountable owner.
- Target dates must be realistic, approved, and risk-based.
- Overdue actions must be escalated to senior management.
- Closure must require evidence of implementation.
- High-rated findings should be independently validated by Internal Audit before closure.
- Where remediation is delayed, management must document interim risk treatment and compensating controls.
- Material changes to agreed actions, due dates, or scope must be approved by the appropriate governance forum.
- Progress should be reported at least monthly until all high-rated actions are closed.

### Recommended Management Reporting Format

|---|---|
| Action status | Not started, in progress, complete pending validation, closed, overdue |
| Risk rating | Critical, high, medium, low, advisory |
| Current risk exposure | Description of risk while action remains open |
| Delivery confidence | Green, amber, red with rationale |
| Key blockers | Dependencies, funding, resource constraints, vendor delays |
| Evidence required for closure | Documents, screenshots, reports, test results, approvals, system records |
| Validation owner | Management, risk function, compliance function, Internal Audit |
| Escalation required | Yes / No with required decision |

| F-10 | Backup restoration schedule, test results, validation approvals |
| F-11 | Policy exception register, approval records, expiry review evidence |
| F-12 | Role-based training matrix, completion reports, escalation records |
| F-13 | Evidence repository standard, repository access controls, sample retained control evidence |

## Distribution & Confidentiality

### Distribution

This report is intended for authorised internal use only. Distribution is limited to individuals and governance bodies with a legitimate need to know.

| Recipient / Forum | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Management Body | Oversight of ICT risk management and operational resilience |
| Audit Committee | Review of audit results, management actions, and remediation progress |
| Executive Committee | Management accountability and resource prioritisation |
| Chief Executive Officer | Awareness of material ICT risk and remediation obligations |
| Chief Information Officer | Ownership of ICT RMF remediation |
| Chief Information Security Officer | Security control remediation and monitoring |
| Chief Risk Officer | Risk oversight, challenge, and risk appetite alignment |
| Chief Operating Officer | Operational resilience and business service continuity |
| Compliance Function | Regulatory alignment and management advisory support |
| Operational Resilience Function | Dependency mapping, testing, and continuity improvements |
| Procurement / Third-Party Risk Function | ICT third-party remediation |
| Legal Function | Contractual and confidentiality considerations |
| External Auditor / Supervisory Authority | Only where formally authorised by [Authorised Role / Governance Forum] |

### Confidentiality Requirements

This report is classified as **Confidential - Internal Audit**. It contains sensitive information regarding ICT controls, vulnerabilities, resilience arrangements, third-party dependencies, and internal risk assessments. Unauthorised disclosure may increase operational, security, legal, regulatory, or reputational risk.

Recipients must comply with the following requirements:

- Do not forward, copy, or distribute this report outside the approved distribution list without written authorisation from [Head of Internal Audit].
- Store the report only in approved secure repositories.
- Do not upload the report to unauthorised external platforms, collaboration tools, or personal storage locations.
- Redact sensitive technical details before any approved external sharing.
- Treat working papers, interview notes, testing results, and supporting evidence as confidential audit material.
- Report any unauthorised disclosure or suspected compromise of this report to [Information Security Contact] and [Head of Internal Audit] immediately.

### External Disclosure

External disclosure of this report, in whole or in part, must be approved by [Head of Internal Audit], [Legal Counsel], and the appropriate executive owner. Where disclosure to a supervisory authority, external auditor, regulator, customer, insurer, or third party is required, the organisation must ensure that:

- The disclosure is legally and contractually permissible.
- Only the minimum necessary information is shared.
- Sensitive technical information is redacted where appropriate.
- A record of disclosure is retained.
- Any follow-up requests are coordinated through authorised channels.

### Record Retention

The final report, management responses, supporting evidence, and closure validation records must be retained in accordance with the organisation’s internal audit record retention requirements.

| Record Type | Minimum Retention Location | Retention Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Final audit report | [Internal Audit Repository] | [Retention Period] |
| Draft report and management responses | [Internal Audit Repository] | [Retention Period] |
| Audit workpapers | [Internal Audit Workpaper System] | [Retention Period] |
| Evidence received from management | [Secure Evidence Repository] | [Retention Period] |
| Action tracking records | [Issue Management System] | [Retention Period] |
| Closure validation evidence | [Internal Audit Repository] | [Retention Period] |

DORA-032.title: Third-Party ICT Provider Strategy
DORA-032.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DORA-TPRM-POL-001] | 1.0 | [Chief Information Security Officer / Head of ICT Risk] | [Effective Date] | Digital Operational Resilience Act | Internal |

## Purpose

This Policy defines the organisation’s strategy and mandatory requirements for managing risks arising from the use of ICT third-party service providers. It establishes a structured, risk-based approach to selecting, contracting, overseeing, and exiting ICT provider arrangements, including the use of a multi-vendor strategy where appropriate to reduce concentration risk and support operational resilience.

The objective of this Policy is to ensure that ICT third-party services supporting the organisation are governed in a manner that protects confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and continuity of business services, and that the organisation remains able to manage disruption, provider failure, security incidents, contractual non-performance, and exit scenarios.

## Scope

This Policy applies to:

- All business units, functions, subsidiaries, branches, and legal entities within [Organisation Name] that procure, use, manage, or rely on ICT third-party services.
- All ICT third-party providers, including cloud service providers, managed service providers, software-as-a-service providers, data centre providers, telecommunications providers, outsourcing providers, software vendors, hardware maintenance providers, and providers of ICT security services.
- All ICT services that support business processes, financial services, customer services, operational resilience, regulatory reporting, transaction processing, data storage, data processing, cybersecurity, identity and access management, business continuity, or disaster recovery.
- All lifecycle stages of ICT third-party arrangements, including strategy, procurement, due diligence, contracting, onboarding, monitoring, change management, renewal, termination, exit, and post-exit assurance.
- Subcontracting chains where the ICT third-party provider uses other parties to deliver services to [Organisation Name].

This Policy applies irrespective of whether the ICT service is delivered on-premises, hosted, cloud-based, hybrid, managed, outsourced, or embedded within a broader business service.

This Policy does not replace procurement, legal, information security, business continuity, data protection, financial crime, or outsourcing requirements. Where multiple policies apply, the stricter requirement shall prevail unless formally approved through the exception process.

## Policy Statements

1. **The organisation shall maintain an approved ICT third-party provider strategy** that supports business objectives, digital resilience, risk appetite, and regulatory obligations.

2. **The ICT third-party provider strategy shall be risk-based** and shall distinguish between low-risk, material, critical, and important ICT services based on the potential impact of provider failure, service disruption, security compromise, data loss, legal non-compliance, or inability to exit.

3. **The organisation shall identify and maintain an inventory of all ICT third-party service providers** used across the organisation, including the business owner, service description, contract owner, risk rating, data types processed, locations of service delivery, subcontractor dependencies where known, and criticality assessment.

4. **The organisation shall identify ICT services supporting critical or important business functions** and ensure such services are subject to enhanced governance, due diligence, contractual protection, monitoring, testing, and exit planning.

5. **The organisation shall avoid unmanaged dependency on a single ICT provider** where such dependency could create unacceptable operational, financial, legal, security, or concentration risk.

6. **The organisation shall implement a multi-vendor or alternative-provider strategy where appropriate** for critical or important ICT services, taking into account service substitutability, technical feasibility, cost, interoperability, data portability, resilience benefits, and risk reduction.

7. **The organisation shall document the rationale where a single-provider strategy is used** for a critical or important ICT service, including compensating controls, exit options, resilience measures, contractual protections, and senior management approval.

8. **The organisation shall assess concentration risk across ICT providers** at least annually and whenever significant provider changes occur, including dependency on the same provider, provider group, technology stack, cloud platform, geographic region, subcontractor, data centre, managed service model, or proprietary technology.

9. **The organisation shall assess whether multiple services rely on the same ICT provider or provider ecosystem** in a manner that could create a single point of failure across business lines, legal entities, regions, or critical operations.

10. **The organisation shall define risk appetite and tolerance thresholds for ICT third-party dependency**, including acceptable levels of exposure to individual providers, service types, locations, subcontractors, and non-substitutable technologies.

11. **The organisation shall perform due diligence before entering into or materially changing an ICT third-party arrangement**, proportionate to the risk and criticality of the service.

12. **Due diligence for ICT providers shall include, as applicable, financial stability, operational resilience, information security, data protection, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, service capacity, technical capability, compliance posture, subcontracting model, auditability, geographic risk, and exit feasibility.**

13. **The organisation shall not enter into a critical or important ICT arrangement until the associated risks have been assessed, documented, reviewed, and accepted by authorised decision-makers.**

14. **The organisation shall ensure that procurement decisions for ICT services are not based solely on cost**, and shall include resilience, security, substitutability, contractual enforceability, concentration risk, and exit viability as decision criteria.

15. **The organisation shall maintain clear ownership for each ICT third-party arrangement**, including a business service owner, contract owner, risk owner, and technical service owner where applicable.

16. **The organisation shall ensure that ICT third-party contracts include appropriate rights and obligations** proportionate to the service risk, including service levels, security requirements, incident notification, audit rights, access rights, data protection obligations, subcontracting controls, reporting requirements, business continuity requirements, termination rights, exit support, and data return or deletion requirements.

17. **The organisation shall ensure that contracts for critical or important ICT services include enforceable exit provisions**, including cooperation requirements, transition assistance, data portability, documentation transfer, knowledge transfer, minimum support periods, and continued service obligations during transition where feasible.

18. **The organisation shall ensure that ICT providers notify the organisation of material changes** that may affect service delivery, security, resilience, compliance, subcontracting, location of service delivery, ownership, financial viability, or ability to meet contractual commitments.

19. **The organisation shall require ICT providers to notify the organisation promptly of incidents** that may affect the confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, or continuity of the services or data provided to the organisation.

20. **The organisation shall maintain a documented onboarding process for ICT providers** that confirms completion of due diligence, risk acceptance, contract approval, access controls, data protection checks, service monitoring arrangements, business continuity expectations, and operational handover.

21. **The organisation shall monitor ICT third-party providers throughout the life of the arrangement**, with monitoring frequency and depth aligned to service criticality and risk.

22. **Monitoring of critical or important ICT providers shall include service performance, security posture, incident history, control assurance, resilience testing results, business continuity capability, subcontractor changes, audit findings, remediation progress, and financial or operational warning indicators.**

23. **The organisation shall define and track key risk indicators and key performance indicators for ICT third-party services**, including thresholds for escalation and management action.

24. **The organisation shall require timely remediation of identified ICT provider risks**, including formal action plans, accountable owners, target dates, and escalation where remediation is delayed or ineffective.

25. **The organisation shall maintain an exit strategy for each critical or important ICT third-party arrangement**, including the conditions that would trigger exit, potential replacement options, transition steps, required internal capabilities, data migration approach, customer or regulatory communication considerations, and residual risks.

26. **The organisation shall periodically test or validate exit plans for critical or important ICT services** to confirm that they are realistic, current, and executable within tolerable disruption limits.

27. **The organisation shall consider substitutability before appointing or renewing a critical or important ICT provider**, including the availability of alternative providers, use of open standards, portability of data, interoperability, licensing constraints, internal skills, and migration complexity.

28. **The organisation shall avoid contractual, technical, operational, or data architecture decisions that create unnecessary lock-in** unless the associated risks are documented, justified, and approved at the appropriate level.

29. **The organisation shall maintain appropriate internal capabilities to oversee ICT third-party services**, including sufficient knowledge of provider services, architecture, resilience arrangements, security controls, contractual obligations, and exit dependencies.

30. **The organisation shall not outsource accountability for operational resilience, information security, risk management, or compliance** to ICT third-party providers.

31. **The organisation shall ensure that subcontracting by ICT providers is transparent and controlled**, especially where subcontractors support critical or important services or access sensitive data, regulated data, production environments, or core infrastructure.

32. **The organisation shall assess the risks of material subcontractors** where those subcontractors could affect service availability, security, compliance, data protection, business continuity, or exit capability.

33. **The organisation shall ensure that ICT third-party provider arrangements support effective incident management**, including clear communication channels, escalation paths, reporting timelines, evidence preservation, root cause analysis, and post-incident remediation.

34. **The organisation shall ensure that ICT providers supporting critical or important services participate in resilience, business continuity, disaster recovery, or crisis exercises where required by the organisation.**

35. **The organisation shall ensure that data handled by ICT providers is protected according to its classification**, including requirements for encryption, segregation, access control, logging, retention, secure deletion, and geographic restrictions where applicable.

36. **The organisation shall ensure that privileged access granted to ICT providers is authorised, monitored, time-bound where practical, and subject to strong authentication and least-privilege principles.**

37. **The organisation shall evaluate ICT third-party risk before renewals, major service changes, geographic changes, material subcontracting changes, mergers, acquisitions, or changes in provider ownership or control.**

38. **The organisation shall ensure that ICT third-party risk assessments are updated when significant incidents, audit findings, control failures, performance deterioration, or geopolitical events materially change the risk profile of a provider or service.**

39. **The organisation shall maintain records sufficient to evidence compliance with this Policy**, including inventories, risk assessments, due diligence results, approvals, contracts, monitoring reports, issue logs, exit plans, test results, and management reporting.

40. **The organisation shall report material ICT third-party risks, concentration risks, unresolved issues, and resilience concerns to senior management and relevant governance forums.**

41. **The organisation shall ensure that critical ICT third-party dependencies are considered in operational resilience planning**, including impact tolerances, business continuity plans, crisis management plans, and disaster recovery arrangements.

42. **The organisation shall ensure that ICT third-party provider strategy decisions are aligned with enterprise architecture, information security, procurement, legal, data protection, financial risk, and operational resilience requirements.**

43. **The organisation shall define minimum assurance requirements for ICT providers** based on service criticality, including independent assurance reports, certifications, penetration testing summaries, resilience evidence, security attestations, or other suitable evidence.

44. **The organisation shall not rely solely on provider self-attestation for critical or important services** where independent assurance, contractual audit rights, or direct testing evidence is reasonably available and proportionate.

45. **The organisation shall maintain a formal escalation process for ICT provider risk issues** that may exceed tolerance levels, affect critical or important services, or require senior management decision-making.

46. **The organisation shall ensure that termination of an ICT third-party arrangement is managed through a controlled process**, including risk assessment, data return or deletion, access revocation, asset recovery, transition assurance, records retention, and closure confirmation.

47. **The organisation shall review the ICT third-party provider strategy at least annually** and whenever there is a material change in business strategy, ICT architecture, regulatory expectations, provider landscape, outsourcing model, or operational resilience requirements.

48. **The organisation shall ensure that employees involved in procuring, approving, managing, or overseeing ICT third-party services understand their responsibilities under this Policy.**

49. **The organisation shall apply enhanced scrutiny to cloud, managed security, core platform, identity, network, data hosting, and business-critical SaaS providers** due to their potential impact on resilience, data protection, access control, and concentration risk.

50. **The organisation shall maintain documented governance for decisions to adopt, continue, expand, reduce, or terminate strategic ICT provider relationships**, including documented risk analysis and approval evidence.

The following minimum requirements apply by ICT provider criticality:

| Provider / Service Category | Minimum Due Diligence | Minimum Contract Requirements | Monitoring Frequency | Exit Planning Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical or important ICT service | Full risk assessment, security review, resilience review, financial and operational assessment, data protection review, subcontractor assessment, exit feasibility review | Full ICT risk and resilience clauses, service levels, audit and access rights, incident notification, subcontracting controls, business continuity obligations, termination rights, exit support, data return/deletion | At least quarterly, with annual formal review | Detailed exit plan required and periodically validated |
| Material ICT service | Risk assessment, security review, data protection review, service continuity review, provider assurance evidence | Service levels, security requirements, incident notification, confidentiality, data protection, termination provisions, subcontractor notification where relevant | At least semi-annually, with annual review | Exit approach required |
| Standard ICT service | Proportionate risk screening, supplier checks, security and data classification review | Standard contractual protections, confidentiality, data handling, service obligations, termination rights | At least annually or upon trigger event | Basic exit considerations required |
| Low-risk ICT service | Basic supplier validation and business owner approval | Standard purchasing terms and confidentiality where applicable | As required | Not normally required unless risk changes |

The following factors shall be considered when determining whether a multi-vendor approach is required:

| Risk Factor | Considerations | Expected Policy Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Criticality of supported business service | Whether disruption would materially affect customers, markets, regulatory reporting, transaction processing, or core operations | Multi-vendor, active-active, active-passive, or tested alternative arrangement shall be considered |
| Provider concentration | Multiple services, entities, or regions dependent on the same provider or provider group | Exposure shall be assessed against tolerance thresholds and reported where elevated |
| Technology lock-in | Proprietary interfaces, bespoke integrations, non-portable data, restrictive licensing, or limited migration options | Lock-in shall be reduced where practical or formally accepted |
| Market substitutability | Availability of viable alternative providers or internal capability | Exit strategy shall reflect realistic replacement options |
| Data portability | Ability to extract data in usable, complete, and timely format | Contract and architecture shall support data return or migration |
| Geographic exposure | Provider operations, data storage, support, or subcontractors in higher-risk locations | Additional due diligence and resilience controls shall be required |
| Subcontractor dependency | Reliance on material subcontractors not directly controlled by the organisation | Transparency, notification, and flow-down obligations shall be required |
| Service interoperability | Ability to integrate with alternative providers or parallel services | Architecture decisions shall support resilience and exit objectives where feasible |
| Cost and complexity | Additional cost, operational burden, and technical complexity of multi-vendor design | Risk reduction shall be balanced against proportionality and approved risk appetite |

## Roles & Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Board of Directors / Governing Body | Approves the overall ICT third-party risk strategy where required; provides oversight of material ICT third-party risks; challenges excessive concentration risk; ensures adequate resources and governance are in place. |
| Senior Management | Ensures this Policy is implemented; approves material risk decisions; reviews significant concentration risks, single-provider dependencies, and critical provider issues; ensures accountability remains within the organisation. |
| Chief Information Security Officer / Head of ICT Risk | Owns this Policy; defines ICT third-party risk standards; oversees risk assessment methodology; reviews security and resilience risks; reports material risks to governance forums. |
| Procurement Function | Ensures ICT provider procurement follows approved sourcing processes; embeds due diligence requirements into purchasing activity; prevents contract execution before required approvals are completed. |
| Legal Function | Ensures ICT contracts contain appropriate rights, protections, obligations, termination provisions, audit rights, data protection terms, subcontracting controls, and exit support provisions. |
| Business Service Owner | Owns the business need for the ICT service; determines business criticality; ensures service risks are understood; supports provider monitoring, exit planning, and continuity requirements. |
| Contract Owner | Maintains the contractual relationship; tracks renewal dates, service obligations, amendments, breaches, and termination provisions; coordinates contract reviews and escalations. |
| Technology / ICT Service Owner | Assesses technical architecture, integration dependencies, security requirements, performance requirements, resilience arrangements, and exit feasibility; supports technical monitoring and transition planning. |
| Third-Party Risk Management Function | Maintains the ICT provider inventory; coordinates due diligence, risk assessments, monitoring, issue tracking, and reporting; supports concentration risk analysis and governance reporting. |
| Business Continuity / Operational Resilience Function | Ensures ICT provider dependencies are reflected in continuity plans, resilience testing, impact analysis, scenario testing, and crisis management arrangements. |
| Data Protection / Privacy Function | Reviews provider processing of personal data; ensures appropriate data protection terms, transfer safeguards, retention controls, and deletion requirements are implemented. |
| Finance Function | Supports assessment of provider financial viability where relevant; reviews cost implications of multi-vendor, exit, transition, and resilience options. |
| Internal Audit | Provides independent assurance over the design and effectiveness of ICT third-party risk management controls, governance, and compliance with this Policy. |
| Employees and Contractors | Use only approved ICT providers and services; follow procurement and onboarding processes; promptly report provider issues, security concerns, or unauthorised ICT service use. |

## Compliance, Monitoring & Enforcement

Compliance with this Policy is mandatory. The organisation shall monitor compliance through a combination of preventive controls, management oversight, independent assurance, and operational reporting.

The following compliance and monitoring activities shall be performed:

| Activity | Responsible Function | Frequency | Evidence |
|---|---|---:|---|
| ICT provider inventory review | Third-Party Risk Management | Quarterly | Updated inventory, change log, completeness attestation |
| Critical and important ICT service review | ICT Risk / Business Owners | At least annually | Criticality assessments, approval records |
| Concentration risk assessment | ICT Risk / Operational Resilience | At least annually and upon material change | Concentration risk report, risk heatmap, management actions |
| Due diligence completion check | Procurement / Third-Party Risk Management | Before contract approval | Due diligence file, risk assessment, approvals |
| Contract compliance review for critical providers | Legal / Contract Owner | At onboarding and renewal | Contract checklist, gap assessment, remediation plan |
| Provider performance and risk monitoring | Contract Owner / Service Owner | Quarterly for critical providers | Service reports, risk indicators, issue logs |
| Provider assurance review | ICT Risk / Information Security | At least annually for critical providers | Assurance reports, certifications, control reviews, exceptions |
| Exit plan review | Business Owner / ICT Service Owner | At least annually for critical providers | Exit plan, validation record, action log |
| Subcontractor dependency review | Third-Party Risk Management / Legal | At least annually for critical providers | Subcontractor register, risk assessment, provider notifications |
| Policy compliance reporting | ICT Risk | Quarterly | Management dashboard, breaches, exceptions, remediation status |
| Independent assurance | Internal Audit | Risk-based audit plan | Audit reports, findings, management responses |

Non-compliance with this Policy may result in one or more of the following actions:

- Suspension or rejection of ICT provider onboarding.
- Escalation to senior management or the relevant risk committee.
- Requirement for remediation before contract execution or renewal.
- Restriction, reduction, or termination of provider services.
- Formal risk acceptance by authorised management.
- Disciplinary action for employees who knowingly bypass required controls.
- Notification to relevant governance, legal, compliance, or regulatory stakeholders where appropriate.

Material breaches of this Policy shall be recorded, investigated, and remediated. Root causes shall be identified and addressed to prevent recurrence.

## Exceptions

Exceptions to this Policy shall be permitted only where there is a documented business justification, risk assessment, compensating controls, defined expiry date, and approval by the appropriate authority.

Exceptions shall not be used to bypass mandatory regulatory, legal, security, or operational resilience requirements. Exceptions for critical or important ICT services shall require enhanced scrutiny and senior management approval.

Each exception request shall include:

| Required Information | Description |
|---|---|
| Exception title | Short description of the requested deviation |
| Policy requirement affected | The specific requirement that cannot be met |
| Business justification | Why compliance is not currently possible or proportionate |
| Provider and service affected | ICT provider name, service name, and business owner |
| Criticality rating | Critical, important, material, standard, or low-risk |
| Risk assessment | Description of risks introduced by the exception |
| Compensating controls | Measures to reduce or monitor the risk |
| Duration | Start date, expiry date, and review date |
| Remediation plan | Actions required to achieve compliance, with owners and dates |
| Approval | Required approval based on risk and criticality |

Minimum approval requirements for exceptions are as follows:

| Exception Type | Minimum Approval |
|---|---|
| Low-risk or administrative exception | Policy Owner or delegated ICT Risk Manager |
| Material ICT service exception | Business Owner, ICT Risk, and Procurement |
| Critical or important ICT service exception | Senior Management and relevant risk governance forum |
| Exception involving significant concentration risk, single-provider dependency, or limited exit capability | Senior Management with documented risk acceptance |
| Exception involving legal, data protection, or contractual limitations | Legal and Data Protection approval, plus ICT Risk approval |

Approved exceptions shall be recorded in the exception register and monitored until closure. Expired exceptions shall not remain valid unless formally reassessed and reapproved.

## Review & Maintenance

This Policy shall be reviewed at least annually and whenever significant changes occur, including:

- Changes to applicable legal or regulatory obligations.
- Material changes to the organisation’s business model, ICT strategy, operating model, or sourcing strategy.
- Introduction of new critical or important ICT services.
- Material changes in the ICT provider landscape or provider concentration profile.
- Significant ICT incidents, provider failures, service disruptions, or security events.
- Internal audit findings, regulatory feedback, control failures, or material risk events.
- Changes to operational resilience, business continuity, information security, data protection, or procurement requirements.

The Policy Owner is responsible for coordinating the review, incorporating stakeholder input, obtaining required approvals, and ensuring the current approved version is published and communicated.

Version history shall be maintained as follows:

| Version | Date | Description of Change | Author | Approval |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | [Effective Date] | Initial approved version | [Author Name / Role] | [Approver / Committee] |
