- Lessons learned and improvement actions.

Tools and environments may include:

- Governance, risk, and compliance platform.
- Supplier management platform.
- Configuration management database.
- Enterprise architecture repository.
- Project management and issue tracking tools.
- Secure document repository.
- Identity and access management tools.
- Privileged access management tools.
- Security information and event monitoring tools.
- Data migration and reconciliation tooling.
- Backup and recovery platforms.
- Test and staging environments.

## Success Metrics

Success metrics must be defined for each provider-specific exit plan and reported through appropriate governance forums. Metrics should measure both exit readiness and exit execution outcomes.

Readiness metrics:

| Metric | Target / Threshold | Evidence Source |
|---|---:|---|
| In-scope providers with approved exit plans | 100% | Provider inventory and exit plan register |
| Exit plans reviewed within required cycle | 100% | Review records |
| Critical dependencies mapped | 100% for in-scope services | Dependency maps and architecture records |
| Contractual exit rights assessed | 100% | Contract review records |
| Material contractual gaps remediated or risk accepted | 100% | Action log and risk acceptance records |
| Data inventories completed for in-scope providers | 100% | Data register |
| Alternative exit options assessed | 100% | Exit options assessment |
| Exit tests completed as scheduled | 100% | Test reports |
| High-risk exit readiness actions overdue | 0 | Action tracking |
| Provider contacts and escalation routes current | 100% | Contact matrix review |

Execution metrics:

| Metric | Target / Threshold | Evidence Source |
|---|---:|---|
| Critical service disruption during exit | Within approved impact tolerance | Service monitoring and incident records |
| Recovery objectives met during transition | 100% for critical service events | Recovery evidence |
| Data reconciliation accuracy | 100% for critical datasets, approved tolerance for non-critical datasets | Reconciliation reports |
| Unauthorised access during transition | 0 events | Security monitoring and access reviews |
| Critical security control gaps at cutover | 0 unless formally accepted | Security checklist |
| Cutover completed within approved window | Target agreed per exit event | Change and cutover records |
| Fallback activation due to failed cutover | Reported and reviewed | Change records and incident logs |
| Provider transition deliverables received on time | Target agreed per exit event | Transition tracker |
| Open critical defects at closure | 0 unless formally accepted | Defect and risk logs |
| Data deletion or return evidence obtained | 100% | Provider certificates and validation records |
| Access revocation completed | 100% | IAM, PAM, network, and certificate records |
| Exit closure report completed | Within 30 days of closure | Closure report |

Quality metrics:

| Metric | Target / Threshold |
|---|---:|
| Exit plan completeness score | At least [90]% based on internal quality checklist |
| Lessons learned actions completed by due date | At least [95]% |
| Audit findings relating to exit planning | No repeat high-risk findings |
| Provider exit readiness rating | Maintained at acceptable level for all high-risk providers |
| Management reporting timeliness | 100% of scheduled reporting cycles |

A provider-specific exit should be considered successful when:

- The critical or important function continues within approved impact tolerances.
- Required data is available, accurate, complete, protected, and usable.
- The replacement or target operating model is accepted by the business and ICT service owner.
- Security, resilience, operational, and compliance controls are operating as intended.
- The exiting provider no longer has unnecessary access, data, connectivity, or operational responsibility.
- Contractual and financial closure activities are complete or controlled through approved residual actions.
- Residual risks are documented, accepted at the appropriate level, and tracked to closure.
- Lessons learned have been captured and used to improve future exit planning.

## Review & Update Triggers

This plan must be reviewed at least annually and whenever a material change could affect the organisation’s ability to execute an orderly exit from an ICT third-party provider supporting a critical or important function.

Mandatory review triggers include:

- Onboarding of a new ICT third-party provider supporting a critical or important function.
- Renewal, extension, renegotiation, or material amendment of an in-scope provider contract.
- Material change to the services, systems, data, locations, subcontractors, or operating model supported by the provider.
- Change in provider criticality, substitutability, concentration risk, or dependency profile.
- Major incident, prolonged outage, cyber event, data breach, control failure, or repeated service level failure involving the provider.
- Material adverse change in the provider’s financial condition, ownership, strategy, operating model, regulatory status, or jurisdictional exposure.
- Significant audit finding, assurance issue, penetration test result, control weakness, or unresolved remediation item involving the provider.
- Change in business impact tolerance, recovery objective, continuity strategy, or service criticality.
- Change in technology architecture, data architecture, cloud strategy, identity model, integration design, or resilience approach.
- Change in legal, regulatory, contractual, data protection, outsourcing, or operational resilience expectations affecting provider exit arrangements.
- Completion of an exit test, tabletop exercise, data extraction test, migration rehearsal, continuity exercise, or actual exit event.
- Identification of a new material subcontractor or fourth-party dependency.
- Merger, acquisition, divestment, product closure, business restructuring, or market exit affecting the supported function.
- Provider notification of service withdrawal, platform end-of-life, location change, subcontractor change, or material terms change.
- Any governance decision to reduce, terminate, replace, insource, or redistribute provider services.

Review activities must include:

- Confirming the provider remains correctly classified.
- Validating that dependency maps and data inventories remain current.
- Confirming contractual exit rights remain adequate and enforceable.
- Reassessing exit options and target operating models.
- Reviewing open risks, issues, and remediation actions.
- Confirming contact details, escalation paths, and provider cooperation arrangements.
- Reviewing test results and lessons learned.
- Updating timelines, resource estimates, budget assumptions, and transition dependencies.
- Confirming evidence remains available and accessible.
- Re-approving material changes through the appropriate governance forum.

Plan ownership and maintenance:

| Activity | Frequency / Trigger | Owner | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plan content review | At least annually | Third-Party Risk Management | Updated plan template or confirmation of no change |
| Provider-specific exit plan review | At least annually and on trigger events | Business Owner | Updated provider exit plan |
| Contractual exit readiness review | At renewal, amendment, or material provider change | Legal / Procurement | Updated contract readiness assessment |
| Technical dependency review | At least annually and after material architecture change | ICT Service Owner | Updated dependency map |
| Data portability review | At least annually or after data model change | Data Owner | Updated data migration assessment |
| Security readiness review | At least annually and before execution | CISO | Updated security transition checklist |
| Exit test scheduling | Annual planning cycle | Operational Resilience Lead | Exit test schedule |
| Governance reporting | Quarterly or as defined by risk level | Third-Party Risk Management | Exit readiness dashboard |
| Lessons learned review | After test or actual exit | Project Manager / Operational Resilience Lead | Lessons learned and action log |

All updates must be version-controlled. Material changes must be approved by the document owner and, where they affect a provider supporting a critical or important function, reported to the relevant governance forum.

DORA-037.title: TPP Concentration Risk Analysis
DORA-037.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DORA-TPP-CRA-001] | 1.0 | [Third-Party Risk Management / ICT Risk Owner] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Digital Operational Resilience Act | Confidential - Internal Use Only |

## Purpose

This report assesses the organisation’s concentration risk arising from its use of third-party providers supporting ICT services, including providers that support critical or important functions. It evaluates both:

- **Single-provider concentration risk** - dependency on individual third-party providers where disruption, failure, insolvency, cyber incident, geopolitical event, contractual constraint, or service degradation could materially affect operations.
- **Aggregate concentration risk** - dependency patterns across multiple business services, legal entities, locations, service types, technology stacks, subcontractors, cloud regions, and market providers that may create systemic or correlated exposure.

The purpose of the report is to provide management with a clear view of current concentration exposure, identify areas requiring mitigation, and support informed decisions on sourcing, exit strategies, resilience investment, and third-party oversight.

This report is intended to support the organisation’s broader ICT risk management, third-party risk management, operational resilience, business continuity, and outsourcing governance arrangements.

## Reporting Period & Scope

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Reporting period | [YYYY-MM-DD] to [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Report date | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Prepared by | [Name / Function] |
| Reviewed by | [Name / Function] |
| Approved by | [Management Body / Committee Name] |
| Organisational scope | [Legal entities, branches, business units, or group scope covered] |
| Geographic scope | [Countries / regions covered] |
| Provider scope | Third-party providers delivering ICT services, including cloud, data centre, managed services, software-as-a-service, telecommunications, payment technology, cyber security services, core platforms, data services, and material subcontracted ICT services |
| Service scope | ICT services supporting critical or important functions, material business services, regulated activities, customer-facing channels, internal operations, and resilience capabilities |
| Exclusions | [Any exclusions and rationale, e.g. providers below materiality threshold, non-ICT suppliers, temporary pilot services] |
| Data sources | Contract register, register of ICT third-party arrangements, CMDB, business service mapping, outsourcing register, procurement records, cloud inventories, incident records, business impact analyses, exit plans, resilience testing results, provider due diligence files, and relationship manager attestations |

For this reporting period, the assessment covered **[number] third-party providers**, of which **[number]** were identified as supporting critical or important functions. The assessment also considered known material subcontractors where information was available through contractual disclosures, provider due diligence, service architecture reviews, or supplier attestations.

The analysis included both direct concentration risks and indirect dependencies, including where multiple providers rely on the same infrastructure, cloud platform, software vendor, data centre, connectivity provider, jurisdiction, or specialist subcontractor.

## Executive Summary

The assessment identified a concentration risk profile of **[Low / Moderate / High / Critical]** overall. The organisation has several well-established third-party governance controls, including contractual due diligence, relationship ownership, service monitoring, and periodic risk reviews. However, the analysis identified material areas where operational resilience could be affected by reliance on a limited number of providers, common technology platforms, and insufficiently mature exit or substitution arrangements.

### Overall Concentration Risk Position

| Risk Area | Rating | Summary |
|---|---|---|
| Single-provider dependency | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of most significant individual provider dependency] |
| Aggregate provider concentration | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of dependency across providers, services, or technology stacks] |
| Critical or important function exposure | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of provider support for critical or important functions] |
| Cloud and hosting concentration | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of cloud, data centre, or hosting exposure] |
| Subcontractor and fourth-party visibility | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of visibility and control over material subcontractors] |
| Exit and substitutability | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of exit feasibility and portability position] |
| Geographic and jurisdictional exposure | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of country, region, and legal exposure] |
| Financial and market dependency | [Low / Moderate / High / Critical] | [Summary of dependency on limited market providers or specialist suppliers] |

### Key Findings

1. **High dependency on [Provider A] for [service area]**
 - [Provider A] supports [number] critical or important functions and [number] material business services.
 - The provider is embedded in core operational workflows with limited near-term substitutability.
 - Exit execution is estimated at [number] months and would require [system migration / data conversion / customer communication / regulatory notification].

2. **Cloud infrastructure concentration across multiple services**
 - [percentage]% of in-scope cloud workloads are hosted on [Cloud Provider].
 - Multiple business services rely on the same cloud region or paired regions.
 - Current resilience arrangements reduce availability risk but do not fully address provider-wide service disruption, account-level compromise, or contractual termination scenarios.

3. **Limited visibility of subcontractor dependencies**
 - For [number] providers, subcontractor information is incomplete, outdated, or not sufficiently granular.
 - Several providers use common subcontractors for hosting, support, connectivity, identity services, or monitoring.
 - The organisation may have correlated exposure that is not fully reflected in direct provider-level risk ratings.

4. **Exit plans require further operational validation**
 - Exit strategies exist for [number] critical or important ICT arrangements, but only [number] have been operationally tested or validated through tabletop exercises.
 - Several exit plans rely on assumptions about data portability, availability of skilled resources, and cooperation from incumbent providers.

5. **Market concentration creates constrained substitution options**
 - In certain service areas, such as [core banking platform / payment processing / market data / identity services / cyber monitoring], there are few viable alternative providers that meet regulatory, technical, security, and integration requirements.
 - Replacement would likely involve extended transformation activity rather than a straightforward provider substitution.

### Management Attention Required

Immediate management attention is recommended for:

| Priority | Area | Required Management Decision |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | [Provider A] concentration | Confirm risk appetite position and approve mitigation plan |
| 2 | Cloud hosting concentration | Decide whether to pursue multi-region, multi-account, or selective multi-provider resilience strategy |
| 3 | Subcontractor transparency | Mandate remediation of incomplete subcontractor disclosures in material arrangements |
| 4 | Exit plan validation | Approve testing schedule for critical or important ICT arrangements |
| 5 | Contractual leverage | Approve contract remediation priorities for audit rights, access rights, termination support, data return, and subcontractor notification |

## Methodology

The concentration risk assessment was performed using a structured, evidence-based approach combining quantitative indicators, qualitative judgement, service criticality, substitutability analysis, and resilience impact assessment.

### Assessment Approach

The methodology consisted of the following steps:

1. **Provider population validation**
 - Reconciled the third-party provider inventory against the ICT third-party register, procurement records, contract repository, and business service mapping.
 - Confirmed whether providers deliver ICT services and whether services support critical or important functions.
 - Removed duplicates and grouped related entities under provider group structures where relevant.

2. **Service and function mapping**
 - Mapped each provider to supported systems, applications, business services, legal entities, customer channels, locations, and operational processes.
 - Identified whether the provider supports critical or important functions.
 - Assessed dependency depth, including whether the provider is essential, important, replaceable, or ancillary to service delivery.

3. **Exposure measurement**
 - Calculated spend concentration, service concentration, system dependency, data dependency, user dependency, transaction volume, and critical function coverage.
 - Identified common platforms, hosting environments, subcontractors, regions, and service dependencies.

4. **Resilience and substitutability review**
 - Reviewed business continuity arrangements, disaster recovery capabilities, exit plans, recovery objectives, operational workarounds, data portability, and alternative providers.
 - Assessed whether disruption to the provider could be absorbed without breaching business impact tolerances.

5. **Contract and governance review**
 - Reviewed contractual rights, termination support, access and audit rights, data return provisions, subcontracting controls, resilience commitments, incident notification obligations, and service level arrangements.
 - Assessed relationship governance, performance monitoring, incident history, and financial stability information.

6. **Risk scoring and management challenge**
 - Applied a concentration risk scoring model using defined indicators and professional judgement.
 - Validated results with service owners, risk owners, procurement, technology, resilience, legal, compliance, and third-party risk teams.
 - Escalated material findings for management review.

### Risk Rating Scale

| Rating | Definition | Management Response |
|---|---|---|
| Low | Dependency is limited, alternatives are available, exit is achievable within acceptable timeframes, and disruption is unlikely to materially affect critical operations. | Monitor through standard third-party governance. |
| Moderate | Dependency is meaningful but manageable; some substitution or workaround exists, although execution may require planning and resources. | Maintain oversight and implement targeted improvements. |
| High | Dependency is significant; disruption could materially affect important operations; alternatives are limited, costly, or slow to implement. | Formal mitigation plan required, with senior management oversight. |
| Critical | Dependency is severe; provider failure or loss could threaten critical operations, cause significant customer harm, breach impact tolerances, or create regulatory concern. | Immediate executive attention required; risk treatment, contingency measures, and board-level visibility expected. |

### Assessment Criteria

| Assessment Dimension | Indicators Considered |
|---|---|
| Criticality | Support for critical or important functions, regulated services, customer-facing operations, payment flows, trading, reporting, security operations, data processing, and continuity capabilities |
| Substitutability | Availability of alternative providers, internal capability, switching complexity, data portability, integration complexity, licensing constraints, specialist expertise, and market maturity |
| Exposure scale | Number of services supported, number of systems dependent, legal entities affected, transaction volumes, customer population, data volumes, financial value, and operational workload |
| Resilience | Availability architecture, disaster recovery capability, regional redundancy, recovery objectives, tested continuity plans, incident response coordination, and fallback processes |
| Contractual control | Termination rights, exit support, audit and access rights, subcontractor controls, data return, data deletion, incident notification, service level commitments, and regulatory cooperation |
| Geographic risk | Provider service locations, data residency, support locations, jurisdictional exposure, geopolitical risk, cross-border transfer considerations, and regional dependency |
| Subcontractor risk | Material subcontractors, common fourth parties, provider reliance on hyperscale cloud, telecommunications, data centres, specialist technology vendors, or offshore support centres |
| Financial and strategic risk | Provider financial health, market position, merger or acquisition activity, strategic importance, product roadmap, end-of-life risk, and commercial leverage |
| Historical performance | Incidents, service level breaches, audit findings, vulnerability remediation, control weaknesses, complaints, and unresolved remediation actions |

### Concentration Indicators Used

| Indicator | Threshold for Heightened Review |
|---|---|
| Provider supports critical or important functions | Any direct or indirect support |
| Provider supports multiple material business services | Three or more services |
| Provider dependency across legal entities | Two or more regulated entities |
| Annual spend concentration | More than [percentage]% of ICT third-party spend |
| Transaction dependency | More than [percentage]% of relevant transaction volume |
| User dependency | More than [percentage]% of workforce or customer access |
| Data dependency | Processing or storing sensitive, regulated, or business-critical data |
| Exit duration | More than [number] months to execute an orderly exit |
| Provider substitution | Fewer than two viable alternative providers |
| Common subcontractor reliance | Same subcontractor used by two or more material providers |
| Cloud region reliance | Concentration of critical workloads in one region or paired region set |
| Unvalidated exit plan | No test, walkthrough, or evidence-based validation in the last [number] months |

## Detailed Findings / Results (with structure)

### 1. Provider Concentration Overview

The in-scope provider population shows a concentration of ICT dependency among a limited number of providers. The top [number] providers account for a significant proportion of ICT service delivery, technology spend, and critical function support.

| Metric | Result | Commentary |

### 2. Highest-Risk Provider Dependencies

### 3. Critical or Important Function Exposure

The assessment identified that several critical or important functions are dependent on a small number of ICT providers. In some cases, a single provider supports multiple functions, increasing the potential impact of provider disruption.

### 4. Cloud, Hosting, and Infrastructure Concentration

Cloud and hosting arrangements represent one of the most significant concentration areas. The organisation benefits from the resilience and scalability of major infrastructure providers; however, dependency on a limited number of cloud platforms and regions increases exposure to provider-wide disruption, misconfiguration, identity compromise, commercial restrictions, or regional unavailability.

- [percentage]% of critical cloud workloads are hosted with [Cloud Provider 1].

- Some resilience designs protect against component or zone failure but may not adequately address provider-wide unavailability or account-level administrative failure.

- Identity, encryption key management, monitoring, and logging services may create additional concentration within the same provider ecosystem.

### 5. Software-as-a-Service Concentration

The organisation relies on several SaaS providers for business-critical workflows, collaboration, customer interaction, compliance reporting, and internal operations.

Key observations:

- Several SaaS services are embedded in business workflows and have limited manual alternatives.
- Data export capabilities vary by provider and may not support rapid restoration into an alternative platform.
- Some SaaS services use the same underlying cloud infrastructure, creating indirect concentration.
- Contractual exit support and data return provisions are inconsistent across providers.

### 6. Cyber Security and Resilience Service Provider Concentration

The organisation uses third parties for cyber security tooling and services, including monitoring, vulnerability management, threat intelligence, endpoint protection, incident response, penetration testing, and managed detection.

Key observations:

- Cyber resilience capabilities depend on a small number of specialist providers.
- A disruption affecting a cyber security provider could impair monitoring, detection, response, or privileged access control.
- Incident response retainer arrangements may be affected during sector-wide events where provider demand exceeds available capacity.
- Dependency on provider-hosted security consoles should be considered in continuity planning.

### 7. Telecommunications and Connectivity Concentration

- Some sites rely on diverse circuits from the same wholesale carrier, limiting true resilience.
- Cloud connectivity uses [Provider] as the primary carrier for [services].

### 8. Subcontractor and Fourth-Party Concentration

Visibility of subcontractors is essential because multiple direct providers may rely on the same underlying infrastructure or specialist service.

| Common Subcontractor / Platform | Used By Direct Providers | Service Provided | Known Critical Dependency | Visibility Level | Concentration Rating |

### 9. Geographic and Jurisdictional Concentration

The assessment reviewed provider delivery locations, data hosting locations, support locations, and subcontractor jurisdictions.

- Support operations for multiple providers are concentrated in [region].
- Certain services depend on data centres or cloud regions located in [region].
- Cross-border data processing arrangements are in place for [services], but dependency mapping should be improved.
- Regional disruption, sanctions, legal restrictions, labour instability, or natural disasters could affect multiple providers simultaneously.

### 10. Contractual and Exit Readiness Results

The review assessed whether contractual rights and practical exit arrangements are sufficient to reduce concentration risk.

| Control Area | In Place for All Critical Arrangements | Partially in Place | Gaps Identified |
|---|---:|---:|---|

Key observations:

- Exit plans are often present as documents but are not consistently validated through exercises.
- Some contracts do not provide sufficient transition assistance for complex migrations.
- Data extraction formats, timelines, and responsibilities are not consistently defined.
- Audit and access rights are stronger in newer contracts than in legacy arrangements.
- Several arrangements require renegotiation to improve subcontractor transparency and exit support.

### 11. Incident and Performance History

Incident history was considered as a risk modifier. Providers with repeated service degradation, delayed incident notification, unresolved control issues, or significant audit findings were reviewed for increased concentration concern.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---|

## Analysis

### Overall Assessment

The organisation’s concentration risk is currently assessed as **[Low / Moderate / High / Critical]**. The rating is driven by the combined effect of reliance on a limited set of providers, dependency on common cloud and infrastructure platforms, incomplete subcontractor visibility, and the varying maturity of exit planning.

The most material risks are not limited to direct provider failure. They also arise from correlated scenarios where multiple services or providers are affected simultaneously by a shared technology dependency, common subcontractor, regional disruption, sector-wide cyber event, or market capacity constraint.

### Key Risk Drivers

#### 1. Operational dependency on a small number of strategic ICT providers

Several providers are deeply embedded in service delivery. For these providers, the organisation cannot easily switch to an alternative without significant migration, testing, data conversion, contractual transition, and operational change.

This creates potential exposure to:

- Prolonged outage or service degradation.
- Provider insolvency or strategic withdrawal from a product line.
- Contract termination or commercial dispute.
- Regulatory concern where the provider supports critical or important functions.
- Reduced negotiating leverage due to operational dependency.

#### 2. Cloud and infrastructure dependency

Cloud and hosted infrastructure arrangements provide strong technical resilience for many failure scenarios, but they also create dependency on provider-controlled environments. A major provider-level incident, identity compromise, account suspension, region-wide outage, or systemic configuration issue could affect multiple business services simultaneously.

The current architecture appears strongest for component-level resilience and weaker for full provider portability.

#### 3. Limited substitutability in specialist service areas

For certain services, there are few alternative providers that meet the organisation’s security, regulatory, functional, integration, data, and resilience requirements. In these areas, exit would be a transformation programme rather than a supplier replacement exercise.

This is particularly relevant for:

- [Core platform services]
- [Payment technology]
- [Regulatory reporting]
- [Identity and access management]
- [Market data services]
- [Managed detection and response]
- [Customer communication services]

#### 4. Subcontractor transparency gaps

The organisation has incomplete visibility over subcontractors for some material arrangements. This limits its ability to understand whether multiple providers depend on the same underlying third party, location, platform, or specialist support service.

Without improved subcontractor mapping, the organisation may underestimate correlated concentration risk.

#### 5. Exit plans are not yet consistently operational

Documented exit strategies exist for several high-risk arrangements, but practical validation remains uneven. Some exit plans lack:

- Confirmed alternative providers.
- Tested data extraction and restoration.
- Defined transition resources.
- Clear decision triggers.
- Updated contact and escalation paths.
- Estimated customer and operational impact.
- Legal and regulatory notification steps.
- Evidence that recovery can occur within acceptable business tolerances.

### Scenario Analysis

The following scenarios were considered to assess the potential operational impact of concentration risk.

| Scenario | Providers / Services Potentially Affected | Expected Impact | Current Resilience | Residual Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Major outage at [Cloud Provider] affecting primary region | [Systems / services] | Loss or degradation of [services] for [duration] | [Multi-zone / multi-region / backup] | [Rating] |
| Failure of [Provider A] supporting [critical function] | [Functions] | Material disruption to [operations/customers/reporting] | [Manual workaround / alternate provider / none] | [Rating] |
| Cyber incident at managed service provider | [Systems / services] | Reduced operational support, possible containment activity, increased internal workload | [Internal support / alternate support / IR plan] | [Rating] |
| Telecommunications provider regional outage | [Sites / channels] | Reduced connectivity, branch or remote working disruption | [Diverse routing / mobile backup / none] | [Rating] |
| Common subcontractor disruption | Multiple direct providers | Correlated failure across services | [Limited visibility / partial mitigation] | [Rating] |
| Provider insolvency or market withdrawal | [Services] | Transition required under time pressure | [Exit plan / transition rights] | [Rating] |
| Legal or geopolitical restriction affecting support location | [Providers using region] | Delayed support, access restrictions, service degradation | [Provider contingency / alternate support] | [Rating] |

### Risk Appetite Alignment

The current concentration profile is **[within / approaching / outside]** the organisation’s stated risk appetite for third-party ICT dependency.

| Risk Appetite Area | Current Position | Appetite Status |
|---|---|---|
| Dependency on single provider for critical or important functions | [Summary] | [Within / Near limit / Outside] |
| Ability to exit material ICT arrangements within acceptable timeframe | [Summary] | [Within / Near limit / Outside] |
| Visibility of material subcontractors | [Summary] | [Within / Near limit / Outside] |
| Cloud and infrastructure resilience | [Summary] | [Within / Near limit / Outside] |
| Geographic and jurisdictional dependency | [Summary] | [Within / Near limit / Outside] |
| Provider performance and incident history | [Summary] | [Within / Near limit / Outside] |

Where exposure exceeds appetite, risk treatment actions are required and should be tracked through the organisation’s risk management process.

## Recommendations & Actions

The following actions are recommended to reduce concentration risk and improve management oversight.

### Priority Action Plan

| Ref | Recommendation | Priority | Owner | Target Date | Success Criteria | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CRA-01 | Approve formal risk treatment plan for [Provider A] due to dependency on [critical service/function]. | High | [Owner] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Risk treatment approved, funded, and tracked through governance forum. | [Open] |
| CRA-02 | Validate exit plan for [Provider A] through a tabletop exercise and evidence-based walkthrough. | High | [Owner] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Exercise completed, assumptions tested, gaps logged, remediation actions assigned. | [Open] |
| CRA-03 | Complete subcontractor mapping for all providers supporting critical or important functions. | High | [Owner] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Material subcontractors recorded, common dependencies identified, register updated. | [Open] |
| CRA-04 | Review cloud concentration strategy and define target resilience approach for critical workloads. | High | [Owner] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Approved strategy covering region, account, backup, recovery, and portability requirements. | [Open] |
| CRA-05 | Remediate contracts lacking adequate exit support, data return, subcontractor notification, and audit access provisions. | High | [Legal / Procurement] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Contract remediation plan approved and priority contracts updated or risk accepted. | [Open] |
| CRA-06 | Identify viable alternative providers for high-risk service categories. | Medium | [Procurement / Service Owners] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Alternatives assessed and documented for each high-risk category. | [Open] |
| CRA-07 | Implement concentration risk dashboard for quarterly management reporting. | Medium | [TPRM / Risk] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Dashboard includes provider, service, spend, cloud, subcontractor, and exit indicators. | [Open] |
| CRA-08 | Enhance onboarding and change processes to require concentration risk assessment before new ICT arrangements or major changes. | Medium | [Procurement / TPRM] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Assessment embedded in sourcing workflow and evidenced for new material ICT arrangements. | [Open] |
| CRA-09 | Conduct joint resilience exercises with selected high-risk providers. | Medium | [Operational Resilience] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Exercises completed for top-risk providers and lessons learned documented. | [Open] |
| CRA-10 | Improve monitoring of provider financial health, market changes, ownership changes, and product roadmap risk. | Medium | [Vendor Management] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Monitoring process established and alerts reviewed through governance forum. | [Open] |

### Recommended Management Decisions

Management is requested to:

1. Confirm whether the overall concentration risk rating of **[rating]** is accepted pending remediation.
2. Approve the priority action plan and assign accountable owners.
3. Confirm escalation of **[Provider A]**, **[Provider B]**, and **[Provider C]** to enhanced oversight.
4. Approve contract remediation priorities for material ICT arrangements.
5. Approve the planned schedule for exit plan validation and provider resilience exercises.
6. Confirm whether selective investment in alternative providers, internal capability, or enhanced resilience architecture is required.
7. Require quarterly reporting on concentration risk indicators and remediation progress.

### Risk Treatment Options

The following treatment options should be considered for high and critical concentration areas.

| Treatment Option | Suitable For | Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| Risk reduction through enhanced resilience | Cloud, hosting, connectivity, security tooling | May include additional regions, backups, segmentation, alternative access paths, or improved monitoring |
| Risk reduction through provider diversification | Services with viable market alternatives | May increase cost and operational complexity |
| Risk reduction through internal capability | Managed services, cyber operations, specialist support | Requires skills, staffing, tooling, and operating model investment |
| Risk reduction through contractual remediation | Legacy or incomplete contracts | Dependent on negotiation leverage and renewal timing |
| Risk reduction through exit planning | Critical or important arrangements | Requires testing, data portability, alternative operating model, and decision triggers |
| Risk acceptance | Low likelihood or high cost mitigation scenarios | Requires senior approval, documented rationale, and periodic review |
| Risk transfer | Insurance or contractual liability mechanisms | Does not replace operational resilience obligations and may not cover customer or regulatory impact |

### Follow-Up and Reporting

Progress against actions will be monitored by **[Committee / Forum]** on a **[monthly / quarterly]** basis. High and overdue actions will be escalated to **[Senior Management / Management Body / Risk Committee]**.

The concentration risk assessment will be refreshed at least annually and additionally when any of the following occur:

- A new ICT provider is onboarded for a critical or important function.
- A material ICT arrangement is renewed, terminated, expanded, or significantly changed.
- A provider changes subcontractors for a material service.
- A material incident occurs involving a provider or common subcontractor.
- The organisation launches a new critical service or materially changes its technology architecture.
- A provider undergoes merger, acquisition, insolvency event, strategic withdrawal, or major service model change.
- Regulatory, geopolitical, or market developments materially alter provider risk.

## Distribution & Confidentiality

This report contains confidential information about the organisation’s ICT dependencies, third-party providers, operational resilience arrangements, concentration exposures, contracts, and risk treatment plans. It must be handled in accordance with the organisation’s information classification and document handling requirements.

### Approved Distribution

| Recipient / Forum | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Management Body / Board Risk Committee] | Oversight of material third-party concentration risk and approval of risk treatment decisions |
| [Executive Risk Committee] | Review of findings, prioritisation, and escalation |
| [ICT Risk Management Function] | Risk assessment, monitoring, and control oversight |
| [Third-Party Risk Management Function] | Provider governance, register updates, and remediation tracking |
| [Procurement / Vendor Management] | Contract remediation, supplier engagement, and market analysis |
| [Legal] | Contractual rights, exit support, subcontractor provisions, and termination arrangements |
| [Operational Resilience / Business Continuity] | Impact tolerance analysis, scenario testing, and exit validation |
| [Information Security] | Cyber dependency assessment and provider security oversight |
| [Service Owners] | Validation of provider dependency and mitigation actions |
| [Internal Audit] | Independent assurance planning and audit evidence review, where appropriate |

### Confidentiality Requirements

- This report must not be shared externally without approval from **[Report Owner / Legal / Compliance]**.
- Extracts may only be shared with third-party providers where necessary and where disclosure has been approved.
- Provider-specific findings must be shared on a need-to-know basis and must not disclose confidential information relating to other providers.
- The report must be stored in **[approved repository]** with access restricted to authorised personnel.
- Retention must follow the organisation’s records management requirements for regulatory and risk management evidence.
- Any suspected unauthorised disclosure must be reported through the organisation’s information security incident process.

### Document Review

This report will be reviewed and updated:

- At least annually.
- Following significant changes to the organisation’s ICT provider landscape.
- Following material provider incidents.
- Following changes to critical or important functions.
- Following material changes in cloud, hosting, subcontractor, or jurisdictional exposure.
- Upon request from senior management, risk management, internal audit, or competent oversight functions.

DORA-038.title: Information Sharing Agreements (Cyber Threat Intel)
DORA-038.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DORA-ISAC-TPL-001] | 1.0 | [Cyber Threat Intelligence / CISO Office] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | DORA | Internal - Confidential |

## Purpose

This template is used to document, assess, approve and maintain voluntary information sharing arrangements relating to cyber threat intelligence.

The purpose of the agreement is to ensure that any sharing or receipt of cyber threat information is:

- Conducted for a legitimate cyber resilience, detection, prevention, response or recovery purpose.
- Limited to information that is appropriate, relevant and proportionate.
- Governed by clear rules on confidentiality, permitted use, onward sharing, data protection, security handling and retention.
- Approved by the appropriate internal stakeholders before participation begins.
- Recorded in a manner that supports auditability, oversight and periodic review.
- Consistent with the organisation’s legal, regulatory, contractual and operational obligations.

This template applies to proposed or existing arrangements with trusted communities, industry bodies, public authorities, financial sector peers, technology providers, managed security service providers, computer emergency response teams, intelligence vendors and other approved cyber threat intelligence partners.

## Instructions

1. Complete this template before entering into, renewing, materially changing or terminating any cyber threat intelligence information sharing arrangement.
2. The requester must provide enough detail for Legal, Privacy, Information Security, Risk, Compliance and the relevant business owner to assess the arrangement.
3. Do not share live incident details, customer information, personal data, confidential business information, regulated information or third-party confidential information until the required approvals are complete.
4. Where urgent sharing is needed to manage an active cyber threat or incident, follow the emergency approval route in this template and complete retrospective documentation within [X business days].
5. All information sharing must follow the agreed handling classification, traffic light protocol or equivalent marking rules stated in the agreement.
6. The arrangement must define what may be shared, who may receive it, how it may be used, how it must be protected and whether onward sharing is permitted.
7. If personal data, customer data, employee data, sensitive business data, privileged information or information received from a third party may be included, consult Legal and Privacy before sharing.
8. If the arrangement involves a third-party ICT service provider, managed service provider, intelligence platform, portal or automated feed, complete the relevant third-party risk and security reviews before onboarding.
9. If the arrangement includes automated technical exchange, such as indicators of compromise, malware signatures, telemetry, vulnerability intelligence, detection rules or API feeds, ensure technical validation and access controls are defined.
10. The approved record must be stored in the designated governance repository and added to the Information Sharing Register.
11. The arrangement must be reviewed at least annually, or sooner if there is a material change in scope, participants, data types, sharing mechanism, threat environment, legal basis, confidentiality expectations or operational dependency.
12. The agreement must not be used to coordinate anti-competitive behaviour, exchange commercially sensitive market information, or share information beyond the cyber resilience purpose.

## Form Fields

| Field | Type | Required | Guidance |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Agreement title | Free text | Yes | Provide the formal name of the information sharing arrangement, community, memorandum, contract, platform or exchange mechanism. |
| Request type | Select one | Yes | Select: New arrangement, Renewal, Material change, Emergency approval, Termination, Periodic review. |
| Request date | Date | Yes | Enter the date the request is submitted for review. |
| Requester name | Free text | Yes | Enter the name of the person proposing or managing the arrangement. |
| Requester role / team | Free text | Yes | Identify the business function, cyber security team, resilience team or operational unit responsible. |
| Business owner | Free text | Yes | Identify the accountable internal owner for the arrangement. This should usually be the CISO, Head of Cyber Threat Intelligence, SOC Manager or relevant senior risk owner. |
| Primary internal contact | Free text | Yes | Name the operational contact responsible for day-to-day participation, receipt, dissemination and record keeping. |
| Secondary internal contact | Free text | Yes | Name the backup contact to support continuity of participation and incident response coverage. |
| External sharing partner / community | Free text | Yes | Identify the organisation, association, community, platform, authority or group with whom information will be shared or received. |
| External contact details | Free text | Yes | Include role-based mailbox, named contact, secure portal details or other approved communication channel. Avoid personal contact details unless necessary. |
| Partner type | Select all that apply | Yes | Select: Financial entity, Public authority, Sector information sharing group, CERT/CSIRT, Law enforcement, ICT service provider, Security vendor, Intelligence provider, Industry association, Other. |
| Arrangement status | Select one | Yes | Select: Proposed, Under review, Approved, Active, Suspended, Expired, Terminated. |
| Proposed start date | Date | Yes | Enter the intended start date for participation or information exchange. |
| Proposed end date / renewal date | Date | Yes | Enter the expected end date, renewal date or review date. Open-ended arrangements must still have a scheduled review date. |
| Purpose of sharing | Long text | Yes | Explain the cyber resilience purpose, such as threat detection, vulnerability awareness, incident response, sector coordination, defensive measures, situational awareness or recovery support. |
| Business justification | Long text | Yes | Explain why the arrangement is needed and how it supports the organisation’s digital operational resilience, security operations or risk reduction objectives. |
| Expected benefits | Long text | Yes | Describe expected benefits, such as earlier warning, improved detection rules, validated indicators, sector coordination, peer benchmarking or faster response. |
| Scope of information to be received | Select all that apply plus comments | Yes | Select applicable categories: Indicators of compromise, tactics and techniques, malware analysis, phishing intelligence, vulnerability intelligence, exploit activity, threat actor profiles, incident trends, detection logic, mitigation guidance, recovery lessons, fraud-related cyber intelligence, third-party threat alerts, other. Add comments where needed. |
| Scope of information to be shared | Select all that apply plus comments | Yes | Identify what the organisation may share. Be specific and limit to approved categories. Avoid broad statements such as “all relevant information”. |
| Information not permitted for sharing | Long text | Yes | List prohibited categories, such as customer personal data, account data, authentication secrets, encryption keys, privileged legal material, confidential client information, unapproved third-party information, sensitive commercial data or unredacted incident records. |
| Personal data involved? | Yes / No / Unknown | Yes | Indicate whether any personal data may be included in information shared or received. If Yes or Unknown, Privacy review is mandatory. |
| Personal data details | Long text | Conditional | If personal data may be involved, describe the categories, source, purpose, minimisation steps, lawful handling basis, redaction approach and any additional safeguards. |
| Sensitive or regulated data involved? | Yes / No / Unknown | Yes | Indicate whether the arrangement may involve protected financial, customer, employee, security, privileged, contractual or regulated information. |
| Sensitive data details | Long text | Conditional | Describe the nature of the sensitive information and the controls used to prevent inappropriate disclosure. |
| Redaction / anonymisation requirements | Long text | Yes | Define how identifying details, customer data, internal system names, IP addresses, hostnames, user details, supplier names or incident specifics will be removed or generalised before sharing, unless explicitly approved. |
| Permitted use by recipient | Long text | Yes | State what the recipient may do with shared information, such as use for defensive cyber security, detection, prevention, response, resilience testing or risk assessment. |
| Prohibited use by recipient | Long text | Yes | State restrictions, such as no public disclosure, no commercial resale, no use for competitive purposes, no attribution to the organisation without approval, no use outside cyber defence, and no onward sharing unless authorised. |
| Onward sharing permitted? | Select one | Yes | Select: Not permitted, Permitted with prior written approval, Permitted within named community only, Permitted under specific handling markings, Other. |
| Onward sharing conditions | Long text | Conditional | If onward sharing is permitted, define recipients, markings, purpose limitation, confidentiality obligations and notification requirements. |
| Sharing frequency | Select one | Yes | Select: Ad hoc, Event-driven, Daily, Weekly, Monthly, Real-time feed, During active incidents only, Other. |
| Sharing method | Select all that apply | Yes | Select: Secure portal, Encrypted email, API feed, TAXII/STIX feed, Secure messaging platform, Conference call, In-person forum, Ticketing system, Managed service channel, Other. |
| Approved communication channels | Long text | Yes | List the authorised channels and any security requirements, such as encryption, MFA, named accounts, role-based access or secure file transfer. |
| Unapproved communication channels | Long text | Yes | Identify channels that must not be used, such as personal email, consumer messaging apps, unapproved file-sharing services or public forums. |
| Classification / handling markings | Select all that apply plus comments | Yes | Identify the classification scheme and sharing restrictions to be used, including any traffic light protocol or equivalent markings. Explain how markings must be applied. |
| Minimum security controls for exchange | Long text | Yes | Define required controls, such as MFA, encryption in transit, access logging, named users, least privilege, secure storage, malware scanning and restricted distribution lists. |
| Access management requirements | Long text | Yes | Define who may access shared intelligence internally, how access is approved, how leavers are removed and how access is reviewed. |
| Internal distribution list | Long text | Yes | List internal roles or teams permitted to receive the intelligence, such as SOC, CSIRT, Vulnerability Management, Fraud Risk, ICT Risk, Resilience, Legal or Executive Crisis Team. |
| Internal dissemination rules | Long text | Yes | Explain how received intelligence may be circulated internally, including need-to-know rules, classification handling and restrictions on copying or forwarding. |
| Operational use | Long text | Yes | Describe how the intelligence will be used in practice, such as detection engineering, SIEM enrichment, EDR blocking, firewall updates, vulnerability prioritisation, incident triage or executive briefings. |
| Automated action permitted? | Yes / No | Yes | State whether received intelligence may trigger automated blocking, detection, enrichment or alerting. If Yes, define validation requirements and rollback controls. |
| Validation requirements | Long text | Yes | Define how intelligence will be assessed before operational use, including source reliability, confidence rating, false positive checks, age, relevance and potential business impact. |
| Incident-related sharing rules | Long text | Yes | Define what may be shared during live incidents, who approves it, how urgent disclosures are documented and how confidentiality is maintained. |
| Emergency sharing approval route | Long text | Yes | Specify the emergency approver roles, minimum consultation requirements and retrospective documentation deadline for urgent threat or incident situations. |
| Legal review required? | Yes / No | Yes | Confirm whether Legal review is required. Legal review is required where there is a formal agreement, confidentiality terms, liability exposure, cross-border sharing, third-party restrictions or sensitive information. |
| Privacy review required? | Yes / No | Yes | Confirm whether Privacy review is required. Privacy review is required where personal data may be included, inferred, enriched or transferred. |
| Compliance review required? | Yes / No | Yes | Confirm whether Compliance review is required. Compliance review is expected for sector arrangements, regulatory engagement, public authority sharing or material information-sharing communities. |
| Third-party risk review required? | Yes / No | Yes | Confirm whether review is required for any vendor platform, managed service, intelligence provider or external system used to process or transmit shared intelligence. |
| Data location / cross-border considerations | Long text | Conditional | Identify whether information may be stored, accessed or transferred outside the organisation’s usual operating jurisdictions. Include relevant safeguards. |
| Confidentiality terms | Long text | Yes | Summarise confidentiality obligations, including who is bound, duration, exceptions and consequences of unauthorised disclosure. |
| Intellectual property / ownership | Long text | Yes | State who owns shared intelligence, whether it may be modified, incorporated into detection content, used in reports or retained after termination. |
| Liability and reliance | Long text | Yes | Describe any limitation of liability, disclaimer of accuracy, reliance expectations and responsibility for validating intelligence before use. |
| Competition / market conduct safeguards | Long text | Yes | Confirm that the arrangement is limited to cyber threat intelligence and does not include pricing, strategy, customer allocation, market conduct, commercially sensitive competitive information or non-cyber operational coordination. |
| Regulatory or public authority interaction | Long text | Conditional | If a regulator, law enforcement body, public authority or sector coordination body is involved, describe the nature of interaction and any notification or confidentiality expectations. |
| Contractual restrictions checked? | Yes / No / N/A | Yes | Confirm whether existing customer, supplier, outsourcing or confidentiality agreements restrict the proposed sharing. |
| Third-party information included? | Yes / No / Unknown | Yes | Indicate whether any information received from suppliers, customers, vendors or partners may be shared. If Yes or Unknown, verify permission before sharing. |
| Threat intelligence quality criteria | Long text | Yes | Define expected quality indicators, such as timeliness, source confidence, technical accuracy, relevance, context, actionability and handling markings. |
| Logging and evidence requirements | Long text | Yes | Specify how sharing events will be recorded, including date, sender, recipient, category, handling marking, approval, channel and summary of content. |
| Metrics to be tracked | Select all that apply plus comments | Yes | Select: Number of items received, number shared, actionable intelligence rate, false positive rate, detections created, incidents supported, vulnerabilities prioritised, time to disseminate, partner responsiveness, other. |
| Retention period for shared information | Free text | Yes | Define how long shared and received information will be retained. Align with records retention, legal requirements and operational need. |
| Secure disposal requirements | Long text | Yes | Describe how records, downloaded files, portal exports, emails or working copies will be deleted or archived when no longer required. |
| Review frequency | Select one | Yes | Select: Quarterly, Semi-annually, Annually, Upon material change, Other. Annual review is the minimum expected for active arrangements. |
| Review triggers | Select all that apply | Yes | Select: Change in partner, change in scope, incident involving shared information, confidentiality breach, new data type, new jurisdiction, new technology platform, regulatory request, poor intelligence quality, termination notice, other. |
| Exit / termination conditions | Long text | Yes | Define when the organisation may suspend or terminate participation, such as breach of confidentiality, unacceptable data risk, misuse, low value, legal restriction or change in business need. |
| Termination actions | Long text | Yes | Define required actions at exit, such as access removal, portal closure, deletion or return of information, final notification, register update and retention of approval records. |
| Residual risks | Long text | Yes | Document remaining risks after controls, such as inaccurate intelligence, inappropriate disclosure, re-identification, partner misuse, operational disruption from false positives or dependency on external feeds. |
| Risk acceptance required? | Yes / No | Yes | Indicate whether any residual risk requires formal acceptance by the relevant risk owner. |
| Risk owner | Free text | Conditional | Identify the person accountable for accepting residual risk, where applicable. |
| Attachments | List | No | Attach draft agreement, terms of participation, community rules, confidentiality terms, privacy assessment, third-party review, technical design, security review or other supporting documents. |
| Overall recommendation | Select one plus comments | Yes | Select: Approve, Approve with conditions, Reject, Defer pending further information, Suspend, Terminate. Include rationale. |
| Conditions of approval | Long text | Conditional | List mandatory conditions, such as redaction requirements, limited recipients, technical controls, annual review, legal wording changes or privacy safeguards. |
| Completion date | Date | Yes | Enter the date the form is finalised for approval. |

## Approval / Routing

The completed template must be routed to the appropriate stakeholders before the arrangement becomes active. Approval may be electronic, provided the approval record is retained and linked to this template.

| Role / Function | Review Responsibility | Approval Required | Timing |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Requester | Completes the template, gathers supporting documents and confirms operational need. | No | Before routing |
| Business Owner | Confirms business justification, scope, operational value and accountability for participation. | Yes | Before Legal and Risk approval |
| Cyber Threat Intelligence Lead / SOC Lead | Confirms technical relevance, handling rules, validation approach and operational use. | Yes | Before activation |
| CISO or Delegate | Confirms alignment with cyber resilience objectives and approves security participation. | Yes | Before activation |
| Legal | Reviews confidentiality, permitted use, liability, contractual restrictions, public authority involvement and competition safeguards. | Conditional | Required for formal agreements, sensitive sharing, legal uncertainty or external commitments |
| Privacy / Data Protection | Reviews personal data risk, redaction, minimisation, lawful handling, cross-border considerations and data subject risk. | Conditional | Required where personal data may be involved or inferred |
| ICT Risk / Operational Resilience | Reviews resilience benefit, operational dependency, risk treatment and register alignment. | Conditional | Required for material arrangements or arrangements supporting critical functions |
| Third-Party Risk Management | Reviews vendor platforms, managed services, external portals, APIs or outsourced intelligence services. | Conditional | Required where an ICT third party is involved |
| Compliance | Reviews regulatory expectations, sector participation, public authority interaction and governance evidence. | Conditional | Required for regulated, sector-wide or public authority arrangements |
| Data / Information Owner | Confirms whether proposed information can be shared and whether restrictions apply. | Conditional | Required where internal, customer, supplier or sensitive data is in scope |
| Risk Owner | Accepts residual risk where controls do not fully mitigate identified exposure. | Conditional | Required where risk acceptance is documented |
| Executive Sponsor | Approves high-impact, cross-border, strategic, sector-level or reputationally sensitive arrangements. | Conditional | Required for high-risk or high-visibility arrangements |

Approval record:

| Approval Stage | Name | Role | Decision | Conditions / Comments | Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Business Owner Review | [Name] | [Role] | [Approve / Reject / Conditional] | [Comments] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Cyber Security Review | [Name] | [Role] | [Approve / Reject / Conditional] | [Comments] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Legal Review | [Name] | [Role] | [Approve / Reject / Conditional / N/A] | [Comments] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Privacy Review | [Name] | [Role] | [Approve / Reject / Conditional / N/A] | [Comments] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Risk / Resilience Review | [Name] | [Role] | [Approve / Reject / Conditional / N/A] | [Comments] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Compliance Review | [Name] | [Role] | [Approve / Reject / Conditional / N/A] | [Comments] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Final Approval | [Name] | [Role] | [Approve / Reject / Conditional] | [Comments] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |

Emergency approval route:

| Situation | Minimum Approval | Permitted Before Full Review | Retrospective Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Imminent threat requiring rapid defensive sharing | CISO or delegated incident commander | Limited sharing of necessary technical indicators or defensive context using approved secure channels | Complete this template and obtain full review within [X business days] |
| Active incident requiring coordination with trusted partner or authority | Incident commander and Legal, where reachable | Limited sharing of relevant facts needed for containment, eradication, coordination or recovery | Document content shared, recipients, justification and approvals within [X business days] |
| Urgent receipt of intelligence via trusted community | Cyber Threat Intelligence Lead or SOC Manager | Receipt and internal use subject to validation and handling markings | Register the source, classification, operational use and any follow-up actions within [X business days] |

No emergency approval may be used to bypass privacy, legal or confidentiality requirements where there is sufficient time to consult the required function. Emergency sharing must be limited to what is necessary for cyber defence or incident management.

## Records & Retention

The approved template and related evidence must be retained as part of the organisation’s cyber governance and operational resilience records.

Records to be retained include:

| Record | Repository / System | Minimum Retention | Owner | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Completed information sharing agreement template | [Governance Repository / GRC System] | [X years] after termination or last use | [Cyber Threat Intelligence / CISO Office] | Retain approved version and any superseded versions. |
| Signed agreement, terms of participation or community rules | [Contract Repository / GRC System] | [X years] after termination | [Legal / Contract Owner] | Include confidentiality terms and amendments. |
| Approval evidence | [GRC Workflow / Email Archive / Repository] | [X years] after approval expiry | [Document Owner] | Retain decisions, conditions and risk acceptances. |
| Privacy, legal, compliance and risk assessments | [GRC System] | [X years] after termination | [Relevant Control Function] | Retain linked assessments and review notes. |
| Third-party risk and security review evidence | [Third-Party Risk System] | [X years] after termination | [Third-Party Risk Management] | Required where a vendor platform or service is used. |
| Information Sharing Register entry | [Information Sharing Register] | Current while active, then [X years] archived | [CISO Office] | Register must reflect status, owner, review date and scope. |
| Sharing event logs | [Threat Intelligence Platform / SOC System / Secure Repository] | [X years] or as operationally required | [SOC / CTI Lead] | Log date, recipient, source, category, marking, channel and summary. |
| Review records | [GRC System] | [X years] after review | [Business Owner] | Include annual reviews, changes, continued need and closure decisions. |
| Termination evidence | [Governance Repository / Contract Repository] | [X years] after termination | [Business Owner / Legal] | Include access removal, deletion or retention instructions and partner notices. |

The Information Sharing Register must contain, at minimum:

| Register Field | Required Content |
|---|---|
| Arrangement name | Formal name of the agreement or community. |
| External partner / community | Entity or group involved in sharing. |
| Internal business owner | Accountable owner for the arrangement. |
| Operational contact | Day-to-day contact for participation. |
| Status | Proposed, active, suspended, expired or terminated. |
| Approved scope | Categories of intelligence that may be shared and received. |
| Sharing method | Approved communication channels or platforms. |
| Handling requirements | Classification, traffic light protocol or equivalent restrictions. |
| Key restrictions | Prohibited information, onward sharing limits and redaction requirements. |
| Approval date | Date of final approval. |
| Review date | Next scheduled review date. |
| Termination date | Date ended, where applicable. |
| Link to evidence | Link to approved template, agreement, reviews and logs. |

Retention and handling requirements:

- Records must be protected according to their classification and stored only in approved repositories.
- Access to agreement records must be limited to personnel with a legitimate governance, legal, risk, compliance, cyber security or audit need.
- Sharing event logs must be sufficient to demonstrate what was shared, with whom, when, under what handling restrictions and under whose authority.
- Working copies, downloaded intelligence and temporary extracts must be deleted when no longer needed unless required for investigation, evidence, resilience analysis or legal hold.
- Records subject to legal hold, investigation, regulatory request or incident review must not be deleted until the hold is released.
- The document owner must ensure that expired or terminated arrangements are marked accordingly in the register and are not used for further information exchange.
- At least annually, the register must be reconciled against active communities, portals, distribution lists, API feeds, vendor services and internal access permissions.
- Any unauthorised sharing, suspected misuse, breach of handling rules or loss of shared intelligence must be reported through the organisation’s security incident reporting process and assessed for any required notifications.

## Purpose

This Annual Compliance Report provides the designated competent authority with a consolidated overview of [Organisation Name]’s compliance with the Digital Operational Resilience Act for the reporting period stated below.

The report summarises the organisation’s digital operational resilience posture, key governance activities, ICT risk management outcomes, material incidents, resilience testing, third-party ICT risk management, remediation progress, and planned improvements. It is intended to demonstrate that [Organisation Name] maintains appropriate arrangements to identify, assess, prevent, detect, respond to, recover from, and learn from ICT-related disruption affecting financial services, customers, counterparties, and market confidence.

This report has been prepared for regulatory reporting purposes and is supported by underlying evidence retained by the relevant control owners, including risk assessments, incident records, testing results, committee minutes, supplier oversight records, audit reports, and remediation tracking.

## Executive Summary

During the reporting period, [Organisation Name] continued to strengthen its digital operational resilience framework across ICT governance, risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party oversight, and executive accountability.

Overall, the organisation has established a structured and operational compliance framework for DORA implementation. Key governance arrangements are in place, including defined management accountability, ICT risk ownership, reporting to senior governance bodies, maintenance of critical asset and service inventories, incident classification and escalation processes, resilience testing activity, and oversight of ICT third-party providers.

The annual assessment identified that the organisation is broadly aligned with DORA expectations, with several areas requiring continued improvement. The most significant improvement themes relate to enhancing the completeness of ICT dependency mapping, strengthening exit and concentration risk analysis for material ICT third-party providers, improving evidence consistency for resilience testing, and reducing remediation ageing for selected ICT risk actions.

No ICT-related incident during the reporting period resulted in confirmed prolonged unavailability of a critical or important function beyond approved tolerance levels. [Number] ICT incidents were assessed under the organisation’s regulatory impact criteria, of which [Number] were classified as major and reported to the competent authority within applicable timelines. Lessons learned activities were completed for all major incidents and tracked through the ICT risk and resilience action plan.

Resilience testing was performed across critical systems, including vulnerability assessments, scenario testing, business continuity exercises, disaster recovery tests, cyber response simulations, and targeted technical assessments. Testing identified [Number] high-priority findings, of which [Number] were closed by the end of the reporting period and [Number] remain under active remediation.

Third-party ICT risk management remained a key focus area. The organisation maintained a register of ICT third-party arrangements, reviewed contracts supporting critical or important functions, conducted due diligence and ongoing monitoring, and escalated material provider risks to the relevant governance bodies. Further work is planned to improve mapping of subcontracting dependencies, strengthen exit planning evidence, and enhance concentration risk metrics.

| ICT asset and service inventory | Partially effective | Key assets recorded; completeness and linkage to business services require enhancement |
| Incident management and reporting | Effective | Classification, escalation, communication, and reporting processes operated during the period |
| Digital operational resilience testing | Largely effective | Annual testing performed; consistency of evidence and retesting discipline to be improved |
| ICT business continuity and recovery | Largely effective | Recovery arrangements tested for priority systems; improvements required for cross-provider recovery scenarios |
| ICT third-party risk management | Partially effective | Register and oversight in place; enhancement required for concentration, subcontracting, and exit analysis |
| Information sharing and threat intelligence | Developing | Threat intelligence used operationally; formal sharing arrangements remain limited |
| Training and awareness | Largely effective | Targeted training delivered; additional role-based training planned for incident and supplier owners |
| Remediation governance | Largely effective | Action tracking in place; ageing and dependency-related delays require closer executive attention |
