### Management Conclusion

Management considers that [Organisation Name] has made substantive progress in embedding DORA-aligned operational resilience practices. The organisation has not identified any unresolved condition that would indicate a systemic inability to manage ICT risk or continue critical or important functions within approved recovery objectives.

The improvement plan set out in this report is being actively governed through [Committee Name], with progress reported to [Board / Management Body Name]. Priority actions have been assigned to accountable owners with target completion dates, funding where required, and measurable outcomes.

## Methodology

### Assessment Approach

The annual compliance assessment was performed using a risk-based methodology designed to evaluate whether the organisation’s digital operational resilience arrangements are designed appropriately, implemented effectively, and operating in practice.

The assessment considered both design effectiveness and operating effectiveness across governance, ICT risk management, incident reporting, testing, third-party risk management, business continuity, recovery, and remediation governance.

The methodology included:

- Review of approved governance documents, including policies, standards, procedures, committee terms of reference, risk appetite statements, and reporting packs.
- Interviews and walkthroughs with accountable executives, ICT risk owners, security operations, incident management, business continuity, procurement, legal, compliance, internal audit, and key business service owners.
- Sampling of ICT risks, incidents, third-party reviews, resilience tests, access controls, vulnerability records, change records, and remediation actions.
- Review of management information provided to governance forums.
- Assessment of registers and inventories, including ICT assets, critical or important functions, third-party providers, contracts, incidents, risks, and resilience testing plans.
- Validation of selected evidence against system records, ticketing tools, governance minutes, supplier reports, and assurance documentation.
- Review of prior-period findings and closure evidence.
- Consideration of internal audit results, external audit observations, regulatory correspondence, penetration test reports, and independent assurance activities.

### Evidence Sources

| Evidence Category | Examples Reviewed |
|---|---|
| Governance records | Board papers, risk committee minutes, management attestations, policy approvals, committee reporting packs |
| ICT risk records | ICT risk assessments, control self-assessments, risk acceptances, risk appetite metrics, issue logs |
| Asset and dependency records | Configuration management data, application inventory, service maps, critical function mapping, data flow records |
| Incident records | Incident tickets, major incident reports, regulatory notification records, communications logs, post-incident reviews |
| Testing evidence | Vulnerability scans, penetration test reports, disaster recovery test results, scenario exercises, tabletop outputs, remediation tickets |
| Continuity and recovery records | Business continuity plans, recovery plans, backup reports, restoration tests, crisis management exercise reports |
| Third-party oversight evidence | Supplier register, due diligence records, contracts, service review minutes, assurance reports, exit plans, performance reports |
| Training records | Completion reports, role-based training materials, awareness communications, phishing simulation results |
| Assurance records | Internal audit reports, second-line reviews, external assurance, management action plans |

### Rating Method

Findings were assessed using the following rating approach.

| Rating | Description | Management Expectation |
|---|---|---|
| Effective | Controls are designed appropriately, implemented, and operating consistently; only minor improvement opportunities identified | Maintain control operation and monitor through normal governance |
| Largely effective | Controls are generally operating, with limited gaps or inconsistent evidence that do not materially weaken resilience | Remediate through tracked management actions |
| Partially effective | Control design or operation is incomplete, inconsistent, or not sufficiently evidenced; potential resilience impact if not remediated | Assign priority remediation, monitor at senior management level |
| Ineffective | Significant weakness in design or operation; material exposure to disruption, regulatory concern, or customer harm | Immediate management action and escalation required |

### Materiality Considerations

The assessment prioritised matters that could affect:

- Continuity of critical or important functions.
- Integrity, availability, authenticity, or confidentiality of ICT systems and data.
- Timely detection, classification, reporting, and management of major ICT-related incidents.
- Ability to recover services within approved recovery objectives.
- Dependency on ICT third-party providers, including concentration and exit risk.
- Customer outcomes, market integrity, financial stability, or regulatory confidence.
- Accuracy and timeliness of regulatory reporting.
- Management body oversight and accountability.

| F-18 | Privileged access review evidence is inconsistent for selected systems | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] |
| F-19 | Threat intelligence outputs are not consistently translated into documented control changes, scenarios, or management reporting | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] |

---

### 9. Information Sharing and External Coordination

#### Result

The organisation participates in selected industry forums, receives threat intelligence from public and private sources, and engages with regulators, law enforcement, sector bodies, and service providers as required.

Formal arrangements for structured cyber threat information sharing are developing. The organisation has not identified any legal or confidentiality barrier preventing responsible participation in relevant information-sharing activities.

#### Evidence Reviewed

| Evidence | Status |
|---|---|
| Threat intelligence feeds and reports | Reviewed |
| Industry forum participation records | Reviewed |
| Regulatory communication records | Reviewed |
| Incident coordination records | Sampled |
| Internal dissemination records | Reviewed |

#### Observations

- Threat information is reviewed by security teams and used in operational monitoring.
- External coordination occurred during relevant incidents and sector alerts.
- There is an opportunity to formalise criteria for sharing indicators, lessons learned, and sector-relevant threat information.
- Legal, compliance, and data protection review steps should be documented for external sharing.

#### Rating

Developing

#### Findings

| Finding ID | Finding | Severity | Owner | Target Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F-20 | Formal information-sharing procedures require completion, including approval criteria, confidentiality protections, and legal review steps | Low | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] |

---

### 10. Training, Awareness, and Competence

#### Result

The organisation delivered ICT risk, cybersecurity, incident management, and operational resilience awareness activities during the reporting period. General cybersecurity awareness training was mandatory for employees and contractors. Targeted training was provided to selected incident responders, system owners, supplier owners, and senior management.

#### Training Summary

#### Observations

- Mandatory awareness completion was tracked and escalated.
- Phishing simulation outcomes improved compared with the prior period.
- Role-based training has begun for incident and supplier owners.
- Additional training is required for business owners of critical or important functions, particularly regarding dependency mapping, recovery expectations, incident escalation, and supplier oversight responsibilities.

Largely effective

---

### 11. Remediation Management and Prior-Period Actions

#### Result

The organisation maintains a central action tracker for DORA-related findings, ICT risk issues, audit findings, incident lessons learned, supplier actions, and resilience testing observations. Progress is reported to [Committee Name] and escalated where actions are overdue or blocked.

#### Observations

- A central tracker exists and is reviewed regularly.
- High-priority actions are escalated to senior management.
- Closure evidence is retained for most completed actions.
- Some actions have been extended multiple times due to dependency on supplier responses, technology migration, or resource constraints.

| F-23 | Overdue high-priority actions require enhanced executive challenge and documented risk acceptance where delays continue | High | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] |

## Analysis

### Overall Compliance Position

The organisation has implemented the core components required for digital operational resilience. Governance, risk management, incident handling, resilience testing, and third-party oversight are operational and subject to management review. The organisation has demonstrated the ability to identify and respond to ICT incidents, perform resilience testing, maintain continuity arrangements, and oversee key ICT service providers.

The strongest areas are incident management, management engagement, baseline cybersecurity operations, and the existence of structured risk and remediation governance. The principal areas requiring continued investment are dependency mapping, end-to-end resilience testing, third-party concentration management, and evidence quality.

### Key Strengths

| Strength | Business Value |
|---|---|
| Established senior governance for ICT risk and resilience | Supports accountability, escalation, and informed decision-making |
| Operating incident classification and reporting process | Enables timely regulatory assessment and coordinated response |
| Active resilience testing programme | Provides practical evidence of recovery capability and identifies control weaknesses |
| Centralised remediation tracking | Improves visibility of risk reduction and management accountability |
| ICT third-party register in place | Supports oversight of outsourced and cloud-based ICT dependencies |
| Security monitoring and vulnerability management | Enhances detection, response, and prevention of cyber disruption |

### Key Risk Themes

#### 1. Incomplete Service and Dependency Mapping

Incomplete mapping between critical or important functions, applications, infrastructure, data flows, suppliers, subcontractors, and recovery dependencies may reduce management’s ability to assess impact quickly during incidents or validate end-to-end resilience.

This risk is most relevant where services rely on multiple internal systems, group services, cloud platforms, managed service providers, or batch processing dependencies.

#### 2. Third-Party Concentration and Exit Risk

The organisation relies on several ICT providers for important services. While supplier oversight is in place, further analysis is required to understand concentration across providers, technologies, geographic regions, subcontractors, and group dependencies.

Exit planning should become more operationally detailed, including transition triggers, data portability, alternative service options, timeframes, cost assumptions, and customer impact considerations.

#### 3. Evidence Consistency

Controls are often operating in practice, but evidence is not always retained consistently. This affects resilience testing, risk acceptance, supplier assurance reviews, access reviews, incident classification decisions, and remediation closure.

Improving evidence standards will strengthen internal governance, regulatory reporting readiness, and auditability.

#### 4. End-to-End Resilience Assurance

Individual tests are being performed, but the organisation should increase scenario-based testing across full business services. This includes internal systems, third-party providers, operational teams, communications, data recovery, manual workarounds, and customer impact management.

#### 5. Remediation Ageing

A small number of high-priority actions remain overdue. Although management is aware of these actions, continued delay may increase residual risk if not supported by documented compensating controls, revised risk assessment, and formal acceptance.

### Trend Assessment

| Area | Trend | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Governance and accountability | Improving | Regular reporting and executive ownership are established |
| ICT risk visibility | Improving | Risk register and metrics are maturing |
| Incident management | Stable / Improving | Process operated effectively during the period |
| Resilience testing | Improving | Broader testing performed, but end-to-end maturity still developing |
| Third-party oversight | Stable | Core process exists; concentration and exit planning need enhancement |
| Asset and dependency mapping | Improving from low baseline | Programme underway but incomplete |
| Cybersecurity operations | Stable | Key controls operating; privileged access and intelligence integration require improvement |
| Remediation discipline | Stable | Tracker in place; ageing and closure standards require stronger challenge |

### Residual Risk View

Based on evidence reviewed, management considers the residual ICT and digital operational resilience risk profile to be within or approaching approved tolerance for most areas, subject to timely completion of the high-priority actions in this report.

The areas most likely to exceed tolerance if remediation is delayed are:

- Critical dependency mapping.
- Third-party ICT concentration and exit planning.
- Recovery objective alignment across business, technology, and supplier arrangements.
- End-to-end testing of critical services.
- Overdue high-priority remediation actions.

### Impact on Customers, Markets, and Regulatory Objectives

No evidence was identified during the reporting period of sustained customer harm, market disruption, or systemic failure arising from ICT disruption. Customer-affecting incidents were managed through established procedures, and material incidents were assessed for regulatory reporting.

The planned improvements are expected to reduce the likelihood and impact of future ICT disruption by improving impact analysis, recovery coordination, supplier resilience, and management decision-making.

## Recommendations & Actions

### Management Action Plan

The following actions have been approved or proposed to address the findings in this report.

| Action ID | Related Finding(s) | Action | Priority | Owner | Target Date | Success Criteria |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-01 | F-01 | Implement an integrated digital operational resilience dashboard for senior management covering critical functions, incidents, testing, suppliers, risk appetite, and remediation | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Dashboard approved, produced monthly/quarterly, and reviewed by governance forum |
| A-02 | F-02 | Clarify local accountability and oversight responsibilities for group-provided ICT services | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Responsibility matrix approved and embedded in reporting and escalation procedures |
| A-03 | F-03 | Standardise risk acceptance records for ICT risks, including rationale, expiry date, compensating controls, and senior approval | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Updated template implemented and applied to all high and critical ICT risk acceptances |
| A-04 | F-04, F-05, F-06 | Complete mapping of critical or important functions to ICT assets, infrastructure, data flows, third-party services, recovery objectives, and owners | High | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Approved dependency maps completed for all critical or important functions |
| A-05 | F-07 | Enhance incident classification records for non-reportable and near-threshold incidents | Low | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Classification rationale documented for all assessed incidents |
| A-06 | F-08 | Expand incident communication playbooks for customer, regulator, supplier-led, and multi-jurisdictional scenarios | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Playbooks approved and tested in at least one scenario exercise |
| A-07 | F-09, F-11 | Define minimum evidence standards for resilience testing and retesting | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Test evidence checklist implemented and used for all priority tests |
| A-08 | F-10 | Introduce annual end-to-end scenario testing for selected critical business services involving internal teams and material ICT providers | High | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | At least [Number] end-to-end tests completed with lessons learned tracked |
| A-09 | F-12, F-13 | Align business continuity plans, recovery objectives, technical recovery plans, supplier commitments, and manual workaround procedures | High | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Recovery alignment confirmed for all critical or important functions |
| A-10 | F-14 | Develop and validate operational exit plans for all material ICT providers supporting critical or important functions | High | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Exit plans approved, reviewed, and tested through tabletop or walkthrough |
| A-11 | F-15 | Implement third-party ICT concentration risk metrics and reporting | High | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Metrics reported to senior governance forum and used in supplier risk decisions |
| A-12 | F-16 | Improve subcontractor and fourth-party dependency data collection for critical ICT providers | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Dependency data recorded and reviewed for all material ICT providers |
| A-13 | F-17 | Standardise supplier assurance review documentation, including exceptions and complementary responsibilities | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Supplier assurance review template implemented and sampled for quality |
| A-14 | F-18 | Strengthen privileged access review evidence and recertification tracking for priority systems | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Reviews completed for all priority systems with exceptions remediated |
| A-15 | F-19, F-20 | Formalise use and sharing of threat intelligence, including legal review, dissemination, and integration with testing and risk assessment | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Procedure approved and evidence of use retained |
| A-16 | F-21 | Complete role-based DORA and resilience training for critical function owners, incident leads, system owners, and supplier owners | Medium | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Training completion meets [Percentage]% target |
| A-17 | F-22, F-23 | Strengthen remediation closure criteria, ageing escalation, and risk acceptance for delayed actions | High | [Owner] | [DD MMM YYYY] | Revised action governance implemented and overdue actions reduced by [Percentage]% |

### Prioritised Roadmap

| Timeframe | Priority Activities |
|---|---|
| 0-3 months | Finalise board dashboard, improve incident classification evidence, standardise risk acceptance, define resilience testing evidence requirements, escalate overdue high-priority actions |
| 3-6 months | Complete critical dependency mapping, align recovery objectives, enhance supplier assurance reviews, improve privileged access evidence, complete role-based training |
| 6-9 months | Implement third-party concentration metrics, complete material provider exit plans, improve subcontractor visibility, perform end-to-end scenario test |
| 9-12 months | Validate remediation effectiveness, perform second end-to-end resilience scenario, update annual reporting evidence pack, refresh maturity assessment |

### Management Commitments

Management commits to:

- Maintain active oversight of the action plan through [Committee Name].
- Provide progress updates to [Board / Management Body Name] at least [Monthly / Quarterly].
- Escalate overdue high-priority actions and obtain documented risk acceptance where delays materially affect resilience.
- Retain evidence supporting action closure, including testing or independent validation where appropriate.
- Notify the competent authority of material developments where required.
- Incorporate lessons learned from incidents, testing, audits, supplier reviews, and regulatory feedback into the resilience framework.

### Requested Regulatory Engagement

[Organisation Name] welcomes feedback from the competent authority on this report and is available to provide supporting evidence, walkthroughs, or further clarification upon request.

The organisation proposes the following engagement points, if considered useful by the competent authority:

### Confidentiality Classification

DORA-040.title: Continuous Monitoring Dashboard
DORA-040.content:
## What This Evidences

The Continuous Monitoring Dashboard evidences ongoing monitoring of ICT controls and third-party provider performance for DORA operational resilience purposes. It demonstrates that the organisation is actively tracking control health, ICT risk indicators, incident trends, vulnerabilities, service availability, and third-party performance against agreed obligations.

This artifact is operational evidence that must be collected from the organisation’s own systems. It must not be authored manually as a standalone document. The dashboard should be exported or captured from live monitoring, security, IT service management, risk, or third-party management tools used by the organisation.

## Where To Collect It From

Collect the dashboard from the organisation’s operational monitoring environment, typically one or more of the following:

- SIEM or security monitoring platform: [SIEM / Log Monitoring Tool]
- IT service management platform: [ITSM Tool]
- Security posture or vulnerability management tool: [Vulnerability Management Tool]
- Cloud or infrastructure monitoring platform: [Infrastructure / Cloud Monitoring Tool]
- Third-party risk management portal: [TPRM Tool]
- Service provider performance portal: [Provider Portal]
- Governance, risk, and compliance platform: [GRC Tool]
- Business continuity or operational resilience dashboard: [Resilience Dashboard Tool]

If monitoring is split across multiple tools, collect the primary integrated dashboard and any supporting dashboard exports needed to show complete coverage.

## How To Collect

1. Log in to [Dashboard Tool / Portal] using an account with read-only or reporting access.
2. Navigate to the dashboard used for ICT control and third-party performance monitoring, such as [Dashboard Name].
3. Confirm the reporting period is set to [Start Date] through [End Date].
4. Confirm filters include relevant business units, critical ICT services, important systems, and material third-party providers.
5. Verify the dashboard refresh timestamp or last data ingestion time is visible.
6. Export the dashboard using the tool’s built-in export function, preferably as PDF.
7. If export is unavailable, capture full-page screenshots showing the URL, timestamp, filters, and all relevant dashboard panels.
8. Export supporting data tables where available, such as CSV or Excel files for incidents, SLA breaches, vulnerabilities, alerts, or third-party KPIs.
9. Save the exported dashboard and supporting files using the agreed evidence naming convention.
10. Record collection details in the evidence register, including collector name, collection date, source system, and reporting period.

## What To Capture

Capture enough information to show active, complete, and timely monitoring, including:

- Dashboard name and source system
- Reporting period covered
- Date and time of export or screenshot
- Last data refresh or ingestion timestamp
- Scope filters applied, including entities, services, systems, and providers
- ICT control status indicators, such as pass, fail, warning, overdue, or degraded
- Security event trends and high-priority alerts
- ICT incident volumes, severity, ageing, and unresolved incidents
- Vulnerability counts by severity, ageing, and remediation status
- Patch or configuration compliance metrics
- Backup, recovery, and availability status for critical systems
- Service availability and performance metrics
- Third-party SLA, KPI, and incident performance
- Open actions, overdue remediation, and accountable owners
- Exception, breach, or threshold alerts
- Links or identifiers for underlying records, tickets, risks, or provider reports

## Frequency & Owner

- Collection frequency: Monthly, or more frequently for critical ICT services and material third-party providers.
- Event-driven collection: Also collect after major incidents, material SLA breaches, significant control failures, or regulatory reporting events.
- Evidence owner: [ICT Risk / Operational Resilience Owner].
- Collection operator: [SOC / IT Operations / GRC Analyst / TPRM Analyst].
- Review owner: [Head of ICT Risk / CISO / Operational Resilience Lead].

## Retention & Storage

Store the exported dashboard and supporting data in [Evidence Repository / GRC Tool / Document Management System]. Retain evidence for [Retention Period] in line with regulatory, audit, and internal recordkeeping requirements.

Storage must preserve integrity and traceability. Use access controls, version history, immutable storage where available, and a consistent naming convention such as:

- [YYYY-MM]_[Dashboard Name]_[Reporting Period]_[Source System]_Export.pdf
- [YYYY-MM]_[Metric Type]_[Source System]_SupportingData.csv

Do not overwrite previous dashboard exports.

## Acceptance Criteria

An auditor will usually accept the evidence as sufficient where it:

- Is exported or captured directly from an operational system, not manually recreated
- Shows the dashboard source, date, reporting period, scope, and refresh timestamp
- Covers relevant ICT controls, critical systems, and material third-party providers
- Includes clear metrics, thresholds, exceptions, and status indicators
- Shows unresolved issues, overdue actions, incidents, vulnerabilities, and SLA breaches
- Provides traceability to underlying tickets, alerts, risks, or provider records
- Demonstrates periodic monitoring over time, not a one-off snapshot
- Is retained in a controlled repository with collection and ownership details
- Matches the organisation’s defined monitoring scope and operational resilience obligations

ISO41-001.title: FMS Project Charter
ISO41-001.content:
| Metadata | Value |
|---|---|
| Document ID | FMS-PLAN-001 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Owner | [Executive Sponsor / Facilities Director] |
| Effective Date | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Framework | ISO 41001:2018 — Facility Management Systems |
| Classification | Internal |

## Purpose & Objectives

This FMS Project Charter formally authorises the implementation of a Facility Management System (FMS) aligned with ISO 41001:2018 and establishes the mandate, leadership commitment, governance, authority, and resources required to implement, operate, maintain, and continually improve the FMS.

The Charter supports ISO 41001:2018 by demonstrating that top management has approved the FMS initiative, accepts accountability for the effectiveness of the FMS, and commits to providing direction, resources, oversight, and integration of facility management requirements into organisational processes.

The objectives of this Charter are to:

- Establish formal executive sponsorship and organisational authority for the FMS implementation.
- Confirm top management commitment to ISO 41001:2018 requirements, including leadership, strategic alignment, resource provision, risk-based thinking, performance evaluation, and continual improvement.
- Define the scope, implementation approach, governance model, responsibilities, resources, milestones, and success metrics for the FMS project.
- Ensure facility management objectives are aligned with organisational strategy, stakeholder needs, compliance obligations, and the demand organisation’s core business objectives.
- Provide a structured implementation plan to achieve readiness for ISO 41001:2018 conformity assessment and, where applicable, certification.
- Enable transparent monitoring and reporting of FMS implementation progress to senior leadership.
- Ensure the FMS is established as an integrated management system rather than a standalone documentation exercise.
- Mandate participation by relevant functions, including facilities, procurement, finance, health and safety, human resources, information technology, legal, sustainability, business continuity, security, quality, and operational business units.

The intended outcomes of the FMS implementation are:

- A documented, implemented, and maintained FMS that conforms to ISO 41001:2018.
- Clear facility management governance, accountabilities, decision rights, and escalation paths.
- Facility management policies, objectives, processes, performance indicators, and controls that support organisational effectiveness.
- Defined mechanisms for understanding demand organisation needs and translating them into facility management requirements.
- Improved consistency, reliability, safety, sustainability, service quality, cost transparency, and user satisfaction across facility management services.
- Evidence that top management demonstrates leadership and commitment through active participation, resourcing, communication, and review.

## Scope

This Charter applies to the planning and implementation of the FMS for the organisation’s facility management activities within the defined FMS scope.

The initial FMS implementation scope includes:

| Scope Element | Included |
|---|---|
| Organisation | [Organisation Name] |
| Facilities / Sites | [Head Office], [Operational Sites], [Warehouses], [Regional Offices], and other facilities approved by the FMS Steering Committee |
| Facility Management Services | Hard services, soft services, maintenance management, workplace services, space management, cleaning, security coordination, utilities management, waste management, contractor management, service desk coordination, facility-related procurement, and facility performance monitoring |
| Internal Functions | Facilities Management, Procurement, Finance, Health and Safety, Security, Sustainability, Legal, Human Resources, Information Technology, Risk Management, Business Continuity, and relevant business units |
| External Parties | Facility service providers, maintenance contractors, landlords, managing agents, outsourced FM partners, consultants, regulators, certification bodies, and other interested parties |
| Management System Components | Context analysis, stakeholder needs, scope definition, leadership governance, FMS policy, objectives, risks and opportunities, operational planning and control, support processes, performance evaluation, internal audit, management review, corrective action, and continual improvement |
| Standard | ISO 41001:2018 |

The implementation will address the requirements of ISO 41001:2018 across the following management system areas:

- Organisational context and interested party requirements.
- Leadership commitment and governance.
- Facility management policy and objectives.
- Roles, responsibilities, authorities, and competence.
- Resource planning and provision.
- Risk and opportunity management.
- Operational planning and control of facility management services.
- Communication, documented information, and knowledge management.
- Performance monitoring, measurement, analysis, and evaluation.
- Internal audit and management review.
- Nonconformity, corrective action, and continual improvement.

The following are outside the initial implementation scope unless specifically approved by the FMS Steering Committee:

- Full ISO 41001 certification for facilities not listed in the approved FMS scope.
- Capital project delivery governance unrelated to ongoing facility management operations.
- Technical engineering redesign of facilities, except where required to meet FMS objectives or compliance obligations.
- Replacement of enterprise systems unless approved as a dependency or remediation action.
- Non-facility-related service management processes.
- Legal compliance determinations outside facility management obligations.

Scope changes require documented approval by the FMS Steering Committee and must include impact assessment for resources, timeline, risk, stakeholder commitments, and certification readiness.

## Assumptions & Dependencies

The FMS implementation is based on the following assumptions:

| Assumption | Impact if Invalid | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Top management will actively sponsor and support the FMS implementation. | Delays in decision-making, insufficient authority, and weak evidence for ISO 41001. | Executive Sponsor |
| Required subject matter experts will be available to participate in workshops, reviews, audits, and approvals. | Incomplete process definition, weak implementation evidence, and missed milestones. | FMS Project Manager |
| Existing facility management processes, contracts, performance data, and documented information can be accessed for review. | Inability to assess current-state maturity and establish baseline performance. | Facilities Management Lead |
| The organisation will provide budget and resources proportionate to the approved FMS scope. | Reduced implementation quality, delayed certification readiness, or scope reduction. | Executive Sponsor / Finance Lead |
| Existing operational controls can be improved rather than fully replaced in most areas. | Increased implementation effort, cost, and organisational disruption. | FMS Project Manager |
| External service providers will cooperate with FMS requirements, including performance reporting, documented procedures, and audit participation. | Gaps in operational control and supplier assurance. | Procurement Lead |
| Relevant legal, regulatory, safety, environmental, and contractual requirements can be identified and integrated into the FMS. | Compliance risk and incomplete conformity with ISO 41001 planning requirements. | Legal / Compliance Lead |
| Senior leadership will participate in management review and performance evaluation activities. | Insufficient evidence of leadership commitment and governance oversight. | Executive Sponsor |

Key dependencies include:

| Dependency | Description | Required By | Dependency Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Executive Approval | Formal approval of Charter, FMS scope, implementation mandate, and resource allocation. | Project initiation | Executive Sponsor |
| FMS Governance Structure | Establishment of Steering Committee, project team, working groups, and escalation routes. | Planning phase | Executive Sponsor |
| Current-State Assessment | Review of existing FM processes, contracts, compliance obligations, service levels, KPIs, risks, and documentation. | Gap assessment | FMS Project Manager |
| Stakeholder Engagement | Identification and consultation of demand organisation stakeholders, end users, service recipients, regulators, suppliers, and internal functions. | Context and requirements definition | Facilities Management Lead |
| Budget Approval | Funding for internal effort, consulting support if required, training, audits, tools, communication, and certification activities. | Resource mobilisation | Finance Lead |
| Document Control Capability | Method for creating, approving, publishing, retaining, and controlling FMS documented information. | Documentation development | Quality / Document Control Lead |
| Supplier Participation | Cooperation of outsourced FM providers and contractors in process alignment, reporting, controls, and audits. | Operational implementation | Procurement Lead |
| Data Availability | Availability of facilities asset data, maintenance records, service requests, energy usage, space utilisation, cost data, incident records, and supplier KPIs. | Performance baseline and metrics | Facilities Data Owner |
| Internal Audit Capability | Competent internal auditors trained in ISO 41001 or supported by qualified external resources. | Readiness assessment | Internal Audit Lead |
| Management Review Scheduling | Scheduled executive review of FMS performance, risks, objectives, resources, audit results, and improvement actions. | Final readiness and ongoing governance | Executive Sponsor |

Constraints and risks affecting the implementation include:

| Constraint / Risk | Potential Effect | Planned Response |
|---|---|---|
| Competing operational priorities | Limited availability of FM and business stakeholders | Secure executive mandate, schedule workshops in advance, escalate resource conflicts |
| Inconsistent FM practices across sites | Increased process harmonisation effort | Use phased implementation and define minimum mandatory FMS requirements |
| Poor facility data quality | Weak baseline and unreliable performance indicators | Conduct data quality review and assign data remediation actions |
| Supplier contractual limitations | Difficulty enforcing reporting or process changes | Review contract clauses and incorporate FMS requirements at renewal or variation |
| Limited management system maturity | Need for additional training and change management | Provide targeted awareness, templates, coaching, and role-specific guidance |
| Change fatigue | Low engagement or resistance to new processes | Use clear communication linking FMS benefits to business outcomes |
| Undefined FM service expectations | Misalignment between facility services and demand organisation needs | Conduct stakeholder requirements analysis and service level review |

## Approach / Phases

The FMS implementation will follow a structured, phased approach designed to establish leadership commitment, define the management system, implement controls, evaluate performance, and prepare for certification or formal conformity assessment.

### Phase 1 — Initiation and Leadership Mandate

The purpose of this phase is to establish executive authority, governance, and commitment in accordance with ISO 41001:2018.

Key activities:

- Approve this FMS Project Charter.
- Appoint the Executive Sponsor, FMS Project Manager, FMS Steering Committee, process owners, and working group members.
- Confirm project objectives, scope, budget, authority, escalation routes, and decision-making protocols.
- Communicate top management commitment to the FMS across relevant functions and facilities.
- Confirm alignment between FMS objectives and organisational strategy, business requirements, sustainability objectives, compliance obligations, risk appetite, and service expectations.
- Establish project reporting cadence and leadership oversight arrangements.
- Confirm requirements for use of internal or external ISO 41001 expertise.

Primary outputs:

- Approved FMS Project Charter.
- Confirmed FMS governance structure.
- Resource and budget authorisation.
- FMS project communication from top management.
- Project plan and stakeholder engagement plan.

### Phase 2 — Current-State Review and Gap Assessment

The purpose of this phase is to evaluate existing facility management arrangements against ISO 41001:2018 requirements and identify required actions.

Key activities:

- Review existing FM policies, procedures, contracts, service specifications, performance reports, risk registers, compliance registers, asset records, and service level agreements.
- Assess leadership involvement, governance effectiveness, accountability, and resource sufficiency.
- Identify internal and external interested parties and their facility management requirements.
- Review demand organisation needs, business objectives, service expectations, and facility-related risks.
- Conduct site-level and service-level gap assessments.
- Evaluate existing supplier management, operational controls, maintenance practices, workplace services, emergency arrangements, and reporting mechanisms.
- Identify legal, regulatory, contractual, safety, environmental, accessibility, and sustainability obligations relevant to the FMS.
- Establish a prioritised implementation action plan.

Primary outputs:

- ISO 41001 gap assessment report.
- Interested party and requirements register.
- FMS risk and opportunity register.
- Initial compliance obligations register.
- Current-state process inventory.
- Prioritised remediation and implementation plan.

### Phase 3 — FMS Design and Documentation

The purpose of this phase is to design the management system structure and create required documented information.

Key activities:

- Define and approve the FMS scope statement.
- Develop the FMS Policy for approval by top management.
- Establish measurable FMS objectives aligned with strategic and operational priorities.
- Define governance structures, roles, responsibilities, authorities, and interfaces.
- Define facility management processes and their interactions.
- Develop required plans, procedures, registers, and templates.
- Establish document control, record retention, version management, and approval processes.
- Define competence requirements for FMS roles and develop training materials.
- Develop communication requirements for internal and external stakeholders.
- Define performance indicators, monitoring methods, data owners, reporting frequency, and review mechanisms.

Primary outputs:

- Approved FMS scope.
- Approved FMS Policy.
- FMS objectives and implementation plans.
- FMS process architecture and process interaction map.
- Roles and responsibilities matrix.
- Documented procedures and operational controls.
- FMS documented information register.
- Competence and training matrix.
- FMS KPI framework and reporting template.

### Phase 4 — Implementation and Operational Integration

The purpose of this phase is to implement the designed FMS and integrate it into routine facility management operations.

Key activities:

- Communicate approved FMS policy, objectives, roles, and expectations.
- Train personnel and contractors according to defined competence requirements.
- Implement facility management processes across in-scope services and sites.
- Align supplier requirements, contract management practices, service reporting, and performance reviews with the FMS.
- Implement risk and opportunity controls.
- Establish operational planning and control processes for in-scope FM activities.
- Integrate FMS requirements into procurement, contractor management, maintenance planning, work order management, service desk processes, incident management, health and safety coordination, sustainability reporting, and business continuity interfaces.
- Begin routine monitoring of FMS KPIs and service performance.
- Capture evidence of implementation, including meeting minutes, training records, approved documents, service reports, audit trails, and corrective actions.

Primary outputs:

- Implemented FMS processes.
- Training and competence records.
- Operational control evidence.
- Supplier performance records.
- Updated risk and opportunity register.
- KPI reports and performance dashboards.
- Records demonstrating communication and leadership engagement.

### Phase 5 — Performance Evaluation and Internal Assurance

The purpose of this phase is to evaluate the effectiveness of the implemented FMS and identify corrective actions before certification or formal review.

Key activities:

- Conduct internal audits against ISO 41001:2018 and organisational FMS requirements.
- Evaluate compliance with legal, regulatory, contractual, and stakeholder requirements.
- Review performance against FMS objectives and KPIs.
- Assess effectiveness of operational controls, supplier performance, risk treatment, and documented information management.
- Record nonconformities, observations, and improvement opportunities.
- Assign corrective actions with owners, due dates, and verification criteria.
- Conduct management review with top management participation.
- Confirm resource adequacy and leadership commitment for ongoing FMS operation.

Primary outputs:

- Internal audit programme and audit reports.
- Nonconformity and corrective action register.
- Compliance evaluation results.
- Management review agenda, minutes, decisions, and actions.
- Updated FMS performance report.
- Certification or conformity readiness assessment.

### Phase 6 — Certification Readiness and Transition to Business-as-Usual

The purpose of this phase is to finalise implementation, support external assessment where applicable, and transition the FMS into ongoing governance.

Key activities:

- Close priority corrective actions and verify effectiveness.
- Conduct final readiness review.
- Prepare evidence pack for external auditor or independent reviewer.
- Support Stage 1 and Stage 2 certification audit activities where certification is pursued.
- Respond to external audit findings and corrective action requests.
- Confirm ongoing FMS governance calendar, reporting cycle, internal audit programme, and management review schedule.
- Transfer ownership of FMS maintenance activities to business-as-usual process owners.
- Confirm continual improvement pipeline and resource planning.

Primary outputs:

- Certification readiness confirmation.
- External audit evidence pack.
- Certification audit reports, where applicable.
- Corrective action responses.
- Business-as-usual FMS governance calendar.
- Continual improvement register.
- Lessons learned report.

- At least quarterly during active implementation.
- Prior to certification readiness review or formal conformity assessment.
- During management review where project governance, scope, resources, risks, or leadership commitments require amendment.
- Upon transition from project implementation to business-as-usual FMS governance.

| Change in top management, Executive Sponsor, or FMS Project Manager | Confirm leadership commitment, authority, accountability, and continuity | Top Management / Executive Sponsor |
| Change to FMS scope, facilities, services, or organisational boundaries | Assess impact on deliverables, timeline, resources, risks, and certification readiness | FMS Steering Committee / Top Management |
| Material change to facility management strategy or organisational objectives | Reconfirm alignment of FMS objectives with strategic direction | Top Management |
| Significant budget increase or resource constraint | Reassess feasibility, schedule, scope, and prioritisation | Executive Sponsor / Finance Lead |
| Major supplier, outsourcing, or contract change affecting FM services | Update dependencies, operational controls, supplier requirements, and responsibilities | Procurement Lead / Steering Committee |
| New or changed legal, regulatory, contractual, safety, environmental, or stakeholder requirements | Update compliance obligations, controls, objectives, and implementation plan | Legal / Compliance Lead |
| Significant facility incident, service failure, audit finding, or compliance breach | Reassess risks, controls, resources, and management oversight | FMS Steering Committee |
| Internal audit identifies systemic FMS governance or implementation weaknesses | Update approach, milestones, responsibilities, or resources | Executive Sponsor |
| Certification body feedback or external audit findings affect implementation priorities | Update corrective action plan, timeline, and readiness criteria | FMS Project Manager / Steering Committee |
| Merger, acquisition, divestment, relocation, or major portfolio change | Reassess FMS scope, context, stakeholders, resources, and implementation plan | Top Management |
| System replacement or major change to FM, document control, reporting, or risk systems | Update dependencies, evidence collection, controls, and responsibilities | IT / Systems Lead |
| Transition to business-as-usual governance | Replace project milestones with ongoing FMS governance, audit, review, and improvement cycles | Facilities Management Lead / Executive Sponsor |

All updates to this Charter must be version controlled and approved in accordance with the organisation’s document control requirements. Superseded versions must be retained as documented information to evidence the evolution of leadership commitment, mandate, and resource decisions throughout FMS implementation.
