- Externally supplied equipment, materials, spare parts, consumables, and products that affect facility performance or compliance.
- Subcontracted services used by approved FM providers where the organisation has responsibility for controlling outsourced processes.

This procedure applies throughout the outsourcing and contractor lifecycle:

1. Needs definition and risk assessment.
2. Supplier selection and evaluation.
3. Contracting and service level definition.
4. Onboarding and induction.
5. Operational delivery and supervision.
6. Performance monitoring and review.
7. Nonconformance management and corrective action.
8. Contract change, renewal, suspension, termination, or offboarding.

This procedure applies to employees, contractors, service providers, subcontractors, procurement personnel, contract managers, facilities management personnel, health and safety personnel, security personnel, and any other party involved in specifying, procuring, managing, receiving, or verifying externally provided FM services.

Out of scope:

- Non-FM procurement that does not affect facility management operations or FMS performance.
- Employment contracts for directly employed staff.
- Informal user requests that do not result in externally provided FM services or products.

Where corporate procurement, legal, health and safety, information security, or financial procedures impose additional requirements, those requirements must be applied in conjunction with this procedure.

## Prerequisites & Inputs

Before initiating outsourcing or contractor engagement, the responsible FM representative must ensure the following prerequisites and inputs are available or obtained.

| Input / Prerequisite | Description | Source / Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Defined FM requirement | Clear statement of the required externally provided process, service, product, outcome, or works. | Requestor / FM Manager |
| Operational need or business case | Justification for outsourcing or contractor engagement, including link to facility objectives, user needs, asset needs, compliance, or service continuity. | Requestor / FM Manager |
| Scope of work / specification | Documented description of deliverables, locations, assets, service boundaries, working hours, exclusions, dependencies, and acceptance criteria. | FM Manager / Technical Lead |
| Risk assessment | Assessment of operational, health and safety, environmental, security, compliance, asset, business continuity, and reputational risks. | FM Manager / H&S / Security |
| Applicable legal and regulatory requirements | Statutory obligations relevant to the service or works, including permits, licences, certifications, inspections, and reporting obligations. | Legal / Compliance / FM |
| Budget approval | Approved funding or budget allocation for the outsourced service or contractor works. | Finance / Budget Owner |
| Procurement route | Defined sourcing method, including competitive tender, framework agreement, approved supplier list, emergency procurement, or direct award justification. | Procurement |
| Evaluation criteria | Criteria for selection, including competence, certification, technical capability, service quality, capacity, cost, risk, sustainability, safety, and prior performance. | Procurement / FM Manager |
| Contract template or purchase terms | Approved contractual terms, including service levels, reporting, insurance, data protection, safety, confidentiality, access, and termination provisions. | Legal / Procurement |
| FM system requirements | Applicable procedures, operational controls, asset registers, maintenance plans, work order processes, reporting formats, and FMS objectives. | FM Manager |
| Site access requirements | Access control, identification, induction, security clearance, key management, permits, and working restrictions. | Security / FM |
| Permit-to-work requirements | Required permits for high-risk activities such as hot works, confined spaces, electrical work, working at height, isolation, excavation, or impairment of life safety systems. | H&S / FM |
| Insurance and accreditation requirements | Required levels of public liability, professional indemnity, employer’s liability, licences, certifications, and competence records. | Procurement / Legal / FM |
| Communication plan | Named contacts, escalation routes, meeting schedule, reporting methods, and emergency contact arrangements. | FM Manager / Contract Manager |
| Existing supplier performance data | Historic supplier ratings, nonconformities, incident history, audit findings, complaints, and service performance records. | Contract Manager / Procurement |
| Approved supplier list status | Confirmation whether the supplier is pre-qualified, conditionally approved, new, suspended, or removed. | Procurement |

No external FM provider or contractor may begin work until the applicable prerequisites for their risk classification have been completed, approved, and recorded.

## Step-by-Step Procedure (numbered)

1. **Identify the need for externally provided FM services or products**

 1.1. The requestor or FM Manager identifies a requirement for an externally provided service, product, process, specialist competence, temporary resource, project, or contractor activity.

 1.2. The FM Manager confirms whether the requirement affects the FMS, facility operations, users, assets, compliance obligations, safety, security, environmental performance, business continuity, or service quality.

 1.3. If the requirement affects the FMS, this procedure must be followed.

 1.4. The FM Manager documents the business need, expected outcome, service location, affected assets, required timing, known constraints, and whether the requirement is planned, reactive, urgent, or emergency.

2. **Classify the outsourced service or contractor risk level**

 2.1. The FM Manager, with support from Health and Safety, Security, Compliance, Procurement, or Technical Leads as required, performs a risk classification before sourcing the provider.

 2.2. The classification must consider:

 - Criticality of the facility or asset affected.
 - Impact on users, customers, visitors, staff, or vulnerable persons.
 - Legal or regulatory implications.
 - Safety risk, including high-risk work.
 - Environmental impact.
 - Security and access requirements.
 - Business continuity implications.
 - Required technical competence or statutory qualification.
 - Data, systems, or confidential information access.
 - Use of subcontractors.
 - Past performance or incident history.
 - Complexity and duration of the service or works.

 2.3. The risk classification must be recorded using the following model unless an equivalent approved corporate model is used.

 | Risk Level | Description | Examples | Minimum Control Requirements |
 |---|---|---|---|
 | Low | Limited impact on FMS performance, low safety/security exposure, routine supply or low-risk service. | Office consumables, low-risk ad hoc support, non-critical furniture installation. | Approved purchase terms, basic supplier checks, delivery verification, site rules where applicable. |
 | Medium | Regular service or work affecting facility user experience, asset condition, operational continuity, or moderate compliance exposure. | Cleaning, landscaping, non-critical maintenance, waste services, minor works. | Supplier evaluation, documented scope, contract or purchase order, induction, insurance checks, performance monitoring. |
 | High | Work or service affecting critical assets, statutory compliance, safety systems, significant user impact, security-sensitive areas, or business continuity. | Fire systems maintenance, electrical works, lift maintenance, security guarding, HVAC for critical areas, hot works, working at height. | Formal tender/evaluation, competence verification, contract with SLAs/KPIs, H&S review, permits, supervision plan, scheduled performance reviews, audit rights. |
 | Critical | Outsourced process central to FM service delivery, legal compliance, life safety, critical infrastructure, or organisation-wide continuity. | Total FM provider, integrated FM contract, data centre facilities operations, life safety systems, emergency response services. | Executive approval, detailed due diligence, contract governance board, business continuity requirements, formal transition plan, robust KPIs, audit programme, contingency plan. |

 2.4. The level of control applied to the provider must be proportionate to the risk level and the potential impact of the externally provided process, product, or service on the organisation’s FMS.

3. **Define the scope, requirements, and acceptance criteria**

 3.1. The FM Manager or appointed Technical Lead prepares a documented scope of work or service specification.

 3.2. The specification must define, as applicable:

 - Service objectives and expected outcomes.
 - Facilities, locations, zones, rooms, assets, systems, or users covered.
 - Service boundaries, exclusions, assumptions, and dependencies.
 - Required service hours, response times, completion times, availability, and coverage.
 - Statutory, regulatory, technical, and industry standard requirements.
 - Competence, licence, certification, and training requirements.
 - Health, safety, environmental, and security requirements.
 - Required method statements, risk assessments, permits, and safe systems of work.
 - Materials, parts, equipment, and product requirements.
 - Sustainability and environmental requirements, where applicable.
 - Information, reporting, records, and evidence to be provided.
 - Business continuity, emergency response, resilience, and contingency requirements.
 - Access, identification, confidentiality, and conduct requirements.
 - Subcontractor approval requirements.
 - Performance indicators, service levels, and acceptance criteria.
 - Nonconformance, defect, rework, and corrective action expectations.

 3.3. The FM Manager must ensure that requirements are sufficiently clear to enable objective evaluation, contract control, service monitoring, and acceptance or rejection of delivered services.

4. **Select the appropriate sourcing method**

 4.1. Procurement and the FM Manager determine the sourcing method in accordance with procurement rules and the risk classification.

 4.2. Acceptable sourcing methods include:

 - Use of an approved supplier list.
 - Competitive quotation.
 - Formal tender or request for proposal.
 - Framework agreement.
 - Direct award with documented justification.
 - Emergency engagement where immediate action is required to protect life, safety, assets, security, compliance, or business continuity.

 4.3. Direct award or emergency sourcing must be justified, approved, and retrospectively reviewed where normal sourcing controls cannot be completed before work begins.

 4.4. High and Critical risk engagements must not proceed without documented Procurement, FM, and appropriate management approval, except where emergency procedures apply.

5. **Evaluate and select the provider**

 5.1. Procurement coordinates supplier evaluation with input from the FM Manager, Technical Lead, Health and Safety, Security, Legal, Finance, and other subject matter experts as required.

 5.2. Evaluation must be based on documented criteria proportionate to the risk classification.

 5.3. Evaluation criteria must include, where applicable:

 - Technical competence and relevant experience.
 - Capacity and resources to deliver the service.
 - Relevant qualifications, licences, accreditations, memberships, and statutory approvals.
 - Understanding of the scope and proposed delivery methodology.
 - Health and safety performance, including incident history.
 - Environmental and sustainability performance.
 - Quality management arrangements.
 - Business continuity and emergency response capability.
 - Security suitability and access control arrangements.
 - Financial stability.
 - Insurance coverage.
 - References and prior performance.
 - Subcontractor management arrangements.
 - Cost, value for money, and whole-life cost considerations.
 - Ability to meet reporting, records, and FMS integration requirements.

 5.4. The FM Manager must confirm that the provider can meet the defined acceptance criteria and service requirements.

 5.5. The outcome of evaluation must be documented and retained.

 5.6. Providers must not be selected solely on lowest price where service quality, safety, statutory compliance, asset integrity, or FMS performance may be adversely affected.

6. **Complete due diligence and pre-qualification checks**

 6.1. Before award or mobilisation, Procurement and the FM Manager complete due diligence appropriate to risk level.

 6.2. Due diligence checks must include, as applicable:

 | Due Diligence Check | Low | Medium | High | Critical |
 |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
 | Supplier identity and contact verification | Required | Required | Required | Required |
 | Insurance certificates | As applicable | Required | Required | Required |
 | Trade licences / statutory registrations | As applicable | As applicable | Required | Required |
 | Competence certificates and qualifications | As applicable | Required | Required | Required |
 | Health and safety policy and performance | As applicable | Required | Required | Required |
 | Risk assessments and method statements | As applicable | As applicable | Required before work | Required before work |
 | Financial stability check | Optional | As applicable | Required | Required |
 | References or prior performance review | Optional | Required | Required | Required |
 | Security screening requirements | As applicable | As applicable | Required where relevant | Required where relevant |
 | Environmental controls / waste licences | As applicable | As applicable | Required where relevant | Required where relevant |
 | Business continuity capability | Optional | As applicable | Required where relevant | Required |
 | Data protection / confidentiality assessment | As applicable | As applicable | Required where relevant | Required where relevant |
 | Subcontractor control process | Optional | Required where used | Required | Required |
 | Site visit or capability audit | Optional | Optional | As applicable | Required where significant |

 6.3. Any gaps identified during due diligence must be resolved before contract award or explicitly accepted through the exceptions process.

 6.4. Evidence of due diligence must be retained in the supplier or contract file.

7. **Approve provider selection and establish contractual controls**

 7.1. Procurement prepares the contract, purchase order, framework call-off, statement of work, or service agreement.

 7.2. Legal review is required for High and Critical risk contracts, material contract deviations, complex liability provisions, data access, long-term outsourcing, or significant commercial exposure.

 7.3. The contract or purchase terms must include, as applicable:

 - Defined scope, deliverables, and service boundaries.
 - Service levels, KPIs, response times, completion times, and performance thresholds.
 - Compliance with applicable laws, regulations, permits, licences, and standards.
 - Compliance with organisation FM procedures, site rules, health and safety rules, security rules, environmental requirements, and emergency procedures.
 - Requirements for competence, training, certification, and supervision.
 - Requirements for risk assessments, method statements, permits, and safe systems of work.
 - Requirements for reporting, records, certificates, inspection evidence, maintenance logs, and completion documentation.
 - Requirements for product conformity, warranties, manuals, test certificates, and asset documentation.
 - Requirements for subcontractor notification, approval, flow-down of obligations, and control.
 - Right of access, inspection, audit, and performance review by the organisation.
 - Nonconformance, corrective action, service credit, rework, suspension, and termination provisions.
 - Change control requirements.
 - Confidentiality, data protection, security, and access requirements.
 - Insurance and indemnity requirements.
 - Emergency response and business continuity requirements.
 - Exit, handover, knowledge transfer, return of assets, and offboarding obligations.

 7.4. The FM Manager confirms that the contract includes the operational controls necessary to meet ISO 41001:2018 requirements.

 7.5. Work must not commence until contract approval, purchase order approval, or other authorised engagement mechanism is in place, except under approved emergency arrangements.

8. **Prepare the mobilisation and transition plan**

 8.1. For recurring, Medium, High, or Critical services, the FM Manager and provider must agree a mobilisation plan before service commencement.

 8.2. For significant outsourcing or Critical services, a formal transition plan must be approved by the FM Manager and relevant governance stakeholders.

 8.3. The mobilisation or transition plan must include, as applicable:

 | Mobilisation Element | Required Detail |
 |---|---|
 | Key contacts | Provider account manager, site supervisor, contract manager, emergency contacts, escalation contacts. |
 | Service start date | Mobilisation milestones, go-live date, handover points, blackout periods. |
 | Resource plan | Staffing, skills, shift patterns, backup resources, supervision. |
 | Site familiarisation | Facility layout, restricted areas, plant rooms, access routes, welfare facilities, emergency exits. |
 | Asset and system familiarisation | Asset registers, critical systems, maintenance plans, operating manuals, known issues. |
 | Induction and training | Site induction, safety briefing, security briefing, environmental briefing, task-specific training. |
 | Permits and approvals | Permit-to-work requirements, access badges, keys, parking, equipment approvals. |
 | Documentation | RAMS, method statements, certificates, insurance, licences, work instructions, reporting templates. |
 | Communication | Meeting schedule, operational reporting, emergency communication, user communications. |
 | Performance baseline | Initial service levels, inspection criteria, current asset condition, open work orders. |
 | Contingency arrangements | Backup provider, emergency response, temporary service arrangements. |
 | Acceptance of mobilisation | Sign-off criteria and responsible approver. |

 8.4. The FM Manager verifies completion of required mobilisation activities before authorising routine service delivery.

9. **Onboard the provider and individual contractor personnel**

 9.1. The FM Manager or designated Site Representative ensures provider personnel complete mandatory onboarding before accessing the site or commencing work.

 9.2. Onboarding must be proportionate to the activity and must include, as applicable:

 - Site induction.
 - Health and safety induction.
 - Emergency procedures.
 - Security and access control briefing.
 - Environmental and waste management requirements.
 - Conduct expectations and user interaction rules.
 - Incident, near miss, hazard, and defect reporting processes.
 - Work order or service management system use.
 - Permit-to-work process.
 - Isolation and lockout/tagout requirements.
 - Restricted areas and access limitations.
 - Confidentiality and information handling requirements.
 - Use of personal protective equipment.
 - Welfare, parking, delivery, storage, and housekeeping rules.

 9.3. For High-risk work, the Site Representative must verify task-specific competence and review risk assessments and method statements before work starts.

 9.4. Access badges, keys, system accounts, or permits must be issued only for approved personnel and must be limited to the access necessary to perform the contracted work.

 9.5. Onboarding records must be retained.

10. **Control subcontracting**

 10.1. Providers must not subcontract any material part of the outsourced FM service unless permitted by the contract and approved by the FM Manager.

 10.2. The provider remains accountable for subcontractor performance unless otherwise specified in the contract.

 10.3. The FM Manager must ensure subcontractors are subject to controls equivalent to those applied to the primary provider, proportionate to risk.

 10.4. Subcontractors must meet the same competence, induction, safety, security, reporting, and documentation requirements applicable to the work.

 10.5. The provider must maintain a current list of subcontractors used for the organisation’s services and provide it upon request.

 10.6. Unapproved subcontractor use must be treated as a contractual nonconformance and escalated.

11. **Authorise work and manage day-to-day service delivery**

 11.1. Work must be initiated through an approved work order, service request, planned maintenance schedule, permit, project instruction, purchase order, or contract instruction.

 11.2. The Site Representative confirms that the provider has authority to perform the specific task and that required permits, isolations, access approvals, and documentation are in place.

 11.3. The provider must deliver the service in accordance with:

 - Contractual requirements.
 - Approved scope of work.
 - Service level agreements.
 - Applicable laws and regulations.
 - Organisation FM procedures and site rules.
 - Approved risk assessments and method statements.
 - Permit-to-work requirements.
 - Manufacturer and technical standards.
 - Environmental, safety, security, and quality requirements.

 11.4. Any change to work scope, method, timing, materials, risk profile, affected asset, service interruption, or access requirement must be approved before implementation.

 11.5. The provider must immediately report incidents, near misses, hazards, defects, service failures, statutory noncompliance, security breaches, environmental spills, damage to assets, or user-impacting issues.

 11.6. The FM Manager or Site Representative monitors work execution through supervision, inspections, work order review, site walk-throughs, user feedback, and performance reporting.

12. **Verify delivered services, works, and products**

 12.1. The FM Manager, Site Representative, Technical Lead, or authorised recipient must verify that delivered services, works, or products meet specified requirements before acceptance.

 12.2. Verification methods may include:

 - Visual inspection.
 - Functional testing.
 - Review of completion certificates.
 - Review of statutory test certificates.
 - Review of maintenance logs.
 - User acceptance.
 - Sample quality checks.
 - Technical inspection.
 - Asset data update verification.
 - Environmental or waste transfer documentation review.
 - Security or access log review.
 - Performance against SLA or KPI data.

 12.3. Acceptance criteria must be based on the contract, specification, service level, applicable standard, work order, or defined inspection checklist.

 12.4. Products and materials must be checked for conformity, correct specification, damage, certification, safe storage requirements, warranties, and compatibility with relevant facility systems.

 12.5. Nonconforming services, works, or products must not be accepted unless formally approved through the exceptions process.

 12.6. Payment approval must be linked to evidence of satisfactory delivery where contractually and operationally appropriate.

13. **Monitor provider performance**

 13.1. The Contract Manager monitors provider performance throughout the contract lifecycle.

 13.2. Monitoring frequency and method must be proportionate to provider risk level, service criticality, performance history, and contractual requirements.

 13.3. Performance monitoring may include:

 - SLA and KPI reporting.
 - Work order completion analysis.
 - Planned preventive maintenance compliance.
 - Reactive response and resolution times.
 - Statutory compliance completion rates.
 - Quality inspections and audits.
 - Safety observations and incident reviews.
 - Environmental performance reviews.
 - User satisfaction and complaint analysis.
 - Asset downtime and reliability trends.
 - Financial and commercial reviews.
 - Contract meeting minutes and action tracking.
 - Review of corrective actions.
 - Periodic supplier requalification.

 13.4. Minimum monitoring frequency is defined below unless more frequent monitoring is required by contract or risk assessment.

 | Risk Level | Minimum Monitoring Activities | Minimum Frequency |
 |---|---|---|
 | Low | Delivery checks, issue review, invoice validation where applicable. | Per delivery or engagement |
 | Medium | KPI review, service quality checks, complaints review, contract manager review. | Monthly or quarterly |
 | High | KPI review, compliance check, safety review, performance meeting, corrective action review. | Monthly |
 | Critical | Formal governance meeting, executive dashboard, risk review, audit/inspection plan, continuity review. | Monthly, with quarterly senior review |

 13.5. Performance indicators must be appropriate to the service and may include the following.

 | KPI Category | Example KPI | Typical Target / Threshold |
 |---|---|---|
 | Responsiveness | Emergency response time achieved | ≥ 95% within contracted time |
 | Completion | Planned preventive maintenance completed on schedule | ≥ 98% by due date |
 | Statutory compliance | Statutory inspections completed before expiry | 100% |
 | Quality | Inspection pass rate | ≥ 95% |
 | Safety | Reportable incidents attributable to provider | 0 target; all investigated |
 | Corrective action | Corrective actions closed by due date | ≥ 95% |
 | User satisfaction | Service complaints resolved within target | ≥ 90% |
 | Asset reliability | Repeat failures after maintenance | Monitored and trended |
 | Reporting | Monthly report submitted complete and on time | 100% |
 | Environmental | Waste transfer documentation complete | 100% where applicable |

 13.6. Performance data must be retained and used for supplier reviews, contract renewal decisions, corrective actions, and continual improvement of the FMS.

14. **Conduct provider review meetings**

 14.1. The Contract Manager schedules provider review meetings in accordance with risk level and contractual requirements.

 14.2. Review meetings must be documented and include, as applicable:

 - Review of previous actions.
 - SLA and KPI performance.
 - Statutory compliance status.
 - Planned and reactive work performance.
 - Safety incidents, near misses, hazards, and observations.
 - Security, access, and conduct issues.
 - Environmental performance and waste documentation.
 - User feedback, complaints, and compliments.
 - Audit and inspection results.
 - Resource, competence, and staffing matters.
 - Subcontractor performance.
 - Open risks and issues.
 - Asset condition trends and recommendations.
 - Change requests and upcoming works.
 - Business continuity and emergency preparedness.
 - Innovation and improvement opportunities.
 - Corrective actions and deadlines.

 14.3. Actions must be assigned to named owners with target dates and tracked to closure.

 14.4. Persistent failure to close actions must be escalated in accordance with this procedure.

15. **Manage nonconforming externally provided services**

 15.1. Any externally provided service, process, product, or work that does not meet specified requirements must be recorded as a nonconformance, defect, service failure, incident, or complaint as applicable.

 15.2. Examples of nonconformance include:

 - Failure to meet contractual SLA or KPI requirements.
 - Incomplete or poor-quality work.
 - Failure to provide required statutory certificates or maintenance records.
 - Use of unapproved materials or parts.
 - Work performed outside approved scope or method.
 - Unsafe work or breach of permit conditions.
 - Unauthorised subcontracting.
 - Security breach or access violation.
 - Environmental breach or waste documentation failure.
 - Failure to report incidents or hazards.
 - Repeated user complaints.
 - Failure to maintain required insurance, licence, or accreditation.

 15.3. The Contract Manager assesses the severity and impact of the nonconformance.

 15.4. Immediate containment action must be taken where there is risk to life, safety, security, asset integrity, legal compliance, environment, or business continuity.

 15.5. Corrective action must be requested from the provider for significant, repeated, or high-risk nonconformities.

 15.6. Corrective action requests must include:

 | Field | Required Information |
 |---|---|
 | Nonconformance reference | Unique identifier or linked incident/work order number. |
 | Provider | Supplier or contractor name. |
 | Description | Clear statement of the issue and requirement not met. |
 | Date identified | Date and time detected. |
 | Impact | Safety, compliance, service, asset, user, financial, or environmental impact. |
 | Immediate containment | Actions taken to control risk or prevent further impact. |
 | Root cause requirement | Whether root cause analysis is required. |
 | Corrective action required | Required remedial and preventive actions. |
 | Owner | Provider and internal responsible owners. |
 | Due date | Required closure date. |
 | Verification method | How closure will be verified. |
 | Status | Open, in progress, overdue, verified, closed. |

 15.7. The Contract Manager verifies corrective action effectiveness before closure.

 15.8. Repeated or serious nonconformities must be considered in supplier performance ratings, contract remedies, escalation, suspension, renewal decisions, or termination.

16. **Control contract changes and variations**

 16.1. Any change to scope, service level, price, duration, delivery model, subcontracting arrangement, risk profile, site access, materials, critical personnel, or statutory obligation must be controlled.

 16.2. The Contract Manager reviews the proposed change for impact on:

 - FMS objectives and operational performance.
 - User needs and service delivery.
 - Legal and regulatory compliance.
 - Health and safety.
 - Security and access.
 - Environmental performance.
 - Asset condition and lifecycle.
 - Business continuity.
 - Cost and budget.
 - Contractual obligations and risk allocation.
 - Records, reporting, and acceptance criteria.

 16.3. Changes must be documented through an approved variation, change order, contract amendment, revised statement of work, or updated purchase order.

 16.4. High and Critical risk changes require approval by the FM Manager and Procurement, with Legal, Health and Safety, Security, Finance, or senior management approval where applicable.

 16.5. Changes must be communicated to affected stakeholders and reflected in operational plans, work instructions, asset data, service levels, and monitoring arrangements.

17. **Maintain provider records and FMS integration**

 17.1. The Contract Manager ensures provider information and service outputs are captured in the relevant FMS, contract management system, procurement system, asset management system, document repository, or work order system.

 17.2. Provider records must be accurate, current, accessible to authorised personnel, protected from unauthorised alteration, and retained in accordance with records retention requirements.

 17.3. Service outputs must update relevant facility records, including:

 - Asset registers.
 - Maintenance histories.
 - Compliance certificates.
 - Inspection reports.
 - Drawings and schematics.
 - Operation and maintenance manuals.
 - Risk assessments.
 - Defect logs.
 - Warranty records.
 - Permit records.
 - Planned maintenance schedules.
 - Business continuity contacts.
 - Emergency response plans.

 17.4. The FM Manager must ensure that externally provided information required for FMS operation and evaluation is available when needed.

18. **Requalify and renew providers**

 18.1. Providers must be periodically requalified based on risk, performance, contract duration, and changes in service scope or regulatory requirements.

 18.2. Requalification must include review of:

 - Current insurance coverage.
 - Licences and certifications.
 - Performance history.
 - Nonconformities and corrective actions.
 - Safety and environmental performance.
 - Security or access issues.
 - User feedback.
 - Financial or operational stability where relevant.
 - Continued ability to meet FMS and contractual requirements.

 18.3. Minimum requalification frequency is:

 | Risk Level | Minimum Requalification Frequency |
 |---|---|
 | Low | At renewal or before repeat use where records are older than 36 months |
 | Medium | Every 24 months or at contract renewal |
 | High | Annually or at contract renewal |
 | Critical | Annually and before any major renewal, extension, or material scope change |

 18.4. Contract renewal decisions must consider provider performance, risk, value, compliance, user needs, lessons learned, and alignment with FM objectives.

 18.5. Providers with unacceptable performance must not be renewed without documented senior management approval and an agreed improvement plan.

19. **Suspend, terminate, or offboard providers**

 19.1. A provider may be suspended, restricted, removed from the approved supplier list, or terminated where there is serious or repeated failure to meet requirements.

 19.2. Grounds for suspension or termination may include:

 - Serious safety breach.
 - Statutory noncompliance.
 - Security breach.
 - Fraud, unethical conduct, or misrepresentation.
 - Loss of required licence, insurance, certification, or competence.
 - Persistent SLA or KPI failure.
 - Failure to implement corrective actions.
 - Unauthorised subcontracting.
 - Material breach of contract.
 - Insolvency or inability to deliver.
 - Conduct that creates unacceptable risk to the organisation, users, assets, or FMS.

 19.3. Before termination, the Contract Manager must consult Procurement and Legal unless immediate action is required to protect life, safety, security, compliance, or critical operations.

 19.4. Offboarding must ensure controlled exit and continuity of facility services.

 19.5. Offboarding activities must include, as applicable:

 | Offboarding Activity | Required Action |
 |---|---|
 | Access removal | Retrieve badges, keys, passes, parking permits, system accounts, remote access, and access codes. |
 | Asset return | Recover organisation tools, equipment, documents, devices, uniforms, drawings, and manuals. |
 | Work closure | Close or transfer open work orders, defects, permits, projects, and planned maintenance tasks. |
 | Records transfer | Obtain final certificates, maintenance records, warranties, as-built drawings, asset data, logs, and reports. |
 | Knowledge transfer | Conduct handover with replacement provider or internal team. |
 | Data and confidentiality | Confirm return, deletion, or protection of organisation information as contractually required. |
 | Financial closure | Validate final invoices, credits, service credits, retention, and disputed amounts. |
 | Subcontractor closure | Confirm subcontractor removal and return of access privileges. |
 | Lessons learned | Record performance issues, risks, and improvement actions. |
 | Supplier status update | Update approved supplier list to active, inactive, suspended, terminated, or not approved. |

 19.6. The FM Manager must confirm that offboarding does not create unacceptable service, compliance, safety, or continuity risk.

20. **Manage emergency contractor engagement**

 20.1. Emergency engagement may be used only where immediate action is required to protect life, safety, security, environment, assets, statutory compliance, or business continuity.

 20.2. The FM Manager or authorised delegate may approve emergency engagement where standard sourcing controls cannot be completed before work starts.

 20.3. Even in emergencies, minimum controls must be applied where practicable:

 - Confirm supplier identity and competence.
 - Confirm insurance or known approved supplier status where possible.
 - Conduct safety briefing and site induction.
 - Apply permit-to-work requirements for high-risk activities.
 - Restrict access to necessary areas.
 - Record scope, authorisation, timing, and reason for emergency engagement.
 - Supervise work proportionate to risk.
 - Verify completion before acceptance.

 20.4. A retrospective review must be completed within a reasonable period after the emergency event, including documentation of supplier details, work performed, risks, approvals, costs, records, and any follow-up actions.

 20.5. If an emergency provider may be used again, normal due diligence and approval must be completed before repeat non-emergency use.

## Roles & RACI

The following roles are responsible for implementing this procedure.

| Role | Key Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Facilities Management Manager | Owns this procedure; ensures externally provided FM services are controlled; approves risk classification; ensures requirements align with FMS objectives; approves High/Critical FM operational controls. |
| Contract Manager | Manages provider lifecycle; monitors performance; maintains contract records; leads review meetings; manages nonconformities, corrective actions, and offboarding. |
| Procurement | Manages sourcing, supplier evaluation, approved supplier status, commercial negotiation, purchase orders, procurement records, and supplier due diligence coordination. |
| Requestor / Service Owner | Defines business need and confirms service requirements; participates in acceptance and performance feedback. |
| Technical Lead / Subject Matter Expert | Defines technical specifications; verifies competence; reviews method statements; inspects technical delivery; confirms technical acceptance. |
| Health and Safety Representative | Reviews safety risk, RAMS, permits, incidents, competence, and compliance with safety requirements. |
| Security Representative | Reviews site access, restricted areas, identification, background checks where applicable, and security incidents. |
| Legal | Reviews contractual terms, liability, termination, data protection, confidentiality, and significant contract deviations. |
| Finance / Budget Owner | Confirms budget availability, payment approvals, financial controls, and commercial reporting. |
| Provider / Contractor | Delivers services in accordance with contract and site requirements; maintains competence; controls subcontractors; reports incidents; provides records; implements corrective actions. |
| Site Representative | Coordinates local access, induction, permits, supervision, work verification, and site-level issue escalation. |
| Senior Management | Approves Critical outsourcing arrangements, significant exceptions, high-risk terminations, and escalated unresolved performance issues. |

RACI matrix:

| Activity | FM Manager | Contract Manager | Procurement | Technical Lead | H&S | Security | Legal | Finance | Provider | Senior Management |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Identify outsourcing need | A | C | C | C | C | C | I | C | I | I |
| Risk classify service/provider | A | R | C | C | C | C | I | I | I | I |
| Define scope and acceptance criteria | A | R | C | R | C | C | I | C | C | I |
| Select sourcing method | C | C | A/R | C | I | I | I | C | I | I |
| Evaluate provider | A | R | R | C | C | C | C | C | I | I |
| Complete due diligence | C | R | A/R | C | C | C | C | C | R for own evidence | I |
| Approve provider selection | A | R | A/R | C | C | C | C | C | I | A for Critical |
| Establish contract controls | C | R | A/R | C | C | C | A/R where required | C | C | A for Critical |
| Mobilise and onboard provider | A | R | C | C | C | C | I | I | R | I |
| Approve subcontractors | A | R | C | C | C | C | C | I | R for disclosure | I |
| Authorise and supervise work | A | R | I | C | C | C | I | I | R | I |
| Verify service delivery | A | R | I | R/C | C | C | I | C | C | I |
| Monitor performance | A | R | C | C | C | C | I | C | R for reporting | I |
| Manage nonconformance | A | R | C | C | C | C | C | C | R for corrective action | I |
| Approve contract changes | A | R | A/R | C | C | C | C where required | C | C | A for Critical |
| Suspend or terminate provider | A | R | R | C | C | C | A/R where required | C | I | A for Critical/high impact |
| Offboard provider | A | R | C | C | C | C | C | C | R | I |
| Review procedure effectiveness | A/R | C | C | C | C | C | I | I | I | C |

RACI key:

- **R** = Responsible for performing the activity.
- **A** = Accountable for final decision or outcome.
- **C** = Consulted before action or decision.
- **I** = Informed of outcome or status.

## Records & Outputs

The following records must be created, maintained, and retained as evidence that externally provided FM processes, products, and services are controlled in accordance with ISO 41001:2018.

| Record / Output | Description | Owner | Minimum Retention |
|---|---|---|---|
| Outsourcing request / business need | Record of requirement, justification, location, timing, and service impact. | FM Manager / Requestor | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Risk classification record | Documented assessment of provider/service risk level and required controls. | FM Manager | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Scope of work / service specification | Defined service requirements, deliverables, acceptance criteria, and compliance obligations. | FM Manager / Technical Lead | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Procurement evaluation records | Tender documents, quotations, evaluation scorecards, award justification, direct award rationale. | Procurement | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Supplier due diligence evidence | Insurance, licences, certifications, references, financial checks, H&S records, security checks. | Procurement / Contract Manager | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Approved supplier list entry | Supplier approval status, category, risk rating, restrictions, and review date. | Procurement | Current + 6 years |
| Contract / purchase order / statement of work | Formal engagement terms and service obligations. | Procurement / Legal | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Mobilisation / transition plan | Onboarding, handover, service start, resource, and readiness activities. | Contract Manager | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Induction and access records | Site induction, safety briefing, access badges, keys, system access, permits issued. | Site Representative / Security | Current + 3 years, or longer if legal requirement applies |
| RAMS and permit-to-work records | Risk assessments, method statements, permits, isolations, approvals, and close-outs. | H&S / FM | As legally required; minimum 3 years |
| Work orders and completion records | Service requests, task completion, evidence, photos, certificates, approvals. | Contract Manager / Site Representative | Minimum 6 years, or asset lifecycle where relevant |
| Statutory compliance certificates | Inspection, test, maintenance, calibration, and certification evidence. | FM Manager / Technical Lead | As legally required; minimum 6 years |
| Product conformity records | Delivery notes, certificates of conformity, warranties, manuals, technical data sheets. | Contract Manager | Asset lifecycle or minimum 6 years |
| KPI and SLA reports | Provider performance data, dashboards, trend analysis, and service metrics. | Contract Manager | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Review meeting minutes | Provider governance meeting records, decisions, issues, and actions. | Contract Manager | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Nonconformance and corrective action records | Service failures, defects, incidents, root cause, corrective actions, verification. | Contract Manager | Minimum 6 years |
| Audit and inspection reports | Supplier audits, site inspections, quality reviews, safety audits. | Contract Manager / H&S | Minimum 6 years |
| Contract change records | Variations, amendments, change approvals, revised scope and pricing. | Procurement / Contract Manager | Contract duration + 6 years |
| Requalification records | Periodic supplier reassessment and renewal recommendation. | Procurement / Contract Manager | Current + 6 years |
| Suspension / termination records | Decision records, notices, legal review, risk assessment, continuity actions. | Procurement / Contract Manager | Minimum 6 years |
| Offboarding checklist | Access removal, asset return, records transfer, final invoice validation, lessons learned. | Contract Manager / Security | Minimum 6 years |
| Emergency engagement record | Emergency justification, approval, work details, retrospective review, follow-up actions. | FM Manager | Minimum 6 years |

Records must be:

- Legible, accurate, complete, and traceable to the provider, contract, asset, site, and service where applicable.
- Stored in approved repositories such as [Contract Management System], [FM System], [Procurement System], or [Document Repository].
- Protected from unauthorised access, alteration, loss, or destruction.
- Available for internal audits, management review, external audits, regulatory inspection, and performance evaluation.
- Disposed of only in accordance with the organisation’s records retention and disposal requirements.

## Exceptions & Escalation

Exceptions to this procedure are permitted only where justified, risk-assessed, approved, and recorded.

1. **Exception criteria**

 Exceptions may be considered where:

 - Emergency conditions prevent completion of normal controls before work begins.
 - A sole supplier is required due to proprietary systems, warranty constraints, statutory necessity, urgent continuity needs, or specialist competence.
 - Full due diligence evidence is temporarily unavailable but risk can be controlled through compensating measures.
 - A contractual term cannot be adopted but equivalent controls are established.
 - A temporary deviation is required to maintain critical facility operations.

2. **Exception approval**

 The following approval levels apply.

 | Exception Type | Required Approval |
 |---|---|
 | Low-risk procedural deviation | FM Manager |
 | Medium-risk deviation or missing due diligence item | FM Manager and Procurement |
 | High-risk deviation affecting safety, compliance, security, or critical assets | FM Manager, Procurement, relevant control function, and Senior Management |
 | Critical outsourcing deviation or acceptance of material nonconformance | Senior Management, Legal, Procurement, and FM Manager |
 | Emergency engagement | FM Manager or authorised delegate, with retrospective review |

3. **Exception record**

 Each exception must include:

 - Description of the deviation.
 - Reason for exception.
 - Provider and service affected.
 - Risk assessment.
 - Compensating controls.
 - Approval authority.
 - Expiry date or review date.
 - Required corrective or follow-up actions.
 - Evidence of closure.

4. **Escalation triggers**

 The Contract Manager must escalate to the FM Manager where any of the following occur:

 - Serious safety incident or near miss involving a provider.
 - Statutory compliance failure or missed mandatory inspection.
 - Security breach, unauthorised access, or loss of keys/badges.
 - Environmental incident or regulatory reporting issue.
 - Service failure affecting business continuity or critical operations.
 - Repeated KPI failure or unresolved corrective action.
 - Use of unapproved subcontractors.
 - Loss of provider insurance, licence, certification, or competence.
 - Contract dispute or material commercial issue.
 - Evidence of fraud, unethical behaviour, or misrepresentation.
 - Provider insolvency or inability to deliver.
 - Any issue likely to affect ISO 41001 conformity or FMS performance.

5. **Escalation path**

 | Escalation Level | Trigger | Escalation Recipient | Expected Action |
 |---|---|---|---|
 | Level 1 | Routine service issue or minor nonconformance | Contract Manager / Site Representative | Corrective action request and local follow-up. |
 | Level 2 | Repeated minor issue or moderate service impact | FM Manager | Performance review, recovery plan, increased monitoring. |
 | Level 3 | Serious safety, compliance, security, or critical service issue | FM Manager, H&S/Security/Compliance, Procurement | Immediate containment, formal corrective action, management notification. |
 | Level 4 | Material breach, unresolved high-risk issue, termination risk, or Critical provider failure | Senior Management, Legal, Procurement, FM Manager | Executive decision, contract remedies, continuity plan, suspension or termination. |

6. **Immediate stop-work authority**

 The FM Manager, Site Representative, Health and Safety Representative, Security Representative, or authorised manager may stop contractor work immediately where there is imminent risk to life, safety, security, environment, statutory compliance, critical assets, or business continuity.

 Work may restart only when:

 - The risk has been assessed.
 - Required corrective actions have been implemented.
 - Required permits or approvals are in place.
 - The authorised representative confirms that work may safely resume.

## Review

This procedure must be reviewed at least annually, or sooner where any of the following occur:

- Changes to ISO 41001:2018 requirements, applicable law, regulatory obligations, or organisational FM requirements.
- Significant outsourcing, insourcing, or contractor management changes.
- Introduction of a new Critical or High-risk outsourced FM service.
- Significant provider failure, incident, audit finding, legal issue, or nonconformance.
- Material changes to procurement, contract management, health and safety, security, or FM systems.
- Management review identifies the need for improved control of externally provided processes, products, or services.
- Lessons learned from emergencies, contract transitions, provider termination, or service continuity events indicate procedural gaps.

The Facilities Management Manager is responsible for coordinating the review with Procurement, Contract Management, Health and Safety, Security, Legal, Finance, and relevant operational stakeholders.

The review must assess:

- Whether the procedure remains suitable, adequate, and effective.
- Whether controls remain proportionate to provider risk and FMS impact.
- Whether provider selection and onboarding controls are consistently applied.
- Whether monitoring, KPI, inspection, and review mechanisms provide reliable evidence of conformity.
- Whether nonconformities and corrective actions are timely and effective.
- Whether records are complete, accessible, and audit-ready.
- Whether subcontractor controls remain adequate.
- Whether emergency engagement and exception processes are being used appropriately.
- Whether lessons learned and improvement opportunities have been incorporated.

Review outputs must include:

- Updated procedure version, where changes are required.
- Approved action plan for improvement items.
- Communication or training requirements.
- Updates to templates, checklists, supplier evaluation criteria, or monitoring dashboards.
- Evidence of approval and publication.

Version history must be maintained.

| Version | Date | Summary of Changes | Approved By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | [Effective Date] | Initial issue. | Facilities Management Manager |

ISO41-015.title: Emergency Preparedness & Response Plan
ISO41-015.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Control Reference | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| [FM-PLAN-EPR-001] | 1.0 | Facilities Management / Health, Safety & Environment | [Effective Date] | ISO 41001:2018 Facility Management Management System | — Operational Planning and Control | Internal |

## Purpose & Objectives

This Emergency Preparedness & Response Plan defines the planning approach, responsibilities, resources, milestones, and success measures for establishing and maintaining effective emergency preparedness and response arrangements for facility-related incidents, including fire, evacuation, and utility outage scenarios.

The plan supports ISO 41001:2018, which requires the organisation to plan, implement, and control the processes needed to meet facility management requirements and implement actions determined through planning. This includes establishing criteria for operational processes, controlling planned changes, and ensuring outsourced or externally provided processes are controlled where they affect facility management performance.

The objectives of this plan are to:

1. Establish a structured emergency preparedness and response programme covering:
 - Fire detection, alarm, response, and evacuation.
 - Building evacuation and assembly management.
 - Utility outages, including electricity, water, gas, heating, ventilation, cooling, telecommunications, and critical facility services.
2. Ensure emergency response arrangements are integrated into facility management operational planning and control.
3. Define emergency response roles, responsibilities, escalation paths, and decision authorities.
4. Identify critical dependencies, resources, and external interfaces required for emergency response.
5. Provide a phased implementation approach for emergency planning, testing, corrective action, and continual improvement.
6. Ensure emergency arrangements are documented, communicated, exercised, monitored, and reviewed.
7. Support protection of life safety, property, environment, service continuity, and compliance obligations.
8. Ensure changes to facilities, occupancy, services, contractors, and operational processes are assessed for emergency preparedness impacts before implementation.

This plan is not a step-by-step evacuation procedure; rather, it defines the programme-level plan for preparing, implementing, exercising, and maintaining emergency response capability as part of the facility management system.

## Scope

This plan applies to all facilities, workplaces, occupied areas, plant rooms, shared spaces, external premises areas, and facility services under the organisation’s facility management responsibility.

The plan covers emergency preparedness and response planning for the following event categories:

| Emergency Category | Included Scenarios | Primary Facility Management Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| Fire and smoke | Confirmed fire, smoke detection, manual call point activation, suspected fire, fire alarm activation, sprinkler discharge | Life safety systems, evacuation, fire service access, fire compartmentation, emergency lighting, alarm monitoring, fire wardens, post-incident recovery |
| Evacuation | Full building evacuation, partial evacuation, phased evacuation, shelter-in-place where directed | Assembly points, occupant accounting, accessibility needs, visitor management, contractor evacuation, re-entry control |
| Electrical utility outage | Loss of mains power, brownout, local distribution failure, generator failure, UPS depletion | Emergency lighting, life safety systems, access control, lifts, critical equipment, generator fuel, business continuity interfaces |
| Water utility outage | Loss of potable water, sanitation impact, sprinkler system impairment, water contamination | Welfare facilities, hygiene, cooling systems, fire suppression availability, building closure criteria |
| Gas outage or leak | Gas supply interruption, suspected leak, gas detection activation | Isolation points, evacuation, hazardous atmosphere risk, contractor response, statutory notification |
| Heating, ventilation and cooling outage | HVAC failure, ventilation failure, temperature excursion, smoke control system impairment | Indoor environmental quality, critical area temperature, occupant welfare, fire safety interfaces |
| Telecommunications outage | Loss of telephony, internet, radio, alarm monitoring link, building management system connectivity | Emergency communications, escalation, security monitoring, remote system visibility |
| Lift or vertical transport failure | Lift entrapment, lift outage affecting evacuation or accessibility | Rescue arrangements, accessibility support, maintenance contractor response |
| Building management or control system failure | BMS failure, access control failure, security system failure, automated alarm failure | Manual monitoring arrangements, emergency access, alarm escalation, temporary controls |

The scope includes:

- Emergency preparedness planning and implementation.
- Identification of emergency response requirements arising from facility operations.
- Coordination with fire safety, health and safety, security, business continuity, environmental, and crisis management arrangements.
- Emergency roles, training, drills, and exercises.
- Communication and escalation arrangements.
- Maintenance and readiness of emergency equipment and facility systems.
- Contractor, tenant, visitor, and supplier interfaces affecting emergency response.
- Planning for temporary controls during impairment of life safety or utility systems.
- Post-exercise and post-incident review.
- Documented information required to demonstrate operational control under ISO 41001:2018.

The scope excludes:

- Detailed emergency procedures and work instructions, which are maintained separately.
- Enterprise-wide crisis management strategy, except where facility management interfaces are required.
- IT disaster recovery, except for dependencies on facility utilities and building infrastructure.
- Occupational health and safety legal compliance programmes owned outside Facilities Management, except for coordination requirements relevant to facilities and building operations.

Interfaces with related documents include, where applicable:

| Related Document / Process | Relationship to this Plan |
|---|---|
| Fire Safety Management Plan | Defines fire risk controls, inspection regimes, and fire system maintenance requirements |
| Evacuation Procedure | Provides step-by-step evacuation instructions for occupants and response teams |
| Business Continuity Plan | Defines continuity priorities and recovery requirements after facility disruption |
| Crisis Management Plan | Defines executive decision-making and external stakeholder management during major incidents |
| Utility Outage Procedure | Defines operational response steps for specific utility failures |
| Contractor Management Procedure | Ensures contractors understand emergency arrangements and impairment controls |
| Preventive Maintenance Plan | Ensures emergency systems and critical utilities are inspected, tested, and maintained |
| Change Management Procedure | Ensures facility changes are assessed for emergency preparedness impact |
| Incident Reporting and Investigation Procedure | Captures emergency incidents, lessons learned, corrective actions, and evidence |

## Assumptions & Dependencies

The following assumptions underpin this plan:

1. The organisation maintains legal occupancy rights and operational control for the facilities in scope.
2. Facility layouts, occupancy levels, operating hours, critical services, and emergency system inventories are known or can be verified.
3. Emergency response arrangements will be proportionate to:
 - Facility size and complexity.
 - Occupancy profile.
 - Operating hours.
 - Vulnerable occupants or accessibility requirements.
 - Hazard profile.
 - Regulatory obligations.
 - Criticality of services delivered from the facility.
4. Life safety takes priority over property protection, operational continuity, and asset preservation.
5. Emergency response arrangements will align with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements in [Jurisdiction].
6. Emergency services retain authority over incident command once they assume control.
7. Contractors, tenants, visitors, and service providers will be required to comply with site emergency arrangements.
8. Where facilities are leased or multi-tenant, responsibilities will be agreed with landlords, managing agents, and other duty holders.
9. Emergency preparedness will be incorporated into planned and unplanned facility changes.
10. Emergency response exercises and drills will be scheduled to minimise operational disruption while achieving sufficient realism and coverage.

Key dependencies include:

| Dependency | Description | Owner / Interface | Required Control |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fire detection and alarm systems | Systems used to detect fire, raise alarms, and support evacuation | Facilities Management / Fire Safety Responsible Person / Maintenance Provider | Inspection, testing, maintenance, fault response, impairment management |
| Emergency lighting | Lighting supporting evacuation routes during power failure | Facilities Management / Electrical Contractor | Periodic testing, battery duration verification, defect remediation |
| Means of escape | Exits, escape routes, signage, doors, stairwells, and assembly access | Facilities Management / Security / Building Management | Routine inspections, obstruction control, access control override testing |
| Fire suppression systems | Sprinklers, extinguishers, gaseous suppression, hose reels where applicable | Facilities Management / Fire Protection Contractor | Maintenance, impairment notification, availability monitoring |
| Utilities | Electricity, water, gas, heating, cooling, telecommunications | Facilities Management / Utility Providers | Contact lists, outage procedures, escalation paths, service restoration coordination |
| Emergency communications | PA systems, radios, phones, mass notification tools, signage | Facilities Management / Security / IT | Testing, fallback methods, contact list accuracy |
| Security and access control | Building entry, emergency egress, lockdown and re-entry controls | Security / Facilities Management | Emergency override, muster support, emergency services access |
| Building Management System | Monitoring and control of HVAC, alarms, utilities, and plant | Facilities Management / Controls Contractor | Monitoring availability, manual fallback arrangements |
| Contractor response capability | Specialist contractors for fire, electrical, mechanical, gas, water, lift, and controls systems | Procurement / Facilities Management | Service level agreements, emergency callout, competence assurance |
| Occupant information | Staff, contractors, visitors, tenants, persons requiring assistance | Human Resources / Security / Reception / Tenant Contacts | Muster support, privacy-respecting emergency assistance arrangements |
| External emergency services | Fire, ambulance, police, civil defence, utility emergency teams | Facilities Management / HSE / Security | Site information, access arrangements, liaison protocols |
| Compliance obligations | Fire codes, building regulations, health and safety duties, environmental requirements | Legal / Compliance / HSE / Facilities Management | Legal register updates, inspection evidence, audit readiness |

Constraints and planning considerations include:

- Some emergency controls may be owned by landlords, property managers, or shared-service providers.
- Utility restoration time may be outside organisational control.
- Facility occupancy patterns may vary due to hybrid working, shift work, events, or contractors.
- Vulnerable persons and persons requiring assistance may change over time.
- Emergency exercises may require coordination with tenants, neighbouring premises, emergency services, or local authorities.
- Planned impairments to fire systems or utilities may require compensating controls before work proceeds.

## Approach / Phases

The emergency preparedness and response implementation will be delivered through the following phases. Each phase produces documented outputs suitable for management review, audit evidence, and ongoing operational control.

### Phase 1 — Initiation and Governance

The organisation will establish governance arrangements for emergency preparedness and response within the facility management system.

Key activities:

1. Confirm facilities and services in scope.
2. Appoint the Emergency Preparedness Plan Owner.
3. Confirm relationship with fire safety, health and safety, security, business continuity, and crisis management functions.
4. Identify legal and other requirements applicable to fire, evacuation, utilities, emergency systems, and occupancy.
5. Define emergency planning criteria consistent with ISO 41001:2018, including:
 - Required process outcomes.
 - Process control criteria.
 - Documented information requirements.
 - Control of planned changes.
 - Control of outsourced services affecting emergency readiness.
6. Establish an emergency preparedness steering group or working group where facility complexity requires cross-functional coordination.
7. Define reporting requirements to senior management.

Expected outputs:

- Confirmed scope register.
- Emergency preparedness governance structure.
- Emergency planning terms of reference.
- Legal and compliance obligation register update.
- Emergency preparedness implementation schedule.

### Phase 2 — Facility Risk, Scenario, and Impact Assessment

The organisation will assess facility emergency scenarios and operational impacts to ensure response arrangements are risk-based and proportionate.

Key activities:

1. Identify emergency scenarios for each facility, including:
 - Fire and smoke.
 - Full or partial evacuation.
 - Power outage.
 - Water outage.
 - Gas leak or outage.
 - HVAC failure.
 - Telecommunications outage.
 - Lift entrapment or outage.
 - Failure of BMS, access control, alarm monitoring, or security systems.
2. Review facility characteristics, including:
 - Occupancy load.
 - Building height and layout.
 - Evacuation routes.
 - Hazardous areas.
 - Critical plant and equipment.
 - Persons requiring assistance.
 - External access and emergency service approach routes.
3. Assess consequences for:
 - Life safety.
 - Statutory compliance.
 - Essential facility services.
 - Environmental protection.
 - Business continuity.
 - Security.
 - Reputation.
4. Identify control requirements and gaps against current arrangements.
5. Prioritise actions based on risk, legal obligations, and operational criticality.

Example assessment record:

| Scenario | Potential Impact | Existing Controls | Gap / Required Action | Priority | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fire alarm activation during normal hours | Life safety risk, evacuation required, emergency service response | Fire alarm, wardens, exits, assembly points | Verify warden coverage for hybrid workdays | High | Facilities / HSE |
| Loss of mains power | Emergency lighting activation, access control impact, plant shutdown | UPS for selected systems, emergency lighting | Confirm generator runtime and fuel contract | Medium | Facilities |
| Water outage | Sanitation unavailable, welfare impact, possible closure | Utility contact process | Define closure decision criteria after [X] hours | Medium | Facilities / HSE |
| Gas leak in plant area | Explosion risk, evacuation, emergency service attendance | Gas isolation valves, contractor support | Update site plan showing isolation points | High | Facilities |
| Telecoms outage | Emergency escalation impaired | Mobile phones, security radios | Confirm radio coverage in basement and plant rooms | Medium | Security / Facilities |

Expected outputs:

- Facility emergency scenario register.
- Emergency risk and impact assessment.
- Gap analysis.
- Prioritised action plan.

### Phase 3 — Emergency Response Strategy and Control Design

The organisation will define emergency response strategies and operational controls for each scenario.

Key activities:

1. Define emergency response levels, such as:
 - Local incident.
 - Site emergency.
 - Major facility disruption.
 - Crisis escalation.
2. Define activation criteria for:
 - Evacuation.
 - Shelter-in-place.
 - Utility outage response.
 - Emergency services notification.
 - Business continuity escalation.
 - Building closure.
 - Re-entry after evacuation.
3. Define minimum emergency control requirements for each facility.
4. Establish criteria for continuing operations during utility outage, including:
 - Minimum lighting.
 - Safe temperatures.
 - Water and sanitation availability.
 - Fire protection availability.
 - Emergency communication capability.
 - Security and access control status.
5. Define impairment controls for unavailable emergency systems, including:
 - Fire watch.
 - Temporary detection or communications.
 - Restricted hot work.
 - Area closure.
 - Additional security patrols.
 - Notification to insurers, landlords, authorities, or emergency services where required.
6. Establish emergency service access arrangements, including:
 - Premises information packs.
 - Keys or access devices.
 - Site plans.
 - Utility isolation points.
 - Hazard information.
7. Define contractor emergency callout requirements and service levels.
8. Define records to be retained as documented information under operational control.

Expected outputs:

- Emergency response strategy.
- Emergency response matrix.
- Building closure and re-entry criteria.
- Utility outage decision criteria.
- Emergency system impairment process.
- Contractor emergency response requirements.

Example response matrix:

| Event | Immediate Objective | Activation Criteria | Escalation Trigger | Minimum Records |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fire alarm | Evacuate safely and confirm incident status | Alarm activation, smoke/fire observed, manual call point | Confirmed fire, injury, failed evacuation, fire system impairment | Alarm log, warden report, incident report |
| Full evacuation | Account for occupants and prevent unsafe re-entry | Fire alarm, emergency service instruction, credible threat | Missing person, accessibility assistance required, prolonged exclusion | Muster report, re-entry authorisation |
| Power outage | Maintain life safety and determine operational viability | Loss of mains power or critical electrical distribution | Emergency lighting compromise, generator failure, critical service outage | Outage log, utility notification, recovery record |
| Water outage | Preserve welfare and assess closure requirements | Loss of potable water or sanitation | Fire suppression impairment, no sanitation, contamination notice | Utility report, closure decision record |
| Gas leak | Protect life and isolate hazard | Gas odour, detector alarm, contractor or utility notification | Confirmed leak, explosion risk, emergency services required | Isolation record, emergency services report |
| HVAC failure | Maintain safe indoor environment | Loss of heating, cooling, ventilation, or smoke control | Temperature outside safe range, critical area impact, smoke control impairment | BMS log, contractor report |

### Phase 4 — Documentation Development

The organisation will develop or update documented emergency preparedness and response information.

Key activities:

1. Develop or update site-specific emergency response procedures.
2. Develop or update evacuation maps and signage.
3. Document emergency role descriptions.
4. Prepare emergency contact lists.
5. Prepare utility isolation diagrams and critical equipment lists.
6. Prepare emergency service information packs.
7. Update contractor callout lists and service-level expectations.
8. Define visitor, contractor, and tenant emergency instructions.
9. Establish controlled document ownership, review frequency, and version control.
10. Ensure documents are accessible during normal operations and emergency conditions.

Required documented information includes:

| Documented Information | Minimum Content | Owner | Review Frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Site Emergency Response Procedure | Activation, evacuation, escalation, emergency contacts, re-entry | Facilities / HSE | At least annually |
| Fire Evacuation Plan | Routes, assembly areas, wardens, accessibility arrangements | Facilities / Fire Safety Responsible Person | At least annually and after changes |
| Utility Outage Procedure | Utility-specific response steps, callouts, closure criteria | Facilities | At least annually |
| Emergency Contact List | Internal and external contacts, contractors, utilities, emergency services | Facilities / Security | Quarterly |
| Emergency Equipment Register | Fire systems, emergency lighting, generators, radios, first aid points, spill kits | Facilities | Semi-annually |
| Emergency Services Pack | Site plans, hazards, isolation points, access arrangements | Facilities / Security | At least annually |
| Emergency Drill Records | Drill scope, participants, results, corrective actions | HSE / Facilities | After each drill |
| Emergency Incident Records | Event timeline, actions taken, decisions, lessons learned | Facilities / HSE / Security | After each incident |

### Phase 5 — Resource Readiness and Implementation

The organisation will implement the planned emergency controls and verify resource readiness.

Key activities:

1. Confirm emergency equipment is present, suitable, inspected, and maintained.
2. Confirm emergency response roles are appointed and covered across operating hours.
3. Confirm evacuation routes, exits, assembly areas, and emergency signage are available and unobstructed.
4. Confirm emergency communications are operational and have fallback arrangements.
5. Confirm contractor emergency callout routes are tested.
6. Confirm utility shut-off and isolation points are accessible and labelled.
7. Confirm emergency services access arrangements.
8. Establish arrangements for persons requiring evacuation assistance.
9. Communicate emergency instructions to workers, contractors, visitors, and tenants.
10. Implement records demonstrating operational control.

Readiness verification checklist:

| Readiness Area | Verification Activity | Evidence Required | Frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fire alarm | Test activation and monitoring path | Test certificate or log | As required by local regulation / maintenance plan |
| Emergency lighting | Functional and duration test | Inspection report | As required by local regulation / maintenance plan |
| Escape routes | Walkthrough inspection | Inspection checklist | Monthly or risk-based |
| Assembly points | Confirm signage, capacity, access | Site inspection record | Quarterly |
| Emergency communications | Test PA, radios, mass notification, fallback phones | Communications test log | Quarterly |
| Utility isolation | Verify access, labels, responsible persons | Plant room inspection record | Semi-annually |
| Contractor callout | Test contact and response process | Callout verification log | Semi-annually |
| Emergency contacts | Validate phone numbers and escalation order | Updated contact list | Quarterly |
| Accessibility support | Validate assistance arrangements | PEEP or assistance register confirmation, where applicable | Quarterly or after personnel changes |
| Emergency services pack | Verify accuracy and availability | Version-controlled pack | Annually |

### Phase 6 — Training, Awareness, and Communication

The organisation will ensure that relevant personnel understand emergency response expectations and can perform assigned roles.

Key activities:

1. Deliver general emergency awareness to occupants.
2. Deliver role-specific training to:
 - Fire wardens or evacuation marshals.
 - Facilities response staff.
 - Security staff.
 - Reception and visitor management staff.
 - Incident coordinators.
 - Plant room authorised personnel.
 - Contractor supervisors.
3. Communicate emergency instructions during onboarding and induction.
4. Provide site-specific emergency instructions to visitors and contractors.
5. Ensure changes to emergency arrangements are communicated promptly.
6. Maintain training records and competency evidence.

Training matrix:

| Audience | Required Training / Briefing | Frequency | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| All workers | Fire alarm response, evacuation routes, assembly points, reporting hazards | On induction and annually | LMS record or attendance log |
| Fire wardens / evacuation marshals | Sweep procedures, reporting, accessibility support, assembly point coordination | Initial and refresher at least annually | Training certificate |
| Facilities team | Utility isolation, emergency systems, impairment controls, contractor coordination | Initial and annually | Competency record |
| Security / reception | Alarm response, emergency services access, visitor evacuation, re-entry control | Initial and annually | Training log |
| Contractors | Site emergency rules, alarms, evacuation, hot work and impairment notification | Before site work | Contractor induction record |
| Tenants / shared occupants | Site emergency arrangements and coordination requirements | At lease onboarding and annually | Communication record |
| Incident coordinators | Escalation, decision logging, crisis/business continuity interface | Initial and annually | Exercise participation record |

### Phase 7 — Exercises, Drills, and Testing

The organisation will validate emergency preparedness arrangements through planned drills, scenario exercises, and system tests.

Key activities:

1. Establish an annual emergency exercise programme.
2. Conduct evacuation drills at planned intervals and after significant changes.
3. Conduct tabletop exercises for utility outage scenarios.
4. Test emergency communication methods and escalation paths.
5. Include contractors, tenants, security, reception, and facilities teams where relevant.
6. Evaluate exercises against defined success criteria.
7. Record lessons learned, corrective actions, owners, and due dates.
8. Track corrective action closure to completion.
9. Report significant findings to management.

Exercise programme example:

| Exercise Type | Scenario | Participants | Minimum Frequency | Evaluation Focus |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evacuation drill | Fire alarm requiring full evacuation | All occupants present, wardens, security, facilities | At least annually or as required by law | Evacuation time, route effectiveness, assembly management |
| Tabletop exercise | Extended power outage with generator failure | Facilities, security, HSE, business continuity, IT, communications | Annually | Decision-making, escalation, continuity interface |
| Tabletop exercise | Water outage and sanitation loss | Facilities, HSE, HR, communications, site leadership | Every 2 years or risk-based | Closure criteria, welfare decisions, communications |
| Callout test | Emergency contractor response | Facilities, key contractors | Semi-annually | Contact accuracy, response time, escalation |
| Communications test | PA/radio/mobile fallback | Security, facilities, wardens | Quarterly | Coverage, clarity, redundancy |
| Fire system impairment simulation | Planned fire alarm outage | Facilities, fire safety, security, contractor | Annually | Temporary controls, notification, fire watch |

### Phase 8 — Monitoring, Review, and Continual Improvement

The organisation will monitor performance and maintain emergency preparedness arrangements as a controlled facility management process.

Key activities:

1. Monitor emergency readiness indicators.
2. Review incident and exercise outcomes.
3. Track corrective and preventive actions.
4. Review emergency arrangements after changes, incidents, audit findings, or legal changes.
5. Report performance to management review.
6. Retain documented information as evidence of planning and operational control.
7. Integrate improvements into maintenance, procurement, contractor management, training, and change control processes.

Expected outputs:

- Emergency preparedness performance dashboard.
- Corrective action register.
- Management review inputs.
- Updated procedures, contact lists, diagrams, and training records.
- Evidence of operational control and continual improvement.
