### Column Guidance

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Inventory Record ID | Enter a unique identifier for this inventory line, using a consistent format such as SWIFT-INV-0001; do not reuse IDs after retirement. |
| SWIFT Component Category | Select the component category: Messaging Interface, Communication Interface, GUI Workstation, HSM, Jump Host, Database, Middleware, Directory/Authentication, Network Device, Security Device, Management/Monitoring, Other. |
| Asset Role / Function | Describe the specific role the asset performs in the local SWIFT infrastructure, for example production messaging interface server, SWIFTNet communication gateway, operator GUI workstation, HSM used for signing, or administrative jump host. |
| In CSCF Scope | Enter Yes or No to indicate whether the asset is part of the SWIFT local infrastructure subject to SWIFT CSCF control 1.1; if No, explain why in Remarks / Exceptions. |
| SWIFT Service / BIC Supported | Enter the SWIFT service, BIC, logical terminal, or customer environment supported by the asset; use N/A if not directly tied to one service or BIC. |
| Asset Name / Hostname | Enter the approved hostname, device name, or console name exactly as recorded in CMDB, DNS, or the management platform. |
| Product / Technology Name | Enter the product or technology name, for example Alliance Access, Alliance Gateway, Alliance Web Platform, Alliance Connect, HSM management software, Windows Server, Linux, or PAM jump server. |
| Vendor / Manufacturer | Enter the vendor or manufacturer name, for example SWIFT, Thales, Entrust, Microsoft, Red Hat, Cisco, Fortinet, VMware, or other relevant supplier. |
| Model / Platform | Enter the hardware model, virtual platform, appliance type, or cloud/on-prem platform, for example ProLiant DL360, VMware VM, Luna Network HSM, or physical workstation. |
| Serial Number / Asset Tag | Enter the physical serial number and/or internal asset tag; use VM UUID or CMDB asset ID for virtual assets where no serial number exists. |
| Environment | Select one value: Production, Disaster Recovery, Test, Development, UAT, Training, Management, Other. |
| Physical / Hosting Location | Enter the site, data centre, room, rack, secure area, or cloud/private hosting location where the asset resides; include country and city where relevant. |
| Hosting Type | Select one value: Physical Server, Virtual Machine, Appliance, Workstation, Network Device, Security Device, Cloud Instance, SaaS/Hosted, Other. |
| Network Zone | Enter the approved network/security zone name in which the asset resides, for example SWIFT Secure Zone, SWIFT Operator Zone, Management Zone, HSM Zone, DMZ, or Corporate LAN. |
| IP Address(es) | Enter all assigned IPv4/IPv6 addresses and subnet/VLAN where relevant, separated by semicolons; format example: 10.10.20.15/24 VLAN120. |
| MAC Address(es) | Enter network interface MAC address(es) where available, separated by semicolons; use N/A for assets where MAC address is not applicable or not visible. |
| Operating System / Firmware | Enter the operating system or firmware family/name running on the asset, for example Windows Server, RHEL, appliance firmware, HSM firmware, or network OS. |
| OS / Firmware Version | Enter the exact OS or firmware version/build currently installed, for example Windows Server 2022 build 20348, RHEL 9.3, or firmware 7.8.4. |
| Application / Component Version | Enter the installed version of the SWIFT or supporting application/component; include release and patch level where available, or N/A if not applicable. |
| Interface / Connectivity Details | Record the key interfaces, protocols, ports, and connection paths used by the asset for SWIFT operations or administration, for example RDP via jump host only, MQ to messaging interface, HSM TCP port, or SWIFTNet connectivity. |
| Connected SWIFT Components | List the local SWIFT components this asset connects to or depends on, using hostnames or inventory record IDs separated by semicolons. |
| External Connectivity | Enter any connectivity outside the local SWIFT secure environment, for example SWIFTNet, service bureau, vendor support, corporate AD, monitoring, backup network; enter None if no external connectivity exists. |
| Privileged Access Method | Describe how administrative access is performed, for example PAM via jump host, local console only, SSH from management subnet, RDP from jump host, HSM security officer card; include MFA/PAM requirement where applicable. |
| Primary Business Owner | Enter the accountable business owner role or named owner responsible for the SWIFT service supported by this asset. |
| Technical Custodian | Enter the IT or operations team responsible for technical administration and configuration of the asset. |
| Support Team / Supplier | Enter the internal support team, managed service provider, or vendor responsible for support; include support contract reference if maintained. |
| Criticality | Select one value based on business impact: Critical, High, Medium, Low. |
| Data Classification | Select the highest classification of data processed, stored, or accessible by the asset, using the organisation’s classification scheme, for example Restricted, Confidential, Internal, Public, or N/A. |
| HA / DR Role | Enter the high availability or disaster recovery role: Primary, Secondary, DR, Standalone, Cluster Node, Backup, N/A. |
| Backup / Recovery Requirement | State whether backup or recovery is required and the expected recovery objective if known, for example Daily backup, RPO 24h/RTO 4h, configuration backup only, HSM key backup per ceremony, or N/A. |
| Configuration Baseline Reference | Enter the approved secure configuration or build standard reference applicable to the asset, for example SWIFT-SRV-BLD-001, HSM-HARDENING-002, or CIS Windows Server baseline; use N/A only with justification in Remarks / Exceptions. |
| Patch / Maintenance Window | Enter the approved patching or maintenance window/frequency, for example Monthly 3rd Sunday 02:00-04:00 UTC, Quarterly, Vendor-advised, or Change-controlled only. |
| Lifecycle Status | Select one value: Planned, In Build, Active, Suspended, Retiring, Retired. |
| Support Status | Select one value: Supported, Extended Support, End of Support, End of Life, Unknown; End of Support/End of Life must be explained in Remarks / Exceptions. |
| Last Inventory Validation Date | Enter the date this record was last verified against source evidence, in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| Validation Method | Enter how the inventory item was validated, for example CMDB reconciliation, network discovery, console export, HSM inventory export, physical inspection, configuration review, or owner attestation. |
| Evidence Reference | Enter the evidence location or reference supporting the record, such as CMDB CI link, discovery report ID, configuration export path, screenshot reference, rack audit record, or change ticket. |
| Remarks / Exceptions | Enter any relevant limitations, exclusions, discrepancies, temporary configurations, compensating notes, or rationale for N/A values; leave blank only if there are no remarks. |

### Maintenance

Owned by the SWIFT Infrastructure Owner or SWIFT Platform Manager, with review by Information Security/GRC. Update at least quarterly and immediately after any build, decommission, network change, HSM/key infrastructure change, or SWIFT component upgrade, drawing from the CMDB, network discovery, SWIFT platform configuration exports, HSM inventory exports, PAM records, and approved change tickets.

Update at least quarterly and immediately after any build, decommission, network change, HSM/key infrastructure change, or SWIFT component upgrade, drawing from the CMDB, network discovery, SWIFT platform configuration exports, HSM inventory exports, PAM records, and approved change tickets.

SWF-004.title: Swift Data Flow Diagram
SWF-004.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DOC-SWIFT-DFD-001] | 1.0 | [SWIFT Security Officer / CISO] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework | Internal - Restricted |

## Purpose

This template is used to document the organisation’s SWIFT-related data flows, including connectivity to and from SWIFT, supporting infrastructure, security controls, operator access paths, and integration with back-office systems.

The completed Swift Data Flow Diagram must provide a clear, accurate, and reviewable representation of how SWIFT messages, authentication data, operational traffic, administrative access, and related logs move through the organisation’s environment. It supports secure design, risk assessment, incident response, change management, and independent assurance activities.

This template applies to all environments, systems, applications, network zones, service providers, and operational processes that connect to, process, transmit, store, monitor, or administer SWIFT-related services, including:

- SWIFT interface products and messaging components.
- SWIFT connectivity components and network links.
- Back-office applications that generate, approve, consume, reconcile, or archive SWIFT messages.
- Middleware, file transfer, APIs, queues, databases, and integration platforms.
- Security services such as identity providers, privileged access tools, firewalls, monitoring, endpoint protection, and logging platforms.
- Administrative access paths used by internal teams or third parties.
- Segregated environments such as production, disaster recovery, testing, and support environments where SWIFT-related data or connectivity exists.

## Instructions

Complete one Swift Data Flow Diagram record for each distinct SWIFT environment or architecture variant. At minimum, separate records should be maintained for production and disaster recovery environments. Additional records should be created where the architecture, data flow, network segmentation, service provider connectivity, or back-office integration differs materially.

The completed form must be supported by a visual diagram. The diagram may be embedded, attached, or referenced by document link, provided it is version-controlled and reviewed with this form. The diagram must be sufficiently detailed for a qualified reviewer to understand the data flows without relying on informal verbal explanation.

When completing this template:

1. Use current production information, not design assumptions, unless the form is being completed for a planned change.
2. Identify all systems and network zones involved in SWIFT connectivity, message processing, administration, monitoring, backup, and recovery.
3. Clearly distinguish message flows from administrative access, logging, monitoring, backup, file transfer, and support flows.
4. Show the direction of each flow and whether the flow is inbound, outbound, or bidirectional.
5. Identify trust boundaries, segmentation points, security zones, and any connection to external parties or service providers.
6. Include back-office systems and integration components that create, enrich, validate, approve, reconcile, archive, or consume SWIFT messages.
7. Record protocols, ports, authentication methods, encryption mechanisms, and the business purpose for each flow where known.
8. Identify where SWIFT-related data is stored, queued, transformed, logged, backed up, or exported.
9. Include any third-party operational access paths, remote support methods, managed services, or outsourced infrastructure dependencies.
10. Validate the completed form against firewall rules, system inventories, configuration baselines, connectivity records, and change records.
11. Ensure sensitive information is handled according to the classification stated in the metadata block. Do not distribute externally unless formally approved.
12. Submit the completed form for review and approval before implementation of any new or changed SWIFT-related connectivity.

The Swift Data Flow Diagram must be reviewed:

- At least annually.
- Before major SWIFT architecture or connectivity changes.
- After any significant security incident affecting SWIFT-related infrastructure.
- After onboarding, changing, or terminating a service provider involved in SWIFT connectivity or support.
- After material changes to back-office systems, integration platforms, firewalls, remote access, logging, or identity services supporting SWIFT operations.

## Form Fields

| Field | Type | Required | Guidance |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Form Reference | Text | Yes | Unique reference for this completed data flow record, such as `[SWIFT-DFD-PROD-YYYY-001]`. |
| Environment Name | Text | Yes | Identify the environment covered, such as production, disaster recovery, pre-production, testing, or support. |
| Environment Criticality | Dropdown | Yes | Select: Critical, High, Medium, Low. Production SWIFT messaging environments should normally be rated Critical or High. |
| Business Owner | Text | Yes | Name or role accountable for the business process supported by the SWIFT environment. |
| Technical Owner | Text | Yes | Name or role accountable for technical accuracy of the architecture and data flows. |
| SWIFT Security Officer | Text | Yes | Name or role responsible for SWIFT security oversight and review. |
| Diagram Title | Text | Yes | Title of the associated visual data flow diagram. |
| Diagram Version | Text | Yes | Version of the visual diagram reviewed with this form. |
| Diagram Location / Link | URL / Reference | Yes | Provide repository path, document management link, or attachment reference. |
| Date Diagram Last Validated | Date | Yes | Date the diagram was last compared against actual implementation evidence. |
| Validation Method | Multi-line Text | Yes | Describe how the diagram was validated, such as firewall rule review, CMDB comparison, network scan, configuration review, service owner attestation, or change record review. |
| Scope Summary | Multi-line Text | Yes | Briefly describe the SWIFT services, systems, business processes, and connectivity covered by this data flow diagram. |
| Out of Scope Items | Multi-line Text | No | List related systems or environments intentionally excluded and explain why. Avoid leaving ambiguity around back-office or integration systems. |
| SWIFT Connectivity Type | Dropdown / Multi-select | Yes | Select applicable connectivity model and related services used by the organisation. Include direct, service bureau, hosted, managed, or network service provider arrangements where relevant. |
| SWIFT Interface Components | Table | Yes | List all SWIFT interface, gateway, connector, messaging, screening, and operational components in scope. Include hostname, function, environment, owner, and location. |

| Security Zones | Table | Yes | Identify all relevant network or security zones, including SWIFT secure zone, user zone, server zone, management zone, logging zone, backup zone, and external connections. |
| Trust Boundaries | Multi-line Text | Yes | Describe where data crosses from one trust level to another, including internal-to-external, user-to-server, production-to-support, and on-premises-to-cloud boundaries. |
| External Parties | Table | Conditional | Required where any service bureau, cloud provider, network provider, managed service provider, correspondent, vendor, or support party is involved. Include party name, service provided, connection type, and data exchanged. |

| Administrative Access Flows | Table | Yes | Record administrator, operator, vendor, and support access routes. Include jump hosts, privileged access tooling, authentication, and session monitoring. |
| Authentication and Authorisation Flows | Table | Yes | Document identity provider, directory, multi-factor authentication, certificate, key management, and user provisioning flows relevant to SWIFT access. |
| Logging and Monitoring Flows | Table | Yes | Identify security logs, application logs, system logs, transaction logs, alerting feeds, monitoring tools, and destinations such as SIEM or SOC platforms. |
| Backup and Recovery Flows | Table | Yes | Identify backup traffic, replication, snapshot handling, recovery repositories, and offsite or cloud backup destinations for SWIFT-related systems and data. |
| File Storage and Data Repositories | Table | Yes | List databases, file shares, queues, archives, logs, message stores, and backup repositories containing SWIFT-related data. |
| Data Classification | Dropdown | Yes | Select the highest classification of data included in the flows. SWIFT message data, authentication data, and operational security data should be classified appropriately. |
| Sensitive Data Elements | Multi-select / Text | Yes | Identify data types such as payment instructions, account identifiers, customer data, message payloads, operator IDs, certificates, keys, credentials, logs, and audit trails. |
| Encryption in Transit | Table | Yes | Describe encryption mechanisms for each applicable flow. Include where encryption begins and ends. |
| Encryption at Rest | Table | Yes | Describe encryption for message stores, databases, logs, archives, configuration files, backups, and exported data. |
| Network Security Controls | Multi-line Text | Yes | Summarise segmentation, firewall filtering, routing restrictions, intrusion detection, network monitoring, allowlisting, and secure remote access controls. |
| Endpoint and Server Security Controls | Multi-line Text | Yes | Summarise hardening, malware protection, application control, patching, configuration management, vulnerability management, and administrative restrictions. |
| Privileged Access Controls | Multi-line Text | Yes | Describe privileged account handling, approval, authentication, session recording, command restrictions, break-glass access, and periodic review. |
| Change Management Linkage | Text / URL | Conditional | Required for new or changed architecture. Provide change request, project, release, or architecture decision reference. |
| Known Exceptions or Compensating Controls | Table | Conditional | Required where any expected security practice is not fully implemented. Include risk owner, justification, compensating control, target remediation date, and approval status. |
| Open Risks | Table | Conditional | Required where risks have been identified from the data flow review. Include risk description, likelihood, impact, owner, treatment plan, and due date. |
| Incident Response Dependencies | Multi-line Text | Yes | Identify systems, contacts, logs, access methods, and third parties required to investigate or contain a SWIFT-related incident. |
| Operational Dependencies | Multi-line Text | Yes | Identify key services needed for SWIFT operations, such as DNS, NTP, directory services, certificate services, HSMs, monitoring, backup, internet access, or leased lines. |
| Resilience and Failover Flows | Multi-line Text | Yes | Describe how traffic and data move during failover, disaster recovery, degraded operations, or manual contingency processing. |
| Data Retention Points | Table | Yes | Identify where SWIFT-related data is retained, retention duration, owner, protection method, and disposal process. |
| Evidence Reviewed | Table | Yes | List evidence used to validate the data flow diagram, such as firewall exports, network diagrams, CMDB records, system configurations, service provider documents, change tickets, and access reviews. |
| Reviewer Comments | Multi-line Text | No | Record technical, security, audit, or operational review comments. |
| Required Remediation Actions | Table | Conditional | Required where the review identifies incomplete, inaccurate, obsolete, or insecure flows. Include owner and due date. |
| Completion Status | Dropdown | Yes | Select: Draft, Under Review, Approved, Approved with Actions, Rejected, Retired. |
| Prepared By | Text | Yes | Name and role of person completing the form. |
| Date Prepared | Date | Yes | Date the form was completed. |
| Next Review Date | Date | Yes | Date the completed form must next be reviewed. |

## Approval / Routing

The completed Swift Data Flow Diagram form must be routed to the following stakeholders for review and approval. Approval confirms that the data flow representation is accurate, complete for its stated scope, and suitable for use in SWIFT security governance, risk management, change management, and assurance activities.

| Role | Review Responsibility | Approval Required | Name / Role | Date | Decision | Comments |

A completed form may be approved with actions only where:

- The documented data flows are materially accurate.
- Open actions do not conceal or create unacceptable risk.
- Each action has a named owner, due date, and priority.
- Any residual risk is reviewed by the appropriate risk owner.
- The SWIFT Security Officer agrees that the diagram is fit for operational and assurance use.

A form must be rejected and returned for correction where:

- SWIFT connectivity paths are missing or unclear.
- Back-office systems or integration points are omitted.
- Administrative or third-party access paths are not documented.
- Security zones, trust boundaries, or external connections cannot be understood.
- The diagram conflicts with available implementation evidence.
- Encryption, authentication, logging, or monitoring information is materially incomplete.
- Known exceptions or risks are not recorded.

## Records & Retention

The record set must include, where applicable:

- Supporting validation evidence.

SWF-005.title: CSCF Gap Assessment
SWF-005.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DOC-ID] | 1.0 | [SWIFT Security Owner / CISO] | [Effective Date] | SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework - Current Version | Confidential - Internal Use Only |

## Purpose

This report presents the results of the organisation’s gap assessment against the current SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework. It evaluates the design and operating status of security controls that protect the organisation’s SWIFT environment, including the secure zone, operator access, authentication, transaction integrity, logging, monitoring, incident response, and supporting governance processes.

The objectives of this report are to:

- Determine the organisation’s current level of alignment with the SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework.
- Identify gaps between current practices and expected SWIFT security outcomes.
- Assess the business and security risk associated with each gap.
- Provide practical remediation actions, owners, target dates, and evidence expectations.
- Support management oversight, internal assurance, external assessment preparation, and annual SWIFT attestation activities.

This report is intended to be used by technology, cyber security, risk, compliance, audit, operations, and business stakeholders responsible for maintaining a secure SWIFT operating environment.

## Reporting Period & Scope

### Reporting Period

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Assessment period | [Start Date] to [End Date] |
| Evidence review period | [Evidence Start Date] to [Evidence End Date] |
| Management review date | [Management Review Date] |
| Report issue date | [Report Issue Date] |
| Next planned reassessment | [Next Assessment Date] |

### Scope

The assessment covered the organisation’s SWIFT environment and supporting processes, including:

- SWIFT-connected infrastructure and applications.
- Secure zone network architecture and segmentation.
- SWIFT interface systems, messaging interfaces, middleware, gateways, and supporting servers.
- Connectivity components used to exchange messages with SWIFT.
- Privileged and operator access to SWIFT-related systems.
- Authentication mechanisms used for administrative, application, and operator activities.
- End-user workstations used for SWIFT administration or transaction processing.
- Transaction creation, validation, approval, release, and reconciliation processes.
- Logging, monitoring, alerting, and security event review.
- Vulnerability management, patching, anti-malware, and system hardening.
- Backup, recovery, resilience, and business continuity arrangements.
- Incident response and escalation processes for SWIFT-related events.
- Security governance, control ownership, documentation, and evidence management.
- Third-party service providers with access to, or operational responsibility for, SWIFT-related systems or processes.

### In-Scope Environments

| Environment / Component | In Scope | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| SWIFT production interface | Yes | Includes application, server, database, and connectivity components |
| SWIFT test environment | Yes | Reviewed where connected to production-like infrastructure or used for operational testing |
| Secure zone network | Yes | Includes firewalls, routing, segmentation, and access paths |
| Operator workstations | Yes | Includes systems used to create, approve, release, or administer SWIFT transactions |
| Administrative workstations | Yes | Includes privileged access workstations and jump hosts |
| Directory and identity services | Yes | Reviewed for accounts, groups, authentication, and access governance |
| Security monitoring platform | Yes | Includes log collection, alerting, and escalation processes |
| Backup and recovery platforms | Yes | Includes backup scope, protection, restoration testing, and retention |
| Third-party managed services | Yes | Reviewed for contracted responsibilities and evidence availability |
| Corporate systems not connected to SWIFT | Limited | Reviewed only where they provide identity, monitoring, patching, endpoint protection, or administrative access to SWIFT systems |

### Out-of-Scope Items

The following items were not assessed in detail, except where they directly support the SWIFT environment:

- General corporate IT systems with no connectivity, administration path, or dependency relationship with the SWIFT environment.
- Business applications that do not initiate, approve, process, reconcile, or report on SWIFT messages.
- Non-SWIFT payment rails and channels.
- Physical security of offices not hosting SWIFT infrastructure or operator activities.
- Broader enterprise controls not relied upon by the SWIFT environment.

### Assessment Boundaries and Assumptions

- The assessment was performed using evidence provided by control owners and system administrators.
- Control operating effectiveness was assessed only for the evidence period stated above.
- Where sampling was used, conclusions are based on the selected samples and available evidence.
- Third-party controls were assessed based on contracts, service descriptions, assurance reports, control attestations, and evidence made available to the organisation.
- Any systems or processes not disclosed during the assessment may affect the completeness of conclusions.

## Executive Summary

### Overall Assessment Result

The organisation has established several foundational controls to protect its SWIFT environment, including defined ownership, network segmentation, access management processes, logging, endpoint protection, and operational procedures. However, the assessment identified gaps that require remediation to fully meet the expected level of security maturity for a SWIFT-connected organisation.

The most significant areas requiring management attention are:

1. **Secure zone segmentation and access path validation**
 - Network segmentation exists, but firewall rule reviews and traffic validation are not consistently evidenced.
 - Some administrative access paths are not fully documented or risk-assessed.

2. **Privileged access governance**
 - Privileged accounts are assigned to named individuals in most cases, but periodic access recertification and emergency access review are not consistently performed.
 - Several service accounts lack documented ownership, usage justification, and password rotation evidence.

3. **Multi-factor authentication coverage**
 - Strong authentication is deployed for key operator and remote access scenarios.
 - Coverage is incomplete for some administrative paths and supporting infrastructure components.

4. **System hardening, patching, and vulnerability remediation**
 - Baseline hardening standards exist but are not consistently mapped to all SWIFT-related systems.
 - Patch compliance reporting is available, but remediation timeframes and exception approvals are inconsistently documented.

5. **Transaction integrity and maker-checker controls**
 - Dual control is implemented for critical payment activities.
 - Evidence of periodic configuration review and sample-based transaction control testing needs improvement.

6. **Logging, monitoring, and incident response**
 - Logs are collected from key systems, but monitoring use cases specific to SWIFT fraud, misuse, and compromise scenarios require enhancement.
 - Incident response procedures exist but do not sufficiently describe SWIFT-specific containment, notification, and recovery actions.

7. **Evidence management and annual attestation readiness**
 - Evidence is maintained across multiple repositories, with inconsistent naming, ownership, retention, and review status.
 - Control owners require a more structured evidence calendar to support annual attestation and independent assessment.

### Overall Gap Summary

| Rating | Count | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| Meets expectation | [Number] | Control is designed appropriately and evidence demonstrates consistent operation |
| Partially meets expectation | [Number] | Control exists but has design, coverage, consistency, or evidence weaknesses |

### Management Conclusion

The organisation is progressing toward a defensible SWIFT security control posture, but remediation is required before management can confidently assert full alignment with the current framework. Priority should be given to closing gaps that affect secure architecture, privileged access, authentication, transaction integrity, monitoring, vulnerability management, and incident response.

A formal remediation plan should be approved by management, tracked through governance forums, and supported by evidence that demonstrates both control design and operating effectiveness.

## Methodology

### Assessment Approach

The gap assessment was conducted using a structured control-by-control review of the current SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework. Each expected security outcome was assessed against the organisation’s current implementation, supporting processes, and available evidence.

The assessment included the following activities:

- Review of SWIFT environment architecture, data flows, network diagrams, and system inventories.
- Interviews and workshops with control owners, system administrators, security operations, business operations, risk, compliance, and third-party service managers.
- Review of policies, standards, procedures, runbooks, access records, configuration extracts, monitoring outputs, vulnerability reports, and change records.
- Sampling of user access, privileged access, transaction approvals, system changes, patch records, incident tickets, and monitoring alerts.
- Evaluation of evidence against expected control intent, coverage, consistency, and auditability.
- Risk rating of identified gaps based on likelihood, impact, exploitability, and compensating controls.
- Development of remediation recommendations, target actions, and expected evidence.

### Rating Definitions

| Rating | Definition |
|---|---|
| Meets expectation | The control is appropriately designed, implemented across the relevant scope, operating consistently, and supported by sufficient evidence. |
| Partially meets expectation | The control is implemented but has weaknesses in design, coverage, consistency, timeliness, ownership, or evidence quality. |
| Does not meet expectation | The control is not implemented, is materially ineffective, or cannot be evidenced. |
| Not applicable | The control does not apply due to the organisation’s architecture, operating model, or documented business context. |
| Not assessed | The control could not be assessed due to missing evidence, unavailable stakeholders, incomplete scope definition, or unresolved dependency. |

### Risk Rating Definitions

| Risk Level | Definition | Management Response |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Weakness could enable material compromise of the SWIFT environment, unauthorised transactions, major operational disruption, or severe regulatory/reputational impact. | Immediate executive attention and urgent remediation required. |
| High | Weakness materially increases the likelihood or impact of compromise, fraud, operational disruption, or failed attestation. | Remediation should be prioritized and tracked through management governance. |
| Medium | Weakness creates moderate risk or reduces confidence in control effectiveness, but compensating controls may exist. | Remediation should be planned and completed within agreed timelines. |
| Low | Weakness is limited in impact, usually relating to documentation, evidence, consistency, or process maturity. | Remediation should be addressed through normal control improvement activity. |

### Limitations

The assessment was subject to the following limitations:

- Some evidence was provided as screenshots or extracts rather than direct system access.
- Certain third-party control evidence was limited to summary assurance documents.
- Historical evidence for earlier periods was incomplete for selected control activities.
- Some technical configurations were reviewed through administrator walkthroughs rather than independent export.
- Evidence of operating effectiveness was limited where controls were recently implemented or redesigned.
- Any remediation completed after the assessment end date is not reflected unless specifically noted.

| 11 | Logging and monitoring | Partially meets expectation | High | SWIFT-specific monitoring use cases are limited | Develop monitoring use cases and validate log coverage | [Owner] | [Date] |
| 12 | Incident response | Partially meets expectation | High | SWIFT-specific playbooks and exercises are limited | Create playbooks and conduct exercises | [Owner] | [Date] |
| 13 | Backup and recovery | Partially meets expectation | Medium | Recovery testing and dependency mapping are incomplete | Map recovery scope and perform restoration tests | [Owner] | [Date] |
| 14 | Physical security | Meets expectation | Low | Evidence retention could be improved | Store physical access review evidence centrally | [Owner] | [Date] |
| 15 | Third-party management | Partially meets expectation | Medium | Provider responsibility and evidence mapping are incomplete | Formalise third-party responsibility matrix | [Owner] | [Date] |
| 16 | Evidence management | Partially meets expectation | Medium | Evidence collection is inconsistent | Implement evidence calendar and repository standards | [Owner] | [Date] |

## Analysis

### Overall Control Maturity

The assessment indicates that the organisation has implemented many core security capabilities required to protect its SWIFT environment. The control environment is strongest where enterprise security services are mature and consistently applied, such as corporate identity processes, endpoint protection, change management, and incident ticketing.

However, the principal weakness is that several controls are operated as general enterprise controls rather than being tailored, scoped, evidenced, and monitored specifically for the SWIFT environment. For a SWIFT security programme, control effectiveness depends not only on having enterprise controls in place, but also on demonstrating that those controls apply completely and consistently to the secure zone, SWIFT systems, operator workstations, administrative access paths, transaction workflows, and supporting services.

### Key Themes

#### 1. Scope Definition Requires Strengthening

Several gaps are caused by incomplete or fragmented understanding of the full SWIFT control scope. The organisation can identify core SWIFT systems, but supporting components are not always captured in a single authoritative inventory. This affects access reviews, vulnerability scans, patch reports, monitoring coverage, backup scope, third-party responsibilities, and evidence collection.

A reliable SWIFT asset and dependency register is a foundational remediation activity. Without it, control owners may unintentionally omit systems, accounts, logs, backups, or providers from their control activities.

#### 2. Control Evidence Is Not Yet Audit-Ready Throughout the Year

Evidence exists for many controls, but it is collected inconsistently and often depends on manual requests during assessment or attestation periods. Some evidence is retained in operational tools without clear extraction, approval, or review records. Screenshots are used where system-generated reports would provide stronger evidence.

Evidence should demonstrate:

- What was reviewed.
- Who reviewed it.
- When it was reviewed.
- What criteria were applied.
- What exceptions were found.
- How exceptions were resolved.
- Whether unresolved items were escalated or risk-accepted.

#### 3. Privileged Access and Authentication Are Priority Risk Areas

Privileged access to SWIFT systems and supporting infrastructure represents one of the highest-risk areas. While named accounts and approval workflows exist, the organisation requires stronger evidence of periodic recertification, service account governance, emergency access review, and strong authentication coverage.

In particular, the organisation should focus on:

- Administrative access into the secure zone.
- Local administrator access.
- Database administrator access.
- Network device administration.
- Service and application accounts.
- Third-party support accounts.
- Emergency or break-glass accounts.
- Privileged access from non-dedicated workstations.

#### 4. Technical Segmentation Should Be Revalidated

The secure zone architecture is a positive control foundation, but firewall rule review and traffic validation are not sufficiently evidenced. Over time, firewall rules can expand due to operational needs, troubleshooting, migrations, or emergency changes. Without periodic rationalisation, the secure zone may become more exposed than intended.

Network segmentation validation should confirm that:

- Only approved systems can communicate with SWIFT systems.
- Only approved ports and protocols are allowed.
- Administrative access is restricted to approved paths.
- Internet access is blocked or tightly controlled where not required.
- Third-party access is controlled, logged, and time-bound.
- Monitoring covers allowed and attempted unauthorised flows.

#### 5. Monitoring Should Become More SWIFT-Specific

Enterprise monitoring is in place, but the use case library should better reflect SWIFT-specific attack and fraud scenarios. Generic infrastructure alerts are necessary but not sufficient. The organisation should develop scenarios that correlate authentication events, privileged actions, transaction workflow changes, firewall activity, endpoint alerts, and unusual operator behaviour.

Examples of monitoring scenarios to consider include:

- Operator login from unusual location or device.
- Privileged access outside approved maintenance window.
- Multiple failed authentication attempts against SWIFT systems.
- New or modified privileged group membership.
- Firewall rule change affecting the SWIFT secure zone.
- Unexpected outbound traffic from SWIFT systems.
- Malware alert on operator or administrative workstation.
- Change to payment approval workflow or transaction release configuration.
- Transaction volume or value deviation from expected pattern.
- Manual override or exception activity outside normal process.

#### 6. Incident Response Needs SWIFT-Specific Operational Detail

The enterprise incident response plan provides a good foundation, but SWIFT-related incidents require specific playbooks due to the potential for rapid financial impact and complex stakeholder coordination. The organisation should define how it will contain suspected compromise without unnecessarily disrupting critical payments activity, how it will preserve evidence, and how business operations will validate transaction integrity.

Exercises should include technology, payment operations, treasury, legal, compliance, communications, third-party providers, and senior management.

#### 7. Third-Party Accountability Requires Formal Mapping

Where third parties manage infrastructure, connectivity, applications, security operations, or support activities, the organisation remains responsible for understanding and evidencing the control environment. Responsibility mapping should distinguish between controls operated by the organisation, controls operated by providers, and shared controls.

For each provider, the organisation should confirm:

- Which SWIFT-related services are provided.
- Which controls the provider operates.
- What evidence will be provided and how often.
- How security incidents will be notified and escalated.
- How provider access is approved, reviewed, and revoked.
- How vulnerabilities and patches are managed.
- How changes affecting SWIFT are approved.
- How audit and assurance requests will be supported.

### Root Cause Analysis

| Root Cause | Impact | Related Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Fragmented asset and dependency inventory | Incomplete control coverage and evidence uncertainty | Inventory, segmentation, vulnerability management, monitoring, backup |
| Enterprise controls not tailored to SWIFT scope | Controls exist but cannot be fully demonstrated for SWIFT | Access management, endpoint protection, change management, monitoring |
| Manual and annualised evidence collection | Inconsistent audit readiness and late gap identification | Governance, evidence management, attestation readiness |
| Incomplete privileged access governance | Increased risk of unauthorised access and weak accountability | Access management, authentication, monitoring |
| Limited SWIFT-specific incident and monitoring scenarios | Reduced detection and response effectiveness | Logging, monitoring, incident response |
| Incomplete third-party responsibility mapping | Unclear accountability and missing provider evidence | Third-party management, vulnerability management, access management |

### Residual Risk Assessment

If remediation is not completed, the organisation may face elevated residual risk in the following areas:

- Unauthorised access to SWIFT systems or operator functions.
- Credential compromise through incomplete strong authentication coverage.
- Lateral movement into the secure zone through excessive or undocumented network access.
- Delayed detection of suspicious activity or fraudulent transaction patterns.
- Inability to evidence consistent operation of key controls during annual attestation.
- Incomplete response to suspected SWIFT-related compromise.
- Gaps in provider-operated controls affecting the SWIFT environment.

### Positive Observations

The assessment also identified several strengths:

- Management recognises SWIFT security as a priority and has assigned ownership.
- A secure zone concept is implemented for core SWIFT infrastructure.
- Dual control exists for key transaction activities.
- Enterprise processes are available for access management, change management, vulnerability management, monitoring, and incident response.
- Endpoint protection and central logging are deployed across significant portions of the environment.
- Technical and business teams demonstrated strong knowledge of SWIFT operational processes.
- The organisation has prior experience with annual SWIFT attestation activities.

## Recommendations & Actions

### Remediation Principles

The following principles should guide remediation:

- Prioritise actions that reduce the likelihood of unauthorised transactions, credential compromise, and secure zone compromise.
- Establish a single authoritative scope for SWIFT assets, dependencies, access paths, and providers.
- Convert informal or team-dependent practices into documented, repeatable, and evidenced controls.
- Ensure each control has a named owner, evidence owner, review frequency, and escalation path.
- Prefer system-generated reports and ticket-based evidence over screenshots where possible.
- Track all remediation through a central action plan with senior management oversight.
- Validate remediation through independent review before closure.

### Prioritised Action Plan

| Priority | Action | Expected Outcome | Owner | Due Date | Closure Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical / High | Establish authoritative SWIFT asset and dependency register | Complete scope for all controls and evidence activities | [Owner] | [Date] | Approved register, dependency map, review record |
| Critical / High | Validate secure zone segmentation and firewall rules | Confirm only approved traffic and access paths are allowed | [Owner] | [Date] | Firewall review, approved rule matrix, traffic validation report |
| Critical / High | Implement full privileged access recertification | Confirm privileged access is authorised and appropriate | [Owner] | [Date] | Access review report, approvals, exception remediation tickets |
| Critical / High | Close multi-factor authentication coverage gaps | Strong authentication for all high-risk access paths | [Owner] | [Date] | Authentication coverage matrix, configuration evidence, test results |
| Critical / High | Strengthen service account governance | Account ownership, purpose, protection, and rotation are controlled | [Owner] | [Date] | Service account register, vault records, rotation evidence |
| Critical / High | Implement SWIFT-specific monitoring use cases | Improved detection of compromise and transaction misuse | [Owner] | [Date] | Use case library, log source validation, alert test evidence |
| Critical / High | Develop SWIFT-specific incident playbooks | Faster and more coordinated response to SWIFT incidents | [Owner] | [Date] | Approved playbooks, exercise records, lessons learned |
| High | Review transaction workflow controls | Confirm maker-checker, thresholds, and segregation are effective | [Owner] | [Date] | Workflow review, transaction sample testing, exception log |
| High | Map vulnerability scanning and patching to SWIFT assets | Complete visibility and timely remediation | [Owner] | [Date] | Scan coverage report, patch dashboard, exception register |
| Medium | Implement SWIFT workstation hardening baseline | Reduced malware and credential theft risk | [Owner] | [Date] | Approved baseline, compliance report, exception approvals |
| Medium | Add SWIFT impact flag to change management | Better identification and review of SWIFT-affecting changes | [Owner] | [Date] | Updated change template, sample change records |
| Medium | Formalise third-party responsibility matrix | Clear control accountability and evidence expectations | [Owner] | [Date] | Responsibility matrix, provider evidence schedule |
| Medium | Improve backup and recovery evidence | Demonstrable recovery capability for SWIFT services | [Owner] | [Date] | Backup coverage map, restore test results, recovery procedure updates |
| Medium | Implement evidence calendar and repository standards | Improved attestation readiness and evidence consistency | [Owner] | [Date] | Evidence calendar, repository index, quarterly evidence review |
| Low | Improve physical security evidence retention | Centralised evidence for location access controls | [Owner] | [Date] | Physical access review evidence stored in repository |

### Remediation Timeline

| Phase | Timeframe | Focus Areas | Expected Milestones |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 - Stabilise | 0-30 days | Scope, ownership, high-risk access, urgent network exposure | Asset register initiated, control owners assigned, high-risk access review started, firewall review commenced |
| Phase 2 - Reduce High Risk | 31-90 days | Segmentation, privileged access, authentication, transaction controls, vulnerability coverage | Firewall rules rationalised, strong authentication gaps addressed, privileged access recertified, transaction workflow review completed |
| Phase 3 - Strengthen Detection and Response | 91-150 days | Monitoring use cases, incident playbooks, endpoint hardening, third-party assurance | SWIFT monitoring library implemented, incident playbooks approved, provider responsibility matrix completed |
| Phase 4 - Evidence and Assurance | 151-210 days | Evidence management, recovery testing, independent validation, attestation preparation | Evidence repository operational, recovery tests completed, remediation independently validated |
| Phase 5 - Continuous Improvement | Ongoing | Control monitoring, quarterly evidence reviews, exercises, management reporting | Quarterly control health reporting, recurring access reviews, periodic exercises, continuous remediation tracking |

### Required Management Decisions

Management should make the following decisions to support remediation:

| Decision Required | Options / Considerations | Recommended Decision | Decision Owner | Due Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Remediation sponsorship | Assign executive sponsor for SWIFT control remediation | Appoint [Executive Role] as remediation sponsor | [Decision Owner] | [Date] |
| Funding and resourcing | Determine resource needs for identity, network, monitoring, and evidence workstreams | Approve dedicated remediation resources | [Decision Owner] | [Date] |
| Risk acceptance criteria | Define when temporary exceptions are acceptable | Require documented expiry, compensating controls, and senior approval | [Decision Owner] | [Date] |
| Third-party evidence expectations | Determine minimum provider evidence requirements | Require periodic SWIFT-relevant assurance evidence | [Decision Owner] | [Date] |
| Attestation readiness checkpoint | Determine date for independent validation before attestation | Schedule readiness review by [Date] | [Decision Owner] | [Date] |

### Action Tracking Requirements

All remediation actions should be tracked in a central register and reviewed at least monthly until closure. High-risk actions should be reviewed more frequently where deadlines are compressed or dependencies are significant.

The action register should include:

- Unique action identifier.
- Related finding.
- Risk rating.
- Action owner.
- Supporting stakeholders.
- Target date.
- Current status.
- Dependencies.
- Evidence required for closure.
- Closure approval.
- Residual risk assessment.
- Risk acceptance reference, where applicable.

### Closure Criteria

A remediation action should not be closed until:

- The corrective action has been implemented.
- The action owner has provided objective evidence.
- Evidence has been reviewed for completeness and relevance.
- Any exceptions have been documented and approved.
- The risk rating has been reassessed.
- Closure has been approved by the SWIFT security owner or delegated governance forum.

### Recommended Key Risk Indicators

| Indicator | Purpose | Suggested Frequency | Escalation Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Number of overdue high-risk remediation actions | Tracks remediation performance | Monthly | Any high-risk action overdue by more than [Number] days |
| Percentage of SWIFT assets covered by vulnerability scanning | Confirms scan completeness | Monthly | Coverage below [Percentage] |
| Percentage of privileged accounts recertified on time | Confirms access governance | Quarterly | Any recertification cycle missed |
| Number of service accounts without owner or rotation evidence | Tracks credential governance | Monthly | Any account without owner or overdue rotation |
| Percentage of SWIFT log sources reporting successfully | Confirms monitoring coverage | Monthly | Coverage below [Percentage] |
| Number of firewall rules without documented justification | Tracks segmentation hygiene | Quarterly | Any rule lacking owner or business purpose |
| Number of unresolved critical or high vulnerabilities | Tracks exposure | Weekly / Monthly | Any unresolved item beyond approved timeframe |
| Number of SWIFT-specific incident exercises completed | Confirms response readiness | Annually / Semi-annually | No exercise completed within planned cycle |
| Evidence submission completion rate | Tracks attestation readiness | Quarterly | Completion below [Percentage] |

### Recommended Governance Cadence

| Forum | Frequency | Attendees | Agenda |
|---|---|---|---|
| SWIFT remediation working group | Weekly until high-risk actions are closed | Control owners, technology leads, security, operations, risk | Action progress, blockers, evidence quality, dependencies |
| SWIFT security steering update | Monthly | Executive sponsor, CISO, operations leadership, risk, compliance | Risk posture, overdue actions, management decisions, escalations |
| Evidence health check | Quarterly | Evidence owners, compliance, internal assurance | Evidence completeness, quality, repository status, upcoming reviews |
| Access governance review | Quarterly | System owners, identity team, business owners, security | User access, privileged access, service accounts, exceptions |
| Incident response exercise review | At least annually | Security, technology, payment operations, legal, compliance, communications | Scenario testing, lessons learned, playbook updates |

## Distribution & Confidentiality

### Distribution

This report is intended for authorised internal stakeholders with responsibility for SWIFT security, operations, risk management, compliance, audit, and remediation oversight.

| Recipient / Group | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Executive Sponsor] | Executive oversight, funding, and risk decisions |
| [Chief Information Security Officer] | Security ownership and remediation governance |
| [SWIFT Security Owner] | Control accountability and attestation readiness |
| [Head of Technology / Infrastructure] | Technical remediation ownership |
| [Head of Payment Operations] | Transaction control and operational process ownership |
| [Risk and Compliance Team] | Risk tracking, assurance coordination, and management reporting |
| [Internal Audit] | Independent assurance planning and validation |
| [Third-Party/Vendor Management] | Provider control responsibility and evidence coordination |
| [Security Operations Centre] | Monitoring and incident response enhancements |
| [Business Continuity / Resilience Team] | Recovery and continuity action ownership |

Distribution to external parties, including assessors, regulators, correspondent banks, customers, technology providers, or other third parties, requires prior approval from [Report Owner / CISO / Legal].

### Confidentiality Requirements

This report is classified as **Confidential - Internal Use Only** because it contains sensitive information about the organisation’s SWIFT security posture, control gaps, network architecture, access control weaknesses, monitoring coverage, and remediation priorities.

Recipients must:

- Store the report only in approved internal repositories.
- Not forward the report outside approved distribution lists without written authorisation.
- Not extract sensitive details into unsecured emails, presentations, or collaboration channels.
- Protect printed copies and securely dispose of them when no longer required.
- Share only the minimum necessary information with third parties and only through approved channels.
- Report any suspected unauthorised disclosure to [Security Contact / Incident Response Team].

### Handling of Assessment Evidence

Evidence supporting this report must be retained in the approved SWIFT evidence repository for the required retention period. Access to evidence should be restricted to authorised personnel involved in control operation, assurance, remediation, or attestation activities.

Evidence containing credentials, sensitive configurations, personal data, transaction information, cryptographic material, or security architecture details must be handled according to the organisation’s data protection and information classification requirements.

### Report Approval

| Role | Name | Approval Status | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Report Owner | [Name] | [Approved / Pending] | [Date] |
| SWIFT Security Owner | [Name] | [Approved / Pending] | [Date] |
| Chief Information Security Officer | [Name] | [Approved / Pending] | [Date] |
| Executive Sponsor | [Name] | [Approved / Pending] | [Date] |
| Risk / Compliance Representative | [Name] | [Approved / Pending] | [Date] |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [EXAMPLE: CSCF-RP-2025-001] | [EXAMPLE: 2025] | [EXAMPLE: 1.1] | [EXAMPLE: SWIFT Environment Protection] | [EXAMPLE: Mandatory] | [EXAMPLE: Applicable] | [EXAMPLE: Internal CSCF Assessment] | [EXAMPLE: Network segmentation evidence for the secure zone is incomplete for one connectivity path.] | [EXAMPLE: Production SWIFT secure zone, firewall FW-SWIFT-01, Alliance Access environment] | [EXAMPLE: Firewall rule review procedure does not require mapping to CSCF zones.] | [EXAMPLE: High] | [EXAMPLE: Confirm and evidence that SWIFT-related systems are segregated from general IT networks in line with the approved architecture.] | [EXAMPLE: Review firewall rules, update network diagram, remove unauthorised flows, obtain change approval, and store evidence.] | [EXAMPLE: Daily firewall log monitoring for unexpected traffic until rule review is completed.] | [EXAMPLE: Network Security Lead] | [EXAMPLE: Head of Payments Operations] | [EXAMPLE: Infrastructure Manager] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-02-01] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-03-15] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-06-30] | [EXAMPLE: In Progress] | [EXAMPLE: 40] | [EXAMPLE: Change ticket approval CHG0001234] | [EXAMPLE: Network engineer availability and firewall vendor support] | [EXAMPLE: Approved network diagram, firewall rule export, change ticket, and segmentation test results] | [EXAMPLE: https://repository.example.com/swift/cscf/remediation/CSCF-RP-2025-001] | [EXAMPLE: Configuration review and sample traffic test by second-line security assurance] | [EXAMPLE: Security Assurance Manager] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-03-20] | [EXAMPLE: CISO] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-03-25] | [EXAMPLE: Low] | [EXAMPLE: Not Applicable] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-02-15] | [EXAMPLE: Awaiting approved maintenance window for final rule change.] |
| [EXAMPLE: CSCF-RP-2025-002] | [EXAMPLE: 2025] | [EXAMPLE: 5.1] | [EXAMPLE: Logical Access Control] | [EXAMPLE: Mandatory] | [EXAMPLE: Applicable] | [EXAMPLE: External Assessment] | [EXAMPLE: Quarterly privileged access review is not consistently evidenced for all SWIFT application administrators.] | [EXAMPLE: Alliance Access administrators and operating system privileged accounts] | [EXAMPLE: Access review ownership and evidence retention requirements were not formally defined.] | [EXAMPLE: Medium] | [EXAMPLE: Establish repeatable privileged access review with retained evidence and timely revocation of inappropriate access.] | [EXAMPLE: Define review procedure, generate privileged account listing, complete owner review, remove unnecessary access, and retain approval evidence.] | [EXAMPLE: Weekly monitoring of privileged account changes by IAM team.] | [EXAMPLE: IAM Operations Lead] | [EXAMPLE: Payments Operations Manager] | [EXAMPLE: SWIFT Application Owner] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-01-20] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-02-28] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-06-30] | [EXAMPLE: Completed Pending Validation] | [EXAMPLE: 90] | [EXAMPLE: HR leaver feed reconciliation and application account export availability] | [EXAMPLE: IAM analyst time and GRC workflow configuration] | [EXAMPLE: Privileged account report, review sign-off, revocation tickets, and updated access review procedure] | [EXAMPLE: https://grc.example.com/issues/CSCF-RP-2025-002] | [EXAMPLE: Sample test of privileged accounts against approved access review evidence] | [EXAMPLE: Internal Control Testing Team] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-03-05] | [EXAMPLE: SWIFT Security Officer] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-03-08] | [EXAMPLE: Low] | [EXAMPLE: Not Applicable] | [EXAMPLE: 2025-02-28] | [EXAMPLE: First quarterly review completed; validation scheduled with control testing team.] |

### Column Guidance

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Remediation ID | Enter a unique identifier for the remediation item, using a consistent format such as CSCF-RP-YYYY-NNN. |
| SWIFT CSCF Version | Enter the SWIFT CSCF version the remediation relates to, for example 2024, 2025, or the full framework version used for attestation. |
| CSCF Control Reference | Enter the exact SWIFT CSCF control reference being remediated, for example 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.9, 4.1, 5.1, 6.4, or 7.1. |
| Control Title | Enter the official or organisation-adopted title of the SWIFT CSCF control being remediated. |
| Control Type | Enter one of: Mandatory, Advisory, Not Applicable. For this remediation plan, mandatory-control gaps should normally be recorded as Mandatory. |
| Applicability | Enter the applicability decision for the control in the organisation’s SWIFT architecture context, using one of: Applicable, Not Applicable, Partially Applicable. |
| Assessment Source | Enter the source that identified the gap, such as Internal CSCF Assessment, External Assessment, Independent Assessment, Audit Finding, Penetration Test, Vulnerability Assessment, or Management Review. |
| Gap Statement | Describe the specific control gap to be closed, stating what is missing, incomplete, ineffective, or not evidenced; avoid generic statements. |
| Affected Scope | Identify the affected SWIFT environment, architecture type, systems, applications, infrastructure, users, locations, service providers, or processes. |
| Root Cause | State the primary cause of the gap, such as missing procedure, incomplete implementation, legacy configuration, tooling limitation, resource constraint, ownership gap, or third-party dependency. |
| Risk Rating | Enter the current risk rating before remediation using one of: Critical, High, Medium, Low, or according to the organisation’s approved risk methodology. |
| Remediation Objective | State the intended compliant end state that will close the CSCF gap and enable audit evidence to be produced. |
| Remediation Action | Describe the specific action or set of actions to be completed, including configuration, process, technology, governance, evidence, or testing activities. |
| Interim Compensating Control | Describe any temporary mitigating measure in place until full remediation is complete; enter None if no compensating control exists. |
| Action Owner | Enter the named person or role accountable for completing the remediation action. |
| Business Owner | Enter the business process owner accountable for accepting the remediation outcome and related operational impact. |
| Technology Owner | Enter the IT, security, infrastructure, application, or service owner responsible for technical implementation. |
| Target Start Date | Enter the planned remediation start date in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| Target Completion Date | Enter the planned remediation completion date in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| Regulatory or SWIFT Deadline | Enter the required deadline in YYYY-MM-DD format if driven by SWIFT attestation, regulator, audit commitment, or management-approved milestone; otherwise enter Not Applicable. |
| Current Status | Enter one of: Not Started, In Progress, Blocked, Completed Pending Validation, Validated, Closed, Deferred, Cancelled. |
| Percent Complete | Enter the estimated completion percentage as a whole number from 0 to 100. |
| Dependencies | Record any prerequisite activities, approvals, systems, vendors, change tickets, procurement, or related remediation items; enter None if no dependencies exist. |
| Required Resources or Budget | Enter required people, technology, vendor support, funding, or budget reference needed to complete the remediation; enter None if not applicable. |
| Expected Evidence | List the evidence expected to prove remediation, such as approved policy, configuration export, screenshot, access review, test result, change record, monitoring alert, procedure, or independent validation report. |
| Evidence Repository Link | Enter the controlled repository path, GRC record link, SharePoint link, ticket link, or document management reference where evidence will be stored. |
| Validation Method | Describe how closure will be verified, such as control re-test, configuration review, sample testing, walkthrough, vulnerability scan, access recertification, or independent assessment. |
| Independent Validator | Enter the named person, team, second-line function, internal audit, external assessor, or qualified independent reviewer responsible for validating closure. |
| Validation Date | Enter the date validation was completed in YYYY-MM-DD format; leave blank until validation is performed. |
| Closure Approval | Enter the name and role of the person approving closure, such as CISO, SWIFT Security Officer, Control Owner, Risk Owner, or Steering Committee chair. |
| Closure Date | Enter the formal closure date in YYYY-MM-DD format; leave blank until approved for closure. |
| Residual Risk After Remediation | Enter the expected or confirmed residual risk after remediation using one of: Critical, High, Medium, Low, None, or Not Assessed. |
| Exception or Deferral Reference | Enter the approved risk acceptance, exception, or deferral reference if remediation will not be completed by the deadline; otherwise enter Not Applicable. |
| Last Updated Date | Enter the date this remediation item was last updated in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| Comments | Enter concise additional notes, decisions, blockers, meeting outcomes, or clarifications relevant to remediation tracking. |

### Maintenance

Owned by the SWIFT Security Officer or CSCF remediation programme manager, with updates at least weekly during remediation and monthly thereafter until all items are closed. The template draws from CSCF self-assessment results, independent assessment reports, audit findings, GRC issue records, change management tickets, vulnerability tools, IAM records, and evidence repositories.
