## Approach / Phases

The Swift incident response approach follows a structured lifecycle. The phases may run in parallel depending on severity, urgency, and operational impact.

### Phase 1 - Preparation and Readiness

The organisation will maintain Swift-specific incident readiness through the following activities:

- Maintain a current Swift environment diagram covering production, test, disaster recovery, management access, administrative workstations, supporting databases, interfaces, firewalls, jump hosts, monitoring tools, and connectivity paths.
- Maintain an inventory of Swift users, operators, administrators, service accounts, privileged accounts, certificates, authentication mechanisms, and third-party access.
- Define and maintain Swift incident severity criteria aligned to business impact, fraud risk, system integrity, confidentiality exposure, and service availability.
- Maintain secure copies of key Swift configuration baselines, hardening standards, firewall rules, routing rules, access lists, and golden images where applicable.
- Ensure Swift-related logs are collected, time-synchronised, retained, access-controlled, and reviewed.
- Maintain playbooks for likely Swift incident scenarios, including:
 - Suspected unauthorised Swift message creation or modification.
 - Compromise of a Swift operator or administrator account.
 - Malware or ransomware on Swift infrastructure or supporting systems.
 - Compromise of a jump host, privileged workstation, or remote access path.
 - Unauthorised configuration change in Swift systems or security controls.
 - Suspicious payment pattern or attempted fraudulent transfer.
 - Loss of integrity in reconciliation, message archive, or transaction logs.
 - Compromise of an interface between Swift and internal payment systems.
 - Third-party compromise affecting Swift operations.
- Train Swift operators, payments staff, IT administrators, SOC analysts, and incident responders on escalation triggers and immediate containment do’s and don’ts.
- Conduct tabletop exercises and technical simulations involving Swift operations, payments, fraud, legal, compliance, IT, cyber security, and executive stakeholders.
- Maintain a current contact directory and escalation tree, stored in a secure location accessible during outages.
- Ensure forensic tooling, secure evidence storage, clean administrative workstations, emergency credentials, and out-of-band communications are available.
- Pre-agree decision authorities for suspending Swift connectivity, stopping payment release, isolating systems, engaging external forensics, notifying external parties, and resuming service.

### Phase 2 - Detection and Initial Triage

Potential Swift incidents may be detected through:

- Alerts from security monitoring tools, endpoint protection, identity monitoring, network sensors, data loss prevention, or privileged access management systems.
- Suspicious activity reported by Swift operators, payments staff, reconciliation teams, fraud monitoring, counterparties, customers, correspondent banks, or service providers.
- Unusual Swift message volume, value, destination, timing, type, approval pattern, or routing.
- Failed login spikes, access from unusual locations, out-of-hours activity, disabled security controls, unexpected privilege changes, or abnormal administrative activity.
- Unexpected changes to Swift application configuration, message templates, routing tables, certificates, connectivity settings, or interface files.
- Discrepancies between Swift messages, payment systems, accounting records, sanctions screening, fraud monitoring, or reconciliation outputs.
- Indicators from threat intelligence, Swift advisories, regulators, law enforcement, vendors, or industry information-sharing groups.

Initial triage will establish:

- What happened or is suspected to have happened.
- Which Swift systems, users, messages, accounts, interfaces, or service providers may be affected.
- Whether there is evidence of unauthorised access, fraud, data exposure, malware, destructive activity, or service disruption.
- Whether Swift message integrity or payment authorisation integrity may be compromised.
- Whether the event is ongoing.
- Whether immediate containment is required to prevent further loss or damage.
- Whether the incident requires executive escalation.

Minimum information to capture during triage:

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| Incident reference | Unique incident number assigned by the incident management system |
| Date and time detected | Time of first alert, report, or observable event |
| Reporter/source | Person, system, counterparty, vendor, or team that identified the issue |
| Initial description | Plain-language description of the suspected incident |
| Affected assets | Known or suspected Swift systems, accounts, workstations, interfaces, or networks |
| Affected messages | Message references, dates, values, currencies, counterparties, and status where known |
| Business impact | Impact on payment processing, settlement, liquidity, customers, counterparties, or operations |
| Security impact | Suspected compromise of confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, or non-repudiation |
| Current activity | Whether malicious or suspicious activity appears to be continuing |
| Initial severity | Provisional severity rating |
| Immediate actions taken | Isolation, account lockout, payment hold, evidence preservation, or notifications |
| Decision owner | Person accountable for next-stage escalation and response coordination |

### Phase 3 - Severity Classification and Escalation

Swift incidents will be classified using the following severity model.

| Severity | Criteria | Examples | Required Escalation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | Confirmed or strongly suspected compromise affecting Swift message integrity, unauthorised message transmission, active fraud, destructive malware, material outage, or loss of control over Swift privileged access | Fraudulent Swift messages sent or queued; administrator account compromised; ransomware on Swift server; active attacker in Swift segment | Immediate escalation to CISO, CIO, Head of Payments, General Counsel, CRO, executive crisis team, and relevant external response partners |
| High | Credible suspected compromise of Swift-related systems, credentials, interfaces, or payment workflows with potential for financial loss, service disruption, or data exposure | Suspicious operator login; unexplained Swift configuration change; malware on jump host; abnormal payment approval pattern | Escalation to CISO, Swift Service Owner, SOC Manager, Payments Operations, Fraud, Legal, Compliance, and IT leadership |
| Medium | Security event affecting Swift-supporting systems with limited evidence of compromise and no confirmed message or payment impact | Failed login pattern; suspicious file on support server; unauthorised access attempt blocked by controls | Escalation to SOC, Swift Operations, IT Operations, IAM, and Payments Operations as needed |
| Low | Isolated event, policy deviation, or alert with no evidence of compromise, no impact to message integrity, and no operational disruption | Benign misconfiguration; known false positive; user reports suspicious email with no interaction | Managed by SOC or relevant operational team with documented closure |

Escalation principles:

- Any suspected unauthorised Swift message creation, approval, modification, suppression, deletion, or transmission must be treated as at least High severity until disproven.
- Any suspected compromise of Swift administrator credentials, operator credentials, certificates, authentication devices, or privileged access paths must be escalated immediately.
- Any security incident involving the Swift production environment must be reported to the Swift Service Owner and CISO or delegate without delay.
- Any suspected fraud or payment manipulation must involve Payments Operations, Fraud, Legal, Compliance, and senior business management.
- Where there is uncertainty, responders must escalate rather than wait for full confirmation.
- Decisions to suspend Swift connectivity, halt message processing, invoke crisis management, notify external parties, or resume normal operations must be made by authorised decision-makers.

### Phase 4 - Containment

Containment actions must balance fraud prevention, evidence preservation, business continuity, customer impact, and legal considerations.

Potential immediate containment actions include:

- Suspend or hold affected Swift messages pending validation.
- Stop payment release or require additional manual approval for defined message types, currencies, values, branches, counterparties, or users.
- Disable or lock suspected compromised operator, administrator, privileged, service, or third-party accounts.
- Revoke active sessions and require credential reset or authentication re-enrolment.
- Isolate affected Swift servers, workstations, jump hosts, interfaces, or network segments where safe to do so.
- Block suspicious IP addresses, domains, command-and-control indicators, remote access paths, or unauthorised network flows.
- Disable compromised interfaces between Swift and upstream payment systems while preserving transaction data.
- Preserve volatile evidence before shutdown where feasible and authorised.
- Capture forensic images of affected systems or storage where required.
- Preserve relevant logs, alerts, message archives, approvals, reconciliation records, access records, and configuration states.
- Increase monitoring on Swift systems, privileged activity, payment activity, and network flows.
- Move to manual payment validation, dual control, or heightened approval workflows.
- Engage external forensic support if internal capability is insufficient or independence is required.
- Coordinate with correspondent banks, counterparties, or payment schemes to stop, recall, or validate suspicious payments where applicable.

Containment decisions must be documented, including the rationale, decision owner, time, affected systems, business impact, and evidence preserved.

Actions to avoid unless authorised:

- Rebooting or rebuilding suspected compromised systems before evidence is preserved.
- Deleting suspected malicious files without capture and analysis.
- Resetting large numbers of credentials without understanding attacker persistence mechanisms.
- Communicating incident details over potentially compromised channels.
- Resuming Swift processing solely because systems appear operational.
- Making external notifications without Legal, Compliance, and Communications review, except where immediate operational contact is necessary to prevent loss.

### Phase 5 - Investigation and Evidence Management

The investigation will determine the incident scope, root cause, attacker activity, affected assets, affected messages, data exposure, financial exposure, and recovery requirements.

Investigation activities may include:

- Review Swift application logs, operator logs, message logs, audit trails, system logs, database logs, security alerts, and privileged access records.
- Validate all Swift messages during the suspected compromise window against source systems, approval records, sanctions screening, fraud checks, reconciliation outputs, and accounting entries.
- Identify unauthorised or unusual message creation, alteration, cancellation, release, suppression, deletion, replay, or routing.
- Review login activity for Swift users, administrators, service accounts, remote access users, and third-party accounts.
- Analyse endpoint and server evidence for malware, persistence, lateral movement, credential theft, unauthorised tools, script execution, or tampering.
- Review firewall, proxy, DNS, VPN, remote access, identity provider, and network telemetry for suspicious activity.
- Compare current Swift system configurations against approved baselines.
- Review recent changes, emergency access, vendor support sessions, patching activity, system maintenance, and privileged access approvals.
- Determine whether security controls were disabled, bypassed, misconfigured, or ineffective.
- Assess whether data was accessed, copied, exported, altered, encrypted, destroyed, or exposed.
- Identify whether third-party systems or personnel contributed to or were affected by the incident.
- Maintain a detailed investigation timeline.

Evidence handling requirements:

| Requirement | Expected Practice |
|---|---|
| Evidence identification | Record each evidence item with description, source, date, time, collector, and purpose |
| Chain of custody | Document every transfer, access, copy, or analysis action |
| Integrity protection | Use approved hashing or equivalent integrity verification for forensic copies |
| Secure storage | Store evidence in restricted, access-controlled repositories |
| Legal coordination | Involve Legal where privilege, litigation, regulatory notification, or law enforcement referral may apply |
| Time synchronisation | Record time zone and source system clock reliability for each evidence source |
| Minimal alteration | Avoid changing original evidence unless necessary for containment or safety |
| Retention | Retain evidence according to legal, regulatory, contractual, and incident-specific requirements |

### Phase 6 - Eradication and Remediation

Once containment is stable and sufficient evidence has been preserved, eradication will remove attacker access, malware, unauthorised changes, and control weaknesses.

Remediation actions may include:

- Remove malware, unauthorised tools, persistence mechanisms, backdoors, scripts, scheduled tasks, unauthorised services, and rogue accounts.
- Rebuild affected Swift servers, operator workstations, jump hosts, or support systems from trusted sources where compromise is suspected.
- Rotate or revoke affected credentials, certificates, keys, tokens, passwords, service account secrets, and administrative credentials.
- Re-enrol users in strong authentication mechanisms where credential compromise is suspected.
- Correct unauthorised Swift application, interface, routing, certificate, firewall, or access control changes.
- Validate system hardening, patch levels, endpoint protection, logging, file integrity monitoring, time synchronisation, and secure configuration.
- Close unauthorised network paths and remove temporary access introduced during response.
- Review and remediate access for all Swift operators, administrators, service accounts, third parties, and support personnel.
- Strengthen payment approval controls, segregation of duties, transaction verification, and reconciliation where weakness contributed to the incident.
- Apply compensating controls where full remediation cannot be completed before service restoration.
- Confirm vendors and service providers have remediated any related compromise in their environments.

Eradication is complete only when:

- Known malicious activity has stopped.
- Known attacker access paths have been removed.
- Affected credentials and secrets have been secured.
- Affected systems have been cleaned or rebuilt to trusted state.
- Swift configurations have been validated against approved baselines.
- Payment integrity controls are functioning.
- Monitoring is in place to detect recurrence.
- Business, technology, security, and risk owners agree that recovery may proceed.

### Phase 7 - Recovery and Service Restoration

Recovery must ensure that Swift services resume from a trusted state and that message processing integrity is confirmed.

Recovery activities include:

- Confirm the trusted status of Swift infrastructure, operator workstations, administrative access paths, interfaces, and supporting network services.
- Validate restored systems against approved security baselines and configuration records.
- Confirm endpoint protection, monitoring, logging, backup, access control, and time synchronisation are operating.
- Reconcile Swift messages, source system records, sanctions screening results, fraud monitoring outputs, acknowledgements, accounting records, and settlement records for the incident window.
- Verify suspicious, held, rejected, cancelled, recalled, or delayed payments before release or closure.
- Conduct heightened review of payment queues and message creation activity before returning to normal processing.
- Confirm third-party connectivity and support access are secure before re-enablement.
- Obtain formal approval from authorised business, technology, security, and risk decision-makers before resuming normal Swift operations.
- Continue enhanced monitoring for a defined post-recovery period.
- Communicate recovery status to approved internal and external stakeholders.

Recovery decision checklist:

| Recovery Gate | Required Confirmation | Approver |
|---|---|---|
| Technical trust | Systems are rebuilt, cleaned, patched, hardened, monitored, and validated | [Infrastructure Lead] |
| Access trust | User, administrator, service, and third-party access has been reviewed and secured | [IAM Lead] |
| Message integrity | Swift messages and payment records have been reconciled and validated | [Head of Payments Operations] |
| Security confidence | No ongoing malicious activity is detected and monitoring coverage is sufficient | [CISO / Incident Commander] |
| Legal and regulatory readiness | Notification obligations and evidence preservation needs have been assessed | [General Counsel / Compliance Lead] |
| Business readiness | Operational teams can process safely under normal or heightened controls | [Swift Service Owner] |
| Executive approval | Material risks are understood and accepted for service restoration | [Executive Sponsor / Crisis Team Lead] |

### Phase 8 - Communications and Notifications

Communications must be accurate, timely, controlled, and appropriate to the audience. Information must be shared on a need-to-know basis and using trusted channels.

Internal communications may include:

- Incident commander briefings to executive management and crisis management team.
- Status updates to Swift operations, payments operations, IT, security, fraud, compliance, legal, risk, finance, treasury, and customer-facing teams.
- Operational instructions for payment holds, manual validation, enhanced approvals, or system access restrictions.
- Staff awareness notices where user action is required, such as credential reset, phishing reporting, or use of alternative communication channels.

External communications may include:

- Notifications to Swift through approved support or reporting channels where the incident affects the security or integrity of Swift-related operations.
- Notifications to regulators or supervisory authorities where required.
- Engagement with law enforcement for suspected criminal activity or fraud.
- Contact with correspondent banks, counterparties, customers, payment intermediaries, or service providers to validate, stop, recall, or investigate suspicious transactions.
- Notifications to cyber insurer or breach response panel where coverage may apply.
- Public or media statements coordinated by Communications and Legal.

Communication principles:

- Do not speculate on cause, attribution, loss, or impact before facts are established.
- Do not disclose technical indicators, investigative details, or control weaknesses beyond approved recipients.
- Use out-of-band channels if normal communications may be compromised.
- Maintain a record of all material communications, decisions, recipients, times, and approvals.
- Ensure external statements are approved by Legal, Compliance, Communications, and executive leadership as appropriate.
- Align customer, regulator, counterparty, and media communications to avoid inconsistent messaging.

### Phase 9 - Post-Incident Review and Improvement

A post-incident review must be completed for all High and Critical Swift incidents and for Medium incidents where there are material lessons learned.

The review will assess:

- Timeline of detection, escalation, containment, investigation, eradication, recovery, and communications.
- Root cause and contributing factors.
- Effectiveness of Swift-specific controls, including access control, segregation, monitoring, logging, hardening, reconciliation, and approval workflows.
- Whether incident severity was correctly assessed and escalated.
- Whether evidence was preserved appropriately.
- Whether fraud prevention and payment validation actions were effective.
- Whether third-party support met expectations.
- Whether communication was timely, accurate, and appropriately controlled.
- Whether recovery occurred from a trusted state.
- Whether there were policy, procedure, training, technology, resourcing, or governance gaps.

Post-incident outputs:

| Output | Description | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Incident report | Formal record of facts, impact, response actions, timeline, decisions, and conclusions | [Incident Commander] |
| Root cause analysis | Technical and process analysis of how the incident occurred and persisted | [Security Investigation Lead] |
| Payment impact assessment | Confirmed or potential financial impact, message impact, and reconciliation outcome | [Head of Payments Operations] |
| Control improvement plan | Corrective actions with owners, due dates, risk ratings, and validation requirements | [CISO / Risk Owner] |
| Lessons learned record | Practical improvements to playbooks, monitoring, training, escalation, and communications | [Incident Response Manager] |
| Executive summary | Business-level summary for senior management and governance committees | [CISO] |

Corrective actions must be tracked to closure through the organisation’s risk, audit, or issue management process.

| Legal and compliance advisors | Notification assessment, privilege, regulatory engagement, evidence handling, and external communication review |
| Communications specialists | Stakeholder messaging, executive updates, media handling, and customer communication support |
| Vendor support contacts | Emergency support for Swift components, managed services, infrastructure, monitoring, and forensic tooling |

### Technology and Tooling

| Tooling Area | Required Capability |
|---|---|
| Security information and event monitoring | Central collection and correlation of Swift-related logs and alerts |
| Endpoint detection and response | Detection, isolation, investigation, and remediation of compromised systems |
| Network detection and traffic analysis | Visibility into Swift segment traffic, remote access, and suspicious communications |
| Privileged access management | Monitoring and control of administrator access, session recording, and emergency access |
| Identity monitoring | Detection of unusual login activity, privilege changes, and account misuse |
| File integrity monitoring | Detection of unauthorised changes to critical Swift files and configurations |
| Backup and recovery tooling | Restoration from trusted backups and validation of recovery points |
| Forensic imaging and analysis tools | Evidence capture, integrity verification, malware analysis, and timeline reconstruction |
| Secure evidence repository | Restricted storage for logs, images, reports, screenshots, and chain-of-custody records |
| Case management system | Incident tracking, action management, timeline recording, and reporting |
| Out-of-band communications | Secure communications independent of potentially compromised corporate systems |
| Payment reconciliation tools | Validation of Swift messages against source, approval, accounting, and settlement records |

### Documentation and Reference Materials

Required documentation must be current, access-controlled, and available during an incident:

- Swift environment architecture diagrams.
- Swift asset inventory.
- Swift account and access inventory.
- Network segmentation diagrams and firewall rule summaries.
- Data flow diagrams for Swift message processing.
- Approved Swift configuration baselines.
- Payment processing and approval procedures.
- Reconciliation and exception handling procedures.
- Fraud escalation and payment recall procedures.
- Disaster recovery and backup procedures for Swift services.
- Vendor support contracts and emergency contacts.
- Incident contact directory and escalation matrix.
- Evidence handling procedures and chain-of-custody templates.
- External notification decision workflow.
- Swift-specific detection use cases and alert handling guides.
- Recent change records affecting Swift systems.
- Recent access review records for Swift users and administrators.
- Recent exercise reports and corrective action trackers.

### Budget and External Support

The annual Swift incident response budget should include provision for:

- Forensic retainer or emergency forensic support.
- Swift specialist support where not covered by existing maintenance arrangements.
- Security monitoring and logging enhancements.
- Training and exercises for Swift stakeholders.
- Secure evidence storage and forensic tooling.
- Out-of-band communication services.
- Travel or on-site support during major incidents, where applicable.
- Legal, regulatory, and breach response support.
- Independent review or assurance of remediation following material incidents.

## Success Metrics

The effectiveness of this plan will be measured using readiness, response, recovery, and improvement metrics.

| Metric | Target | Measurement Method | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Swift incident response plan review completion | At least annually | Approved review record | Incident Response Manager |
| Swift stakeholder training completion | 100% of in-scope personnel annually | Training records | CISO |
| Critical contact directory accuracy | Validated quarterly | Contact test results | Incident Response Manager |
| Swift incident tabletop exercise completion | At least annually | Exercise report | CISO |
| Technical simulation completion | At least annually or after major change | Simulation report | SOC Manager |
| Swift asset inventory accuracy | Reviewed quarterly and after major change | Inventory reconciliation | Swift Service Owner |
| Swift logging coverage for critical assets | 100% of identified critical assets | Logging coverage assessment | SOC Manager |
| Time to acknowledge Critical Swift alert | Within 15 minutes | Case management timestamps | SOC Manager |
| Time to escalate Critical Swift incident to CISO | Within 30 minutes | Incident timeline | Incident Commander |
| Time to complete initial payment impact assessment for Critical incident | Within 1 hour | Payment impact record | Head of Payments Operations |
| Evidence preservation for High and Critical incidents | 100% where technically feasible | Evidence log and chain-of-custody record | Security Investigation Lead |
| Post-incident review completion for High and Critical incidents | Within 30 business days of recovery | Approved review report | Incident Response Manager |
| Corrective action closure | Within agreed due dates based on risk | Issue tracker | Risk Management |
| Reconciliation completion after suspected message integrity incident | 100% of affected window | Reconciliation report | Head of Payments Operations |
| Recovery approval evidence | 100% of High and Critical recoveries | Recovery gate checklist | Incident Commander |
| Repeat incident due to same root cause | Zero material repeats | Incident trend analysis | CISO |

Qualitative success indicators:

- Swift operators and payments staff understand when and how to escalate suspicious activity.
- Incident responders can quickly identify Swift dependencies, access paths, logs, and business owners.
- Payment integrity can be assessed rapidly during suspected compromise.
- Technical teams can isolate affected Swift components without unnecessary disruption.
- Executive leadership receives clear, timely, decision-ready information.
- External communications are controlled, accurate, and legally reviewed.
- Recovery decisions are based on evidence of technical trust and payment integrity.
- Lessons learned result in measurable control improvements.

## Review & Update Triggers

This plan must be reviewed at least annually and whenever a significant trigger occurs.

Review triggers include:

- A suspected or confirmed Swift security incident.
- A material cyber incident elsewhere in the organisation that could affect Swift response assumptions.
- Significant change to Swift architecture, connectivity, hosting, interface design, network segmentation, authentication, monitoring, or payment workflows.
- Onboarding, termination, or material change of a third-party provider supporting Swift services.
- Introduction of new Swift message types, payment products, business units, currencies, branches, or high-risk transaction flows.
- Material changes to regulatory, supervisory, contractual, or Swift-related security expectations.
- Significant findings from internal audit, external assurance, penetration testing, red team exercises, vulnerability assessments, or control testing.
- Failure or weakness identified during tabletop exercises, simulations, recovery testing, or actual response.
- Changes in executive ownership, Swift service ownership, incident response leadership, SOC provider, or key response personnel.
- Changes to legal entity structure, operating model, outsourcing model, or geographic footprint affecting Swift operations.
- Threat intelligence indicating increased targeting of Swift customers, financial institutions, payment infrastructure, or relevant technology providers.
- Discovery that contact lists, escalation paths, diagrams, inventories, or recovery information are inaccurate.
- Material changes to logging, retention, evidence handling, or security monitoring capabilities.
- Post-incident corrective actions requiring updates to this plan or related playbooks.

Each review must confirm:

- The plan remains aligned to the current Swift environment and operating model.
- Roles, decision authorities, and escalation routes remain accurate.
- Contact details and external support arrangements are current.
- Detection, containment, evidence, recovery, and communication activities remain practical and tested.
- Dependencies and assumptions remain valid.
- Lessons learned and audit findings have been incorporated.
- Approved changes have been communicated to relevant stakeholders.

Plan changes must be version-controlled, approved by the document owner, and retained according to the organisation’s document management requirements.

SWF-017.title: Cyber Threat Intelligence & ISAC Procedure
SWF-017.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DOC-ID] | 1.0 | Cyber Security Operations Manager | [Effective Date] | SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework | Internal |

## Purpose

This procedure defines how [Organisation Name] receives, assesses, disseminates, acts upon, and records cyber threat intelligence from the Swift Information Sharing and Analysis Centre (Swift ISAC).

The objective is to ensure that relevant Swift community threat information is used in a timely and controlled manner to protect the organisation’s Swift infrastructure, connected systems, payment operations, and supporting processes.

This procedure supports the organisation’s ability to:

- Monitor Swift-specific cyber threats, fraud indicators, attack techniques, and security advisories.
- Identify whether Swift ISAC intelligence is relevant to the organisation’s environment.
- Take timely defensive action where indicators, tactics, vulnerabilities, or fraud patterns are applicable.
- Share relevant intelligence with appropriate internal stakeholders on a need-to-know basis.
- Maintain evidence that Swift ISAC information is reviewed and acted upon.
- Escalate urgent or high-impact intelligence through incident response and management channels.

## Scope

This procedure applies to all Swift-related cyber threat intelligence received from Swift ISAC and other official Swift security communication channels used by [Organisation Name].

In scope are:

- Swift ISAC alerts, advisories, reports, indicators, threat bulletins, and related communications.
- Swift customer security updates relevant to the organisation’s Swift environment.
- Threat intelligence related to:
 - Swift infrastructure.
 - Swift interfaces and messaging platforms.
 - Payment operations and transaction monitoring.
 - Fraud scenarios affecting Swift users.
 - Compromised credentials or privileged access paths.
 - Malware, command-and-control infrastructure, suspicious IP addresses, domains, file hashes, and other indicators.
 - Vulnerabilities or misconfigurations that may affect Swift-connected systems.
- Internal analysis, triage, distribution, and response activities arising from Swift ISAC information.
- Evidence records used to demonstrate that intelligence was reviewed, assessed, and actioned.

Out of scope are:

- General threat intelligence unrelated to Swift or financial messaging, unless it affects Swift-connected systems.
- Public media reporting that has not been validated by an approved intelligence source.
- Formal incident response activities after an event is declared; these are managed under the Cyber Security Incident Response Procedure.
- External intelligence sharing by [Organisation Name] unless separately authorised by Legal, Compliance, Communications, and senior management.

This procedure applies to:

- Security Operations Centre personnel.
- Cyber Threat Intelligence analysts.
- Swift Operations team members.
- Payment Operations staff.
- Infrastructure and network administrators supporting Swift systems.
- Identity and Access Management personnel supporting Swift access.
- Fraud monitoring teams.
- Incident Response team members.
- Risk, Compliance, and Internal Audit stakeholders requiring evidence of review and action.

## Prerequisites & Inputs

Before this procedure can operate effectively, the following prerequisites must be in place.

### Access and subscriptions

| Requirement | Description | Responsible Role | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Swift ISAC access | Approved personnel have active access to Swift ISAC or approved Swift security intelligence channels. | Swift Security Officer | Access approval record |
| Named recipients | Primary and backup recipients are designated for Swift ISAC communications. | Cyber Security Operations Manager | Distribution list or role assignment |
| Secure mailbox or portal account | Swift ISAC alerts are received through an approved secure mailbox, portal, or workflow queue. | Security Operations Centre Lead | Mailbox or platform configuration record |
| Out-of-hours monitoring | Urgent security notifications can be reviewed outside normal business hours. | Cyber Security Operations Manager | On-call rota |
| Need-to-know distribution | Internal distribution lists are restricted to authorised staff. | Information Security Manager | Distribution list membership review |

### Required inputs

The following inputs are used during this procedure:

- Swift ISAC alerts and advisories.
- Swift security notifications and customer communications.
- Internal Swift asset inventory.
- Network diagrams showing Swift infrastructure zones and connectivity.
- Current Swift environment architecture, including interfaces, gateways, connectors, jump servers, and administration systems.
- Current list of privileged accounts for Swift systems.
- Current list of payment operations systems that send, receive, screen, reconcile, or monitor Swift messages.
- Security monitoring use cases and detection rules.
- Vulnerability management records.
- Change management records.
- Incident response playbooks.
- Fraud monitoring rules and transaction investigation procedures.
- Threat intelligence platform records, where used.
- Security information and event management logs, endpoint security telemetry, firewall logs, proxy logs, email security logs, and authentication logs.

### Approved handling requirements

Swift ISAC information must be handled as sensitive security information. Personnel must:

- Use only approved systems to store, process, or distribute Swift ISAC material.
- Avoid forwarding Swift ISAC content to unauthorised recipients.
- Redact sensitive indicators or contextual information before broader internal sharing where full details are not required.
- Mark internal summaries with the appropriate classification.
- Follow any confidentiality, redistribution, or handling instructions included in the Swift ISAC communication.
- Escalate any suspected breach of handling requirements to the Information Security Manager.

### Severity classification

Each Swift ISAC item must be assessed using the following internal severity model.

| Severity | Criteria | Initial Response Target | Example Action |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Critical | Active exploitation, confirmed compromise of Swift users, highly relevant indicators, or urgent defensive action required for Swift infrastructure. | 1 hour | Activate incident response triage; search for indicators; implement emergency blocking where approved. |
| High | Credible threat or vulnerability likely to affect the organisation’s Swift environment or payment operations. | 4 hours | Conduct exposure assessment; update detections; raise priority remediation tasks. |
| Medium | Relevant intelligence requiring monitoring, tuning, validation, or planned control improvement. | 2 business days | Add indicators to monitoring; brief Swift Operations and Fraud teams. |
| Low | Informational item with limited or no current applicability but useful for awareness or trend analysis. | 5 business days | Record review outcome; retain for threat landscape reporting. |

## Step-by-Step Procedure (numbered)

1. **Receive Swift ISAC intelligence**

 1.1. The designated recipient monitors the approved Swift ISAC channel at least once each business day.

 1.2. During out-of-hours periods, alerts marked urgent or equivalent must be routed to the on-call Security Operations contact.

 1.3. The recipient must verify that the communication originated from an approved Swift source or approved internal forwarding route.

 1.4. The recipient must not open attachments, links, or files in an uncontrolled environment if authenticity is uncertain.

 1.5. The recipient records the item in the Cyber Threat Intelligence Register or approved case management system.

 Minimum log details:

 | Field | Required Entry |
 |---|---|
 | Intelligence ID | Unique internal reference |
 | Source | Swift ISAC or approved Swift channel |
 | Date and time received | [Date/Time] |
 | Received by | Name or role |
 | Subject/title | Advisory or alert title |
 | Source classification | As marked by source |
 | Internal classification | Internal handling classification |
 | Initial severity | Critical, High, Medium, or Low |
 | Status | New, Under Review, Action Required, Monitoring, Closed |
 | Assigned analyst | Name or role |

2. **Perform initial authenticity and handling check**

 2.1. Confirm that the advisory is from an approved Swift source or trusted internal distribution channel.

 2.2. Check whether the advisory contains redistribution restrictions.

 2.3. Apply the appropriate internal classification marking.

 2.4. Store the original item in the approved restricted repository.

 2.5. If the communication appears suspicious, potentially fraudulent, or inconsistent with expected Swift communications, escalate to the Security Operations Centre Lead before further distribution.

3. **Triage the intelligence**

 3.1. The assigned analyst reviews the intelligence for:

 - Threat actor activity affecting Swift users.
 - Malware, tools, techniques, or infrastructure relevant to the organisation.
 - Fraud scenarios involving financial messaging or payment workflows.
 - Vulnerabilities affecting Swift-connected infrastructure or supporting platforms.
 - Indicators of compromise.
 - Recommended defensive measures.
 - Urgency and potential business impact.
 - Required action by Swift customers.

 3.2. The analyst assigns or confirms the internal severity using the severity classification table in this procedure.

 3.3. The analyst identifies affected or potentially affected internal areas, including:

 - Swift interface servers.
 - Messaging gateways.
 - Operator workstations.
 - Jump hosts and administration workstations.
 - Identity and access management components.
 - Network security devices protecting Swift zones.
 - Payment screening, sanctions screening, fraud monitoring, and reconciliation platforms.
 - Backup and recovery systems supporting Swift operations.
 - Third-party service providers supporting Swift systems.

 3.4. The analyst records the initial triage outcome.

 Example triage record:

 | Item | Assessment |
 |---|---|
 | Relevance to Swift environment | Relevant / Partially relevant / Not relevant |
 | Likelihood of applicability | High / Medium / Low |
 | Potential impact | Operational / Financial / Fraud / Confidentiality / Integrity / Availability |
 | Indicators available | Yes / No |
 | Immediate defensive action required | Yes / No |
 | Incident suspected | Yes / No |
 | Recommended next step | [Action] |
 | Analyst | [Name] |
 | Date/time completed | [Date/Time] |

4. **Determine whether the intelligence is relevant**

 4.1. Compare the intelligence against the current Swift asset inventory and architecture.

 4.2. Check whether referenced technologies, operating systems, software versions, network paths, ports, account types, or business processes exist in the organisation.

 4.3. Where the intelligence relates to fraud or payment manipulation, consult Payment Operations and Fraud Monitoring to determine whether the scenario could apply to the organisation’s transaction flows.

 4.4. Where the intelligence includes vulnerability information, consult Vulnerability Management and Infrastructure teams to confirm exposure.

 4.5. Where the intelligence includes indicators of compromise, determine whether those indicators can be searched in available logs and monitoring tools.

 4.6. Classify the relevance as follows:

 | Relevance | Meaning | Required Action |
 |---|---|---|
 | Relevant | Directly applicable to the organisation’s Swift environment, technologies, processes, or threat exposure. | Proceed with detailed analysis and action plan. |
 | Partially relevant | Some elements apply, but not all conditions are present. | Conduct targeted review and document limitations. |
 | Not currently relevant | No known applicability based on current environment. | Record rationale and retain for trend awareness. |
 | Unknown | Insufficient information to determine applicability. | Seek clarification, perform additional checks, or escalate. |

5. **Search for indicators of compromise**

 5.1. If indicators of compromise are provided, the Security Operations Centre must determine which indicators can be searched using available tools.

 5.2. Searches may include:

 - Endpoint detection and response telemetry.
 - Security event logs.
 - Firewall logs.
 - Proxy and web gateway logs.
 - DNS logs.
 - Email security logs.
 - Authentication logs.
 - Privileged access logs.
 - Swift application and platform logs.
 - Database activity logs where applicable.
 - Payment operations monitoring alerts.
 - File integrity monitoring alerts.

 5.3. Indicator searches must prioritise Swift-related systems, privileged administration systems, and payment operations environments.

 5.4. Search windows must cover the period recommended in the advisory. If no period is specified, the default lookback period is 90 days, subject to log retention availability.

 5.5. Record the search results, including systems searched, tools used, time window, analyst, and outcome.

 Indicator search log:

 | Indicator Type | Indicator | Data Source Searched | Time Window | Result | Analyst | Date/Time |
 |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
 | IP / Domain / Hash / Filename / Account / Other | [Indicator] | [System] | [Period] | Match / No match / Unable to search | [Name] | [Date/Time] |

 5.6. If a match is found, immediately escalate to the Security Operations Centre Lead and follow the Cyber Security Incident Response Procedure.

6. **Assess exposure and control coverage**

 6.1. For relevant or partially relevant intelligence, the analyst coordinates with technical owners to assess exposure.

 6.2. The assessment must consider:

 - Whether affected software, protocols, services, or configurations are present.
 - Whether security patches or compensating controls are already in place.
 - Whether network segmentation limits exposure.
 - Whether privileged access paths could be abused.
 - Whether multi-factor authentication is enforced where applicable.
 - Whether transaction controls would detect or prevent fraudulent activity.
 - Whether monitoring rules already detect the described behaviour.
 - Whether backup, recovery, and business continuity arrangements are adequate for the scenario.
 - Whether third-party providers could be affected.

 6.3. If exposure cannot be confirmed, the analyst must record the uncertainty and escalate to the relevant technical owner for validation.

 6.4. Control gaps must be logged as remediation actions or risk items.

7. **Define response actions**

 7.1. The analyst prepares a response action plan for relevant or partially relevant intelligence.

 7.2. Actions may include:

 - Adding indicators to detection platforms.
 - Blocking malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, or file hashes.
 - Updating firewall, proxy, endpoint, email, or DNS controls.
 - Applying patches or configuration changes.
 - Disabling exposed services.
 - Increasing monitoring of privileged activity.
 - Reviewing recent Swift operator activity.
 - Reviewing payment message anomalies.
 - Increasing scrutiny of high-risk transactions.
 - Updating fraud monitoring scenarios.
 - Revalidating user access to Swift systems.
 - Conducting threat hunting.
 - Notifying third-party service providers.
 - Initiating incident response.
 - Raising a risk acceptance request where remediation is not feasible within target timeframes.

 7.3. Each action must have an owner, target date, priority, and evidence requirement.

 Action plan template:

 | Action ID | Action | Owner | Priority | Target Date | Evidence Required | Status |
 |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
 | [ID] | [Action] | [Role/Name] | Critical / High / Medium / Low | [Date] | [Evidence] | Open / In Progress / Complete / Deferred |

8. **Obtain approval for protective changes**

 8.1. Routine detection updates may be approved by the Security Operations Centre Lead.

 8.2. Changes to production infrastructure, network controls, Swift systems, or payment processing systems must follow the Change Management Procedure unless emergency action is required.

 8.3. Emergency defensive actions may be approved by the Cyber Security Operations Manager, Chief Information Security Officer, or designated incident commander when delay could materially increase risk.

 8.4. Emergency changes must be retrospectively documented and reviewed in accordance with the Change Management Procedure.

 8.5. Any action that may disrupt Swift messaging, payment processing, settlement, reconciliation, or regulatory reporting must be reviewed with Swift Operations and Payment Operations before implementation unless an active compromise requires immediate containment.

9. **Distribute internal intelligence summary**

 9.1. For relevant, partially relevant, Critical, or High severity intelligence, the analyst prepares an internal summary.

 9.2. The summary must be concise, actionable, and tailored to the audience.

 9.3. The summary must not include sensitive source material beyond what recipients need to perform their role.

 9.4. Distribution must be limited to authorised stakeholders.

 Typical distribution:

 | Recipient Group | When Included | Purpose |
 |---|---|---|
 | Security Operations Centre | All actionable intelligence | Monitoring, detection, triage, escalation |
 | Swift Operations | Intelligence affecting Swift infrastructure or operations | Exposure validation and operational action |
 | Payment Operations | Intelligence affecting payment workflows or fraud scenarios | Transaction monitoring and business controls |
 | Fraud Monitoring | Fraud typologies, payment manipulation indicators, mule or beneficiary patterns | Fraud detection and investigation |
 | Infrastructure and Network Teams | Technical indicators, vulnerabilities, configuration issues | Control updates and remediation |
 | Identity and Access Management | Credential, authentication, and privileged access risks | Access review and control hardening |
 | Risk and Compliance | High-impact issues, accepted risks, evidence tracking | Oversight and reporting |
 | Senior Management | Critical items or material business impact | Decision-making and resource support |

 9.5. The internal summary should include:

 - Source and date received.
 - Internal severity.
 - Relevance assessment.
 - Potential impact.
 - Required actions.
 - Owners and target dates.
 - Escalation status.
 - Handling restrictions.

10. **Implement detection and prevention measures**

 10.1. The Security Operations Centre adds relevant indicators and behavioural detection logic to approved monitoring tools where technically feasible.

 10.2. Network or endpoint blocking must be coordinated with the relevant technical owners.

 10.3. Detection logic should be tested to confirm it does not create excessive false positives or disrupt operations.

 10.4. Where indicators are volatile or likely to change, behavioural detection and threat hunting logic should be considered in addition to static indicators.

 10.5. Implemented rules must be documented with:

 - Rule name.
 - Purpose.
 - Intelligence source reference.
 - Systems covered.
 - Date implemented.
 - Owner.
 - Review date.
 - Alert handling instructions.

11. **Conduct threat hunting where required**

 11.1. Threat hunting is required when:

 - The intelligence is assessed as Critical or High.
 - Indicators are incomplete but behaviours are described.
 - Similar organisations have been targeted.
 - There is a plausible attack path into Swift systems.
 - Initial indicator searches identify suspicious activity.
 - Management or the incident commander requests additional assurance.

 11.2. The threat hunt must define:

 - Hypothesis.
 - Systems in scope.
 - Data sources.
 - Time period.
 - Query logic or analytic method.
 - Findings.
 - Follow-up actions.

 Threat hunt record:

 | Field | Required Entry |
 |---|---|
 | Hunt ID | [ID] |
 | Trigger | Swift ISAC intelligence reference |
 | Hypothesis | [Statement] |
 | Scope | [Systems/Data Sources] |
 | Lookback period | [Period] |
 | Analyst | [Name] |
 | Findings | [Summary] |
 | Escalation required | Yes / No |
 | Evidence location | [Repository/Case Link] |

12. **Coordinate with Payment Operations and Fraud Monitoring**

 12.1. Where the intelligence describes fraudulent payment behaviour, message manipulation, account takeover, mule accounts, unusual counterparties, or operational deception, the analyst must notify Payment Operations and Fraud Monitoring.

 12.2. Payment Operations and Fraud Monitoring must assess whether current controls detect the described scenario.

 12.3. Actions may include:

 - Reviewing recent payment messages for similar patterns.
 - Enhancing transaction monitoring scenarios.
 - Applying temporary additional approval checks.
 - Reviewing beneficiary changes.
 - Reviewing unusual payment timing, value, currency, geography, or counterparties.
 - Validating callback or dual-control procedures for high-risk transactions.
 - Confirming reconciliation processes are operating effectively.
 - Briefing relevant payment operations supervisors.

 12.4. Any suspected fraudulent or unauthorised payment must be escalated immediately under the incident response and financial crime procedures.

13. **Engage third parties where applicable**

 13.1. If Swift-related systems are hosted, supported, monitored, or managed by third parties, the analyst must determine whether the intelligence affects those services.

 13.2. Third-party engagement must be coordinated through the contract owner, vendor manager, or service owner.

 13.3. Requests to third parties may include:

 - Confirmation of exposure.
 - Confirmation of patch status.
 - Indicator search results.
 - Monitoring updates.
 - Evidence of control implementation.
 - Confirmation that no compromise has been identified.
 - Planned remediation dates.

 13.4. Third-party responses must be retained with the intelligence case record.

 13.5. If a third party cannot provide timely assurance for Critical or High severity intelligence, the matter must be escalated to the Cyber Security Operations Manager and Vendor Risk Manager.

14. **Escalate suspected compromise**

 14.1. If intelligence review, indicator searches, threat hunting, fraud monitoring, or operational checks identify signs of compromise, the Security Operations Centre Lead must initiate incident triage.

 14.2. Signs of compromise may include:

 - Matching indicators on Swift-related systems.
 - Unexpected administrative access.
 - Unauthorised changes to Swift configurations.
 - Suspicious message creation, modification, approval, or release.
 - Unusual remote access activity.
 - Endpoint malware detections.
 - Unexplained service failures or log tampering.
 - Evidence of credential theft.
 - Fraudulent or suspicious payment activity.
 - Attempts to disable monitoring or security controls.

 14.3. Once an incident is suspected, incident handling takes priority over routine intelligence processing.

 14.4. The intelligence case remains open and linked to the incident record.

15. **Track remediation to completion**

 15.1. The assigned analyst or case owner tracks all action items until completion, approved deferral, or risk acceptance.

 15.2. Action owners must provide evidence that actions have been completed.

 Acceptable evidence may include:

 - Screenshots of updated security rules.
 - Change records.
 - Vulnerability scan results.
 - Patch deployment reports.
 - Configuration exports.
 - Log search results.
 - Threat hunt reports.
 - Access review records.
 - Payment monitoring rule changes.
 - Third-party assurance responses.
 - Incident records.
 - Management approvals.

 15.3. Overdue Critical or High actions must be escalated to the Cyber Security Operations Manager.

 15.4. Deferred actions must have a documented reason, compensating controls, revised target date, and approval.

16. **Close the intelligence case**

 16.1. The case may be closed when:

 - The intelligence has been assessed.
 - Relevance has been determined.
 - Indicator searches or exposure assessments have been completed where applicable.
 - Required actions have been completed or formally accepted.
 - Escalations have been resolved or linked to active incident, risk, or change records.
 - Evidence has been stored in the approved repository.
 - The case owner has documented the closure rationale.

 16.2. The case owner updates the final status in the Cyber Threat Intelligence Register.

 16.3. For Critical and High severity intelligence, closure must be reviewed by the Security Operations Centre Lead or Cyber Security Operations Manager.

 Closure record:

 | Field | Required Entry |
 |---|---|
 | Intelligence ID | [ID] |
 | Final severity | Critical / High / Medium / Low |
 | Final relevance | Relevant / Partially relevant / Not currently relevant / Unknown |
 | Actions completed | Yes / No |
 | Incident raised | Yes / No |
 | Risk raised or accepted | Yes / No |
 | Closure summary | [Summary] |
 | Closed by | [Name] |
 | Closure approval | [Name/Role] |
 | Date closed | [Date] |

17. **Report trends and lessons learned**

 17.1. The Cyber Threat Intelligence function prepares periodic summaries of Swift-related intelligence activity.

 17.2. Reporting frequency is monthly, unless the Cyber Security Operations Manager requires more frequent reporting due to heightened threat conditions.

 17.3. The report should include:

 - Number of Swift ISAC items received.
 - Number assessed as relevant or partially relevant.
 - Number by severity.
 - Indicator matches identified.
 - Incidents initiated.
 - Key threat themes.
 - Recurring control gaps.
 - Open and overdue actions.
 - Third-party dependencies.
 - Recommendations for control improvement.

 17.4. Lessons learned from Critical or High items must be considered for updates to monitoring, incident playbooks, fraud controls, training, and Swift security procedures.

## Roles & RACI

### Role descriptions

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Chief Information Security Officer | Provides executive oversight, resolves material escalations, approves significant risk decisions, and ensures adequate resources. |
| Cyber Security Operations Manager | Owns this procedure, ensures operational readiness, manages escalations, and oversees timely response to Swift ISAC intelligence. |
| Security Operations Centre Lead | Coordinates triage, monitoring, indicator searches, threat hunting, and incident escalation. |
| Cyber Threat Intelligence Analyst | Reviews Swift ISAC information, assesses relevance, prepares summaries, creates action plans, and maintains records. |
| Swift Security Officer | Maintains Swift security contact details, ensures approved Swift ISAC access, and coordinates with Swift Operations on applicable items. |
| Swift Operations Manager | Assesses operational impact to Swift systems, supports remediation, and validates actions affecting Swift infrastructure. |
| Payment Operations Manager | Assesses payment process impact, implements temporary or permanent operational controls, and escalates suspicious payment activity. |
| Fraud Monitoring Lead | Reviews fraud-related intelligence, tunes fraud detection scenarios, and coordinates suspicious transaction review. |
| Infrastructure and Network Teams | Validate technical exposure, implement patches, configuration changes, network blocks, and supporting controls. |
| Identity and Access Management Lead | Reviews access-related intelligence, validates privileged access controls, and implements access changes. |
| Vulnerability Management Lead | Confirms exposure to vulnerabilities, tracks remediation, and provides scan or patch evidence. |
| Incident Response Manager | Takes over coordination when suspected compromise or active incident criteria are met. |
| Vendor Risk Manager | Coordinates third-party assurance where vendors support Swift-related systems or services. |
| Risk and Compliance Manager | Reviews risk treatment, maintains evidence for assurance, and supports management reporting. |
| Internal Audit | Independently reviews adherence to this procedure as part of planned assurance activities. |

### RACI matrix

| Activity | CISO | Cyber Security Operations Manager | SOC Lead | CTI Analyst | Swift Security Officer | Swift Operations | Payment Operations | Fraud Monitoring | Infrastructure / Network | IAM | Vulnerability Management | Incident Response | Vendor Risk | Risk & Compliance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maintain Swift ISAC access | I | A | C | I | R | C | I | I | I | I | I | I | I | C |
| Receive and log intelligence | I | A | C | R | C | I | I | I | I | I | I | I | I | I |
| Verify authenticity and handling restrictions | I | A | C | R | C | I | I | I | I | I | I | I | I | C |
| Perform triage and severity assessment | I | A | R | R | C | C | C | C | C | C | C | C | I | C |
| Assess relevance to Swift environment | I | A | C | R | C | R | C | C | C | C | C | I | C | I |
| Search indicators of compromise | I | A | R | R | I | C | C | C | C | C | C | C | I | I |
| Conduct threat hunting | I | A | R | R | I | C | I | C | C | C | C | C | I | I |
| Define response action plan | I | A | R | R | C | C | C | C | C | C | C | C | C | C |
| Implement technical controls | I | A | C | C | I | C | I | I | R | R | R | I | C | I |
| Implement payment or fraud controls | I | A | I | C | I | C | R | R | I | I | I | C | I | C |
| Escalate suspected compromise | I | A | R | R | C | C | C | C | C | C | C | R | I | C |
| Coordinate third-party assurance | I | A | C | C | C | C | I | I | C | C | C | I | R | C |
