| 13 | Managed projects | Delivery predictability | CIO, Business Leaders, PMO | Projects are planned, controlled and closed with clear accountability |
| 14 | Managed changes | Controlled change | CIO, Operations, Business Leaders | Technology changes are assessed, approved, implemented and reviewed to reduce disruption |
| 15 | Managed enterprise architecture | Simplification and future readiness | CIO, Architecture, Finance, Business Leaders | Technology decisions follow architectural direction and reduce unnecessary complexity |

### 7. Current-State Observations

The analysis identified several recurring themes in the current state.

| Observation | Evidence / Source | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Technology governance forums exist but decision rights are not consistently documented | Stakeholder interviews; committee material review | Decisions may be delayed, duplicated or escalated inconsistently |
| Investment approval is more mature than benefits realisation tracking | Portfolio review; Finance input | The organisation may not be able to confirm whether expected value is achieved |
| Risk reporting is fragmented across cyber, operations, projects and suppliers | Risk register review; stakeholder interviews | Executive management may lack an integrated view of technology risk |
| Service levels are not consistently defined for all business-critical services | Service reporting review; business stakeholder input | Service expectations may be unclear or difficult to enforce |
| Data ownership is inconsistent across key datasets | Data governance review; business workshops | Data quality and accountability issues may affect reporting and compliance |
| Supplier oversight varies by contract size and business owner maturity | Procurement review; risk input | Critical third-party dependencies may not be managed consistently |
| Continuity arrangements exist for some services but testing coverage is variable | Continuity documentation review | Recovery confidence may be overstated for some critical services |
| Audit and compliance evidence is often assembled manually | Compliance and internal audit input | Assurance activities may be inefficient and reactive |
| Project prioritisation is affected by capacity constraints and competing business demands | Portfolio and stakeholder review | Delivery predictability and strategic focus may be reduced |
| Technology workforce planning is not consistently linked to future demand | HR and CIO input | Skills gaps may affect security, delivery, data and operational performance |

### 8. Risk and Impact Summary

| Risk Area | Description | Likelihood | Impact | Overall Concern |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Strategic misalignment | Technology spend and delivery may not consistently support enterprise priorities | Medium | High | High |
| Benefits leakage | Approved initiatives may not realise expected business value | Medium | High | High |
| Cybersecurity exposure | Security control gaps or inconsistent oversight may increase likelihood of incidents | Medium | High | High |
| Service disruption | Critical services may experience outages, performance degradation or recovery failures | Medium | High | High |
| Data quality failure | Inaccurate or inconsistent data may affect decisions, reporting or compliance | Medium | Medium / High | Medium / High |
| Supplier dependency | Critical outsourced services may not be governed with sufficient performance and risk oversight | Medium | High | High |
| Compliance failure | Incomplete evidence or unclear control ownership may affect regulatory or audit outcomes | Medium | High | High |
| Change disruption | Poorly controlled changes may cause avoidable incidents or operational instability | Medium | Medium / High | Medium / High |
| Resource constraint | Skills and capacity limitations may delay priority initiatives or weaken controls | Medium | Medium | Medium |
| Governance inefficiency | Unclear roles and forums may slow decisions and reduce accountability | Medium | Medium / High | Medium / High |

## Analysis

### Overall Assessment

The organisation has a clear need to strengthen governance and management practices for information and technology. The stakeholder input indicates that the highest-value implementation focus should be placed on governance structure, value delivery, risk optimisation, strategic alignment, portfolio management, security, data, service reliability and resilience.

The findings suggest that the organisation is not starting from a blank position. Existing governance forums, policies, risk practices, project processes and operational controls provide a foundation. However, these practices require better integration, clearer accountability and stronger measurement to meet stakeholder expectations.

The most important gap is not the absence of activity, but the inconsistent connection between governance decisions, business outcomes, risk appetite, technology delivery and performance reporting. COBIT implementation should therefore be positioned as an operating model improvement rather than a documentation exercise.

### Key Patterns

#### 1. Governance Accountability Requires Clarification

Stakeholders identified uncertainty around who makes which information and technology decisions, when decisions must be escalated, and how competing priorities are resolved. This affects portfolio prioritisation, risk acceptance, security exceptions, architecture decisions and supplier-related decisions.

A formal governance model should clarify:

- Decision-making bodies and their mandates.
- Authority levels and escalation paths.
- Ownership of enterprise information and technology outcomes.
- Accountability for risk, value, resources and performance.
- Reporting responsibilities to executive management and the board.

#### 2. Value Delivery Needs More Discipline After Approval

The organisation appears to place reasonable emphasis on initiative approval, but benefits tracking after implementation is less consistent. This creates a risk that technology investment decisions are justified by expected benefits that are not later measured or realised.

Improvement should focus on:

- Mandatory benefits profiles for significant initiatives.
- Named business benefits owners.
- Baseline measures before implementation.
- Post-implementation benefit reviews.
- Reporting of realised, delayed and unrealised benefits.
- Integration of benefits data into portfolio governance.

#### 3. Risk Reporting Should Be Integrated

Technology risk information is available from multiple sources, including cybersecurity, operations, projects, suppliers, audit and compliance. However, the lack of an integrated technology risk view limits the ability of senior management to understand cumulative exposure and make risk-based decisions.

An improved model should include:

- Common risk taxonomy for technology-related risks.
- Risk appetite linkage.
- Consistent risk scoring and escalation.
- Key risk indicators.
- Risk treatment tracking.
- Integration with enterprise risk management.
- Board-level reporting for material risks.

#### 4. Service Management Requires Stronger Business Alignment

Business stakeholders expressed a need for clearer service expectations, more meaningful service reporting and better handling of recurring issues. Technology service management should be aligned with business-critical processes rather than only technical components.

Improvement should include:

- Defined business-facing services.
- Service owners and business owners.
- Service level expectations and performance measures.
- Incident, problem and change trend analysis.
- Regular service review meetings.
- Capacity, availability and continuity planning for critical services.

#### 5. Data Governance Is a Material Business Enabler

Data quality and ownership issues affect reporting, compliance, analytics and management decision-making. Stakeholders expect business-critical data to be treated as an enterprise asset with defined ownership and controls.

Improvement should include:

- Identification of critical data domains.
- Assignment of business data owners and stewards.
- Data quality rules and monitoring.
- Data classification and protection requirements.
- Data lifecycle, retention and disposal expectations.
- Issue management for data defects.
- Integration with reporting, analytics and compliance processes.

#### 6. Third-Party Risk Requires Consistent Oversight

Supplier dependency is increasing, particularly for cloud, managed services and specialised platforms. Supplier oversight practices should be risk-based and aligned to service criticality, data sensitivity and operational dependency.

Improvement should include:

- Supplier criticality classification.
- Clear contract ownership.
- Service performance reporting.
- Security and resilience obligations.
- Right-to-audit or assurance evidence arrangements.
- Exit and transition planning for critical services.
- Periodic supplier risk reviews.

### Prioritisation Logic

The recommended priority objectives were selected based on four main considerations:

| Consideration | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Stakeholder importance | Objectives linked to repeated and high-criticality stakeholder needs were prioritised |
| Risk reduction | Objectives that address material cyber, operational, compliance, supplier and continuity risks were prioritised |
| Value contribution | Objectives that improve investment outcomes, benefits realisation and strategic alignment were prioritised |
| Foundation dependency | Objectives that enable other practices, such as governance structure and strategy management, were prioritised early |

### Implementation Implications

The analysis indicates that the first phase of COBIT implementation should focus on establishing the governance foundation and improving visibility over the highest-risk and highest-value areas. Attempting to implement all objectives at once would likely dilute management attention and reduce effectiveness.

A phased implementation approach is recommended:

| Phase | Focus | Indicative Timeframe | Expected Outputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | Governance foundation and prioritised objective design | Months 1-3 | Governance model, objective owners, reporting structure, initial performance measures, implementation roadmap |
| Phase 2 | Value, risk, portfolio, security and service improvements | Months 4-9 | Portfolio controls, benefits tracking, integrated risk reporting, security governance improvements, service level framework |
| Phase 3 | Data, supplier, continuity and operational maturity improvements | Months 10-15 | Data ownership model, supplier risk process, continuity testing improvements, operational performance reporting |
| Phase 4 | Measurement, assurance and continuous improvement | Months 16-18 | KPI and risk indicator dashboards, assurance plan, management reviews, improvement backlog |

## Recommendations & Actions

### Recommended Actions

| Action ID | Recommendation | Owner | Priority | Target Date | Expected Deliverable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RA-01 | Establish or confirm the enterprise governance structure for information and technology, including committees, mandates, decision rights and escalation paths | [Executive Sponsor / CIO / GRC] | High | [Date] | Approved governance operating model |
| RA-02 | Appoint accountable owners for each priority governance and management objective | [Executive Sponsor] | High | [Date] | Objective ownership matrix |
| RA-03 | Define the first-phase COBIT implementation roadmap using the priority objectives in this report | [CIO / GRC / PMO] | High | [Date] | Approved implementation roadmap |
| RA-04 | Develop a performance measurement model covering value, risk, resources, delivery, service and compliance outcomes | [CIO / GRC / Finance] | High | [Date] | KPI and reporting framework |
| RA-05 | Implement a benefits realisation process for significant technology-enabled investments | [Finance / PMO / Business Owners] | High | [Date] | Benefits management process and reporting template |
| RA-06 | Create an integrated technology risk reporting process aligned with enterprise risk management | [Risk / CIO / Security] | High | [Date] | Technology risk dashboard and escalation process |
| RA-07 | Define business-facing technology services and agree service ownership, service expectations and review cadence | [CIO / Service Owners / Business Leaders] | High | [Date] | Service catalogue and service review framework |
| RA-08 | Establish a data governance model for critical data domains, including ownership, quality and protection responsibilities | [Data Governance Lead / Business Owners] | High | [Date] | Data ownership register and data governance charter |
| RA-09 | Strengthen supplier governance for critical technology suppliers using a risk-based oversight model | [Procurement / CIO / Risk / Legal] | Medium / High | [Date] | Supplier criticality register and review process |
| RA-10 | Validate continuity and recovery arrangements for business-critical technology services | [Business Continuity / CIO / Operations] | High | [Date] | Continuity test plan and remediation tracker |
| RA-11 | Standardise project and change governance requirements for technology-enabled initiatives | [PMO / CIO / Change Manager] | Medium / High | [Date] | Project and change governance standard |
| RA-12 | Prepare an assurance plan for priority objectives to validate design and operating effectiveness | [Internal Audit / GRC / Risk] | Medium / High | [Date] | Assurance and review plan |

### Priority Objective Implementation Actions

| Priority Objective | Immediate Action | Success Indicator |
|---|---|---|
| Ensured governance framework setting and maintenance | Document governance forums, decision rights, roles and reporting lines | Governance model approved and operating with scheduled reporting |
| Ensured benefits delivery | Require benefits profiles and named benefits owners for significant initiatives | Benefits are tracked and reported after implementation |
| Ensured risk optimisation | Consolidate cyber, operational, project, supplier and data risks into an integrated view | Executive management receives regular technology risk reporting |
| Managed strategy | Align technology strategy and roadmap to enterprise strategic priorities | Technology roadmap approved and linked to business outcomes |
| Managed portfolio | Apply consistent prioritisation criteria across initiatives | Portfolio decisions reflect value, risk, capacity and strategic fit |
| Managed security | Confirm security governance, risk reporting and control improvement priorities | Security risks and remediation actions are visible and tracked |
| Managed data | Identify critical data domains and assign owners | Data ownership and quality responsibilities are formally assigned |
| Managed service agreements | Define business-facing services and service expectations | Service reviews are conducted using agreed measures |
| Managed operations | Strengthen operational monitoring, incident trends and problem management | Recurring incidents reduce and operational reporting improves |
| Managed continuity | Validate recovery requirements and test coverage for critical services | Recovery plans are tested and gaps are remediated |

### Proposed Objective Ownership Matrix

| Objective Area | Accountable Owner | Supporting Functions | Oversight Body |
|---|---|---|---|
| Governance framework | [Executive Sponsor] | CIO, GRC, Risk, Legal, Internal Audit | [Governance Committee] |
| Benefits delivery | [Chief Financial Officer / Business Sponsor] | PMO, CIO, Finance, Business Owners | [Investment Committee] |
| Risk optimisation | [Chief Risk Officer] | CIO, Security, Compliance, Internal Audit | [Risk Committee] |
| Technology strategy | [Chief Information Officer] | Business Leaders, Architecture, Finance | [Executive Committee] |
| Portfolio management | [Portfolio Owner / PMO Lead] | CIO, Finance, Business Sponsors | [Portfolio Committee] |
| Security | [Chief Information Security Officer] | CIO, Risk, Legal, HR, Operations | [Security Committee] |
| Data | [Chief Data Officer / Data Governance Lead] | Data Owners, Legal, Compliance, Security | [Data Governance Committee] |
| Service management | [Head of IT Service Management] | Service Owners, Operations, Business Representatives | [Service Review Board] |
| Operations | [Head of Technology Operations] | Infrastructure, Applications, Security, Service Desk | [Operational Review Forum] |
| Continuity | [Business Continuity Manager] | CIO, Operations, Risk, Business Owners | [Resilience Committee] |
| Supplier management | [Head of Procurement / Vendor Management] | CIO, Legal, Risk, Security | [Supplier Governance Forum] |

### Suggested Performance Measures

| Measurement Area | Example Measure | Reporting Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Governance effectiveness | Percentage of key information and technology decisions made through approved governance forums | Quarterly |
| Benefits delivery | Percentage of significant initiatives with approved benefits profiles and named benefits owners | Monthly / Quarterly |
| Benefits realisation | Percentage of expected benefits realised within agreed timeframe | Quarterly |
| Portfolio alignment | Percentage of portfolio spend mapped to enterprise strategic priorities | Quarterly |
| Risk management | Number of material technology risks outside appetite with approved treatment plans | Monthly / Quarterly |
| Security | Percentage of high-risk security remediation actions completed on time | Monthly |
| Service performance | Percentage of critical services meeting agreed service expectations | Monthly |
| Incident management | Number of recurring high-impact incidents | Monthly |
| Continuity | Percentage of critical services with tested recovery plans within required timeframe | Quarterly |
| Data governance | Percentage of critical data domains with assigned owners and defined quality measures | Quarterly |
| Supplier management | Percentage of critical suppliers reviewed according to risk-based schedule | Quarterly |
| Compliance readiness | Percentage of required control evidence available and current | Quarterly |

### Management Decision Required

Management is requested to:

| Decision | Required By | Decision Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Confirm acceptance of the prioritised governance and management objectives | [Date] | [Executive Sponsor / Governance Committee] |
| Approve the recommended phased implementation approach | [Date] | [Executive Committee] |
| Assign accountable owners for priority objectives | [Date] | [Executive Sponsor] |
| Approve development of the COBIT implementation roadmap | [Date] | [Governance Committee / CIO] |
| Confirm reporting cadence for implementation progress and performance measures | [Date] | [Governance Committee] |

## Distribution & Confidentiality

### Distribution

This report is intended for internal governance, management and assurance use. Distribution is limited to authorised personnel with a legitimate business need.

| Recipient / Group | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Board / Board Committee | Oversight of governance, risk, value and resilience implications |
| Executive Management | Decision-making, prioritisation and resource allocation |
| Governance Committee | Review and oversight of COBIT implementation activities |
| Chief Information Officer and Technology Leadership | Planning and execution of governance and management improvements |
| Risk and Compliance Function | Risk alignment, compliance monitoring and control oversight |
| Finance Function | Investment governance, cost oversight and benefits tracking |
| Security Leadership | Security governance and risk management alignment |
| Data Governance Leadership | Data ownership, quality and lifecycle improvement planning |
| Procurement / Vendor Management | Supplier governance and third-party risk management |
| Internal Audit | Assurance planning and independent review coordination |
| PMO / Portfolio Management Function | Roadmap planning, delivery governance and implementation tracking |

### Confidentiality Requirements

This report is classified as **Internal Confidential** and must be handled in accordance with the organisation’s information handling requirements.

The report may contain sensitive information relating to:

- Governance structures and decision-making.
- Technology risks and control gaps.
- Cybersecurity and resilience priorities.
- Supplier dependencies.
- Investment and portfolio performance.
- Internal audit, compliance and remediation activities.
- Strategic technology direction.

Recipients must:

- Not distribute the report outside the approved recipient list without authorisation from [Report Owner / Executive Sponsor].
- Store the report only in approved repositories or document management systems.
- Avoid copying report content into unsecured communication channels.
- Redact sensitive findings before sharing extracts with third parties.
- Ensure any external sharing is reviewed by Legal, Risk or Compliance as appropriate.
- Retain and dispose of the report in accordance with the organisation’s records retention requirements.

### External Sharing

External sharing is not permitted unless formally approved by [Authorising Role]. Where sharing with external auditors, regulators, consultants or service providers is required, the following conditions apply:

| Requirement | Description |
|---|---|
| Approval | Written approval must be obtained from [Authorising Role] |
| Minimum necessary disclosure | Only relevant sections or extracts should be shared |
| Confidentiality protection | A confidentiality agreement or equivalent obligation must be in place where appropriate |
| Redaction | Sensitive security, risk, supplier or commercial information must be redacted where not required |
| Tracking | External distribution must be recorded by [Document Owner / GRC Function] |

### Review and Maintenance

This report should be reviewed:

- Annually as part of governance planning.
- When the enterprise strategy materially changes.
- Following a major technology incident, cyber incident or business disruption.
- Following significant regulatory, contractual or market changes.
- When there is a major change to the technology operating model, outsourcing arrangement or digital transformation roadmap.
- Before each major phase of the COBIT implementation roadmap.

The report owner is responsible for coordinating updates, validating stakeholder inputs and presenting revised findings to the appropriate governance body.

### Column Guidance

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Assessment ID | Enter a unique identifier for the design factor assessment line, using format DFA-YYYY-NNN, e.g. DFA-2026-001. |
| Assessment Date | Enter the date the design factor assessment was performed, in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| COBIT Design Factor Number | Enter the COBIT 2019 design factor number from 1 to 11 only. |
| COBIT Design Factor Name | Enter one of the COBIT 2019 design factors: Enterprise Strategy; Enterprise Goals; Risk Profile; I&T-Related Issues; Threat Landscape; Compliance Requirements; Role of IT; Sourcing Model for IT; IT Implementation Methods; Technology Adoption Strategy; Enterprise Size. |
| Design Factor Dimension / Attribute | Enter the specific dimension, sub-factor, goal, issue, risk category, or attribute being assessed within the selected design factor, using the terminology from the COBIT 2019 Design Guide or the organisation's approved assessment workbook. |
| COBIT Allowed Rating / Category Used | Enter the rating scale or allowed category set applied for this dimension, such as Importance 1-5, Impact 1-5, Low/Medium/High, Insignificant/Normal/High, Support/Factory/Turnaround/Strategic, Outsourcing/Cloud/Insourced/Hybrid, Agile/DevOps/Traditional, First mover/Follower/Slow adopter, Small/Medium/Large. |
| Assessment Value | Enter the organisation's selected rating, score, percentage, or category for this design factor dimension, consistent with the allowed rating/category used in the previous column. |
| Weight / Importance | Enter the relative weighting or importance applied to this design factor dimension, as a numeric value from 0 to 100 or 1 to 5, according to the organisation's COBIT design factor scoring method. |
| Rationale for Assessment | Enter a concise explanation of why the selected value was assigned, referencing business context, strategy, risk exposure, regulatory obligations, operating model, or technology environment. |
| Evidence / Source Reference | Enter the document, system, report, interview, workshop record, risk register entry, strategy document, audit report, or policy used as evidence; include version/date or link/reference ID where available. |
| Data Owner / Contributor | Enter the role or named stakeholder who provided or owns the input, such as CIO, CISO, CRO, Head of Compliance, Enterprise Architect, CFO, Business Unit Owner, or IT Service Owner. |
| Governance Objective Impact | Enter the COBIT governance or management objectives affected by this factor, using COBIT objective references such as EDM01, APO12, BAI03, DSS05, MEA03; list multiple references separated by semicolons. |
| Management Objective Priority Adjustment | Enter the resulting priority direction for affected COBIT objectives: Increase, Decrease, No Change, or To Be Determined; optionally include a numeric target priority if the COBIT toolkit scoring model is used. |
| Affected Governance System Component | Enter the governance system component impacted: Processes; Organizational Structures; Information Flows and Items; People, Skills and Competencies; Policies and Procedures; Culture, Ethics and Behavior; Services, Infrastructure and Applications. |
| Implication for Governance System Design | Enter the design implication arising from the assessment, such as strengthen objective, simplify objective, add control focus, assign additional accountability, increase assurance, adjust sourcing oversight, or no design change. |
| Assumptions / Constraints | Enter any assumptions, limitations, missing data, dependencies, or boundary conditions that affect the assessment; write Not applicable if none. |
| Validation Status | Enter one of: Draft, Under Review, Validated, Approved, Rejected, Superseded. |
| Approver | Enter the role or name of the person or governance body approving the assessment result, such as CIO, Executive Committee, IT Governance Board, Risk Committee, or Steering Committee. |
| Approval Date | Enter the date the assessment line was approved, in YYYY-MM-DD format; leave blank until approved. |
| Review Notes | Enter reviewer comments, challenge points, required follow-up actions, or decision notes; leave blank if no comments. |

### Maintenance

Owned by the COBIT Governance Lead or Enterprise GRC Manager, with input from IT, risk, compliance, architecture, security, and business stakeholders; updated during initial COBIT 2019 design, after major strategic or operating model changes, and at least annually. Source data should be drawn from the COBIT 2019 Design Guide assessment workbook/toolkit, enterprise strategy, goals cascade, risk register, issue log, compliance obligations register, sourcing records, technology roadmap, architecture repository, and stakeholder workshops.

| Assessment ID | Assessment Period | Assessment Date | COBIT Domain | COBIT Governance/Management Objective ID | COBIT Governance/Management Objective Name | Objective Type | In Scope | Scope Rationale | Business Unit / Process Area | Process Owner | Assessment Facilitator | Assessment Method | COBIT Design Factor / Focus Area Context | Target Capability Level | Target Level Justification | Current Assessed Capability Level | Capability Gap | Level 1 Achievement Rating | Level 1 Evidence Summary | Level 2 Achievement Rating | Level 2 Evidence Summary | Level 3 Achievement Rating | Level 3 Evidence Summary | Level 4 Achievement Rating | Level 4 Evidence Summary | Level 5 Achievement Rating | Level 5 Evidence Summary | Key Practices Assessed | Work Products / Evidence Reviewed | Assessment Findings | Key Weaknesses / Deficiencies | Risk / Business Impact | Recommended Improvement Actions | Action Owner | Action Due Date | Improvement Priority | Management Response | Residual Risk Acceptance | Assessor Conclusion | Approval Status | Approver | Approval Date | Next Reassessment Date |

APO12.02; APO12.03; APO12.04; APO12.05; APO12.06] | [EXAMPLE: Risk register extract EV-001; risk committee minutes EV-002; KRI dashboard EV-003] | [EXAMPLE: Risk process is defined and operating, but quantitative performance management is inconsistent] | [EXAMPLE: Incomplete KRI thresholds and inconsistent business unit risk scoring] | [EXAMPLE: May reduce management's ability to identify deteriorating risk exposure in time] | [EXAMPLE: Define mandatory KRI thresholds and implement monthly exception reporting] | [EXAMPLE: Head of Risk] | [EXAMPLE: 2026-06-30] | [EXAMPLE: High] | [EXAMPLE: Accepted; remediation to be tracked through risk transformation plan] | [EXAMPLE: No] | [EXAMPLE: Target not met; current capability assessed at level 3 with gap to level 4] | [EXAMPLE: Draft] | [EXAMPLE: Chief Risk Officer] | [EXAMPLE: ] | [EXAMPLE: 2026-10-10] |

### Column Guidance

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Assessment ID | Enter a unique identifier for this assessment row, using format COBIT-CA-YYYY-NNN, e.g. COBIT-CA-2026-001. |
| Assessment Period | Enter the period covered by the assessment in format YYYY-MM-DD to YYYY-MM-DD. |
| Assessment Date | Enter the date the assessment conclusion was recorded, in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| COBIT Domain | Enter the COBIT 2019 domain code only: EDM, APO, BAI, DSS, or MEA. |
| COBIT Governance/Management Objective ID | Enter the COBIT 2019 objective reference, e.g. EDM01, APO12, BAI06, DSS05, or MEA01. |
| COBIT Governance/Management Objective Name | Enter the official COBIT 2019 governance or management objective name being assessed. |
| Objective Type | Enter one of: Governance Objective, Management Objective. |
| In Scope | Enter Yes or No to indicate whether this COBIT objective is included in the current assessment scope. |
| Scope Rationale | Enter the reason the objective is included or excluded, referencing business criticality, regulatory need, risk exposure, design factor, or management decision. |
| Business Unit / Process Area | Enter the organisational unit, function, service, or process area to which the assessment applies. |
| Process Owner | Enter the accountable owner for the COBIT objective or process, using name and role/title. |
| Assessment Facilitator | Enter the person or team coordinating the assessment, using name and role/title. |
| Assessment Method | Enter the method used, e.g. Self-assessment, Facilitated workshop, Independent internal assessment, External assessment, or Hybrid. |
| COBIT Design Factor / Focus Area Context | Enter any relevant COBIT 2019 design factors, focus areas, enterprise goals, risk profile, regulatory drivers, or tailoring assumptions that affect the target capability. |
| Target Capability Level | Enter the agreed target capability level as an integer from 0 to 5. |
| Target Level Justification | Explain why the target level is appropriate, referencing risk appetite, enterprise goals, regulatory obligations, service criticality, or stakeholder expectations. |
| Current Assessed Capability Level | Enter the assessed capability level achieved as an integer from 0 to 5, based on the rating rules and evidence. |
| Capability Gap | Enter the numeric difference between target and current capability level, calculated as Target Capability Level minus Current Assessed Capability Level. |
| Level 1 Achievement Rating | Enter the achievement rating for capability level 1 using one of: N - Not achieved, P - Partially achieved, L - Largely achieved, F - Fully achieved, N/A - Not assessed. |
| Level 1 Evidence Summary | Summarise the evidence supporting the level 1 rating, including whether the process achieves its purpose and produces expected outcomes. |
| Level 2 Achievement Rating | Enter the achievement rating for capability level 2 using one of: N - Not achieved, P - Partially achieved, L - Largely achieved, F - Fully achieved, N/A - Not assessed. |
| Level 2 Evidence Summary | Summarise evidence that the process is planned, monitored, adjusted, and work products are appropriately established, controlled, and maintained. |
| Level 3 Achievement Rating | Enter the achievement rating for capability level 3 using one of: N - Not achieved, P - Partially achieved, L - Largely achieved, F - Fully achieved, N/A - Not assessed. |
| Level 3 Evidence Summary | Summarise evidence that the process is defined, standardised, documented, communicated, and deployed consistently across the applicable scope. |
| Level 4 Achievement Rating | Enter the achievement rating for capability level 4 using one of: N - Not achieved, P - Partially achieved, L - Largely achieved, F - Fully achieved, N/A - Not assessed. |
| Level 4 Evidence Summary | Summarise evidence that the process is quantitatively managed using measures, thresholds, performance data, and predictable control of outcomes. |
| Level 5 Achievement Rating | Enter the achievement rating for capability level 5 using one of: N - Not achieved, P - Partially achieved, L - Largely achieved, F - Fully achieved, N/A - Not assessed. |
| Level 5 Evidence Summary | Summarise evidence that the process is continuously improved through innovation, root-cause analysis, optimisation, and measurable improvement outcomes. |
| Key Practices Assessed | List the COBIT practices or activities reviewed for the objective, using COBIT practice references where available, separated by semicolons. |
| Work Products / Evidence Reviewed | List the documents, records, reports, system extracts, tickets, metrics, approvals, meeting minutes, or other evidence reviewed, including evidence IDs or repository links where possible. |

COB-005.title: Gap Analysis (Current vs Target Capability)
COB-005.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [GRC-RPT-COBIT-GAP-001] | 1.0 | [Governance, Risk and Compliance Lead] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | COBIT 2019 | Internal Confidential |

## Purpose

This report presents the results of the current versus target capability gap analysis for the organisation’s implementation of COBIT 2019 governance and management practices.

The report is intended to:

- Identify capability gaps by governance and management objective.
- Compare current performance against the agreed target capability for each objective.
- Highlight key risks arising from the identified gaps.
- Prioritise improvement actions based on business impact, risk exposure, feasibility and dependency.
- Provide management with a practical improvement roadmap to strengthen governance, risk management, control effectiveness, value delivery and performance monitoring.

This report supports management decision-making and provides an evidence-based baseline for the organisation’s COBIT implementation programme.

## Reporting Period & Scope

### Reporting Period

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Assessment period | [Start Date] to [End Date] |
| Fieldwork period | [Start Date] to [End Date] |
| Report date | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| Assessment type | Current versus target capability gap analysis |
| Assessment status | Draft for management review / Final approved report |

### Organisational Scope

This report covers the following organisational areas:

| Area | Included in Scope |
|---|---|
| Corporate governance and executive oversight | Yes |
| Information and technology governance | Yes |
| Enterprise risk management interfaces | Yes |
| IT strategy and portfolio management | Yes |
| Architecture and innovation management | Yes |
| Programme and project management | Yes |
| Service delivery and operations | Yes |
| Information security and cyber risk management | Yes |
| Data management and reporting | Yes |
| Supplier and third-party technology management | Yes |
| Compliance, assurance and internal control monitoring | Yes |

### Business Units and Functions Assessed

The following business units and functions were included:

- [Executive Leadership Team]
- [Board Risk Committee / Technology Committee]
- [Information Technology]
- [Information Security]
- [Enterprise Risk Management]
- [Compliance]
- [Internal Audit]
- [Finance]
- [Procurement]
- [Human Resources]
- [Operations]
- [Data and Analytics]
- [Major Business Unit or Region]

### Systems, Services and Processes Considered

The assessment considered governance and management practices supporting:

- Enterprise technology strategy and investment decisions.
- Technology-enabled business change.
- Operational service delivery.
- Information security and resilience.
- Data governance and reporting.
- Supplier and outsourced service management.
- Risk, compliance and assurance activities.
- Performance measurement and improvement.

Critical platforms and services reviewed included:

| System / Service | Business Criticality | Assessment Coverage |
|---|---:|---|
| [Core Banking / ERP / CRM Platform] | High | Governance, risk, change, service continuity |
| [Identity and Access Management Platform] | High | Security, access governance, monitoring |
| [Cloud Hosting Environment] | High | Supplier management, resilience, operational controls |
| [Data Warehouse / Reporting Platform] | Medium | Data quality, ownership, reporting controls |
| [Service Management Tool] | Medium | Incident, problem, change and service request processes |
| [Project Portfolio Management Tool] | Medium | Investment tracking, delivery oversight |

### Out of Scope

The following items were not assessed in detail:

- Technical penetration testing or vulnerability validation.
- Full internal audit testing of individual controls.
- Legal review of supplier contract terms.
- Financial audit of technology spend.
- Detailed privacy impact assessments for individual applications.
- Detailed maturity assessment of non-technology business processes except where they directly affect technology governance and management.

### Assessment Boundaries

This report provides a management-level capability assessment. It does not certify conformity with any external standard, nor does it replace internal audit, regulatory review or independent assurance activities.

## Executive Summary

The assessment found that the organisation has established several foundational governance and management practices for information and technology, including executive-level technology oversight, defined service management processes, a developing risk management function and evidence of structured project governance. However, capability remains uneven across objectives, with stronger performance in operational service delivery than in integrated governance, benefits realisation, data governance, supplier oversight and performance measurement.

The overall current capability is assessed as **Developing**, while the agreed target state for most priority objectives is **Managed and Measured**. This creates a material gap between current operating practices and the level of governance discipline required to support the organisation’s strategic reliance on information and technology.

### Overall Assessment Result

| Dimension | Current Position | Target Position | Gap Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Governance direction and oversight | Partially established | Consistently directed, measured and challenged | Governance bodies exist but decision rights, escalation routes and performance reporting are not yet consistently embedded. |
| Strategy and investment alignment | Developing | Integrated with business planning and benefits tracking | Technology initiatives are linked to business objectives, but portfolio trade-offs and benefits realisation are inconsistent. |
| Risk and security governance | Developing | Risk-based, measurable and enterprise-integrated | Security and technology risks are tracked, but risk appetite, treatment ownership and reporting require stronger integration. |
| Service delivery and operations | Generally established | Measured and continuously improved | Core operational processes exist, but root cause analysis, service performance reporting and process quality metrics are inconsistent. |
| Data, information and reporting | Partially established | Accountable, governed and quality-controlled | Data ownership, quality rules and reporting controls are immature across business functions. |
| Supplier and third-party management | Partially established | Lifecycle-based and risk-tiered | Key suppliers are managed operationally, but risk-based due diligence, performance review and exit planning are not consistently applied. |
| Assurance and continuous improvement | Developing | Evidence-based and risk-prioritised | Internal reviews occur, but assurance planning is not yet fully aligned to technology risk and control priorities. |

### Summary of Capability Ratings

| Capability Level | Description Used in This Report |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Not performed - the objective is largely absent or not consistently executed. |
| 1 | Initial - activities occur informally or reactively, with limited consistency. |
| 2 | Developing - practices are defined in parts of the organisation but not consistently embedded or measured. |
| 3 | Established - practices are documented, assigned and generally followed. |
| 4 | Managed and measured - performance is monitored, risks are actively managed and outcomes are predictable. |
| 5 | Optimised - practices are continuously improved using evidence, automation and benchmarking. |

### Overall Current vs Target Capability

| Objective Group | Average Current Capability | Average Target Capability | Average Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Governance and oversight | 2.1 | 3.8 | 1.7 |
| Strategy, architecture and portfolio | 2.3 | 3.7 | 1.4 |
| Build, acquisition and change | 2.6 | 3.6 | 1.0 |
| Service delivery and operations | 2.8 | 3.7 | 0.9 |
| Security, risk and compliance | 2.4 | 4.0 | 1.6 |
| Monitoring, assurance and performance | 2.0 | 3.8 | 1.8 |

### High-Priority Themes

The most significant improvement themes are:

1. **Clarify governance decision rights and accountability**
 - Management committees are active, but accountabilities for technology value, risk acceptance, investment trade-offs and performance challenge are not consistently documented or enforced.

2. **Strengthen performance measurement**
 - Current reporting focuses on activity and status rather than outcomes, value delivery, risk reduction and service quality trends.

3. **Embed risk-based prioritisation**
 - Technology decisions are not consistently prioritised using agreed business impact, risk appetite, regulatory exposure, operational resilience and customer impact criteria.

4. **Improve benefits realisation**
 - Approved initiatives do not consistently define measurable benefits, owners, baselines, target outcomes and post-implementation review checkpoints.

5. **Mature supplier governance**
 - Supplier performance is reviewed for major providers, but third-party risk tiering, contractual control monitoring, concentration risk and exit readiness require improvement.

6. **Formalise data ownership and quality management**
 - Data governance is not sufficiently embedded across business functions, resulting in inconsistent reporting quality, unclear accountability and manual reconciliation effort.

7. **Increase assurance coverage over technology controls**
 - Assurance activities are fragmented across risk, compliance, internal audit and management review, with limited integrated planning against the highest technology risks.

### Priority Risk Statement

If the identified gaps are not remediated, the organisation may experience:

- Delayed or poorly prioritised technology investment decisions.
- Inability to demonstrate that technology spend delivers intended business value.
- Increased exposure to cyber, operational resilience and third-party failures.
- Inconsistent compliance evidence and audit findings.
- Weak escalation of technology risk to accountable decision-makers.
- Inefficient manual workarounds caused by unclear processes and fragmented data ownership.
- Reduced confidence in management reporting and board oversight.

### Management Conclusion

The organisation has a credible starting point for COBIT implementation, but further work is required to move from process awareness to consistent, measurable and accountable governance. The recommended improvement programme should focus first on objectives with the highest business impact, largest capability gaps and strongest dependency value for other objectives.

## Methodology

### Assessment Approach

The assessment used a structured current versus target capability approach. Each governance and management objective was evaluated against defined practices, evidence of execution, consistency of application, assigned accountability, measurement, risk integration and continuous improvement.

The approach included:

- Review of relevant governance documentation, policies, procedures, committee materials and management reports.
- Interviews and workshops with accountable executives, process owners and control performers.
- Sampling of process evidence such as project approvals, risk registers, service reports, supplier reviews and change records.
- Comparison of current practices against the organisation’s agreed COBIT-aligned target state.
- Rating of current capability and target capability for each assessed objective.
- Identification of gaps, root causes, risk implications and practical improvement actions.
- Prioritisation of actions using impact, urgency, dependency and feasibility criteria.

### Evidence Sources Reviewed

| Evidence Category | Examples Reviewed |
|---|---|
| Governance records | Committee terms of reference, meeting packs, decisions, action logs, escalation records |
| Strategy and planning | Technology strategy, business plans, architecture principles, roadmaps, investment cases |
| Portfolio and project records | Business cases, project status reports, delivery dashboards, benefits registers, post-implementation reviews |
| Risk and compliance | Risk registers, issue logs, control self-assessments, audit findings, compliance attestations |
| Security management | Security policies, risk assessments, incident reports, awareness records, vulnerability summaries |
| Service management | Incident, problem, change, request, availability and service level reports |
| Supplier management | Contracts, service reviews, supplier scorecards, due diligence records, exit plans |
| Data governance | Data ownership records, data quality reports, reporting catalogues, reconciliation logs |
| Assurance records | Internal audit reports, management testing, remediation tracking, control monitoring reports |

### Stakeholders Consulted

| Stakeholder Group | Consultation Method |
|---|---|
| Executive sponsors | Interviews |
| Technology leadership | Interviews and evidence review |
| Information security leadership | Interviews and control walkthroughs |
| Enterprise risk management | Interviews and risk register review |
| Compliance function | Interviews and obligation mapping review |
| Internal audit | Interview and assurance plan review |
| Business process owners | Workshops |
| Project and portfolio managers | Workshops and sample review |
| Service management team | Process walkthroughs |
| Procurement and supplier management | Interviews and supplier file review |

### Rating Method

Each objective was rated using a six-level capability scale from **0** to **5**. Ratings were based on the extent to which practices are performed, documented, assigned, measured, integrated and improved.

A rating was assigned based on the overall strength of evidence, not solely on verbal confirmation. Where evidence was incomplete or inconsistent across business units, the lower rating was applied unless compensating controls were demonstrated.

### Target Capability Setting

Target capability levels were set using the following considerations:

- Business criticality of the related processes.
- Regulatory and contractual expectations.
- Risk appetite and operational resilience needs.
- Dependency on technology for customer, financial and operational outcomes.
- Current and planned digital transformation activity.
- Management’s stated governance objectives.
- Practical implementation capacity over the next planning cycle.

Not every objective requires the highest possible capability. Target capability was assigned based on the level needed to provide effective governance, reliable outcomes and proportionate assurance.

### Prioritisation Criteria

Improvement actions were prioritised using the following criteria:

| Priority Factor | Description |
|---|---|
| Business impact | Degree to which the gap affects strategic outcomes, customers, operations or revenue. |
| Risk exposure | Degree to which the gap increases security, resilience, compliance, financial or reputational risk. |
| Dependency value | Whether closing the gap enables improvement in other objectives. |
| Urgency | Time sensitivity due to audit findings, regulatory expectations, incidents or transformation deadlines. |
| Feasibility | Practical ability to implement within available resources, funding and organisational capacity. |
| Evidence gap | Extent to which current practice cannot be demonstrated through reliable records. |

### Priority Definitions

| Priority | Definition | Expected Management Response |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Significant risk to business objectives, resilience, compliance or governance effectiveness. Immediate executive attention required. | Formal remediation plan within 30 days. |
| High | Material gap that weakens governance, risk management or control reliability. | Remediation plan within 60 days. |
| Medium | Improvement required to increase consistency, efficiency or measurability. | Planned remediation within 90 days. |
| Low | Enhancement opportunity with limited immediate risk. | Consider for continuous improvement backlog. |

### Limitations

The assessment was conducted using available evidence and stakeholder input during the reporting period. The findings represent the observed state at the time of assessment. Subsequent changes to systems, processes, organisational structure, personnel or risk profile may affect the continued accuracy of the results.

## Detailed Findings / Results (with structure)

### 1. Governance and Oversight Objectives

#### 1.1 Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance

| Assessment Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Current capability | 2 - Developing |
| Target capability | 4 - Managed and measured |
| Gap | 2 |
| Priority | High |
| Overall status | Governance structures exist, but the framework is not yet consistently defined, measured or reviewed. |

**Current state**

The organisation has established executive committees and management forums that discuss technology strategy, operational performance, risk and major initiatives. However, the end-to-end governance framework for information and technology is not fully documented. Decision rights, delegated authorities, escalation thresholds and the relationship between committees are not consistently understood.

**Target state**

The organisation should operate a defined and integrated governance framework that sets clear accountabilities, decision rights, escalation paths, reporting expectations and review cycles for information and technology.

**Key gaps**

| Gap | Impact |
|---|---|
| Governance roles and decision rights are not fully documented. | Decisions may be delayed, duplicated or made without the right authority. |
| Committee mandates overlap in areas such as risk, investment and service performance. | Accountability for challenge and approval is unclear. |
| Governance performance is not measured. | Management cannot determine whether governance forums are effective. |
| Action tracking and closure evidence are inconsistent. | Important governance decisions may not be implemented or verified. |

**Evidence observed**

- Committee terms of reference exist for several forums.
- Technology strategy updates are presented to executive stakeholders.
- Meeting minutes and action logs are retained inconsistently.
- Governance reporting varies in format and depth between committees.

**Risk implication**

Weaknesses in governance design may result in unclear accountability for technology outcomes, inconsistent escalation of risks and inefficient decision-making.

---

#### 1.2 Benefits Delivery

| Assessment Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Current capability | 2 - Developing |
| Target capability | 4 - Managed and measured |
| Gap | 2 |
| Priority | High |
| Overall status | Benefits are discussed during investment approval, but tracking after delivery is inconsistent. |

**Current state**

Business cases generally include expected benefits, but these are not always expressed in measurable terms. Benefit owners are not consistently assigned, and post-implementation reviews are not performed for all material initiatives.

**Target state**

Each significant technology-enabled investment should have defined benefits, baseline measures, target outcomes, accountable owners and scheduled reviews to confirm whether benefits were realised.

**Key gaps**

| Gap | Impact |
|---|---|
| Benefit definitions vary in quality and measurability. | Difficult to determine whether investments deliver intended value. |
| Benefit ownership often transfers informally after project closure. | Accountability may be lost once delivery teams move on. |
| Post-implementation reviews are inconsistent. | Lessons learned and value outcomes are not reliably captured. |
| Benefits reporting is not integrated into portfolio governance. | Executives may approve new investment without clear visibility of previous return. |

**Evidence observed**

- Business case templates include a benefits section.
- Several projects track financial benefits during approval.
- Limited evidence of benefits validation after implementation.
- No consolidated benefits realisation dashboard was identified.

**Risk implication**

The organisation may continue funding initiatives without sufficient evidence of value delivery or may miss opportunities to optimise investment outcomes.

---

#### 1.3 Risk Optimisation

| Assessment Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Current capability | 2 - Developing |
| Target capability | 4 - Managed and measured |
| Gap | 2 |
| Priority | Critical |
| Overall status | Technology risks are identified, but risk appetite, treatment tracking and governance reporting require strengthening. |

**Current state**

Technology and security risks are captured in risk registers, and significant risks are periodically reported. However, there is inconsistent linkage between technology risks, business impacts, risk appetite statements, treatment plans and executive risk acceptance.

**Target state**

Technology risk management should be integrated with enterprise risk management, using clear risk ownership, defined appetite, measurable treatment plans and timely escalation to accountable governance bodies.

**Key gaps**

| Gap | Impact |
|---|---|
| Risk appetite is not consistently translated into technology decision criteria. | Management may accept or reject risk inconsistently. |
| Risk treatment plans lack measurable milestones in some cases. | Remediation progress may be difficult to validate. |
| Risk ownership is sometimes assigned to technology teams without business accountability. | Business impact and acceptance may not be properly governed. |
| Reporting focuses on risk status but not always trend, control effectiveness or residual exposure. | Executives may not receive sufficient insight to challenge risk decisions. |

**Evidence observed**

- Enterprise risk register includes technology and cyber risks.
- Security risk assessments are performed for selected systems and projects.
- Risk treatment actions are tracked, but evidence quality varies.
- Board-level risk reporting includes cyber themes, but operational technology risk detail is limited.

**Risk implication**

Without consistent risk appetite alignment and treatment tracking, the organisation may retain unacceptable technology risk or misallocate resources to lower-priority issues.

---

#### 1.4 Resource Optimisation

| Assessment Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Current capability | 2 - Developing |
| Target capability | 3 - Established |
| Gap | 1 |
| Priority | Medium |
| Overall status | Resource planning exists, but capacity, skills and sourcing decisions are not fully integrated. |

**Current state**

Technology resource needs are considered during annual budgeting and major project planning. However, there is limited consolidated visibility of capacity constraints, skills gaps, contractor dependency and competing demand across operations and change delivery.

**Target state**

The organisation should maintain an integrated view of people, skills, funding, tools and supplier capacity required to deliver agreed technology outcomes.

**Key gaps**

| Gap | Impact |
|---|---|
| Capacity planning is not consistently linked to portfolio prioritisation. | Teams may become overcommitted, affecting delivery quality and operational stability. |
| Skills inventories are incomplete. | Workforce development and succession planning may be reactive. |
| Contractor and supplier dependency is not always visible at governance level. | Key person or third-party dependency risks may be underestimated. |

**Evidence observed**

- Annual budget planning includes technology resource requests.
- Project plans identify named resources for major initiatives.
- Skills and capacity reporting is fragmented.
- Some teams maintain informal resource forecasts.

**Risk implication**

Resource constraints may affect delivery timelines, service reliability and the organisation’s ability to execute strategic priorities.

---

### 2. Strategy, Architecture and Portfolio Objectives

#### 2.1 Managed Strategy

| Assessment Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Current capability | 3 - Established |
| Target capability | 4 - Managed and measured |
| Gap | 1 |
| Priority | Medium |
| Overall status | Technology strategy exists and is aligned to business priorities, but measurable outcomes and review cycles need improvement. |

**Current state**

The organisation has a technology strategy that identifies major themes such as cloud adoption, data improvement, cyber resilience, automation and digital enablement. The strategy is referenced in investment discussions, but progress measures are not consistently outcome-based.

**Target state**

Technology strategy should be linked to measurable business outcomes, investment priorities, architecture direction, risk appetite and delivery roadmaps.

**Key gaps**

| Gap | Impact |
|---|---|
| Strategy measures focus on initiative completion rather than business outcomes. | Success may be measured by activity rather than value. |
| Strategy refresh triggers are not formally defined. | Strategy may not adapt quickly to business or risk changes. |
| Linkage between strategic themes and portfolio trade-offs is inconsistent. | Investment decisions may not fully reflect strategic priorities. |

**Evidence observed**

- Approved technology strategy document.
- Annual planning cycle references technology themes.
- Portfolio reporting maps some initiatives to strategic objectives.
- Limited evidence of formal strategy performance review.

**Risk implication**

The organisation may execute technology activities without consistently validating whether they are delivering the intended strategic outcomes.

---

#### 2.2 Managed Enterprise Architecture

| Assessment Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Current capability | 2 - Developing |
| Target capability | 3 - Established |
| Gap | 1 |
| Priority | Medium |
| Overall status | Architecture principles exist, but compliance and lifecycle governance are inconsistent. |

**Current state**

Architecture guidance is available for selected domains, including cloud, integration and security. Architectural review occurs for major projects, but not all technology changes are assessed against architecture standards.

**Target state**

Architecture should guide investment, solution design, technology selection and lifecycle management through defined principles, standards, review gates and exception management.

**Key gaps**

## Analysis

### Overall Capability Pattern

The assessment indicates that the organisation is beyond an ad hoc operating model in most technology governance and management areas. Core processes exist, and many activities are performed by capable teams. However, the organisation has not yet consistently embedded the measurement, accountability, evidence and continuous improvement practices required for a managed governance model.

The strongest areas are:

- Project governance for major initiatives.
- Operational service management.
- Change management process definition.
- Technology strategy formulation.
- Basic risk and security management activities.

The weakest areas are:

- Data governance.
- Innovation management.
- Benefits realisation.
- Integrated performance monitoring.
- Supplier lifecycle risk management.
- Technology control monitoring.
- Continuity testing and recovery validation.

### Root Cause Analysis

| Root Cause | Description | Related Findings |
|---|---|---|
| Fragmented accountability | Responsibilities are assigned within functions but not consistently documented across end-to-end governance objectives. | Governance framework, risk optimisation, data, internal control, supplier management |
| Limited outcome-based measurement | Reporting focuses on activities, project status and operational volumes rather than value, risk reduction and control effectiveness. | Benefits delivery, portfolio, performance monitoring, security |
| Manual evidence and reporting | Evidence collection and management reporting rely heavily on spreadsheets and manual consolidation. | Compliance, control monitoring, performance reporting, supplier management |
| Inconsistent process adoption | Defined processes are followed more consistently for high-profile initiatives than for smaller or business-led technology activity. | Projects, requirements, architecture, change, supplier management |
| Weak integration between governance forums | Committees receive related information but do not always operate from a single integrated view of value, risk, resources and performance. | Governance framework, portfolio, risk, performance monitoring |
| Immature data governance | Data ownership, quality and lineage are not sufficiently embedded across business and technology processes. | Data, reporting, compliance, risk analysis |
| Reactive assurance model | Assurance activities identify issues, but monitoring is not yet consistently risk-based, coordinated or predictive. | Internal control monitoring, assurance, compliance |

### Risk Heat Summary
