 - Duration of processing.
 - Types of personal data.
 - Categories of individuals.
 - Permitted processing operations.
 - Approved locations.
 - Approved subprocessors.
 - Retention, deletion and return requirements.
 - Security requirements.
 - Restrictions on reuse, disclosure and onward transfer.

16. **[Organisation Name] shall not permit Processors to use personal data for their own purposes without reassessment.** 
 If a Processor seeks to use personal data for product improvement, benchmarking, analytics, training models, research, marketing, fraud intelligence, security intelligence, service development or any other independent purpose, the business owner shall refer the matter to the Data Protection Officer and Legal before approval. The role determination, privacy notice, lawful basis, contract terms, risk assessment and data subject implications shall be reassessed.

17. **Where [Organisation Name] acts as Processor, it shall process personal data only under documented instructions.** 
 Business units delivering services to customers or other Controllers shall ensure that [Organisation Name]:
 - Processes personal data only as instructed by the Controller.
 - Does not determine the Controller’s purposes.
 - Does not reuse the Controller’s personal data for unrelated internal purposes.
 - Escalates unclear, incomplete, conflicting or unlawful instructions.
 - Maintains records of received instructions.
 - Assists the Controller as agreed.
 - Uses only approved subprocessors.
 - Returns or deletes personal data at the end of services as contractually required.

18. **Joint Controller arrangements shall be formally allocated and transparent.** 
 Where [Organisation Name] is a Joint Controller with another party, the business owner shall ensure that a written arrangement is agreed before processing begins. The arrangement shall clearly allocate responsibility for:
 - Providing privacy information to individuals.
 - Handling data subject requests.
 - Establishing and documenting processing purposes.
 - Managing security responsibilities.
 - Managing personal data breaches.
 - Managing retention and deletion.
 - Responding to regulator queries.
 - Managing third-party processors and service providers.
 - Handling complaints and disputes.
 - Maintaining evidence of compliance.

19. **Individuals shall be informed of the essential allocation of Joint Controller responsibilities.** 
 Where [Organisation Name] participates in joint controllership, the relevant privacy information shall explain the key aspects of the arrangement in clear language, including how individuals may exercise their rights and which party is the primary contact point where applicable.

20. **Independent Controller data sharing shall be governed by appropriate data sharing terms.** 
 Where [Organisation Name] shares personal data with another independent Controller, the arrangement shall be documented through a contract, data sharing agreement, memorandum of understanding, transfer terms or other approved written instrument. The documentation shall address:
 - Purpose of the sharing.
 - Categories of personal data and individuals.
 - Roles of the parties.
 - Transparency responsibilities.
 - Lawful handling of data subject rights.
 - Security requirements.
 - Retention and deletion expectations.
 - Restrictions on onward sharing.
 - Incident notification expectations.
 - International transfer requirements where relevant.
 - Audit, assurance or cooperation requirements where appropriate.

21. **Affiliates and group companies shall be assessed like external parties.** 
 Processing activities involving affiliates, subsidiaries, parent companies, shared service centres or group entities shall be subject to the same role determination requirements as external third-party arrangements. Corporate group membership shall not automatically determine the privacy role.

22. **Platforms, marketplaces, advertising technologies and analytics tools shall receive enhanced scrutiny.** 
 Business owners shall consult the Data Protection Officer before using technologies where providers may independently determine data use, combine data across customers, set tracking rules, conduct profiling, perform measurement, use identifiers, or use data to improve their own services. Role determination for such tools shall consider technical configuration, contractual terms, actual data flows, provider autonomy and user transparency.

23. **Artificial intelligence and machine learning use shall require explicit role assessment.** 
 Any processing involving model training, model tuning, inference, automated recommendations, classification, scoring, generative artificial intelligence, biometric analysis or automated decision support shall include a documented assessment of whether any party uses personal data for its own purposes, whether data is retained by the provider, and whether the provider determines any essential means of processing.

24. **Subprocessor use shall be controlled.** 
 Where [Organisation Name] appoints a Processor, the Processor shall not engage subprocessors without the required written authorisation. The business owner shall ensure that approved subprocessors are recorded, subject to appropriate obligations, and reviewed where they materially affect processing risk.

25. **Role determination shall be integrated into procurement and contracting.** 
 Procurement, Legal and business owners shall ensure that privacy role determination is completed before contracts involving personal data are signed. Contract templates and negotiation positions shall reflect the approved role determination.

26. **Role determination shall be integrated into project and change governance.** 
 Project managers and system owners shall ensure that role determination is included in privacy screening, solution design, system implementation, data migration, integration, vendor onboarding, product launch and change approval processes.

27. **Conflicting contract terms shall be escalated.** 
 Where a supplier, customer, partner or affiliate proposes contractual terms inconsistent with the factual role determination, the matter shall be escalated to the Data Protection Officer and Legal. Processing shall not proceed until the inconsistency is resolved or an approved exception is granted.

28. **Role determination shall be approved according to risk.** 
 Role determinations shall be reviewed and approved in line with the following minimum approval requirements:

 | Processing Scenario | Minimum Approval Required |
 |---|---|
 | Routine internal Controller processing using approved systems and no new third parties | Business Owner |
 | New Processor appointed by [Organisation Name] | Business Owner, Procurement and Legal |
 | New independent Controller data sharing | Business Owner, Legal and Data Protection Officer |
 | Joint Controller arrangement | Business Owner, Legal and Data Protection Officer |
 | [Organisation Name] acting as Processor for a customer | Business Owner and Legal |
 | Supplier seeks to reuse personal data for its own purposes | Legal and Data Protection Officer |
 | High-risk processing, sensitive data, large-scale monitoring, profiling or artificial intelligence | Data Protection Officer and applicable governance forum |
 | Cross-border processing involving new locations or onward transfers | Legal and Data Protection Officer |

29. **Role determinations shall be retained as accountability evidence.** 
 [Organisation Name] shall retain role determination records, associated approvals, contracts, privacy assessments, data sharing terms, instructions and related correspondence for the duration of the processing activity and for [retention period] thereafter, unless a longer retention period is required by law, litigation hold or organisational policy.

30. **Privacy notices and external communications shall align with approved role determinations.** 
 Business owners shall ensure that privacy notices, consent wording, customer communications, employee notices, website disclosures, contractual notices and other external statements accurately reflect the approved role of [Organisation Name] and relevant third parties.

31. **Data subject request handling shall align with role allocation.** 
 Data subject rights processes shall reflect the approved role determination. Where [Organisation Name] acts as Processor, requests received directly from individuals about Controller data shall be handled according to contract instructions and promptly referred or supported as required. Where [Organisation Name] acts as Controller or Joint Controller, requests shall be handled according to assigned responsibilities and applicable internal procedures.

32. **Personal data breach response shall align with role allocation.** 
 Incident response procedures and contracts shall reflect the role of each party. Processors shall notify Controllers promptly of actual or suspected personal data breaches. Controllers and Joint Controllers shall assess notification obligations, coordinate communications and maintain evidence of decisions.

33. **Role determinations shall be reviewed periodically.** 
 The business owner shall review role determinations at least annually for active processing activities and more frequently where risk, processing complexity or business change requires.

34. **Inconsistent or uncertain role determinations shall be escalated.** 
 If the business owner cannot confidently determine the role, or if parties disagree, the matter shall be escalated to the Data Protection Officer and Legal before processing begins or continues.

35. **Training shall be provided to relevant personnel.** 
 Personnel involved in procurement, contracting, product design, data governance, marketing, analytics, vendor management, HR, customer operations, information security and project delivery shall receive appropriate training on role determination requirements.

36. **Evidence shall be available for audit and assurance.** 
 Business owners, Procurement, Legal and the Data Protection Officer shall maintain evidence sufficient to demonstrate that role determinations were performed, approved, implemented and periodically reviewed.

## Roles & Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Board / Executive Management | Provides oversight of privacy governance and ensures that appropriate resources are available to manage data protection roles and obligations. |
| Data Protection Officer | Owns this Policy, advises on role determination, reviews complex or high-risk assessments, supports accountability evidence, monitors compliance, and escalates significant issues. |
| Legal | Reviews and approves contractual arrangements, data processing terms, data sharing terms, joint controller arrangements and disputed role positions. |
| Business Owner | Ensures role determination is completed for each processing activity, provides factual information about the processing, obtains required approvals, maintains inventory records and ensures the approved role is implemented operationally. |
| Process Owner | Maintains day-to-day compliance for the processing activity, ensures instructions and controls are followed, and reports changes that may affect role determination. |
| Procurement | Ensures privacy role assessment is completed before supplier onboarding or contract signature and coordinates privacy, legal and vendor risk review requirements. |
| Vendor Management | Maintains supplier records, supports subprocessor tracking, coordinates periodic supplier reviews and ensures contractual obligations remain current. |
| Information Security | Reviews security obligations for Controllers, Processors, Joint Controllers and data sharing arrangements and supports assessment of technical and organisational measures. |
| Project Managers | Embed role determination into project initiation, design, implementation and change management activities. |
| System Owners | Ensure system configurations, access permissions, retention settings, integrations and data flows align with the approved role determination. |
| Marketing, Analytics and Product Teams | Assess role implications for campaigns, tracking technologies, analytics, profiling, artificial intelligence, platforms and data sharing before launch. |
| Human Resources | Ensures role determinations are documented for employee and workforce-related processing involving payroll providers, benefits providers, recruitment platforms and other HR service providers. |
| All Personnel | Follow this Policy, provide accurate information for assessments, use personal data only as authorised, and promptly report proposed changes or concerns. |

## Compliance, Monitoring & Enforcement

Compliance with this Policy shall be monitored through a combination of privacy governance activities, procurement controls, contract reviews, processing inventory reviews, supplier assurance, internal audits and periodic management reporting.

The Data Protection Officer, Legal, Procurement and relevant governance forums shall monitor adherence to this Policy, including:

| Monitoring Activity | Frequency | Responsible Role | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Review of new processing activities for role determination completion | Ongoing | Business Owner / Data Protection Officer | Privacy screening records, inventory entries |
| Procurement gate check for personal data processing | Before contract approval | Procurement | Procurement workflow approval, supplier assessment |
| Contract review for correct role terms | Before signature and renewal | Legal | Approved contract or data protection schedule |
| Processing inventory completeness review | At least annually | Data Protection Officer | Inventory review report |
| High-risk and complex role determination review | As needed | Data Protection Officer / Legal | Assessment record and approval |
| Joint Controller and data sharing arrangement review | At least annually | Business Owner / Legal | Agreement review record |
| Processor and subprocessor review | At least annually or upon material change | Vendor Management / Business Owner | Supplier review record |
| Internal audit or assurance testing | According to audit plan | Internal Audit / Compliance | Audit report and remediation plan |
| Training completion monitoring | At least annually | Data Protection Officer / HR | Training completion report |

Non-compliance with this Policy may result in:

- Suspension or delay of processing activities.
- Rejection of supplier onboarding or contract approval.
- Mandatory remediation actions.
- Withdrawal of approval for a processing activity.
- Escalation to executive management or the relevant governance forum.
- Disciplinary action for employees, up to and including termination, in accordance with [HR disciplinary policy].
- Contractual remedies for suppliers or partners, including suspension, termination, audit, indemnity or corrective action requirements.
- Notification to regulators or affected individuals where legally required and approved through the appropriate governance process.

The Data Protection Officer shall report material non-compliance, unresolved disputes, high-risk findings and overdue remediation actions to [Privacy Governance Committee / Risk Committee / Executive Sponsor] according to established reporting procedures.

## Exceptions

Exceptions to this Policy are permitted only where there is a documented business justification, legal review and risk acceptance by the appropriate authority.

Exception requests shall include:

| Required Information | Description |
|---|---|
| Requestor | Name, role and business unit of the person requesting the exception. |
| Processing activity | Description of the processing activity affected. |
| Policy requirement affected | Specific requirement that cannot be met. |
| Proposed deviation | Description of the requested exception. |
| Business justification | Explanation of why the exception is necessary. |
| Privacy risk assessment | Assessment of risks to individuals and to [Organisation Name]. |
| Compensating controls | Measures proposed to reduce risk. |
| Duration | Requested start date and end date. |
| Legal review | Confirmation of Legal review where required. |
| Data Protection Officer opinion | Privacy assessment and recommendation. |
| Approval | Decision by authorised approver. |
| Review date | Date by which the exception must be reassessed. |

The following exception rules shall apply:

1. Exceptions shall not be open-ended and shall have a defined expiry date.
2. Exceptions shall be approved before the affected processing begins or continues, unless urgent circumstances require temporary action to prevent harm.
3. Exceptions involving high-risk processing, Joint Controller arrangements, disputed role determinations, supplier reuse of personal data, or cross-border processing shall require review by the Data Protection Officer and Legal.
4. Expired exceptions shall not be relied upon.
5. Approved exceptions shall be recorded in the privacy exception register.
6. Compensating controls shall be implemented and monitored for the duration of the exception.
7. Exceptions shall be withdrawn where the risk is no longer acceptable, the business justification no longer applies, or required controls are not maintained.

## Review & Maintenance

This Policy shall be reviewed at least annually and whenever there is a material change to:

- Applicable privacy or data protection law.
- Regulatory guidance or enforcement expectations.
- [Organisation Name]’s business model, services, products or operating structure.
- Data sharing practices.
- Supplier, outsourcing or affiliate arrangements.
- Use of platforms, tracking technologies, analytics or artificial intelligence.
- Cross-border processing arrangements.
- Privacy governance processes or accountability requirements.

The Data Protection Officer is responsible for maintaining this Policy. Legal, Procurement, Information Security, Vendor Management, business stakeholders and other relevant functions shall be consulted as appropriate during review.

Policy updates shall be approved by [Approving Authority] and communicated to relevant personnel. Superseded versions shall be retained in accordance with [document retention policy].

| Version | Date | Description of Change | Author | Approver |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | [Date] | Initial version | Data Protection Officer | [Approving Authority] |

GDPR-003.title: Data Protection Officer Appointment
GDPR-003.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DPO-POL-001] | 1.0 | [Chief Privacy Officer / General Counsel] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | GDPR | Internal |

## Purpose

This Policy establishes the mandatory requirements for determining whether the organisation must appoint a Data Protection Officer, for making and maintaining that appointment, and for ensuring the Data Protection Officer can perform their duties independently and effectively.

The objective of this Policy is to ensure that the organisation has appropriate expert oversight of personal data protection where its activities, legal status, scale, or risk profile require a dedicated Data Protection Officer.

## Scope

This Policy applies to:

- [Organisation Name], including all business units, subsidiaries, branches, and controlled entities within scope of the organisation’s privacy governance programme.
- All employees, officers, directors, contractors, consultants, temporary workers, interns, and other personnel who process personal data on behalf of the organisation.
- All processing of personal data carried out by the organisation as a controller or processor.
- All systems, applications, services, products, projects, business processes, and third-party arrangements involving personal data.

This Policy applies where the organisation is required to appoint a Data Protection Officer because it:

- Is a public authority or public body, except where acting in a judicial capacity.
- Conducts regular and systematic monitoring of individuals on a large scale.
- Processes special categories of personal data, or personal data relating to criminal convictions or offences, on a large scale.
- Is otherwise required to appoint a Data Protection Officer under applicable data protection law, supervisory authority guidance, contract, sector requirement, or binding internal governance decision.

Where a formal Data Protection Officer appointment is not legally required, the organisation may appoint a Privacy Lead or equivalent role; however, that role shall not be described as a statutory Data Protection Officer unless the requirements in this Policy are met.

## Policy Statements

1. The organisation shall assess whether a Data Protection Officer is required before commencing any new business activity, product, service, jurisdictional expansion, or operating model that may materially affect personal data processing.

2. The organisation shall document the outcome of each Data Protection Officer requirement assessment, including the rationale for appointment or non-appointment.

3. The organisation shall appoint a Data Protection Officer where its activities meet any mandatory appointment criteria, including public authority status, large-scale regular and systematic monitoring, or large-scale processing of sensitive personal data.

4. The organisation shall ensure that the appointed Data Protection Officer has expert knowledge of data protection law, privacy governance, risk management, security practices, and the organisation’s processing operations.

5. The organisation shall appoint the Data Protection Officer based on professional qualities and ability to perform the role, not based solely on seniority, availability, or administrative convenience.

6. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer has sufficient independence, authority, resources, access, and organisational visibility to perform their duties effectively.

7. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer reports to the highest appropriate management level, such as the Board, Executive Committee, Chief Executive Officer, General Counsel, or equivalent senior leadership body.

8. The organisation shall not instruct the Data Protection Officer on how to reach conclusions in relation to data protection matters.

9. The organisation shall not dismiss, penalise, demote, disadvantage, or otherwise retaliate against the Data Protection Officer for performing their duties.

10. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer has direct and timely access to senior management, relevant committees, records, systems, personnel, audits, risk assessments, contracts, and processing information needed to perform the role.

11. The organisation shall involve the Data Protection Officer properly and in a timely manner in all matters relating to personal data protection, including new initiatives, system changes, vendor selection, mergers and acquisitions, data sharing, high-risk processing, security incidents, and complaints.

12. The organisation shall consult the Data Protection Officer before approving processing activities that may create significant privacy risks for individuals.

13. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer is involved in data protection impact assessments, including advising on necessity, proportionality, safeguards, residual risk, and whether consultation with a supervisory authority is required.

14. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer monitors the organisation’s compliance with data protection law, internal privacy policies, privacy notices, data protection impact assessments, data subject rights processes, training obligations, and processor governance requirements.

15. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer provides advice and guidance to employees, management, and project teams on data protection obligations and privacy risk mitigation.

16. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer acts as a contact point for supervisory authorities in relation to data protection matters.

17. The organisation shall ensure that individuals can contact the Data Protection Officer regarding the processing of their personal data and the exercise of their data protection rights.

18. The organisation shall publish the Data Protection Officer’s contact details in privacy notices, on relevant websites, and in other appropriate communication channels.

19. The organisation shall notify the relevant supervisory authority of the Data Protection Officer’s contact details where legally required.

20. The organisation shall ensure that Data Protection Officer contact details remain current, monitored, and accessible.

21. The organisation shall maintain a documented appointment record for the Data Protection Officer, including appointment date, reporting line, responsibilities, resources, conflict assessment, and contact information.

22. The organisation shall ensure that any outsourced or external Data Protection Officer is appointed under a written agreement that defines responsibilities, availability, confidentiality, reporting arrangements, access rights, escalation routes, and service expectations.

23. The organisation shall ensure that an external Data Protection Officer is sufficiently familiar with the organisation’s structure, operations, systems, data flows, risk profile, and regulatory context.

24. The organisation shall not assign duties to the Data Protection Officer that create a conflict of interest.

25. The organisation shall assess potential conflicts of interest before appointment and whenever the Data Protection Officer’s role, reporting line, duties, or organisational structure changes.

26. The organisation shall not appoint a person as Data Protection Officer where that person determines the purposes or means of personal data processing in a manner that compromises independence.

27. The organisation shall ensure that senior roles with decision-making authority over processing activities are not assigned Data Protection Officer responsibilities unless a documented conflict assessment confirms independence can be preserved.

28. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer is bound by confidentiality or secrecy obligations concerning the performance of their duties, subject to lawful disclosure requirements.

29. The organisation shall provide the Data Protection Officer with adequate time, budget, tools, training, administrative support, legal support, and specialist advice necessary to perform the role.

30. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer receives continuing professional development appropriate to the organisation’s regulatory environment, technologies, processing operations, and risk profile.

31. The organisation shall include the Data Protection Officer in privacy governance forums and risk management processes where personal data matters are discussed.

32. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer has visibility of the organisation’s record of processing activities and may request updates, corrections, and evidence from process owners.

33. The organisation shall require business owners and system owners to cooperate with the Data Protection Officer and provide complete and accurate information within required timelines.

34. The organisation shall ensure that the Data Protection Officer may raise concerns, recommendations, and unresolved risks directly to senior management without obstruction.

35. The organisation shall document management decisions where the organisation chooses not to follow formal Data Protection Officer advice on significant privacy risk matters.

36. The organisation shall ensure that Data Protection Officer advice is considered before accepting high residual privacy risk.

37. The organisation shall appoint a deputy, alternate, or interim contact arrangement where the Data Protection Officer is unavailable for a prolonged period or where continuity is required.

38. The organisation shall ensure that resignation, replacement, extended absence, or removal of the Data Protection Officer is managed through a controlled transition process.

39. The organisation shall update published and supervisory authority contact details promptly when the Data Protection Officer changes.

40. The organisation shall retain records demonstrating compliance with this Policy, including appointment records, conflict assessments, published contact details, supervisory authority notifications, governance reports, advice records, and management decisions.

The following appointment and review records shall be maintained as a minimum:

| Record | Minimum Content | Owner | Retention |
|---|---|---|---|
| DPO Requirement Assessment | Legal basis for appointment decision, processing context, scale, sensitivity, monitoring activities, conclusion, approver | [Privacy Office / Legal] | [Retention Period] |
| DPO Appointment Record | Name or service provider, appointment date, reporting line, responsibilities, resources, contact details | [Privacy Office / HR / Legal] | Duration of appointment plus [Retention Period] |
| Conflict of Interest Assessment | Current duties, decision-making authority, independence risks, safeguards, approval | [Privacy Office / Legal] | Duration of appointment plus [Retention Period] |
| Supervisory Authority Notification | Contact details submitted, date submitted, authority notified, confirmation evidence | [Privacy Office] | Duration of appointment plus [Retention Period] |
| Published Contact Register | Locations where DPO contact details are published, update dates, verification evidence | [Privacy Office / Communications] | [Retention Period] |
| DPO Advice and Escalation Log | Matter, advice given, decision owner, acceptance or rejection of advice, residual risk | [DPO] | [Retention Period] |

The following indicative timelines shall apply unless a shorter legal, contractual, or risk-based timeline is required:

| Activity | Required Timeline |
|---|---:|
| Assess whether a DPO is required for a new high-risk initiative | Before design approval or procurement commitment |
| Complete conflict of interest assessment before appointment | Before appointment is confirmed |
| Publish DPO contact details after appointment | Within [10] business days |
| Notify supervisory authority of DPO contact details where required | Within [10] business days |
| Update contact details after DPO change | Within [5] business days |
| Provide requested processing information to the DPO | Within [10] business days, or sooner for urgent matters |
| Escalate unresolved significant privacy risks to senior management | Within [5] business days of identification |
| Review DPO appointment and resources | At least annually |

## Roles & Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Board / Senior Management | Approves the organisation’s privacy governance approach; ensures the Data Protection Officer has independence, authority, and resources; considers escalated privacy risks; supports a culture of compliance. |
| Chief Executive Officer / Executive Sponsor | Ensures the Data Protection Officer has access to senior leadership; resolves organisational barriers; supports enforcement of this Policy across business units. |
| Data Protection Officer | Advises on data protection obligations; monitors compliance; supports privacy risk management; advises on data protection impact assessments; acts as a contact point for supervisory authorities and individuals; escalates unresolved risks; maintains appropriate evidence of advice and oversight. |
| Privacy Office / Data Protection Team | Supports the Data Protection Officer; maintains privacy governance records; coordinates assessments, privacy notices, rights requests, training, and compliance monitoring; tracks remediation actions. |
| General Counsel / Legal | Advises on legal requirements; supports appointment decisions; reviews conflict of interest assessments; supports supervisory authority engagement and regulatory interpretation. |
| Human Resources | Supports appointment records, role descriptions, reporting lines, training, confidentiality arrangements, and protection against retaliation or inappropriate disciplinary action. |
| Information Security | Cooperates with the Data Protection Officer on security controls, incidents, breach assessment, technical safeguards, and risk mitigation. |
| Procurement / Vendor Management | Involves the Data Protection Officer in relevant third-party processing arrangements; ensures data protection requirements are reflected in supplier due diligence and contracts. |
| Business Process Owners | Identify and document personal data processing; consult the Data Protection Officer on relevant changes; provide accurate information; implement agreed privacy controls and remediation actions. |
| System Owners | Maintain visibility of systems processing personal data; support access to technical information; implement privacy and security controls; cooperate with assessments and audits. |
| Project and Product Teams | Engage the Data Protection Officer early in initiatives involving personal data; complete required assessments; implement privacy-by-design requirements. |
| All Personnel | Cooperate with the Data Protection Officer; complete required training; follow privacy policies and procedures; report privacy risks, incidents, and concerns promptly. |
| Internal Audit / Compliance | Provides independent assurance over compliance with this Policy and the effectiveness of the Data Protection Officer governance model. |

## Compliance, Monitoring & Enforcement

Compliance with this Policy is mandatory.

The organisation shall monitor compliance through appropriate governance and assurance activities, including:

- Periodic review of whether the organisation is required to maintain a Data Protection Officer.
- Annual assessment of the Data Protection Officer’s independence, resources, reporting line, and access to information.
- Review of conflict of interest assessments.
- Review of whether the Data Protection Officer is involved in material personal data processing decisions.
- Testing of published contact details and mailbox monitoring.
- Review of supervisory authority notification records where applicable.
- Review of Data Protection Officer advice logs, escalations, and management responses.
- Review of data protection impact assessment records to confirm timely Data Protection Officer involvement.
- Review of privacy training, incident management, rights request handling, vendor governance, and records of processing activities.
- Internal audit, compliance testing, or external assurance where appropriate.

The Data Protection Officer shall provide periodic reporting to senior management on privacy compliance and risk matters. Reporting shall include, where applicable:

| Reporting Area | Example Metrics |
|---|---|
| DPO Involvement | Number of projects reviewed, data protection impact assessments advised on, high-risk matters escalated |
| Compliance Monitoring | Policy exceptions, overdue remediation actions, training completion, audit findings |
| Data Subject Rights | Request volumes, response timeliness, escalations, complaints |
| Incidents and Breaches | Incidents reviewed, breach assessments supported, lessons learned |
| Third Parties | Supplier reviews, high-risk processors, contractual gaps |
| Regulatory Engagement | Supervisory authority communications, complaints, inquiries, notifications |
| Resource Adequacy | Staffing, budget, training needs, access issues, independence concerns |

Non-compliance with this Policy may result in disciplinary action, contract remedies, access restrictions, remediation requirements, supplier management action, or other corrective measures appropriate to the severity and circumstances of the breach.

Retaliation against the Data Protection Officer or any person raising a good-faith privacy concern is prohibited and shall be treated as a serious breach of this Policy.

Where non-compliance creates significant risk to individuals or the organisation, the matter shall be escalated to senior management and, where appropriate, the Board or relevant governance committee.

## Exceptions

Exceptions to this Policy are permitted only where:

- The exception is lawful.
- The exception is documented.
- The privacy risk has been assessed.
- The Data Protection Officer has been consulted.
- Compensating controls are defined where appropriate.
- The exception is approved by [General Counsel / Chief Privacy Officer / Executive Sponsor].
- The exception has a defined expiry date and review date.

Exceptions shall not be used to avoid a legally required Data Protection Officer appointment or to undermine the independence, authority, or duties of the Data Protection Officer.

Exception requests shall include:

| Required Information | Description |
|---|---|
| Requestor | Name, role, business unit |
| Requirement Affected | Specific Policy requirement for which an exception is requested |
| Business Justification | Reason the requirement cannot be met |
| Risk Assessment | Privacy, legal, operational, and reputational risks |
| DPO Consultation | Evidence of Data Protection Officer input |
| Compensating Controls | Measures to reduce risk |
| Approval | Name and role of approver |
| Expiry Date | Date by which the exception must be reviewed or closed |

All approved exceptions shall be recorded in the privacy exception register and reviewed at least quarterly until closure.

## Review & Maintenance

This Policy shall be reviewed at least annually and whenever there is a material change to:

- Applicable data protection law or supervisory authority expectations.
- The organisation’s legal status, ownership, structure, or operating model.
- The scale, nature, scope, or sensitivity of personal data processing.
- The organisation’s use of monitoring, profiling, automated decision-making, artificial intelligence, analytics, or tracking technologies.
- The organisation’s processing of special categories of personal data or criminal offence data.
- The Data Protection Officer’s role, reporting line, resourcing, or appointment status.
- The organisation’s privacy risk profile, audit findings, incidents, complaints, or regulatory engagement.

The Policy Owner shall ensure that this Policy remains accurate, approved, communicated, and aligned with the organisation’s privacy governance framework.

Material changes to this Policy shall be approved by [Approving Authority]. Minor administrative updates, such as formatting, owner details, or contact information, may be approved by the Policy Owner.

The current approved version of this Policy shall be made available to all relevant personnel through [Policy Portal / Intranet / GRC System]. Previous versions shall be retained in accordance with the organisation’s document retention requirements.

GDPR-004.title: Representative Designation (non-EU)
GDPR-004.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [POL-GDPR-REP-001] | 1.0 | Data Protection Officer / Privacy Office | [Effective Date] | GDPR | Internal |

## Purpose

This Policy defines the mandatory requirements for designating, maintaining, and managing an EU representative where [Organisation Name] is not established in the European Union but offers goods or services to individuals in the European Union or monitors their behaviour within the European Union.

The purpose of the EU representative is to provide an accessible contact point in the European Union for individuals, supervisory authorities, and other relevant parties regarding [Organisation Name]'s processing of personal data subject to GDPR requirements.

## Scope

This Policy applies to:

- [Organisation Name] and all subsidiaries, business units, functions, and personnel involved in processing personal data of individuals located in the European Union.
- Processing activities carried out by [Organisation Name] as a controller, processor, or both, where [Organisation Name] is not established in the European Union.
- Products, services, websites, applications, platforms, analytics, marketing activities, customer support, sales operations, and monitoring activities involving individuals in the European Union.
- Third parties acting on behalf of [Organisation Name] where their processing may create or affect the requirement to designate an EU representative.

This Policy does not replace the need to appoint a Data Protection Officer where such appointment is separately required, nor does it transfer [Organisation Name]'s accountability for compliance to the EU representative.

## Policy Statements

1. [Organisation Name] shall assess whether an EU representative is required before commencing or materially changing any processing activity involving individuals located in the European Union.

2. [Organisation Name] shall designate an EU representative where it is not established in the European Union and processes personal data of individuals in the European Union in connection with:
 - offering goods or services to those individuals, whether paid or free of charge; or
 - monitoring their behaviour within the European Union, including through tracking, profiling, behavioural advertising, analytics, geolocation, or similar technologies.

3. [Organisation Name] shall document the outcome of each EU representative applicability assessment, including the business rationale, processing context, data subjects affected, categories of personal data processed, and the decision reached.

4. [Organisation Name] shall not rely on an exemption from appointing an EU representative unless the Privacy Office has formally documented that the processing is only occasional, does not include large-scale processing of special category or criminal offence data, and is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms.

5. [Organisation Name] shall not treat repeated, ongoing, systematic, targeted, or revenue-generating processing of individuals in the European Union as occasional.

6. Where an EU representative is required, [Organisation Name] shall appoint the representative in writing before the relevant processing activity begins.

7. The EU representative shall be established in one of the European Union member states where the individuals whose personal data is processed are located.

8. Where [Organisation Name] processes personal data of individuals in multiple European Union member states, the Privacy Office shall select the representative's location based on factors including the main markets served, volume of affected individuals, language requirements, regulatory accessibility, and operational effectiveness.

9. [Organisation Name] shall ensure the EU representative has a written mandate to act on behalf of [Organisation Name] regarding GDPR-related communications with supervisory authorities and individuals.

10. The written mandate shall clearly define the EU representative's authority, duties, communication channels, escalation routes, service levels, confidentiality obligations, record-keeping obligations, and limits of authority.

11. [Organisation Name] shall ensure the EU representative is able to communicate effectively in the language or languages appropriate to the individuals and supervisory authorities with whom it is expected to interact.

12. [Organisation Name] shall ensure the EU representative has sufficient competence, availability, and resources to perform its role effectively.

13. [Organisation Name] shall conduct due diligence before appointing an EU representative, including evaluation of the representative's experience, independence, capacity, information security controls, data protection knowledge, financial stability, and ability to support regulatory communications.

14. [Organisation Name] shall execute a written agreement with the EU representative before disclosing any personal data or confidential information to the representative.

15. The agreement with the EU representative shall include, at minimum:
 - the identity and contact details of [Organisation Name] and the EU representative;
 - the scope of processing activities covered;
 - the member state where the EU representative is established;
 - the representative's communication and escalation obligations;
 - obligations to support supervisory authority and individual enquiries;
 - confidentiality and security requirements;
 - retention and return or deletion requirements for records;
 - requirements for notifying [Organisation Name] of requests, complaints, investigations, or regulatory correspondence;
 - service levels for acknowledging and forwarding communications;
 - audit, assurance, and monitoring rights;
 - termination and transition requirements.

16. [Organisation Name] shall ensure the EU representative is identified in relevant external privacy notices, data protection notices, and other appropriate communications to individuals in the European Union.

17. The published contact details of the EU representative shall include, at minimum, the representative's legal name, postal address in the European Union, and a dedicated contact method for privacy-related communications.

18. [Organisation Name] shall keep the EU representative's contact details accurate, complete, and easily accessible to individuals and supervisory authorities.

19. [Organisation Name] shall ensure the EU representative is provided with sufficient information about relevant processing activities to respond appropriately to supervisory authority and individual enquiries.

20. [Organisation Name] shall make available to the EU representative current records of processing activities that relate to individuals in the European Union, unless a documented and approved legal basis exists for limiting access.

21. [Organisation Name] shall ensure the EU representative can access or request relevant records without undue delay when responding to supervisory authority enquiries.

22. The EU representative shall not be appointed as a symbolic or nominal contact only; it shall have a practical ability to facilitate communication between [Organisation Name], supervisory authorities, and individuals.

23. [Organisation Name] shall maintain a central register of EU representative assessments, appointments, agreements, notices, communications, and reviews.

24. [Organisation Name] shall require business units to notify the Privacy Office before launching or changing any product, service, campaign, website, app, analytics tool, monitoring activity, or market expansion that may involve individuals in the European Union.

25. [Organisation Name] shall include EU representative requirements in privacy impact assessments, vendor onboarding reviews, product launch reviews, and international market entry assessments where relevant.

26. [Organisation Name] shall ensure that the EU representative is informed of material changes to processing activities involving individuals in the European Union, including changes to:
 - categories of individuals affected;
 - categories of personal data processed;
 - purposes of processing;
 - geographic markets served;
 - use of profiling, tracking, or monitoring technologies;
 - data sharing arrangements;
 - high-risk processing activities;
 - supervisory authority interactions;
 - privacy complaints or disputes.

27. [Organisation Name] shall establish documented communication procedures with the EU representative for receiving, escalating, and responding to:
 - supervisory authority enquiries;
 - individual rights requests;
 - privacy complaints;
 - investigation notices;
 - requests for records of processing;
 - data breach-related enquiries;
 - requests for clarification about [Organisation Name]'s privacy notices or processing activities.

28. [Organisation Name] shall require the EU representative to acknowledge receipt of supervisory authority communications and forward them to the Privacy Office within the agreed service level.

29. [Organisation Name] shall require the EU representative to forward individual privacy enquiries or complaints to the Privacy Office within the agreed service level.

30. [Organisation Name] shall retain accountability for responding to supervisory authorities and individuals, even where communications are routed through the EU representative.

31. [Organisation Name] shall not instruct the EU representative to withhold, delay, alter, or suppress legitimate communications from individuals or supervisory authorities.

32. [Organisation Name] shall ensure that personal data shared with the EU representative is limited to what is necessary for the representative to perform its duties.

33. [Organisation Name] shall ensure that any transfer of personal data to or from the EU representative is protected by appropriate contractual, technical, and organisational safeguards.

34. [Organisation Name] shall ensure that the EU representative maintains appropriate confidentiality, access control, secure communication, incident reporting, and record protection measures.

35. [Organisation Name] shall require the EU representative to notify the Privacy Office without undue delay of any suspected or confirmed compromise, unauthorised disclosure, loss, or misuse of personal data or confidential information relating to [Organisation Name].

36. [Organisation Name] shall review the continued suitability of the EU representative at least annually and whenever there is a material change in processing operations, regulatory exposure, market presence, or representative performance.

37. [Organisation Name] shall replace the EU representative where the representative is no longer suitably located, competent, available, independent, secure, contractually bound, or able to perform the role effectively.

38. [Organisation Name] shall ensure that termination or replacement of an EU representative does not create a gap in required representation.

39. [Organisation Name] shall update privacy notices, internal registers, supervisory authority communications, and related documentation promptly when the EU representative is appointed, replaced, or its contact details change.

40. [Organisation Name] shall retain evidence of EU representative designation and related compliance activities in accordance with the applicable records retention schedule.

41. [Organisation Name] shall ensure that employees and relevant contractors involved in EU-facing processing understand when to involve the Privacy Office and the EU representative.

42. [Organisation Name] shall not launch EU-targeted offerings or monitoring activities without completing required privacy review steps, including assessment of EU representative obligations.

43. Where [Organisation Name] acts as a processor for a customer and an EU representative may be required for [Organisation Name]'s processing role, [Organisation Name] shall assess and document its own obligation independently of the customer's compliance position.

44. Where [Organisation Name] acts as a controller and engages processors outside the European Union, [Organisation Name] shall ensure such processors provide information necessary to support [Organisation Name]'s EU representative assessment and related compliance obligations.

45. The Privacy Office shall maintain the following minimum service levels for EU representative communications unless stricter timelines are required by law, contract, or supervisory authority instruction:

| Communication Type | EU Representative Acknowledgement to Sender | Forwarding to Privacy Office | Internal Triage by Privacy Office |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Supervisory authority enquiry or investigation notice | Within 1 business day | Within 1 business day | Within 1 business day of receipt |
| Individual rights request | Within 2 business days | Within 2 business days | Within 3 business days of receipt |
| Privacy complaint | Within 2 business days | Within 2 business days | Within 3 business days of receipt |
| Data breach-related enquiry | Within 1 business day | Same business day where practicable | Same business day where practicable |
| General privacy enquiry | Within 5 business days | Within 5 business days | Within 5 business days of receipt |

46. [Organisation Name] shall maintain the following minimum evidence set for audit and accountability purposes:

| Evidence Item | Responsible Owner | Minimum Retention |
|---|---|---:|
| EU representative applicability assessment | Privacy Office | [Retention Period] |
| Appointment approval record | Privacy Office | [Retention Period] |
| Executed EU representative agreement | Legal / Privacy Office | [Retention Period] |
| Due diligence records | Privacy Office / Procurement | [Retention Period] |
| Published privacy notice showing representative details | Privacy Office / Marketing | [Retention Period] |
| Records of processing shared with representative | Privacy Office | [Retention Period] |
| Communications log with representative | Privacy Office | [Retention Period] |
| Supervisory authority correspondence | Privacy Office / Legal | [Retention Period] |
| Individual requests or complaints routed through representative | Privacy Office | [Retention Period] |
| Annual representative review | Privacy Office | [Retention Period] |

## Roles & Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Board / Executive Leadership | Ensure [Organisation Name] has appropriate governance, funding, and oversight for GDPR compliance, including EU representative designation where required. |
| Data Protection Officer / Privacy Office | Own this Policy; assess whether an EU representative is required; approve designation decisions; maintain records; oversee representative performance; coordinate responses to supervisory authorities and individuals. |
| Legal Department | Review and approve the written mandate, contract terms, regulatory communications, liability considerations, and termination or replacement arrangements. |
| Procurement / Vendor Management | Support due diligence, contracting, onboarding, periodic review, and offboarding of the EU representative as a service provider. |
| Business Unit Owners | Notify the Privacy Office of EU-facing processing activities; provide accurate information about products, services, markets, data subjects, personal data, monitoring activities, and processing purposes. |
| Marketing / Digital / Product Teams | Ensure EU-targeted websites, apps, campaigns, tracking technologies, and customer journeys are reviewed before launch and that privacy notices include accurate representative details where required. |
| Information Security | Assess and advise on security safeguards for information shared with the EU representative; support incident response involving the representative. |
| Records Management | Ensure EU representative-related records are retained, protected, retrievable, and disposed of in line with approved retention requirements. |
| EU Representative | Act as the designated point of contact in the European Union; receive and forward communications; support supervisory authority and individual enquiries; maintain confidentiality; protect records; comply with the written mandate. |
| Employees and Contractors | Follow this Policy, escalate EU-related processing plans to the Privacy Office, and cooperate with requests for information needed to support representative obligations. |

## Compliance, Monitoring & Enforcement

Compliance with this Policy is mandatory.

The Privacy Office shall monitor compliance through periodic reviews, privacy impact assessment checks, product launch reviews, vendor reviews, records sampling, and review of communications with the EU representative.

The following monitoring activities shall be performed at the stated minimum frequency:

| Monitoring Activity | Owner | Frequency |
|---|---|---:|
| Review of EU representative applicability assessments | Privacy Office | Quarterly |
| Verification that privacy notices include current representative details | Privacy Office / Marketing | Quarterly |
| Review of EU representative communication logs and service levels | Privacy Office | Quarterly |
| Review of representative due diligence and contractual status | Privacy Office / Procurement | Annually |
| Review of records of processing provided or available to the representative | Privacy Office | Annually |
| Review of market expansion and EU-targeting activities | Privacy Office / Business Owners | At launch and upon material change |
| Review of representative performance and suitability | Privacy Office / Legal | Annually |
| Testing of escalation process for supervisory authority communications | Privacy Office | Annually |

Non-compliance with this Policy may result in corrective action, including suspension of processing activities, withdrawal of product launch approval, mandatory remediation plans, contract review, supplier replacement, disciplinary action, or other measures permitted by [Organisation Name]'s policies and applicable law.

Material non-compliance, regulatory correspondence, unresolved representative performance issues, or failure to appoint a required EU representative shall be escalated to [Executive Committee / Risk Committee / Board Committee] through established governance channels.

## Exceptions

Exceptions to this Policy are permitted only where formally approved by the Data Protection Officer or Privacy Office and Legal Department.

An exception request shall include:

- the specific Policy requirement for which an exception is requested;
- the business justification;
- the processing activities affected;
- the categories and approximate volume of individuals affected;
- the categories of personal data involved;
- the countries or markets affected;
- the risk assessment;
- compensating controls;
- proposed duration of the exception;
- accountable owner;
- remediation plan and target completion date.

Exceptions shall not be approved where they would knowingly result in unlawful processing, prevent individuals or supervisory authorities from contacting [Organisation Name], or create an unmanaged regulatory risk.

All exceptions shall be documented in the Privacy Exceptions Register and reviewed at least quarterly until closed.

| Exception Attribute | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Approval authority | Data Protection Officer / Privacy Office and Legal Department |
| Maximum initial duration | [Maximum Duration, e.g., 90 days] |
| Review frequency | At least quarterly |
| Required record location | [Privacy Exceptions Register / GRC System] |
| Closure requirement | Evidence that the exception is no longer needed or that remediation has been completed |

## Review & Maintenance

This Policy shall be reviewed at least annually and whenever there is a material change to:

- [Organisation Name]'s establishment, corporate structure, or operating locations;
- EU market presence, customer base, or targeting strategy;
- products, services, websites, applications, or monitoring technologies involving individuals in the European Union;
- processing activities, purposes, data categories, or data subject groups;
- legal or regulatory requirements;
- supervisory authority expectations or enforcement trends;
- the EU representative's location, capability, ownership, performance, or contractual status;
- incident, complaint, or audit findings relating to EU representative obligations.

The Data Protection Officer / Privacy Office is responsible for maintaining this Policy, coordinating stakeholder review, obtaining approvals, and ensuring updated versions are communicated to relevant personnel.

Policy changes shall be recorded in the document control history maintained by [Policy Management System / GRC System]. The current approved version shall be made available through [Intranet / Policy Portal / Document Repository].

GDPR-005.title: GDPR Gap Analysis
GDPR-005.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [GDPR-GAP-001] | 1.0 | Data Protection Officer | [Effective Date] | GDPR | Confidential - Internal Use Only |

## Purpose

This report presents the results of a comprehensive GDPR gap analysis performed to assess the organisation’s current readiness against GDPR obligations and recognised privacy governance practices.

The purpose of this report is to:

- Identify areas where current privacy practices meet GDPR expectations.
- Highlight gaps, risks, and weaknesses requiring remediation.
- Assess the maturity of privacy governance, operational controls, documentation, and accountability mechanisms.
- Provide practical recommendations and prioritised actions to improve compliance readiness.
- Support management decision-making, resource allocation, and remediation planning.

This report is intended for senior management, the Data Protection Officer, Legal, Compliance, Information Security, IT, HR, Procurement, Marketing, Product, and other business functions involved in the collection, use, sharing, retention, or protection of personal data.

## Reporting Period & Scope

### Reporting Period

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Assessment period | [Start Date] to [End Date] |
| Fieldwork completed | [Date] |
| Report issued | [Date] |
| Assessment type | GDPR readiness and gap analysis |
| Assessment status | Draft for management review / Final |

### Organisational Scope

The assessment covered the following organisational areas:

| Business Area | Included in Scope | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Executive management and governance | Yes | Accountability, oversight, reporting, privacy risk ownership |
| Legal and compliance | Yes | GDPR interpretation, policies, contracts, notices, regulatory readiness |
| Data Protection Officer function | Yes | Independence, resources, advisory role, monitoring activities |
| Information security | Yes | Technical and organisational safeguards for personal data |
| IT operations | Yes | Systems, access controls, logging, backups, incident support |
| Human resources | Yes | Employee data, recruitment, onboarding, monitoring, retention |
| Sales and marketing | Yes | Consent, communications, lead management, profiling, preferences |
| Customer service | Yes | Customer records, identity checks, requests, complaint handling |
| Procurement and vendor management | Yes | Processor due diligence, contracts, vendor oversight |
| Product and service delivery | Yes | Privacy by design, data minimisation, lifecycle controls |
| Finance | Yes | Billing data, payment records, retention, access permissions |
| Internal audit / risk management | Partial | Review of privacy risk tracking and assurance activity |

### Data Processing Scope

The assessment considered personal data processed in the following contexts:

- Customer and prospective customer records.
- Employee, contractor, and applicant records.
- Supplier and business contact data.
- Website and digital analytics data.
- Marketing and communications data.
- Support tickets and service records.
- Account, billing, invoicing, and payment-related data.
- System logs and security monitoring records where they contain identifiable information.
- Special category or sensitive personal data, where applicable.
- Personal data processed by third-party service providers.

### Systems and Repositories Reviewed

| System / Repository | Business Owner | Data Type | Assessment Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| [CRM System] | Sales / Marketing | Customer, prospect, communications history | Included |
| [HRIS Platform] | Human Resources | Employee and applicant records | Included |
| [Support Platform] | Customer Service | Tickets, customer identifiers, support history | Included |
| [Finance System] | Finance | Billing and payment-related records | Included |
| [Marketing Automation Platform] | Marketing | Campaign, consent, preference data | Included |
| [Cloud Storage / Collaboration Platform] | IT / Business Units | Mixed personal data | Included |
| [Identity Provider] | IT / Security | User identities, access logs | Included |
| [Website / Analytics Platform] | Digital / Marketing | Cookie identifiers, analytics, tracking data | Included |
| [Vendor Management Repository] | Procurement | Supplier contracts and assessments | Included |
| [Incident Management Platform] | Security / IT | Security events and incident records | Included |

### Exclusions and Limitations

The following limitations applied:

- The assessment was based on interviews, document review, system walkthroughs, sampling, and management representations.
- No full technical penetration test or source code review was performed as part of this report.
- Legal opinions on specific disputed processing activities were outside the scope unless already documented by the organisation.
- The assessment did not validate every individual record or transaction.
- Some evidence was unavailable or incomplete at the time of review, as noted in the detailed findings.
- The report reflects the status of controls and documentation during the assessment period and may not reflect subsequent changes.

## Executive Summary

### Overall Readiness Rating

The organisation has established several foundational GDPR compliance elements, including privacy notices, basic data subject request handling, security controls, and contractual safeguards with key vendors. However, the current privacy programme is not yet consistently embedded across all business functions, and several important accountability, documentation, monitoring, and operational controls require improvement.

Overall GDPR readiness is assessed as:

| Readiness Area | Rating |
|---|---|
| Governance and accountability | Partially Effective |
| Records of processing and data mapping | Needs Improvement |
| Lawful basis and transparency | Partially Effective |
| Consent and preference management | Needs Improvement |
| Data subject rights handling | Partially Effective |
| Privacy by design and change management | Needs Improvement |
| Data protection impact assessments | Needs Improvement |
| Vendor and processor management | Partially Effective |
| International data transfers | Needs Improvement |
| Security of personal data | Partially Effective |
| Breach detection and notification readiness | Partially Effective |
| Retention and disposal | Needs Improvement |
| Training and awareness | Partially Effective |
| Monitoring and assurance | Needs Improvement |

### Summary Conclusion

The organisation demonstrates a moderate level of GDPR readiness but requires targeted remediation to evidence compliance consistently and defensibly. The most significant gaps relate to incomplete data processing records, inconsistent privacy risk assessments, immature retention practices, limited evidence of privacy by design, insufficient monitoring of processors, and fragmented consent and preference management.

The highest priority actions are to:

1. Refresh and complete the personal data inventory and processing records.
2. Confirm lawful bases for all material processing activities.
3. Strengthen data subject rights handling with clear workflows, logs, identity verification, and deadline tracking.
4. Formalise and enforce privacy impact assessments for new or changed processing.
5. Review and update processor contracts and international transfer safeguards.
6. Implement a practical retention and deletion programme.
7. Improve breach notification readiness through testing and role-based procedures.
8. Establish recurring privacy governance reporting to senior management.

### Key Strengths Identified

The following positive practices were observed:

- A named privacy owner and nominated Data Protection Officer function are in place.
- Core privacy policies and external privacy notices exist.
- Security controls such as access management, multi-factor authentication, endpoint protection, backups, and incident response processes are partially implemented.
- Standard contractual terms are used for many third-party service providers.
- Data subject requests are generally recognised and routed to Legal or Compliance.
- Staff receive general security or compliance awareness training.
- The organisation has a willingness to remediate and improve privacy governance.

### Key Gaps Identified

The most material gaps are summarised below:

| Priority | Gap Area | Business Impact |
|---:|---|---|
| High | Incomplete records of processing activities and data maps | Limits ability to demonstrate accountability and respond accurately to rights requests or incidents |
| High | Lawful basis documentation is inconsistent | Increases risk of unlawful processing and weakens privacy notices |
| High | Data subject request process lacks consistent evidence and deadline tracking | Increases risk of late, incomplete, or inconsistent responses |
| High | Data protection impact assessments are not consistently performed | Privacy risks may not be identified before launch of new systems or activities |
| High | Vendor due diligence and processor monitoring are inconsistent | Increases third-party processing and transfer risk |
| High | Retention rules are incomplete or not technically enforced | Increases over-retention, discovery, breach, and operational risk |
| Medium | Consent and preference management is fragmented | Increases risk of unwanted marketing or invalid consent reliance |
| Medium | Breach notification process has not been fully tested for privacy-specific scenarios | May delay escalation and regulatory decision-making |
| Medium | Employee privacy documentation and monitoring transparency require improvement | Increases employment privacy and trust risk |
| Medium | Privacy training is not role-specific | Staff in high-risk roles may not understand their obligations |
| Medium | International transfer assessments and documentation are incomplete | Increases cross-border data transfer risk |
| Low | Governance metrics and reporting are limited | Reduces management visibility and accountability |

### Overall Risk View

| Risk Level | Number of Findings | General Theme |
|---|---:|---|
| High | 8 | Accountability, processing records, rights handling, privacy impact assessments, vendor controls, retention |
| Medium | 9 | Consent, training, monitoring, breach readiness, transfer documentation, employee privacy |
| Low | 4 | Documentation consistency, reporting cadence, minor procedural improvements |

## Methodology

### Assessment Approach

The gap analysis was conducted using a structured assessment methodology designed to evaluate both documented intent and operational effectiveness.

The assessment included:

- Review of privacy governance documents, policies, procedures, notices, contracts, and registers.
- Interviews with stakeholders across business, technology, legal, compliance, HR, procurement, security, and marketing functions.
- Walkthroughs of selected systems and business processes involving personal data.
- Sample-based testing of selected records, requests, vendor files, and incident logs.
- Review of data flows, retention schedules, transfer mechanisms, and processor arrangements.
- Assessment of evidence supporting accountability and ongoing privacy compliance.
- Identification of gaps, risk ratings, root causes, and recommended remediation actions.

### Evidence Reviewed

The following evidence categories were reviewed:

| Evidence Category | Examples Reviewed |
|---|---|
| Governance documents | Privacy policy, data protection policy, information security policy, governance meeting records |
| Privacy notices | Website privacy notice, employee privacy notice, candidate privacy notice, customer notices |
| Processing documentation | Data inventory, data flow diagrams, processing activity records, business process descriptions |
| Lawful basis records | Consent records, legitimate interest assessments, contract-based processing records |
| Data subject rights records | Request logs, response templates, identity verification steps, escalation emails |
| Vendor documentation | Processor agreements, due diligence questionnaires, contract templates, supplier register |
| Security documentation | Access control procedures, incident response plan, backup policy, logging practices |
| Incident records | Security incident logs, breach assessment templates, escalation records |
| Training records | Completion reports, training content, onboarding materials |
| Retention documentation | Retention schedule, deletion procedures, archive rules, system configuration evidence |
| Marketing records | Consent capture screens, unsubscribe process, preference centre settings |
| Transfer documentation | Data hosting locations, sub-processor lists, transfer safeguards, risk assessments |
| Change records | Project templates, architecture reviews, system change approvals |

### Stakeholders Consulted

| Function | Role / Stakeholder | Consultation Method |
|---|---|---|
| Executive management | [Role / Name] | Interview |
| Legal / Compliance | [Role / Name] | Interview and document review |
| Data Protection Officer | [Role / Name] | Interview |
| Information Security | [Role / Name] | Interview and control walkthrough |
| IT Operations | [Role / Name] | Interview and system review |
| Human Resources | [Role / Name] | Interview and document review |
| Marketing | [Role / Name] | Interview and process walkthrough |
| Sales | [Role / Name] | Interview |
| Customer Service | [Role / Name] | Interview and request-handling walkthrough |
| Procurement | [Role / Name] | Interview and vendor file review |
| Product / Engineering | [Role / Name] | Interview and project review |
| Finance | [Role / Name] | Interview |

### Rating Method

Findings were rated using the following scale:

| Rating | Definition | Typical Management Response |
|---|---|---|
| High | A material gap that may result in unlawful processing, inability to demonstrate compliance, significant data subject impact, regulatory exposure, or business disruption | Immediate remediation required with senior management oversight |
| Medium | A control weakness or documentation gap that may increase compliance or operational risk if not addressed | Timely remediation required through agreed action plan |
| Low | A minor improvement opportunity or documentation inconsistency with limited immediate risk | Address as part of continuous improvement |
| Effective | Requirement is substantially met and supported by evidence | Maintain and monitor |
| Partially Effective | Requirement is addressed in part, but implementation is inconsistent, incomplete, or not fully evidenced | Improve and standardise |
| Not Effective | Requirement is not addressed or evidence is insufficient to demonstrate compliance | Remediate as a priority |
| Not Assessed | Area was outside the available evidence or scope of assessment | Assess separately if relevant |

### Assessment Criteria

The analysis considered whether the organisation can demonstrate that personal data is:

- Collected and used lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
- Processed for specified and legitimate purposes.
- Limited to what is necessary for the stated purpose.
- Kept accurate and updated where required.
- Retained only for as long as needed.
- Protected against unauthorised access, loss, alteration, or disclosure.
- Managed with clear accountability, governance, documentation, and oversight.
- Supported by appropriate rights-handling, breach response, vendor controls, and privacy risk management.

## Detailed Findings / Results (with structure)

### Findings Summary

| ID | Area | Finding | Rating | Control Effectiveness | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F-01 | Governance and Accountability | Privacy governance exists but is not fully embedded across all business functions | High | Partially Effective | Data Protection Officer |
| F-02 | Data Inventory and Processing Records | Processing records are incomplete and not consistently maintained | High | Not Effective | Data Protection Officer / Business Owners |
| F-03 | Lawful Basis | Lawful basis decisions are not consistently documented for all processing activities | High | Partially Effective | Legal / Compliance |
| F-04 | Privacy Notices | Notices exist but do not fully align with all current processing activities | Medium | Partially Effective | Legal / Marketing / HR |
| F-05 | Consent and Preferences | Consent capture and preference management are fragmented across systems | Medium | Partially Effective | Marketing / IT |
| F-06 | Data Subject Rights | Request process is informal and lacks complete workflow evidence | High | Partially Effective | Customer Service / Legal |
| F-07 | Privacy by Design | Privacy review is not consistently integrated into project and change processes | High | Not Effective | Product / IT / DPO |
| F-08 | Privacy Impact Assessments | Assessments are not consistently triggered, completed, or retained | High | Not Effective | DPO / Project Owners |
| F-09 | Vendor Management | Processor due diligence and ongoing monitoring are inconsistent | High | Partially Effective | Procurement / Legal |
| F-10 | International Transfers | Transfer documentation and safeguards are incomplete for some vendors | High | Partially Effective | Legal / Procurement |
| F-11 | Security Controls | Core security controls are present but evidence and coverage vary by system | Medium | Partially Effective | Information Security |
| F-12 | Breach Response | Privacy breach escalation and notification decision records require improvement | Medium | Partially Effective | Security / DPO |
| F-13 | Retention and Disposal | Retention schedule is incomplete and deletion is not consistently enforced | High | Not Effective | Records Owners / IT |
| F-14 | Special Category and Sensitive Data | Enhanced controls for sensitive data are not consistently documented | Medium | Partially Effective | HR / Business Owners |
| F-15 | Employee Privacy | Employee privacy documentation and monitoring transparency require updates | Medium | Partially Effective | HR / Legal |
| F-16 | Children’s Data | No formal documented assessment confirms whether children’s data is processed | Medium | Not Effective | Product / Legal |
| F-17 | Training and Awareness | Privacy training is general and not sufficiently role-based | Medium | Partially Effective | HR / DPO |
| F-18 | Accountability Evidence | Evidence is dispersed and not maintained in a central compliance repository | Medium | Partially Effective | Compliance |
| F-19 | Monitoring and Assurance | No formal privacy compliance monitoring plan is in place | Medium | Not Effective | DPO / Internal Audit |
| F-20 | Data Accuracy and Quality | Data correction and quality controls vary by system and process | Low | Partially Effective | Business Owners |
| F-21 | Automated Decision-Making and Profiling | Profiling and automation have not been formally assessed across marketing and product use cases | Medium | Not Effective | Marketing / Product / Legal |

---

### F-01 - Governance and Accountability

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Area | Governance and accountability |
| Rating | High |
| Effectiveness | Partially Effective |
| Owner | Data Protection Officer |
| Status | Open |

#### Observation

The organisation has assigned responsibility for privacy compliance and has appointed or nominated a privacy lead.
