| [POL-CYB-SCOPE-001] | 1.0 | [Chief Information Security Officer] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 | Internal |

## Purpose

This Policy establishes the mandatory requirements for defining, approving, maintaining and communicating the organisational and system boundaries of the cybersecurity programme.

The purpose of scope definition is to ensure that cybersecurity governance, risk management, protection, detection, response and recovery activities are applied consistently to the parts of the organisation, technology environment, information assets, third-party relationships and business processes that are within the cybersecurity programme. Clear scope enables effective prioritisation, accountability, risk ownership, resource allocation, control implementation, assurance planning and cybersecurity performance measurement.

This Policy supports the organisation’s cybersecurity profile by ensuring that all relevant assets, systems, services, data, users, locations, suppliers and operational dependencies are identified and assigned appropriate cybersecurity oversight.

## Scope

This Policy applies to all organisational units, personnel, workers, contractors, systems, applications, infrastructure, cloud services, data repositories, business processes, products, services, facilities and third-party arrangements that are owned, operated, managed, used or relied upon by [Organisation Name].

The cybersecurity programme scope shall include, at minimum:

- Corporate information technology environments, including endpoints, networks, servers, identity services, collaboration platforms and business applications.
- Cloud services and externally hosted platforms used for organisational business.
- Operational technology, industrial control systems, building management systems, internet-of-things devices and other connected technologies where applicable.
- Systems, services and data supporting critical business functions, regulated activities, customer services or safety-related operations.
- Information assets processed, stored or transmitted by the organisation, regardless of format or hosting location.
- Third-party services that store, process, transmit, access or materially support organisational information, systems or business operations.
- Business processes that create, use, depend upon or protect information and technology assets.
- Interfaces, integrations, data flows and shared responsibility boundaries between internal and external environments.
- Subsidiaries, branches, locations, remote working environments and managed service arrangements included in organisational operations.

The cybersecurity programme scope shall be documented at both organisational and system levels:

| Scope Level | Description | Minimum Documentation Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Organisational scope | Defines which business units, legal entities, locations, functions, products, services and operational activities are included in the cybersecurity programme. | Approved scope statement, business process inventory, accountable executives and exclusions with justification. |
| System scope | Defines the technology assets, data, users, interfaces, suppliers, dependencies and operating environments included for a specific system, platform or service. | System boundary description, asset inventory, data classification, ownership, dependencies, third-party connections and applicable security requirements. |

This Policy does not replace detailed asset management, risk management, supplier management, data governance, business continuity or system security documentation. Those documents shall align to the approved cybersecurity programme scope and shall not contradict approved boundaries.

## Policy Statements

1. The organisation shall maintain a formally approved cybersecurity programme scope that defines the organisational, technical, operational and third-party boundaries of cybersecurity governance and risk management activities.

2. The cybersecurity programme scope shall be based on business objectives, mission requirements, legal and regulatory obligations, risk exposure, operational dependencies, information sensitivity and the criticality of systems and services.

3. The scope shall identify all included organisational units, business functions, locations, products, services, information assets, technology environments, suppliers and external dependencies that require cybersecurity oversight.

4. The scope shall define system boundaries for in-scope systems, including infrastructure components, applications, databases, interfaces, networks, cloud services, privileged access paths, management planes, user groups and data flows.

5. Each in-scope system, service or business process shall have an assigned business owner and a technical owner responsible for maintaining accurate scope information and supporting cybersecurity requirements.

6. The organisation shall maintain an inventory of in-scope assets and services sufficient to support cybersecurity risk assessment, control implementation, vulnerability management, incident response, recovery planning and assurance activities.

7. The scope shall include externally provided services where the supplier stores, processes, transmits, accesses, manages, protects or materially supports organisational information, systems or operations.

8. Shared responsibility boundaries for cloud services, managed services, outsourced processes and third-party platforms shall be documented and approved before production use.

9. Data types within scope shall be identified and classified according to organisational data classification requirements, including personal information, confidential business information, regulated data, intellectual property, financial information and operationally sensitive information.

10. Critical business functions and supporting technology dependencies shall be identified within the cybersecurity programme scope to enable prioritised risk treatment, resilience planning, response and recovery activities.

11. The scope shall define relevant internal and external interfaces, including application programming interfaces, network connections, remote access paths, data exchanges, third-party integrations and administrative access channels.

12. The organisation shall document any exclusions from the cybersecurity programme scope, including the business justification, risk assessment, compensating arrangements, accountable owner and approval authority.

13. Scope exclusions shall not be used to avoid cybersecurity accountability for systems, services, suppliers or data that present material risk to the organisation, customers, employees, partners or regulatory obligations.

14. New systems, services, suppliers, business processes, locations, products or significant technology changes shall not be placed into production until their cybersecurity scope status has been assessed and recorded.

15. Scope definition shall be integrated into enterprise architecture, change management, procurement, supplier onboarding, project delivery, mergers and acquisitions, system development and service retirement processes.

16. The cybersecurity programme scope shall be used to determine applicability of cybersecurity policies, standards, risk assessments, control requirements, monitoring activities, incident response obligations and assurance reviews.

17. In-scope systems and services shall be subject to cybersecurity risk assessment at a frequency appropriate to their criticality, exposure, data sensitivity and threat environment.

18. High-impact systems, internet-facing services, privileged access systems, regulated data platforms and critical operational dependencies shall be explicitly identified within the scope documentation.

19. The scope shall distinguish between production, development, testing, disaster recovery, backup, administrative and monitoring environments where cybersecurity responsibilities or risks differ.

20. The organisation shall maintain a documented relationship between business processes, information assets, systems, suppliers and responsible owners to support traceability of cybersecurity obligations.

21. The scope shall be communicated to relevant stakeholders, including executive leadership, risk owners, system owners, technology teams, security personnel, procurement teams, legal and compliance functions, and relevant suppliers.

22. Cybersecurity roles, responsibilities and accountabilities shall be assigned for all in-scope areas and shall be sufficiently clear to support decision-making, escalation and assurance.

23. Changes to scope shall be assessed for cybersecurity impact before approval, including effects on risk exposure, control coverage, monitoring, incident response, resilience and compliance obligations.

24. Material scope changes shall be approved by the designated cybersecurity governance body or authorised executive prior to implementation, unless emergency action is required to protect the organisation.

25. Emergency scope changes made to protect operations or reduce immediate risk shall be documented, reviewed and formally approved as soon as practicable after implementation.

26. The organisation shall retain historical records of approved scope versions, scope decisions, exclusions, approvals and material changes for audit, assurance and incident investigation purposes.

27. The scope shall be reviewed at planned intervals and whenever material organisational, technical, regulatory, supplier or threat changes occur.

28. Cybersecurity metrics, reporting and assurance activities shall be aligned to the approved scope and shall clearly identify any known coverage gaps.

29. Where scope boundaries are unclear, the relevant asset, process, supplier, data set or system shall be treated as in scope until a formal determination is approved.

30. The cybersecurity programme scope shall be maintained in a controlled repository accessible to authorised stakeholders and protected against unauthorised modification.

## Roles & Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Board of Directors / Governing Body | Provides oversight of the cybersecurity programme scope, confirms that material risks are visible and ensures adequate resources are available to manage in-scope cybersecurity obligations. |
| Executive Leadership | Approves organisational scope decisions that materially affect business operations, risk appetite, funding, regulatory exposure or strategic priorities. |
| Chief Information Security Officer | Owns this Policy, establishes scope definition requirements, ensures alignment with the cybersecurity programme, reviews material exclusions and reports scope-related risks to leadership. |
| Cybersecurity Governance Committee | Reviews and approves material scope definitions, boundary changes, exclusions, risk acceptance decisions and scope-related escalations. |
| Business Owners | Identify business processes, information assets, critical services, regulatory obligations and third-party dependencies within their area; approve business-level scope information and risk ownership. |
| System Owners | Define and maintain system boundaries, asset relationships, user groups, interfaces, data types, dependencies and operational environments for systems under their ownership. |
| Technology Owners | Maintain technical inventories, architecture records, integration details, hosting information, network boundaries and administrative access paths for in-scope systems and services. |
| Risk Management Function | Supports risk-based scoping decisions, validates risk assessments for exclusions and ensures scope decisions are reflected in enterprise risk records where appropriate. |
| Legal and Compliance Function | Advises on legal, regulatory, contractual and data protection obligations that affect cybersecurity scope. |
| Procurement and Supplier Management | Ensures cybersecurity scope requirements are considered during supplier selection, contracting, onboarding, monitoring, renewal and termination. |
| Enterprise Architecture | Ensures solution designs, technology standards and architecture records reflect approved cybersecurity boundaries and dependencies. |
| Project and Change Managers | Ensure new or changed systems, services, suppliers and business processes are assessed for cybersecurity scope impact before implementation. |
| Internal Audit / Independent Assurance | Provides independent review of the effectiveness, completeness and operation of scope definition and maintenance practices. |
| Employees, Contractors and Third Parties | Comply with applicable cybersecurity requirements for systems, services, data and processes within scope and promptly report suspected scope gaps or inaccuracies. |

The following minimum ownership model shall be applied to in-scope systems and services:

| Required Ownership Field | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Business Owner | Named individual accountable for business use, risk acceptance and prioritisation. |
| Technical Owner | Named individual or role accountable for technical operation and maintenance. |
| Data Owner | Named individual or role accountable for data classification, use and protection requirements. |
| Security Contact | Named individual or team accountable for cybersecurity coordination and issue escalation. |
| Supplier Owner | Named individual accountable for supplier relationship management where external services are involved. |

## Compliance, Monitoring & Enforcement

Compliance with this Policy is mandatory for all in-scope personnel, systems, services, projects, suppliers and business processes.

The organisation shall monitor compliance through a combination of governance review, asset inventory reconciliation, architecture review, project assurance, supplier review, cybersecurity risk assessment, incident analysis, control testing and internal audit.

At minimum, the following monitoring activities shall be performed:

| Monitoring Activity | Frequency | Responsible Role | Expected Evidence |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Review of organisational cybersecurity scope | At least annually | Chief Information Security Officer | Approved scope statement, governance minutes and change log |
| Review of system boundary documentation for critical systems | At least annually | System Owner | Current boundary diagram, asset list, data flows and owner approvals |
| Reconciliation of in-scope systems against asset inventory | At least quarterly | Technology Owner | Inventory reconciliation record and remediation actions |
| Review of scope exclusions | At least annually and upon material change | Cybersecurity Governance Committee | Approved exclusions register and risk assessment records |
| Supplier scope validation for material suppliers | At onboarding, renewal and at least annually | Supplier Management | Supplier assessment, contract requirements and service boundary records |
| Change impact review for material technology or business changes | Before approval or implementation | Change Manager | Change record with cybersecurity scope assessment |
| Assurance testing of scope definition process | Based on audit plan | Internal Audit / Independent Assurance | Audit report, findings and management actions |

The organisation shall maintain a cybersecurity scope register or equivalent controlled record containing, at minimum:

| Required Record | Description |
|---|---|
| Scope Identifier | Unique identifier for the organisational area, system, service or process. |
| Scope Description | Clear description of what is included. |
| Owner | Accountable business and technical owners. |
| Included Assets | Key systems, applications, infrastructure, data stores and services. |
| Included Data Types | Data categories and classifications processed, stored or transmitted. |
| Interfaces and Dependencies | Internal and external connections, integrations and service dependencies. |
| Third Parties | Suppliers or partners supporting or accessing the scope area. |
| Criticality | Business and operational importance. |
| Scope Status | In scope, out of scope, pending assessment or retired. |
| Approval Status | Draft, approved, under review or expired. |
| Last Review Date | Date of most recent validation. |
| Next Review Date | Date of next planned review. |

Non-compliance with this Policy may result in one or more of the following actions:

- Required remediation plan with assigned owner and due date.
- Escalation to the relevant business owner, executive sponsor or governance committee.
- Suspension or delay of project go-live, supplier onboarding, system change or production release.
- Additional cybersecurity review, risk assessment or independent assurance.
- Formal risk acceptance by an authorised executive where remediation cannot be completed within required timeframes.
- Contractual remedies for supplier non-compliance.
- Disciplinary action for personnel, up to and including termination, in accordance with organisational policies and applicable law.

Where a scope gap creates immediate or material cybersecurity risk, the Chief Information Security Officer or authorised delegate may require interim risk reduction measures, including access restriction, network isolation, enhanced monitoring, vulnerability remediation, supplier action, change rollback or temporary service suspension.

## Exceptions

Exceptions to this Policy shall be permitted only where there is a documented business need and the resulting cybersecurity risk has been assessed, approved and assigned to an accountable risk owner.

All exception requests shall include:

| Exception Information | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Requestor | Name and role of the person requesting the exception. |
| Affected Area | Business unit, system, service, supplier, process or data affected. |
| Policy Requirement | Specific requirement from this Policy for which exception is requested. |
| Business Justification | Reason the requirement cannot currently be met. |
| Risk Assessment | Cybersecurity, operational, legal, regulatory and business impact of the exception. |
| Compensating Measures | Temporary controls or safeguards to reduce risk. |
| Duration | Requested start and end date; open-ended exceptions are not permitted. |
| Risk Owner | Accountable person accepting the residual risk. |
| Approval | Required approval from the Chief Information Security Officer and, where material, the cybersecurity governance body or authorised executive. |
| Review Date | Date when the exception will be reassessed. |
| Remediation Plan | Actions required to return to compliance, with owners and target dates. |

Exceptions shall be time-bound and shall not exceed [maximum exception period, e.g., 12 months] without renewed assessment and approval. Exceptions involving critical systems, regulated data, internet-facing services, privileged access, safety-related operations or material suppliers shall require heightened review and executive-level approval.

Expired exceptions shall be treated as non-compliance unless formally renewed before expiry. Exception records shall be retained in accordance with organisational record retention requirements and made available for audit or assurance review.

## Review & Maintenance

This Policy shall be reviewed at least annually and whenever significant changes occur to the organisation, technology environment, threat landscape, regulatory obligations, business strategy, operating model, supplier ecosystem or cybersecurity programme.

The Chief Information Security Officer is responsible for coordinating review and maintenance of this Policy. Policy updates shall be reviewed by relevant stakeholders, approved through the organisation’s policy governance process and communicated to affected personnel.

The cybersecurity programme scope and supporting scope records shall be reviewed and updated when any of the following occur:

- Creation, acquisition, merger, divestiture or closure of a business unit, legal entity, location, product or service.
- Introduction, replacement, retirement or material change of a system, platform, cloud service, network, application or operational technology environment.
- Onboarding, termination or material change of a supplier, managed service provider, cloud provider or outsourced business process.
- Identification of new critical business functions, regulated activities or sensitive data processing.
- Significant change to data flows, integrations, remote access, privileged access, hosting location or administrative control.
- Cybersecurity incident, near miss, audit finding, regulatory finding or material control failure indicating that scope records may be incomplete or inaccurate.
- Significant change in threats, vulnerabilities, business impact, legal obligations or risk appetite.
- Discovery of assets, data stores, services, connections or suppliers not previously recorded in the approved scope.

Version history shall be maintained for this Policy and for the approved cybersecurity programme scope, including the date of change, description of change, author, reviewer and approver.

| Version | Date | Description of Change | Author | Approver |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Initial issue | [Name / Role] | [Name / Role] |

NIST-002.title: Stakeholder Communication Plan
NIST-002.content:
# Stakeholder Communication Plan

| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [DOC-ID] | 1.0 | [Cybersecurity Program Owner] | [Effective Date] | NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 | Internal Use |

## Purpose & Objectives

This Stakeholder Communication Plan defines how [Organisation Name] will identify, engage, inform, and receive input from internal and external stakeholders as part of its cybersecurity governance and risk management activities.

The purpose of this plan is to ensure that cybersecurity-related information is communicated to the right stakeholders, at the right time, using appropriate channels, in a form that supports informed decision-making, accountability, and coordinated action.

The objectives of this plan are to:

- Establish a structured approach for cybersecurity communications across business, technology, risk, legal, compliance, executive, and external stakeholder groups.
- Ensure stakeholders understand their cybersecurity responsibilities, decision rights, dependencies, and escalation paths.
- Support executive oversight by providing timely, relevant, and accurate reporting on cybersecurity risk, performance, priorities, and issues.
- Promote two-way communication so that stakeholder feedback, business context, regulatory expectations, and operational constraints are considered in cybersecurity planning.
- Improve coordination during cybersecurity initiatives, material risk decisions, third-party interactions, audits, assessments, and incident response activities.
- Maintain consistent messaging for internal and external parties, including employees, customers, suppliers, regulators, insurers, and other interested parties.
- Protect sensitive cybersecurity information by applying appropriate classification, need-to-know access, and approved communication channels.
- Provide auditable evidence that stakeholder communication is planned, executed, reviewed, and improved over time.

## Scope

This plan applies to cybersecurity governance communications for [Organisation Name], including communications related to cybersecurity strategy, risk management, roles and responsibilities, policies, controls, third-party dependencies, performance reporting, significant issues, and stakeholder engagement.

The scope includes communications with the following stakeholder groups:

| Stakeholder Group | Examples | Communication Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Board and executive leadership | Board committee, CEO, COO, CFO, CIO, CISO, General Counsel | Cybersecurity risk posture, strategic priorities, funding needs, major decisions, regulatory exposure, material incidents, risk acceptance |
| Cybersecurity and technology teams | Security operations, infrastructure, cloud, architecture, application teams, identity teams | Security initiatives, technical risks, control performance, remediation plans, operational dependencies, incident trends |
| Risk, compliance, legal, and audit teams | Enterprise risk, privacy, legal, internal audit, compliance management | Risk register updates, obligations, assurance activities, policy exceptions, audit findings, evidence needs |
| Business unit leaders | Product owners, process owners, regional leaders, department heads | Business impact of cybersecurity risks, process responsibilities, change impacts, resilience requirements |
| Workforce | Employees, contractors, temporary staff | Security expectations, awareness messages, acceptable use, reporting obligations, policy changes |
| Third parties | Suppliers, managed service providers, cloud providers, consultants, outsourcing partners | Security requirements, assessment requests, incident notification expectations, remediation obligations, service dependencies |
| Customers and clients | Enterprise customers, consumers, account representatives | Security posture statements, service-impact communications, assurance responses, incident-related notices where approved |
| Regulators and government bodies | Supervisory authorities, sector regulators, law enforcement where applicable | Required notifications, supervisory engagement, formal responses, evidence submissions |
| Insurers and external advisors | Cyber insurers, breach counsel, forensic providers, external auditors | Risk information, claim-related communication, assurance coordination, specialist support |

This plan covers planned, recurring, event-driven, and escalation communications. It does not replace the Incident Response Plan, Crisis Communications Plan, Legal Notification Procedure, or Public Relations protocols. Where those documents apply, this plan supports coordination and stakeholder alignment but does not override approved incident, legal, or media communication processes.

The following communication types are in scope:

- Cybersecurity strategy and roadmap updates.
- Governance forums, steering committee updates, and executive briefings.
- Risk assessments, risk register updates, and risk acceptance decisions.
- Cybersecurity performance metrics and management reporting.
- Policy, standard, and procedure changes.
- Cybersecurity awareness and workforce communications.
- Third-party cybersecurity communications.
- Audit, assurance, and assessment communications.
- Regulatory and contractual cybersecurity communications.
- Significant cybersecurity issues, exceptions, and remediation updates.
- Stakeholder feedback and consultation related to cybersecurity governance.

The following are out of scope, except where they intersect with cybersecurity governance:

- General corporate communications unrelated to cybersecurity.
- Marketing communications not involving cybersecurity claims or assurance statements.
- Routine IT service communications that do not affect cybersecurity risk or stakeholder obligations.
- Technical change notifications managed solely through IT service management processes.

## Assumptions & Dependencies

This plan is based on the following assumptions:

- [Organisation Name] has assigned executive accountability for cybersecurity governance.
- A cybersecurity leadership function exists and is responsible for coordinating cybersecurity risk communication.
- Stakeholders can be identified through organisational structure, business ownership records, supplier records, risk registers, systems inventories, and governance forums.
- Communication channels such as email, collaboration tools, intranet, ticketing systems, governance meetings, and executive reporting packs are available and approved for business use.
- Sensitive cybersecurity information will be classified, handled, and distributed in accordance with the organisation’s information classification and handling requirements.
- Legal, privacy, regulatory, and contractual notification requirements will be reviewed by authorised personnel before external disclosure.
- Business units are expected to participate in cybersecurity governance where cybersecurity risks affect their processes, customers, systems, data, or suppliers.
- Third-party communications are coordinated through approved supplier management, procurement, legal, or relationship management channels.
- Workforce communications will align with HR, corporate communications, and security awareness practices.

Successful execution of this plan depends on:

| Dependency | Description | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Stakeholder register | Current list of internal and external stakeholders, contacts, roles, interests, and escalation paths | Cybersecurity Governance Lead |
| Communication channels | Approved tools and forums for different communication types and sensitivity levels | IT / Corporate Communications |
| Information classification rules | Requirements for labelling, storing, sharing, and restricting access to sensitive information | Information Security |
| Cybersecurity metrics | Defined metrics, data sources, reporting cadence, and owners | Cybersecurity Program Owner |
| Risk management process | Process for recording, assessing, treating, escalating, and accepting cybersecurity risks | Enterprise Risk Management |
| Incident response process | Defined process for incident classification, escalation, notification, and communication | Incident Response Lead |
| Legal and regulatory review | Review of external statements, notifications, contractual disclosures, and regulator engagement | Legal / Compliance |
| Supplier governance process | Mechanism for communicating security expectations, assessments, and remediation with third parties | Procurement / Third-Party Risk |
| Executive governance forum | Regular forum for review of cybersecurity posture, risks, priorities, and decisions | Executive Sponsor |

Key constraints include:

- Cybersecurity information may be sensitive and must not be shared broadly without a valid business need.
- External communications may require legal, regulatory, contractual, executive, or public relations approval.
- Stakeholder availability may affect consultation and approval timelines.
- Reporting quality depends on timely and accurate input from technology, business, risk, and supplier teams.
- Global, regional, or sector-specific obligations may require tailored communications.

## Approach / Phases

The communication approach will be implemented in structured phases to ensure stakeholder engagement is planned, repeatable, measurable, and aligned to cybersecurity governance needs.

### Phase 1 - Stakeholder Identification and Analysis

The Cybersecurity Governance Lead will maintain a stakeholder register that identifies relevant internal and external stakeholders and documents their communication needs.

Activities include:

- Identify stakeholder groups connected to cybersecurity governance, risk, compliance, operations, business ownership, suppliers, customers, and oversight.
- Determine each stakeholder’s role in cybersecurity decision-making, execution, review, or assurance.
- Assess the information needs of each stakeholder group, including preferred level of detail, frequency, format, sensitivity, and required decisions.
- Identify communication expectations from contracts, regulations, customer commitments, insurance arrangements, and internal governance practices.
- Define escalation contacts for urgent cybersecurity matters.
- Document stakeholder dependencies, including business units that own critical processes, systems, data, or suppliers.

The stakeholder register will include, at minimum:

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| Stakeholder group | Name of stakeholder category or forum |
| Primary contact | Named individual or role responsible for receiving communications |
| Business area | Function, department, geography, or service area |
| Interest or dependency | Why the stakeholder needs cybersecurity information |
| Communication type | Reports, briefings, alerts, workshops, approvals, consultations |
| Frequency | Regular cadence or trigger-based timing |
| Sensitivity level | Expected classification and sharing restrictions |
| Decision authority | Whether the stakeholder informs, approves, accepts, funds, or executes decisions |
| Escalation path | Contact route for urgent or unresolved matters |

### Phase 2 - Communication Planning and Message Design

For each stakeholder group, communications will be designed to be clear, purposeful, and appropriate to the audience.

Activities include:

- Define the intended outcome of each communication, such as awareness, consultation, decision, approval, escalation, or evidence gathering.
- Establish standard communication types, owners, frequencies, templates, and approval requirements.
- Develop audience-specific messaging that explains cybersecurity risks in business terms, including likelihood, impact, options, residual exposure, and required action.
- Align messages with approved risk appetite, business priorities, and governance expectations.
- Determine when communications require legal, privacy, compliance, executive, customer success, supplier management, or public relations review.
- Define rules for communicating sensitive topics such as vulnerabilities, control weaknesses, incidents, audit findings, regulatory concerns, or supplier failures.
- Establish a process for recording key decisions, action items, approvals, and stakeholder feedback.

The following communication matrix will be used as the baseline:

| Communication Type | Audience | Purpose | Frequency / Trigger | Owner | Channel | Approval Required |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cybersecurity executive dashboard | Board and executive leadership | Provide concise view of risk posture, key risks, metrics, investment needs, and decisions | Quarterly or as requested | CISO / Cybersecurity Program Owner | Board pack / executive meeting | CISO, Executive Sponsor |
| Cybersecurity steering update | Executive sponsor, technology leaders, business leaders, risk, legal, compliance | Track roadmap, risks, dependencies, issues, and decisions | Monthly | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Steering committee meeting | CISO |
| Cybersecurity risk register update | Risk owners, enterprise risk, business process owners, technology owners | Review risk status, treatment plans, acceptances, and escalations | Monthly or upon material change | Risk Management Lead | Risk system / working session | Risk Owner |
| Policy and standard change notice | Workforce, process owners, technology teams, third parties where applicable | Communicate new or changed cybersecurity requirements | As needed | Policy Owner | Email / intranet / supplier portal | CISO, Legal if external |
| Security awareness message | Workforce | Reinforce expected behaviours and reporting routes | Monthly or campaign-based | Security Awareness Lead | Email / intranet / LMS / collaboration tool | Cybersecurity Governance Lead |
| Third-party security communication | Suppliers, managed service providers, procurement, relationship managers | Communicate security requirements, assessment needs, remediation expectations, and incidents affecting services | Onboarding, annually, upon material change, or trigger event | Third-Party Risk Lead | Supplier portal / email / contract management system | Procurement, Legal as needed |
| Customer assurance response | Customers, sales, account managers, legal | Provide approved security posture information and responses to assurance requests | Upon request | Customer Assurance Lead | Approved questionnaire platform / email | Legal, CISO as needed |
| Audit and assessment communication | Internal audit, external assessors, control owners | Coordinate evidence requests, findings, remediation, and management responses | Per audit plan or assessment schedule | Compliance Lead | Audit portal / meetings / email | Control Owner |
| Significant issue escalation | Executive sponsor, affected business owners, risk, legal, technology leaders | Escalate material cybersecurity risks, major control failures, unresolved remediation, or business-impacting issues | Within agreed escalation timeframe after identification | Cybersecurity Program Owner | Meeting / secure email / risk system | CISO |
| Incident stakeholder communication | Incident response team, executives, legal, affected business units, external parties as approved | Support timely and controlled communication during cybersecurity incidents | Per incident severity and response process | Incident Response Lead | Incident bridge / secure channels / approved statements | Legal, Executive Sponsor, Communications as applicable |

### Phase 3 - Channel Selection and Information Handling

Communication channels will be selected based on urgency, audience, sensitivity, and required evidence.

Approved channels may include:

- Executive and board reporting packs.
- Governance committee meetings.
- Secure email distribution lists.
- Collaboration platforms with restricted access.
- Risk management, audit, compliance, and ticketing systems.
- Learning management systems.
- Intranet pages and knowledge bases.
- Supplier portals and contract management platforms.
- Customer assurance platforms.
- Secure file transfer tools for sensitive evidence.

The following handling principles apply:

- Cybersecurity information must be shared only with authorised recipients who have a business need to know.
- Sensitive technical details, vulnerability information, incident details, exploit information, investigation findings, and unremediated control weaknesses must be restricted.
- External communications must use approved messaging and must not disclose sensitive technical or operational information unless authorised.
- Draft communications containing sensitive cybersecurity information must be stored in approved repositories.
- Distribution lists must be reviewed periodically to ensure access remains appropriate.
- Meeting minutes must record decisions and actions without unnecessarily exposing sensitive details.
- Communications involving legal advice, regulatory matters, incidents, customer impact, or contractual commitments must be coordinated with Legal before release.
- Public statements, media responses, and customer-facing cybersecurity claims must be approved through the organisation’s external communications process.

### Phase 4 - Execution and Engagement

Communication owners will deliver communications according to the defined cadence and trigger events.

Execution activities include:

- Prepare communication materials using approved templates and current data.
- Validate accuracy with relevant subject matter experts before distribution.
- Obtain required approvals before issuing communications.
- Deliver communications through approved channels.
- Record delivery evidence, such as meeting agendas, minutes, attendance records, sent communications, dashboard versions, decision logs, and action trackers.
- Capture questions, objections, decisions, and requested changes.
- Assign and track follow-up actions to named owners with due dates.
- Escalate overdue responses, unresolved issues, or decisions that exceed delegated authority.

Stakeholder engagement methods may include:

- Executive briefings.
- Steering committee meetings.
- Risk review workshops.
- Business impact discussions.
- Supplier security reviews.
- Customer assurance sessions.
- Policy consultation sessions.
- Awareness campaigns.
- Tabletop exercises and lessons-learned sessions.
- Audit opening, status, and close-out meetings.

### Phase 5 - Monitoring, Feedback, and Continuous Improvement

The Cybersecurity Governance Lead will monitor whether communications are effective and will adjust the plan as needed.

Monitoring activities include:

- Track delivery against the communication schedule.
- Review attendance and participation in governance forums.
- Monitor completion of required stakeholder actions.
- Measure response times for approvals, evidence requests, risk decisions, and escalations.
- Assess stakeholder understanding through surveys, workshops, assurance feedback, and management reviews.
- Review whether communications resulted in timely decisions and risk treatment progress.
- Identify repeated misunderstandings, delays, information gaps, or unclear ownership.
- Update the stakeholder register and communication matrix when organisational, regulatory, technology, supplier, or risk conditions change.
- Report significant communication issues to the Cybersecurity Program Owner and executive sponsor.

Continuous improvement actions may include:

- Revising message formats to improve clarity.
- Changing frequency or audience for recurring reports.
- Introducing additional briefings for high-risk initiatives.
- Improving dashboard metrics and visualisation.
- Updating templates and approval workflows.
- Providing targeted training to stakeholders with recurring issues.
- Refining escalation criteria and decision logs.

## Milestones & Timeline (markdown table)

| Milestone | Description | Target Date | Owner | Deliverable / Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Confirm plan ownership | Assign accountable owner and supporting roles for cybersecurity stakeholder communications | [Date] | Executive Sponsor | Approved ownership record | Not Started |
| Identify stakeholder groups | Compile internal and external stakeholder groups relevant to cybersecurity governance | [Date] | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Initial stakeholder list | Not Started |
| Complete stakeholder analysis | Document stakeholder interests, communication needs, decision rights, channels, and escalation paths | [Date] | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Stakeholder register | Not Started |
| Define communication matrix | Establish communication types, frequency, owners, channels, and approval requirements | [Date] | Cybersecurity Program Owner | Approved communication matrix | Not Started |
| Validate information handling requirements | Confirm classification and handling rules for sensitive cybersecurity communications | [Date] | Information Security Lead | Handling guidance / approved distribution rules | Not Started |
| Align with legal and external communication processes | Confirm approval path for customer, regulator, media, insurer, and third-party communications | [Date] | Legal / Compliance | External communication approval workflow | Not Started |
| Develop reporting templates | Create templates for executive dashboard, steering update, risk update, issue escalation, and decision log | [Date] | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Approved templates | Not Started |
| Launch recurring governance communications | Begin regular delivery of executive, steering, risk, and operational cybersecurity communications | [Date] | CISO / Cybersecurity Program Owner | Meeting calendar, reports, minutes | Not Started |
| Launch workforce communication cadence | Establish cybersecurity awareness and policy communication schedule | [Date] | Security Awareness Lead | Awareness calendar and messages | Not Started |
| Launch third-party communication cadence | Integrate cybersecurity communication with supplier onboarding, annual review, and remediation processes | [Date] | Third-Party Risk Lead | Supplier communication records | Not Started |
| Implement communication evidence repository | Create central repository for approved communication artefacts, decision logs, and evidence | [Date] | Compliance Lead | Repository structure and access list | Not Started |
| Conduct first effectiveness review | Review timeliness, stakeholder feedback, action closure, and reporting quality | [Date] | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Effectiveness review summary | Not Started |
| Update plan based on lessons learned | Revise plan, communication matrix, stakeholders, channels, or templates as needed | [Date] | Cybersecurity Program Owner | Updated plan and change log | Not Started |

## Roles & Responsibilities

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Board / Board Committee | Receive cybersecurity risk and performance information; challenge management where appropriate; provide oversight of material cybersecurity matters; review significant risk decisions and major investment needs. |
| Executive Sponsor | Champion cybersecurity governance communications; ensure stakeholder participation; resolve cross-functional barriers; approve escalations requiring executive direction. |
| Chief Information Security Officer or Equivalent | Own overall cybersecurity messaging and governance reporting; ensure communications support cybersecurity strategy, risk management, and accountability; approve sensitive or material cybersecurity communications. |
| Cybersecurity Program Owner | Coordinate execution of this plan; ensure communication activities align with cybersecurity priorities; monitor progress, decisions, and issues; report communication effectiveness to leadership. |
| Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Maintain stakeholder register and communication matrix; manage recurring governance communications; coordinate templates, evidence, decision logs, and action tracking; perform effectiveness reviews. |
| Enterprise Risk Management Lead | Align cybersecurity communications with enterprise risk processes; ensure risk information is presented consistently; coordinate risk escalation, risk acceptance, and risk reporting. |
| Legal Counsel | Review external communications involving legal obligations, regulatory matters, contractual commitments, incident notifications, litigation risk, or privileged information; advise on disclosure constraints. |
| Compliance Lead | Coordinate communications for audits, assessments, regulatory requests, and evidence submissions; maintain documentation evidence where required. |
| Privacy Officer / Data Protection Lead | Advise on communications involving personal data, privacy obligations, data subject impact, or data protection authority engagement. |
| Corporate Communications / Public Relations | Review and approve public, media, customer-facing, or reputation-sensitive communications; ensure consistency with corporate messaging. |
| Security Awareness Lead | Plan and deliver workforce cybersecurity awareness communications; measure engagement and completion; tailor messages based on risk trends and behaviours. |
| Incident Response Lead | Coordinate stakeholder communications during cybersecurity incidents in alignment with incident response and crisis communication processes; ensure timely escalation and controlled information sharing. |
| Third-Party Risk Lead | Communicate cybersecurity requirements, assessments, remediation expectations, and security events with suppliers; coordinate with procurement and relationship owners. |
| Procurement / Supplier Relationship Managers | Support supplier communication, contract alignment, escalation, and remediation tracking; ensure suppliers receive approved cybersecurity requirements. |
| Business Unit Leaders | Participate in cybersecurity communications affecting their operations; provide business context; assign owners for actions; make or escalate business risk decisions. |
| Technology and System Owners | Provide accurate technical input for cybersecurity reporting; communicate control status, vulnerabilities, remediation progress, and operational dependencies. |
| Internal Audit | Coordinate audit communications, evidence requests, management responses, and reporting of assurance results; maintain independence in assurance activities. |
| HR / People Function | Support workforce communications, training expectations, onboarding messages, and disciplinary or behavioural matters related to cybersecurity where applicable. |
| All Workforce Members | Read and follow cybersecurity communications relevant to their role; complete required training; report cybersecurity concerns through approved channels. |

A responsibility assignment model may be used for key communication activities:

| Activity | Accountable | Responsible | Consulted | Informed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maintain stakeholder register | Cybersecurity Program Owner | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Business Units, Risk, Legal, Compliance | CISO |
| Approve communication plan | Executive Sponsor | Cybersecurity Program Owner | CISO, Legal, Risk, Compliance | Steering Committee |
| Prepare executive dashboard | CISO | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Technology Owners, Risk, Compliance | Board / Executive Leadership |
| Communicate material cybersecurity risk | CISO | Cybersecurity Program Owner | Risk Owner, Legal, Business Owner | Executive Sponsor |
| Issue workforce security communications | Security Awareness Lead | Security Awareness Lead | HR, Corporate Communications, CISO | Workforce |
| Communicate with suppliers on cybersecurity matters | Third-Party Risk Lead | Supplier Relationship Manager | Legal, Procurement, Security SMEs | CISO / Business Owner |
| Respond to customer security assurance requests | Customer Assurance Lead | Security / Compliance SMEs | Legal, Sales, CISO | Account Team |
| Coordinate regulatory cybersecurity communication | Legal / Compliance | Compliance Lead | CISO, Privacy, Risk | Executive Sponsor |
| Communicate during cybersecurity incidents | Incident Response Lead | Incident Communications Coordinator | Legal, PR, Business Owners, CISO | Approved stakeholder groups |
| Review communication effectiveness | Cybersecurity Program Owner | Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Stakeholders, Risk, Compliance | Executive Sponsor |

## Resources

The following resources are required to implement and sustain this plan.

### People Resources

| Resource | Purpose | Estimated Commitment |
|---|---|---|
| Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Day-to-day coordination of stakeholder communications, registers, templates, action tracking, and evidence | [Commitment] |
| Cybersecurity Program Owner | Oversight of plan execution, escalation, performance review, and stakeholder alignment | [Commitment] |
| Security Metrics / Reporting Analyst | Prepare dashboards, collect metrics, validate data, and maintain reporting packs | [Commitment] |
| Enterprise Risk Representative | Align risk communications, risk register updates, and risk acceptance records | [Commitment] |
| Legal / Compliance Representative | Review external, regulatory, contractual, and sensitive communications | [Commitment] |
| Corporate Communications Representative | Support messaging quality, public-facing communications, and awareness campaigns | [Commitment] |
| Third-Party Risk Representative | Coordinate supplier communications and third-party security obligations | [Commitment] |
| Business Unit Representatives | Provide business input, receive communications, and coordinate actions within their areas | [Commitment] |
| Technology Subject Matter Experts | Provide technical input, control status, remediation updates, and risk context | [Commitment] |

### Tools and Repositories

| Tool / Repository | Intended Use | Minimum Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Governance calendar | Schedule recurring cybersecurity communication forums and reporting deadlines | Accessible to relevant stakeholders |
| Stakeholder register | Maintain stakeholder details, roles, interests, contacts, and communication requirements | Access controlled and reviewed periodically |
| Risk management system | Record cybersecurity risks, treatment plans, acceptances, escalations, and status updates | Supports reporting and evidence retention |
| Compliance / audit repository | Store evidence of communications, approvals, meeting minutes, and audit responses | Version controlled and access restricted |
| Collaboration platform | Support working sessions, action tracking, and controlled document sharing | Appropriate permissions and retention settings |
| Secure email / distribution lists | Distribute approved communications to defined audiences | Distribution lists owned and periodically validated |
| Reporting dashboard | Present cybersecurity metrics, risk trends, and program status | Data sources defined and reviewed for accuracy |
| Learning management system | Deliver and track workforce awareness communications and training | Completion tracking and reporting enabled |
| Supplier management platform | Communicate security requirements and track supplier assurance activities | Linked to supplier ownership and contract records |
| Customer assurance repository | Store approved security responses, questionnaires, and standard assurance statements | Legal and security approval workflow supported |

### Templates and Supporting Materials

The following templates should be maintained:

- Stakeholder register.
- Communication matrix.
- Executive cybersecurity dashboard.
- Cybersecurity steering committee update.
- Cybersecurity risk update.
- Material issue escalation brief.
- Decision log.
- Action tracker.
- Policy change notice.
- Workforce awareness message.
- Supplier cybersecurity communication.
- Customer assurance response.
- Audit evidence request tracker.
- Lessons learned and feedback log.

### Budget and Support Requirements

Budget may be required for:

- Reporting and dashboard tooling.
- Governance, risk, and compliance platform enhancements.
- Secure collaboration and file transfer capabilities.
- Security awareness content and campaign delivery.
- Translation or localisation of workforce communications.
- External legal, regulatory, forensic, or public relations support for sensitive communications.
- Training for executives, risk owners, communication owners, and spokespersons.
- Supplier assurance platforms or external assessment services.

## Success Metrics

The effectiveness of this plan will be measured using qualitative and quantitative indicators. Metrics will be reviewed at least quarterly by the Cybersecurity Program Owner and reported to the appropriate governance forum.

| Metric | Target / Indicator | Data Source | Review Frequency | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stakeholder register completeness | All identified stakeholder groups documented with owner, contact, cadence, and escalation path | Stakeholder register | Quarterly | Cybersecurity Governance Lead |
| Communication schedule adherence | Planned communications delivered on time, with documented evidence | Governance calendar / evidence repository | Monthly | Cybersecurity Governance Lead |
| Executive reporting timeliness | Executive cybersecurity reports issued according to agreed reporting cycle | Board / executive reporting pack | Quarterly | CISO |
| Action closure rate | Stakeholder actions closed by due date or formally re-baselined | Action tracker | Monthly | Cybersecurity Program Owner |
| Risk decision timeliness | Material risk decisions made within agreed decision timeframe | Risk management system | Monthly | Enterprise Risk Management Lead |
| Stakeholder participation | Required stakeholders attend governance forums or provide delegated representation | Meeting attendance records | Monthly | Forum Chair |
| Approval cycle time | Communications requiring approval completed within agreed timeframe | Approval workflow / email records | Monthly | Communication Owner |
| External communication compliance | External cybersecurity communications reviewed and approved before release | Legal / compliance records | Quarterly | Legal / Compliance |
| Workforce engagement | Awareness message open rates, training completion, and campaign participation meet targets | Learning management system / awareness platform | Monthly or campaign-based | Security Awareness Lead |
| Supplier response rate | Suppliers respond to cybersecurity communications, assessments, or remediation requests within required timeframes | Supplier management platform | Monthly | Third-Party Risk Lead |
| Audit evidence availability | Communication evidence available and retrievable for audits or reviews | Evidence repository | Quarterly | Compliance Lead |
| Stakeholder satisfaction | Feedback indicates communications are clear, timely, relevant, and actionable | Survey / interviews / feedback log | Semi-annually | Cybersecurity Governance Lead |
| Escalation effectiveness | Material issues escalated to appropriate decision-makers without avoidable delay | Escalation log / risk system | Quarterly | Cybersecurity Program Owner |
| Reduction in repeat communication issues | Fewer recurring issues related to unclear ownership, missed actions, or inconsistent messaging | Lessons learned log | Quarterly | Cybersecurity Governance Lead |

Success will be demonstrated when:

- Stakeholders understand their cybersecurity responsibilities and escalation paths.
- Cybersecurity risks and decisions are communicated in business-relevant terms.
- Executive leadership receives consistent and timely cybersecurity information.
- External communications are controlled, reviewed, and traceable.
- Communication evidence is available for audit, assurance, and management review.
- Stakeholder feedback leads to measurable improvements in governance communication.
- Significant cybersecurity issues are escalated promptly and resolved through defined decision channels.

## Review & Update Triggers

This plan will be reviewed at least annually and whenever a material change affects cybersecurity stakeholder communication needs.

The Cybersecurity Program Owner is responsible for ensuring reviews are performed and updates are approved. The Cybersecurity Governance Lead is responsible for maintaining the working version of the plan, stakeholder register, communication matrix, and related templates.

Update triggers include:

- Significant change to the organisation’s structure, leadership, operating model, or governance forums.
- Change in cybersecurity strategy, risk appetite, or major cybersecurity program priorities.
- Introduction of new business lines, products, services, geographies, or customer segments.
- Material change in the technology environment, including cloud adoption, outsourcing, mergers, acquisitions, or major system transformation.
- Identification of new critical business processes, systems, data sets, or third-party dependencies.
- Material cybersecurity incident, crisis event, or lessons learned exercise.
- Significant control failure, audit finding, regulatory issue, or unresolved remediation concern.
- Change in legal, regulatory, contractual, insurance, or customer communication expectations.
- Significant supplier issue, supplier incident, or change in outsourced service arrangements.
- Stakeholder feedback indicating communications are unclear, incomplete, delayed, or not actionable.
- Repeated missed actions, late decisions, ineffective escalations, or inconsistent messaging.
- Change in communication channels, collaboration tools, reporting platforms, or information handling requirements.
- Change in classification requirements affecting cybersecurity information.
- Results from audits, assessments, tabletop exercises, management reviews, or maturity assessments.
- New or revised corporate communications, incident response, crisis management, privacy, legal notification, or supplier management processes.

Each review will consider:

- Whether stakeholder groups remain current and complete.
- Whether communication frequency and formats remain appropriate.
- Whether owners and escalation paths are accurate.
- Whether sensitive information is being handled appropriately.
- Whether recurring reports support decision-making.
- Whether external communication approvals are effective.
- Whether evidence is retained and retrievable.
- Whether metrics indicate communication performance is improving.
- Whether lessons learned have been incorporated.

Material changes to this plan must be approved by the Cybersecurity Program Owner and Executive Sponsor. Minor administrative updates, such as role title changes, contact updates, or template refinements, may be approved by the Cybersecurity Governance Lead in accordance with document management practices.

### Column Guidance

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Profile ID | Enter the unique identifier for this Current Profile report, using the organisation's naming convention, e.g. CSF2-CURRENT-YYYY or CSF2-ASIS-001. |
| Assessment Date | Enter the date this Current Profile assessment was performed in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Function | Enter the CSF 2.0 Function for the subcategory: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, or Recover. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Category ID | Enter the official NIST CSF 2.0 Category identifier, e.g. GV.OC, ID.AM, PR.AA, DE.CM, RS.MA, RC.RP. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Category Name | Enter the official NIST CSF 2.0 Category name corresponding to the Category ID. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory ID | Enter the official NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory identifier being assessed, e.g. GV.OC-01, ID.AM-01, PR.AA-01. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory Outcome | Enter the official NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory outcome statement exactly or materially consistent with the NIST CSF 2.0 text. |
| Applicability | Select whether the subcategory is applicable to the organisation: Applicable, Partially Applicable, Not Applicable, or To Be Determined. |
| Applicability Rationale | Explain why the subcategory is applicable, partially applicable, not applicable, or still to be determined; include business, legal, regulatory, technology, or operating context. |
| In-Scope Business Units | List the business units, departments, regions, or legal entities included in the current-state assessment for this subcategory; use comma-separated names or 'Enterprise-wide'. |
| In-Scope Systems / Assets | List the systems, platforms, applications, data environments, infrastructure, or asset classes covered by the current implementation; use asset register names or IDs where available. |
| Current Implementation Summary | Describe how the organisation currently achieves, partially achieves, or does not achieve the subcategory outcome; focus on actual operating practice, not planned activity. |
| Implementation Status | Select the current implementation state: Not Implemented, Partially Implemented, Largely Implemented, Fully Implemented, Not Applicable, or Unknown. |
| Current Achievement Level | Enter the assessed current achievement level using the organisation's agreed scale, e.g. 0=None, 1=Initial, 2=Developing, 3=Defined, 4=Managed, 5=Optimised. |
| Control / Process References | List internal control IDs, process IDs, procedure IDs, or framework mappings that support this subcategory, e.g. IAM-CTRL-001, IR-PROC-003. |
| Policy / Standard References | List approved policy, standard, or procedure documents that define requirements relevant to this subcategory, including document ID and title where available. |
| Technical Tooling / Platforms | List the tools, platforms, or automated mechanisms currently used to support the subcategory, e.g. SIEM, GRC platform, CMDB, EDR, IAM, ticketing system. |
| Evidence References | Provide references or links to evidence proving the current implementation, such as audit workpaper IDs, screenshots, reports, tickets, configuration exports, meeting minutes, or repository paths. |
| Evidence Date | Enter the date of the most recent evidence reviewed in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| Control Owner | Enter the named role or individual accountable for the control implementation supporting this subcategory. |
| Process Owner | Enter the named role or individual accountable for the business or operational process associated with this subcategory. |
| Risk / Issue References | List related risk register IDs, audit findings, exceptions, issues, or compliance observations linked to the current implementation; enter 'None identified' if none are known. |
| Known Gaps or Limitations | Describe specific shortcomings in the current implementation, including missing coverage, inconsistent operation, lack of evidence, manual dependency, or unresolved exceptions; enter 'None identified' if none are known. |
| Compensating Controls | Describe any alternate controls or practices that reduce risk where the primary expected implementation is absent or incomplete; enter 'None' if not applicable. |
| Dependencies | List dependencies affecting the current implementation, such as third-party services, shared platforms, upstream data feeds, enterprise programmes, or key roles. |
| Last Validated Date | Enter the date the current implementation status was last reviewed or validated in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| Validated By | Enter the name and role of the person or team that validated the current implementation status. |
| Validation Method | Select or describe the method used to validate the current state, e.g. Document Review, Interview, System Walkthrough, Configuration Review, Sample Testing, Control Testing, Audit Result, or Self-Attestation. |
| Confidence Rating | Select the confidence level in the current-state assessment: High, Medium, Low, or Not Assessed; base this on evidence quality, recency, and independence. |
| Notes | Enter any additional context needed to interpret the current profile entry, including assumptions, exclusions, open questions, or reviewer comments. |

### Maintenance

Owned by the Cybersecurity GRC Manager with input from control owners, process owners, and risk management. Updated at least annually, after material business or technology changes, and after major control validation activities; source data is drawn from the GRC platform, risk register, control library, evidence repository, CMDB, IAM/PAM platforms, SIEM/security tooling, ticketing system, and audit issue tracker.

### Column Guidance

| Column | What to enter |
|---|---|
| Target Profile ID | Enter a unique identifier for this target profile line item, using a consistent format such as TP-YYYY-NNN. |
| Business Unit / Scope | Enter the business unit, entity, geography, system boundary, or programme scope to which this target outcome applies. |
| Asset / Service / Process in Scope | Enter the specific critical asset, service, system, data set, supplier service, or business process covered by this target outcome. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Function | Select one NIST CSF 2.0 Function: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, or Recover. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Category | Enter the applicable NIST CSF 2.0 Category name and code, such as GV.RM Risk Management Strategy or PR.AA Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory ID | Enter the exact NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory identifier, such as GV.RM-01, ID.AM-01, PR.AA-01, DE.CM-01, RS.MA-01, or RC.RP-01. |
| NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory Outcome | Enter the official NIST CSF 2.0 Subcategory outcome text for the selected Subcategory ID. |
| Target Outcome Statement | Describe the organisation-specific target outcome to be achieved for this subcategory, written as a measurable future-state statement. |
| Target Implementation Tier | Select the intended NIST CSF 2.0 Implementation Tier for this scope: Tier 1 Partial, Tier 2 Risk Informed, Tier 3 Repeatable, or Tier 4 Adaptive. |
| Current Implementation Tier | Enter the assessed current NIST CSF 2.0 Implementation Tier for this scope: Tier 1 Partial, Tier 2 Risk Informed, Tier 3 Repeatable, Tier 4 Adaptive, or Not Assessed. |
| Target Maturity / Capability Level | Enter the target capability level using the organisation's agreed scale, such as 0 Not Performed, 1 Initial, 2 Managed, 3 Defined, 4 Quantitatively Managed, or 5 Optimised. |
| Current Maturity / Capability Level | Enter the current capability level using the same scale as the target maturity field, or Not Assessed if no assessment has been completed. |
| Risk Scenario / Driver | Describe the risk scenario, business objective, audit finding, incident trend, threat, or strategic driver requiring this target state. |
| Inherent Risk Rating | Select the inherent risk rating before existing controls: Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Very Low. |
| Residual Risk Rating | Select the current residual risk rating after existing controls: Critical, High, Medium, Low, Very Low, or Not Assessed. |
| Target Residual Risk Rating | Select the intended residual risk rating after the target state is implemented: Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Very Low. |
| Risk Priority | Select the priority for achieving this target based on risk reduction and business need: P1 Critical, P2 High, P3 Medium, or P4 Low. |
| Business Criticality | Select the criticality of the asset, service, or process: Mission Critical, High, Medium, or Low. |
| Legal / Regulatory / Contractual Driver | Enter applicable obligations driving the target state, such as GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOX, DORA, ISO 27001, customer contract clause, or None. |
| Threat / Vulnerability Driver | Enter the relevant threat, vulnerability, weakness, incident pattern, control deficiency, or exposure this target state addresses. |
| Target Control Requirement | State the specific control requirement that must exist in the target state, using clear mandatory language such as 'Privileged access must be reviewed monthly.' |
| Mapped Control References | Enter references to mapped internal or external controls, separated by semicolons, such as ISO 27001 A.5.15; CIS 6.1; Internal IAM-CTRL-004. |
| Target State Description | Describe the desired future-state process, technology, governance arrangement, evidence, and operating expectation in sufficient detail for implementation and audit validation. |
| Gap Summary | Summarise the difference between the current state and target state, including missing controls, immature processes, tooling gaps, ownership gaps, or evidence gaps. |
| Required Improvement Actions | List the key actions required to reach the target state, using action-oriented wording and separating multiple actions with semicolons. |
| Dependency / Prerequisite | Enter any dependency that must be completed first, such as tool implementation, policy approval, data owner assignment, supplier onboarding, budget approval, or None. |
| Target Evidence / Artifact | Specify the evidence expected to prove the target state is operating, such as approved policy, risk register entry, access review report, SIEM alert report, incident exercise record, or recovery test results. |
| Metric / KPI / KRI | Enter the measurable indicator used to monitor achievement, including unit and threshold where applicable, such as '% critical assets with owner assigned >= 95%'. |
| Acceptance Criteria | Define the precise conditions that must be met for this target outcome to be considered achieved and auditable. |
| Target Owner | Enter the role or named accountable control owner responsible for achieving and maintaining this target outcome. |
| Accountable Executive | Enter the senior executive accountable for the risk decision and target-state approval. |
| Implementation Lead | Enter the person, role, team, or programme responsible for coordinating delivery of the improvement actions. |
| Target Completion Date | Enter the planned completion date for achieving the target state in YYYY-MM-DD format. |
| Estimated Effort | Enter the estimated effort using a consistent unit such as person-days, story points, or T-shirt size S/M/L/XL. |
| Estimated Cost | Enter the estimated implementation cost in the organisation's reporting currency, including currency code, such as USD 25000. |
| Funding Status | Select the funding status: Not Estimated, Unfunded, Funding Requested, Partially Funded, Funded, or Not Required. |
| Implementation Status | Select the delivery status: Not Started, Planned, In Progress, Blocked, Implemented, Validated, Deferred, or Cancelled. |
| RAG Status | Select the current health status: Red, Amber, Green, or Not Rated. |
| Exception / Risk Acceptance Required | Select Yes or No to indicate whether an exception, deferral, or formal risk acceptance is required for this target outcome. |
| Exception / Risk Acceptance Reference | If applicable, enter the exception or risk acceptance record ID; otherwise enter N/A. |
| Review Frequency | Enter how often this target profile line is reviewed: Monthly, Quarterly, Semi-Annually, Annually, or Event-Driven. |
| Last Reviewed Date | Enter the most recent review date in YYYY-MM-DD format, or leave blank until first review. |
| Approval Status | Select the approval status: Draft, Under Review, Approved, Rejected, or Retired. |
| Approver | Enter the person or governance body approving the target profile line, such as CISO, Risk Committee, CIO, or Business Risk Owner. |
| Approval Date | Enter the approval date in YYYY-MM-DD format, or leave blank until approved. |
| Notes | Enter any additional context needed to interpret the target profile line, avoiding duplicate information already captured in other fields. |

### Maintenance

Owned by the CISO or Head of Cyber Risk/GRC, with updates at least quarterly and whenever risk assessments, business priorities, incidents, regulatory obligations, or major architecture changes occur. Source data should be drawn from the NIST CSF assessment, enterprise risk register, control library/GRC platform, asset inventory/CMDB, audit findings, incident records, and approved business strategy or risk appetite statements.
