### Target State

A suitable target state for [Organisation Name] over the next 12 to 18 months is a **managed cybersecurity programme** where:

- Cybersecurity governance is risk-based and integrated with enterprise decision-making.
- Cyber risk appetite is measurable and operationalised.
- Critical assets, data, services, and suppliers are known and owned.
- Controls are prioritised based on business criticality and threat exposure.
- Privileged access is tightly governed and monitored.
- Detection coverage is mapped to critical assets and threat scenarios.
- Incident response is exercised and continuously improved.
- Recovery capabilities are tested against realistic cyber disruption scenarios.
- Third-party cyber risk is managed throughout the supplier lifecycle.
- Metrics demonstrate control effectiveness and support management action.

### Residual Risk Outlook

If the recommended actions are implemented within the proposed timelines, residual cyber risk is expected to reduce materially in the following areas:

- Reduced likelihood of unmanaged critical asset exposure.
- Reduced impact from compromised privileged credentials.
- Improved ability to detect and respond to high-risk cyber activity.
- Improved confidence in recovery from ransomware or destructive attacks.
- Stronger management visibility into risk acceptance and remediation decisions.
- Improved assurance over suppliers supporting critical services or handling sensitive data.

If action is delayed, residual risk is expected to remain elevated, particularly in relation to ransomware, supplier compromise, cloud misconfiguration, identity compromise, and extended operational disruption.

| A-10 | Conduct regular cyber incident response exercises and track lessons learned. | Medium | [CISO] | [Date] | Exercise schedule approved, executive participation confirmed, actions tracked to closure. |
| A-11 | Execute a cyber recovery validation programme for critical services. | High | [CIO] | [Date] | Restoration tests completed, recovery objectives validated, gaps remediated, results reported to leadership. |
| A-12 | Strengthen third-party cyber risk lifecycle management. | High | [Procurement Lead] | [Date] | Supplier tiering completed, high-risk suppliers reassessed, contract requirements updated, issues tracked. |

### 30-60-90 Day Action Roadmap

| Timeframe | Focus | Actions |
|---|---|---|
| 0-30 days | Mobilise and prioritise | Assign action owners; confirm target dates; approve remediation governance; identify critical services and suppliers; define executive dashboard requirements. |
| 31-60 days | Establish foundations | Draft cyber risk appetite thresholds; begin inventory reconciliation; complete privileged access discovery; define vulnerability remediation standards; select priority detection use cases. |
| 61-90 days | Implement early controls | Launch executive cyber dashboard; approve risk thresholds; perform first privileged access review; begin critical service mapping; schedule cyber recovery and incident response exercises. |
| 3-6 months | Validate and embed | Complete high-priority inventory fields; test recovery for selected critical services; reassess high-risk suppliers; implement improved security operations metrics. |
| 6-12 months | Mature and assure | Expand control coverage; repeat maturity measurement; validate remediation evidence; conduct independent follow-up review; report residual risk reduction to leadership. |

### Remediation Governance

To ensure effective closure of recommendations, [Organisation Name] should manage remediation through a formal improvement programme with the following practices:

- Assign one accountable executive owner for each action.
- Define specific deliverables, milestones, and completion evidence.
- Track actions in a central remediation register.
- Review progress at least monthly.
- Escalate overdue high-priority actions to executive governance.
- Record risk acceptance where remediation is deferred.
- Validate closure through evidence review, not self-attestation alone.
- Report progress using status, risk, due date, and residual risk indicators.

### Remediation Register Template

| A-01 | F-01 | [CISO] | Dashboard design approved | [Date] | Not Started | Approved dashboard template and reporting schedule | High |
| A-02 | F-02 | [Enterprise Risk Lead] | Risk thresholds approved | [Date] | Not Started | Approved cyber risk appetite and tolerance document | High |
| A-03 | F-03 | [CIO] | Critical asset inventory reconciled | [Date] | Not Started | Inventory export with owners, criticality, and data classification | High |
| A-05 | F-05 | [Identity and Access Lead] | Privileged access review completed | [Date] | Not Started | Review results, removals, approvals, exception records | High |

| A-12 | F-12 | [Procurement Lead] | High-risk supplier reassessment completed | [Date] | Not Started | Supplier tiering, reassessment records, issue tracker | High |

### Suggested Key Performance and Risk Indicators

| Percentage of critical assets with assigned business and technical owners | Measures ownership completeness | Monthly |
| Percentage of critical assets covered by vulnerability scanning | Measures exposure visibility | Monthly |
| Percentage of critical assets covered by security monitoring | Measures detection coverage | Monthly |
| High-risk vulnerabilities overdue on critical assets | Measures remediation risk | Weekly / Monthly |
| Privileged accounts reviewed within required timeframe | Measures privileged access governance | Monthly |
| Number of privileged access exceptions past expiry | Measures exception control | Monthly |
| Mean time to triage high-priority alerts | Measures detection responsiveness | Monthly |
| Mean time to contain confirmed incidents | Measures response performance | Monthly |
| Critical services with validated recovery tests | Measures recovery confidence | Quarterly |
| High-risk suppliers reassessed within required timeframe | Measures third-party lifecycle assurance | Quarterly |
| Open supplier security issues past due date | Measures supplier remediation risk | Monthly |
| Cyber risks outside approved tolerance | Measures residual risk against appetite | Monthly |

### Follow-Up Assessment

A follow-up assessment should be performed after completion of the priority remediation activities or within [6 to 12 months], whichever occurs first. The follow-up should validate:

- Closure evidence for high-priority findings.
- Improvement in maturity ratings.
- Reduction in residual risk.
- Effectiveness of governance reporting.
- Operating consistency of key controls.
- Completion of cyber recovery and incident response exercises.
- Continued alignment between cybersecurity priorities and business risk.

## Distribution & Confidentiality

### Distribution

This report is intended for authorised recipients only.

| Recipient / Group | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Board / Risk Committee] | Oversight of cyber risk posture, priority findings, and remediation progress |
| [Executive Leadership Team] | Decision-making, resource allocation, and accountability |
| [Chief Information Security Officer] | Cybersecurity programme ownership and remediation coordination |

Distribution outside the approved recipient list requires written approval from [Authorising Executive / CISO / Legal Counsel].

### Confidentiality Requirements

This report is classified as **Confidential** because it contains sensitive information about cybersecurity maturity, control weaknesses, risk exposure, technology dependencies, and remediation priorities.

Recipients must:

- Use the report only for authorised governance, risk management, assurance, or remediation purposes.
- Not distribute, copy, publish, or disclose the report without approval.
- Store the report in an approved secure repository with access restricted to authorised personnel.
- Avoid including detailed findings in broadly distributed presentations or unprotected communications.
- Ensure any extracts or summaries retain appropriate confidentiality markings.
- Notify [CISO / Legal / Report Owner] immediately if the report is disclosed to an unauthorised party.

### External Sharing

External sharing may be permitted only where there is a legitimate business need and appropriate safeguards are in place. Examples may include customers, regulators, insurers, auditors, or contractual assurance stakeholders.

Before external sharing, the report owner must confirm:

- The recipient has a valid need to know.
- Legal and contractual implications have been reviewed.
- A non-disclosure agreement or equivalent confidentiality protection is in place where appropriate.
- Sensitive technical details are redacted if not required.
- The shared version is approved by [CISO / Legal Counsel / Executive Sponsor].
- A record of external disclosure is retained.

### Retention

This report and supporting assessment evidence must be retained in accordance with [Organisation Name]’s information retention requirements. Unless a longer retention period is required for legal, contractual, regulatory, or assurance purposes, the recommended minimum retention period is **[Retention Period]** from the report issue date.

NIST-033.title: Profile Refresh Cycle
NIST-033.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [GRC-PLAN-CSF-PROFILE-REFRESH] | 1.0 | [Cybersecurity Governance Lead] | [Effective Date] | NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 | Internal |

## Purpose & Objectives

This plan defines the annual cycle for reviewing and refreshing the organisation’s NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 Profiles. It establishes the activities, responsibilities, milestones, evidence expectations, and success measures required to keep the Current Profile and Target Profile aligned with the organisation’s risk environment, business priorities, technology estate, legal and contractual obligations, and cybersecurity strategy.

The objectives of the Profile Refresh Cycle are to:

- Confirm that the Current Profile accurately reflects the organisation’s implemented cybersecurity outcomes and operating reality.
- Reassess the Target Profile against current business objectives, risk appetite, threat conditions, regulatory expectations, and stakeholder needs.
- Identify gaps between the Current Profile and Target Profile and determine whether existing remediation plans remain appropriate.
- Refresh cybersecurity priorities and improvement initiatives based on risk, feasibility, cost, dependency, and business impact.
- Provide management with a clear, evidence-based view of cybersecurity posture and planned improvements.
- Maintain traceability between profile decisions, risk assessments, control assessments, security initiatives, exceptions, and governance approvals.
- Support annual cybersecurity planning, budget development, risk reporting, audit readiness, and executive oversight.

This plan is intended to produce a repeatable, auditable, and business-aligned annual review process rather than a one-time assessment exercise.

## Scope

This plan applies to the annual refresh of the organisation’s NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 Profiles, including:

- Current Profile review and validation.
- Target Profile review and adjustment.
- Gap analysis between current and desired cybersecurity outcomes.
- Prioritisation of cybersecurity improvement actions.
- Review of supporting evidence and documentation.
- Alignment with enterprise risk management, technology planning, security operations, compliance obligations, and business strategy.
- Reporting to accountable management and governance forums.

The Profile Refresh Cycle covers cybersecurity outcomes across the organisation’s defined operating environment, including:

- Business units and corporate functions.
- Information systems, platforms, networks, applications, and cloud services.
- Data assets and information flows.
- Identity, access, and privileged access environments.
- Third-party technology and service dependencies.
- Operational technology, where applicable.
- Security processes, capabilities, tools, and monitoring arrangements.
- Governance, risk management, policy, awareness, and resilience practices.

The refresh cycle includes input from existing assurance and operational activities, such as:

- Cybersecurity risk assessments.
- Internal and external audit results.
- Vulnerability and penetration testing results.
- Incident and problem management records.
- Business continuity and disaster recovery exercises.
- Security operations metrics.
- Supplier assurance reviews.
- Compliance reviews.
- Security architecture reviews.
- Policy exception records.
- Technology roadmap updates.
- Business impact analyses.
- Threat intelligence and industry trend reports.

The following items are out of scope for this plan unless specifically included by the plan owner:

- Full redesign of the cybersecurity framework operating model.
- Detailed technical implementation procedures for individual controls.
- Real-time incident response decision-making.
- Ad hoc risk assessments outside the annual profile refresh process.
- Procurement of specific cybersecurity tools, except where recommendations inform planning and budgeting.
- Formal certification activities against external standards, unless separately authorised.

## Assumptions & Dependencies

The successful execution of this plan depends on the following assumptions and dependencies.

| Category | Assumption or Dependency | Impact if Not Met | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Executive sponsorship | Senior leadership supports the annual profile refresh and expects participation from business and technology stakeholders. | Delayed decisions, weak engagement, or unresolved priorities. | Confirm sponsorship at the start of the cycle and include progress updates in governance forums. |
| Defined profile ownership | The organisation has an assigned owner for maintaining the Current Profile, Target Profile, and related improvement roadmap. | Inconsistent updates and unclear accountability. | Assign a single accountable owner with named contributors before refresh activities begin. |
| Availability of evidence | Control owners and process owners can provide timely evidence of current cybersecurity practices. | Current Profile may be based on opinion rather than verified information. | Issue evidence requests early and define minimum evidence expectations. |
| Current risk information | Enterprise and cybersecurity risk records are up to date enough to inform prioritisation. | Target Profile may not reflect actual risk exposure. | Refresh key cyber risks before or during the profile review. |
| Business participation | Business units provide input on strategic changes, critical services, risk tolerance, and operational constraints. | Target Profile may be misaligned with business priorities. | Conduct structured workshops with required business representation. |
| Asset and service visibility | Inventories of systems, data assets, suppliers, and critical services are sufficiently reliable. | Gaps may be missed or incorrectly scoped. | Validate scope using available inventories and confirm exceptions with asset owners. |
| Security metrics | Security operations, vulnerability management, incident, and assurance metrics are available for trend analysis. | Decisions may rely on subjective assessment. | Use the most recent available metrics and document limitations. |
| Third-party information | Supplier risk information and service dependency data are available for critical third parties. | External dependencies may be underrepresented in the profile. | Prioritise suppliers supporting critical processes and document deferred reviews. |
| Governance cadence | Existing risk, security, and technology governance forums can review and approve outputs. | Delayed approval of the refreshed profile and roadmap. | Reserve agenda time before the refresh begins. |
| Budget planning alignment | The refresh cycle is timed to inform annual budget and planning cycles. | Improvement actions may not be funded or resourced. | Align milestones to the organisation’s planning calendar. |
| Change visibility | Major transformation, cloud migration, merger, outsourcing, or regulatory changes are known to the refresh team. | Target Profile may become outdated soon after approval. | Include change representatives and review strategic roadmaps. |

## Approach / Phases

The Profile Refresh Cycle will be performed annually using a structured, evidence-based approach. Each phase has defined activities, outputs, and decision points.

### Phase 1 - Initiation and Planning

The purpose of this phase is to confirm the refresh scope, stakeholders, schedule, inputs, and governance expectations.

Key activities:

- Confirm the refresh sponsor, accountable owner, and core working group.
- Confirm organisational scope, including business units, systems, services, suppliers, and environments to be reviewed.
- Review the previous year’s Profile, gap analysis, improvement roadmap, management decisions, and outstanding actions.
- Confirm alignment with enterprise risk management, audit planning, budget planning, and technology roadmap cycles.
- Define evidence expectations and submission timelines.
- Identify stakeholder workshops, interviews, and governance meeting dates.
- Confirm communication channels, document repository location, naming conventions, and version control approach.
- Issue a refresh kickoff communication to relevant stakeholders.

Expected outputs:

- Approved refresh schedule.
- Stakeholder list and RACI.
- Evidence request list.
- Confirmed workshop calendar.
- Document repository and version control setup.
- Kickoff communication.

### Phase 2 - Input Collection and Context Review

The purpose of this phase is to collect and analyse information that may affect the Current Profile, Target Profile, and prioritisation of improvement actions.

Key activities:

- Review enterprise objectives, strategic plans, and major business changes.
- Review technology changes, including cloud adoption, platform modernisation, major application changes, remote working models, and infrastructure changes.
- Review changes to critical business services and data flows.
- Review updated asset, application, data, and supplier inventories.
- Review legal, regulatory, contractual, and customer security obligations.
- Review recent cybersecurity incidents, near misses, security events, and lessons learned.
- Review threat intelligence relevant to the organisation’s sector, geography, technology stack, and operating model.
- Review vulnerability trends, patching performance, exposure management, and remediation backlogs.
- Review audit findings, assurance results, penetration testing reports, red team exercises, and compliance reviews.
- Review cybersecurity risk register updates, accepted risks, exceptions, and risk treatment plans.
- Review business continuity, disaster recovery, crisis management, and resilience test results.
- Review progress against the prior improvement roadmap.

Expected outputs:

- Context summary.
- Evidence register.
- Updated list of material changes since the previous refresh.
- Summary of risk, threat, assurance, and operational themes.
- Prior-year roadmap progress assessment.

### Phase 3 - Current Profile Validation

The purpose of this phase is to validate the organisation’s current cybersecurity posture against the cybersecurity outcomes selected for the organisation’s profile.

Key activities:

- Review each profile outcome and confirm whether it is fully achieved, partially achieved, not achieved, not applicable, or requires further validation.
- Assess implementation consistency across business units, systems, environments, and critical services.
- Compare documented processes with actual operating evidence.
- Confirm whether control operation is repeatable, measured, and governed where required.
- Identify areas where evidence is missing, outdated, incomplete, or inconsistent.
- Record confidence levels for profile ratings where appropriate.
- Confirm known exceptions, compensating measures, and accepted risks.
- Validate results with control owners, process owners, and relevant business representatives.

Suggested rating model:

| Rating | Description | Evidence Expectation |
|---|---|---|
| Achieved | The outcome is implemented and operating consistently within the defined scope. | Current documentation, operational records, metrics, and accountable ownership are available. |
| Partially Achieved | The outcome is implemented in some areas or is not operating consistently. | Evidence exists but shows coverage gaps, inconsistent operation, or incomplete adoption. |
| Not Achieved | The outcome is not implemented or cannot be demonstrated. | Evidence is absent or confirms the capability is not in place. |
| Not Applicable | The outcome does not apply to the defined scope or operating model. | Rationale is documented and approved by the profile owner. |
| Requires Validation | Initial information is insufficient to determine status. | Additional evidence, testing, or stakeholder confirmation is required. |

Expected outputs:

- Validated Current Profile.
- Evidence references mapped to profile outcomes.
- List of unresolved evidence gaps.
- Summary of current posture themes.
- List of exceptions and accepted risks relevant to profile outcomes.

### Phase 4 - Target Profile Review

The purpose of this phase is to confirm whether the Target Profile remains appropriate or requires adjustment based on the organisation’s current risk environment and business priorities.

Key activities:

- Review the existing Target Profile for continued relevance.
- Identify changes required due to new business objectives, threats, incidents, audits, regulations, customer expectations, technology changes, or risk appetite updates.
- Confirm desired cybersecurity outcomes for critical services, high-risk assets, sensitive data, and third-party dependencies.
- Consider whether target outcomes should vary by business criticality, data sensitivity, environment type, or risk exposure.
- Review strategic improvement areas such as identity security, resilience, data protection, asset visibility, supply chain risk management, detection and response, vulnerability management, governance, and security culture.
- Validate the Target Profile with executive, risk, technology, legal, compliance, and business stakeholders.
- Document rationale for additions, removals, deferrals, or changes to target outcomes.

Expected outputs:

- Refreshed Target Profile.
- Target Profile change log.
- Documented rationale for significant changes.
- Stakeholder validation record.

### Phase 5 - Gap Analysis and Risk Alignment

The purpose of this phase is to identify and evaluate the differences between the validated Current Profile and the refreshed Target Profile.

Key activities:

- Compare current and target states for each applicable profile outcome.
- Identify capability gaps, coverage gaps, maturity gaps, governance gaps, and evidence gaps.
- Link gaps to relevant risks, business impacts, incidents, audit findings, legal obligations, contractual requirements, and technology dependencies.
- Assess the potential impact of each gap on confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, privacy, resilience, operational continuity, and stakeholder trust.
- Identify whether existing remediation plans, projects, or risk treatments already address the gap.
- Determine whether gaps require new actions, revised timelines, additional funding, risk acceptance, or management escalation.
- Confirm whether any gaps represent systemic issues across multiple functions or environments.

Suggested gap classification:

| Gap Type | Description | Example Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| Capability Gap | A required cybersecurity capability is absent or materially incomplete. | No formal third-party security monitoring process for critical suppliers. |
| Coverage Gap | A capability exists but does not cover all required assets, services, or environments. | Vulnerability scanning excludes some cloud workloads or legacy systems. |
| Consistency Gap | A process exists but is not applied consistently across teams or locations. | Access reviews are performed differently across business units. |
| Evidence Gap | The organisation believes an outcome is achieved but cannot demonstrate it reliably. | Security awareness completion records are incomplete. |
| Governance Gap | Ownership, decision-making, policy, reporting, or oversight is unclear or insufficient. | No defined owner for maintaining security requirements in supplier contracts. |
| Performance Gap | The capability exists but does not meet expected effectiveness, timeliness, or quality. | Critical vulnerabilities are remediated outside agreed timeframes. |
| Resilience Gap | Recovery, continuity, or incident response arrangements do not meet business needs. | Recovery testing does not cover a critical service end to end. |

Expected outputs:

- Gap analysis register.
- Risk-aligned gap summary.
- List of gaps already covered by active initiatives.
- List of gaps requiring new or revised treatment decisions.

### Phase 6 - Prioritisation and Roadmap Refresh

The purpose of this phase is to translate the gap analysis into a practical and risk-based cybersecurity improvement roadmap.

Key activities:

- Prioritise gaps based on risk exposure, business impact, threat relevance, legal or contractual urgency, exploitability, dependency, cost, complexity, and resource availability.
- Confirm whether each gap should be remediated, mitigated, transferred, accepted, deferred, or monitored.
- Identify improvement initiatives, expected outcomes, accountable owners, required resources, target dates, and dependencies.
- Group related improvements into logical workstreams, such as governance, identity, resilience, vulnerability management, supplier assurance, data protection, monitoring, or awareness.
- Identify quick wins, foundational activities, strategic initiatives, and long-term transformation items.
- Align roadmap items with budget planning, project portfolio management, technology strategy, and audit remediation commitments.
- Confirm interim risk management actions for high-priority gaps that cannot be resolved immediately.
- Identify decisions requiring executive approval.

Suggested prioritisation criteria:

| Criterion | High Priority Indicator | Medium Priority Indicator | Lower Priority Indicator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Business impact | Affects critical services, regulated activities, safety, or material revenue. | Affects important services with manageable operational impact. | Affects limited-scope or non-critical services. |
| Threat relevance | Actively targeted by common or emerging threat actors. | Relevant to known threats but not currently the dominant exposure. | Limited current threat relevance. |
| Risk exposure | Gap materially increases likelihood or impact of a significant cyber event. | Gap contributes to risk but has partial compensating controls. | Gap has low residual risk or strong compensating controls. |
| Compliance or contractual urgency | Required to meet a near-term obligation or customer commitment. | Supports compliance improvement but no immediate deadline. | No immediate external obligation. |
| Implementation dependency | Enables multiple other improvements. | Supports one or more related improvements. | Standalone improvement with limited dependencies. |
| Feasibility | Can be delivered quickly with available resources. | Requires moderate planning, funding, or coordination. | Requires substantial investment or long-term transformation. |

Expected outputs:

- Refreshed cybersecurity improvement roadmap.
- Prioritised gap register.
- Proposed treatment decisions.
- Interim risk mitigation actions.
- Funding and resource requirements.
- Executive decision log.

### Phase 7 - Review, Approval, and Communication

The purpose of this phase is to obtain management approval and communicate the refreshed profile and roadmap to relevant stakeholders.

Key activities:

- Prepare an executive summary of profile changes, key risks, priority gaps, and recommended actions.
- Review the Current Profile, Target Profile, gap analysis, and roadmap with the cybersecurity governance forum.
- Resolve comments, challenges, and disputed ratings.
- Obtain formal approval from the accountable executive or governance body.
- Communicate approved priorities to control owners, business units, technology teams, risk management, internal audit, and project portfolio stakeholders.
- Update related governance artefacts, including risk records, security strategy, policy exception records, and audit remediation trackers.
- Archive superseded profile versions in accordance with document retention requirements.

Expected outputs:

- Approved Current Profile.
- Approved Target Profile.
- Approved gap analysis and roadmap.
- Executive summary and decision record.
- Communication record.
- Updated related artefacts.

### Phase 8 - Monitoring and Interim Maintenance

The purpose of this phase is to monitor progress and ensure that material changes are captured between annual refresh cycles.

Key activities:

- Track progress against roadmap actions at an agreed governance cadence.
- Monitor changes in risk, threat, technology, business priorities, and compliance obligations.
- Update profile records when material changes occur outside the annual cycle.
- Escalate delayed or blocked high-priority actions.
- Maintain evidence and decision records throughout the year.
- Capture lessons learned to improve the next refresh cycle.

Expected outputs:

- Roadmap progress reports.
- Updated action status records.
- Interim profile updates where required.
- Lessons learned log.

## Milestones & Timeline (markdown table)

The annual Profile Refresh Cycle should be completed within a defined planning window, ideally aligned with the organisation’s annual risk review and budget planning cycle. The following timeline assumes a twelve-week refresh period. Dates should be adjusted to fit the organisation’s governance calendar.

| Milestone | Target Timing | Key Activities | Primary Owner | Deliverables |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Refresh cycle initiated | Week 1 | Confirm sponsor, scope, stakeholders, repository, schedule, and governance dates. | [Cybersecurity Governance Lead] | Approved refresh schedule, stakeholder list, kickoff notice. |
| Evidence request issued | Week 1 | Distribute evidence request to control owners and process owners. | [GRC Manager] | Evidence request tracker. |
| Context review completed | Weeks 2-3 | Review business changes, risks, threats, incidents, audit results, supplier changes, technology roadmap, and compliance obligations. | [Risk Manager] | Context summary and material change log. |
| Prior roadmap progress assessed | Week 3 | Review completion status, delays, residual risks, and benefits achieved from prior-year actions. | [Cybersecurity Programme Manager] | Roadmap progress assessment. |
| Stakeholder workshops completed | Weeks 3-5 | Conduct workshops with business, technology, security, risk, compliance, and supplier management stakeholders. | [Cybersecurity Governance Lead] | Workshop notes and stakeholder input log. |
| Current Profile validated | Weeks 5-7 | Assess current outcome status using evidence, interviews, metrics, and management confirmation. | [GRC Manager] | Draft Current Profile and evidence register. |
| Target Profile refreshed | Weeks 7-8 | Review and adjust target outcomes based on current risk, business objectives, and strategic priorities. | [CISO or Security Director] | Draft Target Profile and change log. |
| Gap analysis completed | Weeks 8-9 | Identify gaps, link to risks, confirm existing treatments, and classify gap types. | [Cyber Risk Lead] | Gap analysis register. |
| Roadmap prioritisation completed | Weeks 9-10 | Prioritise actions, confirm owners, dependencies, resources, target dates, and interim mitigations. | [Cybersecurity Programme Manager] | Draft improvement roadmap. |
| Management review completed | Week 11 | Present refreshed profile, key gaps, risk implications, and funding or resource decisions. | [CISO or Security Director] | Management review pack and decision log. |
| Approval obtained | Week 12 | Obtain approval from the designated governance body or accountable executive. | [Accountable Executive] | Approved Current Profile, Target Profile, gap analysis, and roadmap. |
| Communication completed | Week 12 | Communicate approved priorities and actions to relevant owners and governance stakeholders. | [Cybersecurity Governance Lead] | Communication record and assigned actions. |
| Post-refresh lessons learned captured | Week 13 | Review process effectiveness and identify improvements for next cycle. | [GRC Manager] | Lessons learned log. |
| Quarterly roadmap monitoring | Quarterly after approval | Track action progress, blockers, risk changes, and required escalations. | [Cybersecurity Programme Manager] | Quarterly roadmap status reports. |

## Roles & Responsibilities

The Profile Refresh Cycle requires coordinated participation from cybersecurity, risk, technology, business, legal, compliance, audit, procurement, and executive stakeholders.

| Role | Responsibilities |
|---|---|
| Accountable Executive | Sponsors the refresh cycle, approves final profile outputs, resolves escalated decisions, and ensures alignment with business priorities and risk appetite. |
| Chief Information Security Officer / Security Director | Provides overall cybersecurity leadership, validates strategic priorities, reviews high-risk gaps, recommends treatment decisions, and presents outcomes to governance forums. |
| Cybersecurity Governance Lead | Owns execution of this plan, coordinates refresh activities, manages stakeholder engagement, ensures documentation quality, and maintains the profile artefacts. |
| GRC Manager | Manages evidence collection, supports profile validation, maintains the evidence register, coordinates documentation updates, and ensures audit-ready records are retained. |
| Cyber Risk Lead | Aligns gaps with risk register entries, supports impact assessment, identifies risk treatment options, and confirms risk acceptance or escalation requirements. |
| Cybersecurity Programme Manager | Maintains the improvement roadmap, tracks action ownership and delivery status, identifies dependencies and resource constraints, and reports progress. |
| Security Operations Lead | Provides incident, monitoring, detection, response, vulnerability, and operational security metrics; validates operational security capabilities. |
| Security Architecture Lead | Reviews technology and architecture implications, identifies design gaps, validates strategic security direction, and supports roadmap feasibility analysis. |
| Identity and Access Management Owner | Provides evidence and status for identity governance, access control, privileged access, authentication, and access review outcomes. |
| Infrastructure and Cloud Owners | Provide evidence for platform security, configuration management, vulnerability management, logging, backup, resilience, and operational controls. |
| Application Owners | Validate application security practices, development lifecycle controls, data protection measures, and remediation commitments for in-scope applications. |
| Data Protection / Privacy Lead | Provides input on sensitive data handling, privacy obligations, data protection risks, breach considerations, and regulatory expectations. |
| Legal and Compliance Representatives | Identify relevant legal, contractual, regulatory, and customer security obligations; review significant compliance implications. |
| Procurement / Third-Party Risk Lead | Provides supplier inventory, supplier assurance results, critical supplier dependencies, contract security requirements, and third-party risk information. |
| Business Unit Representatives | Validate business criticality, operational constraints, service dependencies, risk tolerance, and the business impact of gaps and proposed improvements. |
| Enterprise Risk Management Representative | Ensures alignment with enterprise risk processes, risk appetite, risk reporting, and treatment governance. |
| Internal Audit Representative | Provides assurance results, audit observations, and advisory input while preserving independence from management decision-making. |
| Control Owners | Provide evidence, validate implementation status, confirm gaps, propose remediation actions, and accept assigned roadmap responsibilities. |
| Project and Portfolio Management Office | Aligns profile improvement actions with approved projects, delivery governance, resource planning, and portfolio reporting. |

Responsibility expectations:

- Each profile outcome must have a named owner or accountable function.
- Each identified gap must have a documented treatment decision.
- Each approved roadmap action must have an accountable owner, target date, dependency assessment, and status reporting cadence.
- Risk acceptance decisions must be approved by an appropriate risk owner and recorded in the organisation’s risk management system.
- Disputed ratings or prioritisation decisions must be escalated to the cybersecurity governance forum or accountable executive.

## Resources

The following resources are required to complete the annual Profile Refresh Cycle effectively.

### People and Stakeholder Time

| Resource | Estimated Commitment | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| Cybersecurity Governance Lead | 30-50% allocation for refresh duration | Plan execution, coordination, documentation, stakeholder management. |
| GRC Manager / Analyst | 40-60% allocation for refresh duration | Evidence collection, profile validation, register maintenance. |
| Cyber Risk Lead | 15-25% allocation for refresh duration | Risk alignment, impact analysis, treatment review. |
| Security Operations Lead | 8-16 hours | Metrics, incident themes, vulnerability trends, operational validation. |
| Security Architecture Lead | 8-16 hours | Architecture implications, feasibility, technology dependencies. |
| Control Owners | 4-12 hours each | Evidence provision, rating validation, remediation planning. |
| Business Unit Representatives | 2-6 hours each | Business impact and priority validation. |
| Legal, Compliance, Privacy, Procurement | 2-8 hours each | Obligation review and third-party input. |
| Executive Sponsor / Accountable Executive | 2-4 hours | Direction, review, approval, decision-making. |
| Governance Forum Members | 1-2 scheduled sessions | Review and approval of final outputs. |

### Information and Evidence Sources

The refresh team should use the most current available versions of the following inputs:

- Current Profile.
- Target Profile.
- Prior-year gap analysis.
- Cybersecurity improvement roadmap.
- Enterprise risk register.
- Cybersecurity risk register.
- Control self-assessments.
- Internal and external audit reports.
- Penetration testing and technical assurance reports.
- Vulnerability management reports.
- Incident reports and post-incident reviews.
- Security monitoring and detection metrics.
- Identity and access review records.
- Asset, application, data, and supplier inventories.
- Business impact analysis records.
- Disaster recovery and business continuity test results.
- Policy exception register.
- Third-party assurance reports and supplier risk assessments.
- Security architecture review outputs.
- Cloud and infrastructure configuration compliance reports.
- Security awareness and training records.
- Compliance obligation register.
- Technology and transformation roadmaps.
- Budget and project portfolio records.

### Tools and Repositories

The following tools or repositories should be available:

- Document management repository for controlled profile artefacts.
- Risk management system or risk register.
- GRC platform, where available.
- Ticketing or workflow system for tracking evidence requests and action items.
- Project portfolio management tool for roadmap integration.
- Security information and event management or monitoring reporting tools.
- Vulnerability management platform.
- Identity governance or access review system.
- Asset and configuration management repositories.
- Supplier management or third-party risk management system.
- Collaboration tools for workshops, review comments, and approvals.

### Budget and Funding Considerations

The refresh process itself should be funded as part of normal cybersecurity governance activity. However, outputs may identify funding needs for:

- New or enhanced cybersecurity technologies.
- Specialist assurance activities.
- External advisory support.
- Additional staff or managed services.
- Training and awareness initiatives.
- Remediation of legacy platforms.
- Resilience, recovery, and continuity improvements.
- Supplier assurance and contract uplift activities.
- Security automation and reporting enhancements.

Funding requirements must be documented in the refreshed roadmap and aligned with the organisation’s normal budgeting and investment approval process.

## Success Metrics

The effectiveness of the Profile Refresh Cycle will be measured using completion, quality, timeliness, engagement, decision, and outcome metrics.

| Metric | Target | Measurement Method | Reporting Frequency |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Refresh completed on schedule | 100% completion by approved target date | Compare actual completion date to approved timeline. | Annual |
| Required stakeholders engaged | At least 95% of identified stakeholder groups represented | Attendance records, interview logs, workshop notes. | At cycle close |
| Evidence request completion | At least 90% of requested evidence received or formally dispositioned | Evidence request tracker. | Weekly during refresh |
| Profile outcomes reviewed | 100% of in-scope outcomes reviewed and assigned a status | Current Profile review record. | At cycle close |
| Unresolved validation items | No high-impact validation items unresolved at approval | Validation issue log. | At approval |
| Target Profile changes documented | 100% of material changes supported by rationale | Target Profile change log. | At cycle close |
| Gaps risk-aligned | 100% of significant gaps linked to risk, impact, or obligation rationale | Gap analysis register. | At cycle close |
| Roadmap action ownership | 100% of approved actions assigned to accountable owners | Improvement roadmap. | At approval |
| Roadmap target dates defined | 100% of approved actions assigned target dates or approved deferral rationale | Improvement roadmap. | At approval |
| High-priority gaps addressed | 100% have treatment decisions, interim mitigations, or approved risk acceptance | Gap register and risk records. | At approval and quarterly |
| Executive decisions recorded | 100% of approval and risk treatment decisions documented | Decision log and meeting minutes. | At approval |
| Audit-ready artefacts retained | 100% of final artefacts stored in approved repository | Repository review. | At cycle close |
| Quarterly roadmap reporting completed | 100% of scheduled quarterly updates completed | Governance meeting packs and status reports. | Quarterly |
| Lessons learned captured | Completed within one month after refresh approval | Lessons learned record. | Annual |

Qualitative success indicators include:

- Management can clearly explain current cybersecurity posture and planned improvements.
- Profile ratings are evidence-based and consistently applied.
- The Target Profile reflects business priorities rather than purely technical preferences.
- Improvement actions are realistic, funded where necessary, and integrated with operational planning.
- Risk acceptance decisions are explicit, visible, and approved at the right level.
- The refresh process improves stakeholder understanding of cybersecurity risk and accountability.
- Internal audit or external reviewers can trace profile conclusions to supporting evidence and management decisions.

## Review & Update Triggers

This plan will be reviewed at least annually and updated when necessary to remain aligned with organisational needs and cybersecurity governance practices.

The Profile Refresh Cycle itself must be performed annually. In addition, an interim profile review should be initiated when one or more of the following triggers occur:

| Trigger | Review Expectation |
|---|---|
| Material change in business strategy | Reassess Target Profile priorities and impacted roadmap actions. |
| Major technology transformation | Review Current Profile assumptions, implementation coverage, and new security dependencies. |
| Significant cybersecurity incident | Reassess relevant outcomes, incident lessons learned, risk exposure, and required improvements. |
| Material change in threat environment | Review whether target outcomes and prioritised actions remain sufficient. |
| New or changed legal, regulatory, contractual, or customer security obligation | Assess whether Current Profile and Target Profile require adjustment. |
| Acquisition, divestment, merger, outsourcing, or major organisational restructuring | Reassess scope, ownership, inherited risks, and profile applicability. |
| Introduction of new critical service or high-risk data processing activity | Confirm security outcomes, resilience needs, and data protection expectations. |
| Significant audit finding or assurance result | Update gap analysis and roadmap where findings affect profile outcomes. |
| Material supplier change or third-party failure | Review third-party risk and service dependency outcomes. |
| Major change to risk appetite or enterprise risk priorities | Reassess gap prioritisation and risk treatment decisions. |
| Persistent failure to meet roadmap milestones | Review feasibility, ownership, funding, dependencies, and interim risk treatment. |
| Repeated control failures or performance deterioration | Reassess Current Profile ratings and required corrective actions. |
| Material budget or resource change | Reprioritise roadmap actions and identify risk acceptance implications. |
| Change in cybersecurity leadership or accountable ownership | Confirm continuity of profile ownership, assumptions, and decision records. |
| Lessons learned from exercises or simulations | Update relevant profile outcomes, gaps, and improvement activities. |

Plan update responsibilities:

- The [Cybersecurity Governance Lead] is responsible for reviewing this plan annually.
- Material changes to this plan require approval by the [CISO or Security Director].
- Changes affecting governance authority, funding, risk acceptance, or executive accountability require review by the relevant governance forum.
- Superseded versions must be retained in the approved document repository in accordance with organisational retention requirements.
- The plan owner must ensure that stakeholders are notified when significant changes to the refresh process are approved.

BCM-001.title: BCMS Project Charter
BCM-001.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| [BCMS-PLAN-001] | 1.0 | [BCMS Programme Sponsor / Business Continuity Manager] | [YYYY-MM-DD] | ISO 22301:2019 | Internal |

## Purpose & Objectives

This BCMS Project Charter formally authorises the establishment and implementation of a Business Continuity Management System (BCMS) for [Organisation Name]. It defines the mandate, sponsorship, scope, governance, resources, high-level budget, and delivery approach required to implement a practical and auditable BCMS aligned to ISO 22301:2019.

The BCMS project will enable [Organisation Name] to prepare for, respond to, and recover from disruptive incidents that could affect critical products, services, operations, people, premises, technology, suppliers, and stakeholder commitments.

The objectives of this project are to:

- Establish a formally governed BCMS with visible leadership sponsorship and accountable ownership.
- Define the business continuity scope, including critical activities, locations, services, dependencies, and interested parties.
- Identify and assess the impacts of disruption through a Business Impact Analysis.
- Identify threats, vulnerabilities, and continuity risks that could affect priority operations.
- Define continuity strategies and solutions that support agreed recovery priorities.
- Develop, approve, and maintain business continuity plans, incident response arrangements, communication arrangements, and recovery procedures.
- Define roles, authorities, escalation paths, and decision-making arrangements for disruptive incidents.
- Conduct awareness, training, and exercising to validate capability and improve preparedness.
- Establish performance monitoring, internal review, management review, and continual improvement arrangements.
- Prepare the organisation for internal assurance and, where required, external certification assessment.
- Embed business continuity into business planning, supplier management, technology resilience, change management, and operational governance.

The project is sponsored by [Executive Sponsor Role] and authorised to engage business units, support functions, suppliers, and relevant stakeholders as required to deliver the agreed BCMS outcomes.

## Scope

The initial BCMS implementation scope covers the activities, functions, sites, systems, services, people, third parties, and management arrangements necessary to protect the continuity of priority products and services delivered by [Organisation Name].

The BCMS implementation scope includes:

| Scope Area | Included |
|---|---|
| Organisation | [Organisation Name] and in-scope subsidiaries, divisions, or operating entities |
| Products and services | [List priority products/services or “all customer-facing services delivered by…”] |
| Business functions | [Operations], [Customer Support], [Finance], [IT], [HR], [Facilities], [Legal/Compliance], [Procurement], [Communications], and other functions supporting priority services |
| Locations | [Head Office], [Primary Operations Site], [Data Centre / Cloud Region], [Warehouse / Branches], remote working arrangements, and other material operating locations |
| Technology | Critical applications, infrastructure, networks, end-user computing, cloud platforms, telephony, identity services, data repositories, and recovery environments supporting priority activities |
| People | Employees, contractors, key role holders, crisis management participants, continuity plan owners, and recovery team members |
| Suppliers and partners | Material outsourced service providers, technology vendors, logistics providers, facilities providers, professional services providers, and other dependencies supporting priority activities |
| Interested parties | Customers, regulators, employees, shareholders/owners, suppliers, insurers, emergency services, local authorities, and other parties with continuity-related expectations |
| Governance | BCMS leadership, policy, objectives, risk and impact assessment, planning, exercising, training, monitoring, management review, issue management, and continual improvement |
| Documentation | BCMS policy, scope statement, BIA, continuity risk assessments, continuity strategies, business continuity plans, incident response arrangements, communications plans, exercise records, review records, and improvement logs |

The following are excluded from the initial implementation unless later approved through change control:

- Locations not listed in the agreed BCMS scope.
- Products or services that have been formally assessed as non-critical and approved for exclusion by the BCMS Steering Committee.
- Acquired entities or new business lines not yet integrated into [Organisation Name] governance.
- Supplier internal continuity arrangements beyond the evidence, assurance, and contractual obligations required by [Organisation Name].
- Technical disaster recovery engineering work outside the approved project budget, except where explicitly agreed as a project deliverable.

Exclusions must not undermine the organisation’s ability to maintain or recover priority activities within agreed timeframes. Any exclusion must be risk-assessed, justified, documented, and approved by the BCMS Steering Committee.

The project will define and agree:

- Maximum tolerable periods of disruption for priority activities.
- Recovery time objectives for in-scope activities and services.
- Recovery point objectives for key information and systems where data loss tolerance is relevant.
- Minimum service levels during disruption.
- Resource requirements for recovery, including people, technology, facilities, data, equipment, suppliers, and communications.
- Escalation and authority arrangements for incident management and business continuity activation.
- Evidence required to demonstrate effective implementation and ongoing operation of the BCMS.

## Assumptions & Dependencies

The successful delivery of this project depends on the following assumptions and dependencies.

| Category | Assumption / Dependency | Impact if Not Met | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Leadership commitment | Executive leadership will provide visible support, timely decisions, and authority to resolve conflicts | Delayed implementation, weak adoption, unresolved scope and funding issues | Executive Sponsor |
| Business participation | Business units will nominate knowledgeable representatives and allocate time for workshops, reviews, and plan development | Incomplete impact analysis, unrealistic recovery priorities, weak plans | Business Unit Heads |
| Information availability | Current process maps, system inventories, supplier lists, organisation charts, risk registers, and service catalogues will be made available | Additional discovery effort, inaccurate dependency mapping, timeline delays | BCMS Project Manager |
| Technology input | IT and information security teams will provide application, infrastructure, data, backup, recovery, and resilience information | Recovery objectives may not align to technical capability | CIO / IT Lead |
| Supplier engagement | Material suppliers will respond to continuity due diligence requests and provide evidence of resilience arrangements | Supplier-related continuity gaps may remain unvalidated | Procurement Lead |
| Budget approval | Approved budget will be available for consultancy, tools, training, exercises, technology improvements, travel, and certification activities where applicable | Reduced scope, deferred activities, or lower maturity at implementation | Executive Sponsor |
| Resource availability | Key personnel will be available during agreed project phases | Workshops, approvals, and testing may slip | Functional Managers |
| Change control | Significant organisational, technology, supplier, or premises changes will be communicated to the project | BCMS design may become outdated before go-live | Change Advisory / PMO |
| Existing governance | Risk management, incident management, health and safety, information security, and crisis management processes will be leveraged where practical | Duplication of controls, inconsistent escalation routes, inefficient documentation | Risk / Compliance Lead |
| Certification intent | If external certification is required, certification body selection and assessment dates will be confirmed early | Readiness activities may not align to assessment windows | Executive Sponsor |

Key project assumptions:

- The BCMS will be designed to support actual operational recovery, not only documentation readiness.
- The initial implementation will prioritise the most critical services, activities, dependencies, and risks.
- Existing emergency response, incident management, disaster recovery, cyber incident response, and crisis communications arrangements will be reviewed and integrated where appropriate.
- Business continuity requirements will be risk-based and proportionate to the size, complexity, and stakeholder obligations of [Organisation Name].
- Where recovery objectives exceed current capability, gaps will be recorded, risk-owned, and addressed through approved improvement plans.
- The BCMS will be maintained after project closure through defined business-as-usual governance.

## Approach / Phases

The BCMS project will be delivered through structured phases to ensure clear governance, practical implementation, evidence capture, and readiness for internal or external assurance.

### Phase 1 - Initiation and Mobilisation

The project will be formally launched with approved sponsorship, governance, scope, resources, and communications.

Key activities:

- Confirm executive sponsor, project owner, project manager, and steering committee membership.
- Approve this BCMS Project Charter.
- Confirm implementation scope, objectives, constraints, and high-level deliverables.
- Establish project governance, reporting cadence, issue escalation, and decision-making routes.
- Identify business unit representatives and continuity plan owners.
- Confirm budget, procurement needs, and any external support requirements.
- Prepare stakeholder communication and engagement plan.
- Create project document repository and evidence management structure.
- Align the project with related programmes such as risk management, information security, operational resilience, technology resilience, crisis management, and compliance.

Key outputs:

- Approved Project Charter.
- Project plan and milestone schedule.
- Stakeholder register.
- BCMS governance structure.
- Project risk and issue log.
- Evidence repository.

### Phase 2 - Context, Requirements, and Scope Confirmation

This phase confirms the organisational context and continuity expectations that shape the BCMS.

Key activities:

- Identify internal and external factors affecting business continuity.
- Identify interested parties and their continuity-related needs and expectations.
- Review contractual, regulatory, customer, insurer, and internal commitments.
- Confirm products, services, activities, sites, systems, suppliers, and dependencies in scope.
- Define BCMS boundaries and document justified exclusions.
- Agree BCMS policy direction and high-level objectives.
- Review existing continuity, incident, crisis, recovery, and emergency arrangements.

Key outputs:

- BCMS scope statement.
- Interested party and requirements register.
- Context assessment.
- Initial compliance and obligations summary.
- Draft BCMS policy.
- Existing arrangements gap assessment.

### Phase 3 - Business Impact Analysis and Dependency Mapping

This phase determines the operational impact of disruption and identifies recovery priorities.

Key activities:

- Conduct BIA workshops with each in-scope business function.
- Identify priority activities supporting products and services.
- Assess impacts over time across financial, customer, legal, regulatory, operational, reputational, safety, and strategic dimensions.
- Determine maximum tolerable disruption periods.
- Define recovery time objectives and minimum acceptable operating levels.
- Identify key dependencies, including people, premises, technology, data, equipment, suppliers, records, communications, and interdependent teams.
- Identify critical periods, peak processing times, manual workarounds, and seasonal constraints.
- Validate BIA results with process owners and senior management.
- Resolve conflicts between business expectations and recovery capability.

Key outputs:

- Completed BIA records.
- Prioritised activity list.
- Recovery objectives.
- Dependency maps.
- Minimum resource requirements.
- BIA summary and recommendations.

### Phase 4 - Continuity Risk Assessment

This phase identifies and evaluates risks that could disrupt priority activities and assesses the adequacy of existing controls.

Key activities:

- Identify credible disruptive scenarios relevant to the organisation.
- Assess threats and vulnerabilities affecting in-scope activities and dependencies.
- Review current preventive, detective, response, and recovery controls.
- Evaluate residual continuity risk.
- Identify single points of failure and unacceptable concentrations of dependency.
- Record risk treatment actions and assign owners.
- Align continuity risks with the enterprise risk management process.

Example scenarios to consider:

- Loss of workplace or restricted site access.
- Major technology outage or cloud service failure.
- Cyber incident affecting availability or integrity.
- Loss of key supplier or outsourced service.
- Utility failure.
- Severe weather or natural hazard.
- Pandemic or workforce unavailability.
- Transport disruption.
- Data loss or corruption.
- Telecommunications failure.
- Reputational crisis causing service demand surge.
- Civil unrest, security event, or local emergency.

Key outputs:

- Continuity risk assessment.
- Scenario analysis.
- Risk treatment plan.
- Updated project risk log.
- Recommendations for continuity strategies.

### Phase 5 - Continuity Strategy and Solution Design

This phase defines how the organisation will prevent, respond to, continue, and recover priority activities.

Key activities:

- Define continuity strategies for priority activities and dependencies.
- Compare recovery requirements against current capability.
- Identify gaps requiring investment, process change, supplier action, or risk acceptance.
- Define alternative working arrangements, manual workarounds, cross-training, recovery teams, technology recovery approaches, supplier alternatives, and communication channels.
- Agree minimum service levels during disruption.
- Confirm incident escalation and activation thresholds.
- Develop a continuity strategy approval paper for leadership decision-making.
- Obtain approval for risk treatments, funding, and residual risk acceptance where applicable.

Key outputs:

- Business continuity strategy.
- Recovery capability gap analysis.
- Solution design recommendations.
- Approved risk treatment and investment decisions.
- Residual risk acceptance records.

### Phase 6 - Plan Development and Documentation

This phase creates the documented arrangements needed to operate the BCMS and respond to disruption.

Key activities:

- Develop or update business continuity plans for in-scope functions.
- Develop incident response and escalation arrangements.
- Develop crisis management and strategic decision-making arrangements where required.
- Develop internal and external communications protocols.
- Document contact lists, call trees, role cards, action checklists, site recovery details, technology recovery dependencies, supplier escalation routes, and manual workaround procedures.
- Define document control, approval, review, and distribution arrangements.
- Ensure plans are practical, role-based, accessible, and usable during disruption.
- Align plans with emergency response, cyber incident response, IT disaster recovery, crisis communications, health and safety, and facilities procedures.

Key outputs:

- Business continuity plans.
- Incident response plan or playbook.
- Crisis management plan, if in scope.
- Business continuity communications plan.
- Contact and escalation lists.
- Role cards and action checklists.
- Plan approval records.

### Phase 7 - Awareness, Training, and Competence

This phase ensures people understand their continuity responsibilities and are able to perform assigned roles.

Key activities:

- Develop BCMS awareness materials for all relevant personnel.
- Deliver role-specific training for plan owners, recovery teams, incident managers, communications leads, executives, and support functions.
- Provide guidance on plan activation, escalation, record keeping, communications, and recovery priorities.
- Train business unit representatives on maintaining BIA and continuity plans.
- Record attendance, competence evidence, and follow-up actions.
- Include continuity responsibilities in onboarding and role changes where appropriate.

Key outputs:

- Training needs analysis.
- Awareness communications.
- Training materials.
- Attendance records.
- Competence records.
- Training effectiveness feedback.

### Phase 8 - Exercising, Validation, and Improvement

This phase validates continuity arrangements through realistic tests and exercises.

Key activities:

- Develop an exercise programme based on priority activities and risk scenarios.
- Conduct plan walkthroughs, desktop exercises, communications tests, call tree tests, technology recovery tests, supplier escalation tests, and scenario-based simulations as appropriate.
- Evaluate whether plans support agreed recovery objectives and minimum service levels.
- Capture lessons learned, weaknesses, decision points, and improvement actions.
- Assign owners and due dates for corrective actions.
- Retest significant weaknesses where necessary.

Key outputs:

- Exercise schedule.
- Exercise scripts and objectives.
- Exercise attendance records.
- Exercise reports.
- Lessons learned log.
- Corrective action plan.
- Updated plans and procedures.

### Phase 9 - Performance Evaluation and Readiness Review

This phase confirms whether the BCMS is implemented, operating, and ready for assurance review.

Key activities:

- Define BCMS performance measures and reporting methods.
- Conduct BCMS documentation and implementation review.
- Complete internal review or audit of the BCMS.
- Prepare management review materials.
- Review open risks, issues, nonconformities, improvement actions, and residual risk decisions.
- Confirm whether project deliverables meet defined success criteria.
- Prepare evidence for certification readiness if certification is required.
- Obtain leadership approval for transition to business-as-usual operation.

Key outputs:

- BCMS performance dashboard.
- Internal review or audit report.
- Management review pack.
- Corrective action status report.
- Certification readiness assessment, if applicable.
- Go-live approval.

### Phase 10 - Transition to Business-as-Usual

This phase closes the project and embeds the BCMS into ongoing governance.

Key activities:

- Confirm operational owners for BCMS maintenance.
- Transfer project records to controlled document repositories.
- Establish annual BCMS calendar for BIA review, risk review, plan review, training, exercises, internal review, management review, and improvement tracking.
- Confirm ongoing reporting cadence to leadership.
- Close or transition open actions into the operational improvement plan.
- Conduct project closure review and lessons learned.
- Obtain formal project closure approval.

Key outputs:

- BAU BCMS operating model.
- Annual BCMS activity calendar.
- Open action transition log.
- Project closure report.
- Lessons learned report.
- Sponsor closure approval.

## Milestones & Timeline

The project timeline will be confirmed during mobilisation and adjusted through approved change control. The indicative schedule below assumes a [medium-sized] organisation with multiple business functions and moderate operational complexity.

| Milestone | Key Deliverables | Target Date | Responsible Owner | Approval / Acceptance Criteria |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Project authorised | Approved Project Charter, sponsor confirmation, budget approval | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Executive Sponsor | Charter approved and communicated to leadership team |
| Project mobilisation completed | Project plan, governance forum, stakeholder register, repository, reporting cadence | [YYYY-MM-DD] | BCMS Project Manager | Steering Committee confirms project readiness |
| BCMS scope confirmed | Scope statement, exclusions, interested party register, obligations summary | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Business Continuity Manager | Scope approved by Steering Committee |
| BCMS policy drafted and approved | BCMS policy and objectives | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Executive Sponsor | Policy approved and issued through controlled communication |
| BIA workshops completed | Completed BIA templates for all in-scope functions | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Business Unit Heads | All required workshops completed and records validated |
| BIA results approved | Prioritised activities, recovery objectives, dependency maps | [YYYY-MM-DD] | BCMS Steering Committee | Recovery priorities approved and conflicts resolved |
| Continuity risk assessment completed | Risk assessment, scenario analysis, treatment plan | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Risk Lead | Risks reviewed, rated, and assigned to owners |
| Continuity strategies approved | Strategy document, capability gap analysis, investment decisions | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Executive Sponsor | Strategy approved, funding decisions recorded |
| Business continuity plans developed | Function-level continuity plans, contact lists, escalation paths | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Plan Owners | Plans reviewed and approved by accountable managers |
| Incident and communications arrangements approved | Activation criteria, response structure, communications protocols | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Crisis / Incident Management Lead | Arrangements integrated with existing incident processes |
| Training delivered | Awareness materials, role-based training, attendance records | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Training Lead | Target attendance and competence expectations met |
| Initial exercises completed | Exercise plans, exercise reports, lessons learned | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Business Continuity Manager | Exercises completed and improvement actions assigned |
| Internal review completed | Review or audit report, findings, action plan | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Internal Audit / Compliance Lead | Findings documented and accepted by management |
| Management review completed | Performance report, risks, issues, improvement plan, readiness decision | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Executive Sponsor | Leadership confirms BCMS readiness or required remediation |
| Certification readiness confirmed, if applicable | Evidence pack, readiness assessment, remediation status | [YYYY-MM-DD] | BCMS Project Manager | Critical gaps closed or accepted |
| Project closure approved | BAU handover, annual calendar, closure report, lessons learned | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Executive Sponsor | Sponsor confirms transition to ongoing BCMS operation |

Indicative phase durations:

| Phase | Estimated Duration |
|---|---:|
| Initiation and mobilisation | 2-3 weeks |
| Context, requirements, and scope confirmation | 2-4 weeks |
| Business Impact Analysis and dependency mapping | 4-8 weeks |
| Continuity risk assessment | 2-4 weeks |
| Continuity strategy and solution design | 3-6 weeks |
| Plan development and documentation | 4-8 weeks |
| Awareness, training, and competence | 2-4 weeks |
| Exercising, validation, and improvement | 4-6 weeks |
| Performance evaluation and readiness review | 3-5 weeks |
| Transition to business-as-usual | 1-2 weeks |

Changes to milestones, scope, budget, or success criteria must be recorded in the project change log and approved by the BCMS Steering Committee or Executive Sponsor, depending on materiality.

## Roles & Responsibilities

The BCMS project requires clear ownership, leadership support, cross-functional participation, and disciplined delivery governance.

| Role | Responsibilities | Accountable To |
|---|---|---|
| Executive Sponsor | Authorises the BCMS project; secures funding and resources; communicates leadership commitment; resolves escalated issues; approves major scope, budget, and risk decisions; chairs or delegates management review | Board / Executive Leadership |
| BCMS Steering Committee | Provides oversight; approves key deliverables; reviews progress, risks, issues, and decisions; prioritises remediation; ensures cross-functional alignment | Executive Sponsor |
| BCMS Project Manager | Plans and coordinates project activities; manages schedule, risks, issues, dependencies, and reporting; maintains project documentation; coordinates workshops and approvals; escalates blockers | Executive Sponsor / Steering Committee |
| Business Continuity Manager | Provides BCMS subject matter leadership; defines methodology; supports BIA, risk assessment, strategy, plan development, exercises, and performance reporting; prepares BCMS documentation | Executive Sponsor |
| Business Unit Heads | Nominate representatives; validate priority activities and recovery requirements; approve function-level plans; ensure team participation; own continuity risks and improvement actions for their areas | Executive Leadership |
| Process Owners | Provide process knowledge; identify dependencies and recovery needs; develop and maintain continuity procedures; support testing and exercises | Business Unit Heads |
| Plan Owners | Maintain assigned business continuity plans; ensure contacts and procedures remain current; participate in training and exercises; coordinate updates after changes or incidents | Business Unit Heads |
| Incident / Crisis Management Lead | Aligns continuity activation with incident response and crisis decision-making; defines escalation, command structure, and response records; supports exercises | Executive Sponsor |
| IT / Technology Lead | Provides technology dependency information; confirms recovery capabilities; owns technology recovery actions; aligns business recovery requirements with IT disaster recovery plans | CIO / CTO |
| Information Security Lead | Provides input on cyber disruption scenarios, data integrity risks, incident response integration, and security requirements during recovery | CISO / Security Manager |
| Risk Management Lead | Aligns continuity risk assessment with enterprise risk management; supports risk rating, treatment tracking, and residual risk acceptance | CRO / Risk Committee |
| Compliance / Legal Lead | Identifies legal, regulatory, contractual, and customer obligations; reviews external communication considerations; supports evidence requirements | General Counsel / Compliance Officer |
| Procurement / Supplier Management Lead | Identifies material suppliers; coordinates supplier continuity assurance; supports contractual continuity requirements and supplier remediation | CFO / COO |
| Facilities Lead | Provides site, physical access, utilities, workspace, safety, and alternate location information; supports site-loss scenarios | COO / Facilities Director |
| Human Resources Lead | Supports workforce availability planning, emergency contacts, staff communications, wellbeing considerations, role coverage, and training coordination | CHRO / HR Director |
| Communications Lead | Develops internal and external communications protocols, templates, spokesperson arrangements, and stakeholder notification routes | Executive Sponsor |
| Internal Audit / Assurance Lead | Performs independent review of BCMS implementation and effectiveness; reports findings; tracks management actions | Audit Committee / Senior Management |
| External Advisor, if engaged | Provides specialist guidance, templates, facilitation, independent challenge, and readiness support; does not own management decisions | BCMS Project Manager |
| All Employees and Contractors | Follow continuity instructions; maintain awareness of incident reporting and emergency arrangements; participate in training and exercises where assigned | Line Managers |

Decision rights:

| Decision Type | Decision Maker | Consultation Required |
|---|---|---|
| Project authorisation and closure | Executive Sponsor | Steering Committee |
| BCMS scope and exclusions | Steering Committee | Business Unit Heads, Risk, Compliance |
| Budget approval and material changes | Executive Sponsor | Finance, Steering Committee |
| Recovery objectives | Steering Committee | Business Unit Heads, IT, Risk, Compliance |
| Continuity strategy selection | Executive Sponsor / Steering Committee | Business Unit Heads, IT, Procurement, Facilities |
| Residual risk acceptance | Accountable Executive / Risk Committee | Risk, Compliance, Business Owner |
| Plan approval | Accountable Business Unit Head | Business Continuity Manager |
| Exercise programme approval | Steering Committee | Plan Owners, Incident Lead, IT |
| Certification readiness decision, if applicable | Executive Sponsor | BCMS Project Manager, Internal Audit, Steering Committee |

## Resources

The project will require sufficient people, funding, tools, facilities, and management attention to establish a BCMS that is proportionate, effective, and maintainable.

### People Resources

| Resource | Estimated Commitment | Primary Activities |
|---|---:|---|
| Executive Sponsor | 1-2 hours per month plus decision points | Sponsorship, escalation, approval, leadership communication |
| BCMS Project Manager | 40-100% allocation during implementation | Project planning, coordination, reporting, governance, delivery tracking |
| Business Continuity Manager | 40-100% allocation during implementation | Methodology, facilitation, documentation, training, exercising, assurance readiness |
| Business Unit Representatives | 2-6 hours per workshop plus review time | BIA, dependency mapping, plan development, exercises |
| Plan Owners | 1-3 days per plan during development; periodic maintenance thereafter | Plan drafting, validation, updates, exercises |
| IT Representatives | 2-8 hours per critical service or system review | Application mapping, recovery capabilities, technology recovery alignment |
| Risk and Compliance | 2-6 hours per phase as required | Obligations, risk assessment, acceptance, evidence review |
| Procurement / Supplier Management | 1-4 hours per material supplier review | Supplier dependency validation and assurance |
| HR, Facilities, Communications | Time as required for scenario planning and documentation | Workforce, workplace, stakeholder communications, welfare, site continuity |
| Internal Audit / Assurance | Time as required for review planning and execution | Independent review, findings, recommendations |

### Budget

The approved budget for the BCMS project is [Budget Amount] for the initial implementation period ending [YYYY-MM-DD]. Budget ownership sits with [Budget Owner Role].

Indicative budget categories:

| Budget Category | Description | Estimated Amount |
|---|---|---:|
| Internal staff time | Allocation of business, IT, risk, compliance, and management personnel | [Amount] |
| External advisory support | Specialist facilitation, documentation support, readiness review, or certification preparation | [Amount] |
| Training and awareness | Awareness materials, role-based training, executive briefings, exercise facilitation | [Amount] |
| Tools and repositories | BCMS management tool, document repository, workflow, notification system, or collaboration platform | [Amount] |
| Exercise and testing | Scenario design, facilitation, room booking, simulation tools, technology recovery testing | [Amount] |
| Technology resilience improvements | Backup, recovery, replication, monitoring, remote access, communication resilience, or recovery environment improvements | [Amount] |
| Facilities and workplace continuity | Alternate workspace, access equipment, emergency supplies, signage, site recovery needs | [Amount] |
| Supplier assurance | Supplier assessments, audit support, contractual updates, contingency arrangements | [Amount] |
| Certification assessment, if applicable | Certification body fees, readiness assessment, assessment logistics | [Amount] |
| Contingency | Reserve for approved changes and emerging continuity gaps | [Amount] |

Budget principles:

- Funding decisions will be risk-based and aligned to approved recovery priorities.
