BCM-006.title: Business Impact Analysis (BIA)
BCM-006.content:
| Document ID | Version | Owner | Effective Date | Framework | Classification |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| BIA-REP-[YYYY]-[NN] | 1.0 | Business Continuity Manager | [DD Month YYYY] | ISO 22301:2019 | Confidential - Internal Use Only |

## Purpose

This Business Impact Analysis Report documents the results of the organisation-wide assessment of business activities, supporting resources, disruption impacts, and recovery requirements.

The purpose of this report is to:

- Identify the organisation’s most time-critical products, services, processes, and dependencies.
- Determine the maximum tolerable period of disruption for each assessed process.
- Define recovery time objectives and recovery point objectives to support business continuity planning.
- Establish minimum business continuity objectives for critical activities.
- Provide a prioritised basis for continuity strategies, recovery plans, resource allocation, and testing.
- Support management decisions on resilience, investment, risk treatment, and continuity capability.

This report is intended to be used by executive management, process owners, risk owners, business continuity personnel, IT service owners, crisis management teams, and internal assurance functions.

## Reporting Period & Scope

### Reporting Period

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Assessment period | [DD Month YYYY] to [DD Month YYYY] |
| Interviews and workshops completed | [DD Month YYYY] to [DD Month YYYY] |
| Data validation period | [DD Month YYYY] to [DD Month YYYY] |
| Management review date | [DD Month YYYY] |
| Report issue date | [DD Month YYYY] |
| Next scheduled review | [DD Month YYYY] or following material business change |

### Organisational Scope

This BIA covers the following business units, locations, services, and enabling functions:

| Area | Included in Scope | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Executive management | Yes | Strategic decision-making, crisis leadership, external stakeholder approval |
| Operations / service delivery | Yes | Core customer-facing service delivery activities |
| Sales / customer management | Yes | Customer communications, order intake, account support |
| Finance | Yes | Payroll, billing, receivables, payables, cash management |
| Human resources | Yes | Workforce coordination, payroll inputs, staff welfare support |
| Information technology | Yes | Applications, infrastructure, data, service desk, access management |
| Procurement / supplier management | Yes | Critical third-party coordination, purchase approvals |
| Legal / compliance | Yes | Regulatory reporting, contractual obligations, legal response |
| Facilities / physical security | Yes | Site availability, access control, workplace support |
| Communications / marketing | Partial | Crisis communications and stakeholder messaging only |
| [Business Unit / Region] | [Yes / No / Partial] | [Scope note] |

### Products and Services in Scope

The following products and services were assessed to determine continuity priorities:

| Product / Service | Business Owner | Customer / Stakeholder Group | Included |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Core Product / Service 1] | [Role / Name] | [Customer group] | Yes |
| [Core Product / Service 2] | [Role / Name] | [Customer group] | Yes |
| [Internal Enabling Service] | [Role / Name] | Internal departments | Yes |
| [Excluded Product / Service] | [Role / Name] | [Customer group] | No - [reason] |

### Disruption Scenarios Considered

The BIA considered impacts arising from the unavailability, degradation, or compromise of the following resources:

- People and key skills.
- Premises and facilities.
- Technology platforms, applications, and data.
- Third-party suppliers and outsourced services.
- Utilities and telecommunications.
- Records, information, and knowledge assets.
- Specialist equipment, materials, and logistics.
- Regulatory, legal, and contractual operating permissions.

The BIA did not assume a single cause of disruption. Instead, it assessed the consequences of disruption regardless of whether the cause is cyber incident, facility loss, supplier failure, severe weather, workforce shortage, technology outage, civil disruption, or another credible event.

### Key Definitions Used in This Report

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption | The longest period a process, product, service, or activity can be unavailable or severely degraded before the resulting impact becomes unacceptable to the organisation. |
| Recovery Time Objective | The target time within which a process, activity, system, or resource should be restored after disruption. This must be shorter than the maximum tolerable period of disruption. |
| Recovery Point Objective | The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. |
| Minimum Business Continuity Objective | The minimum acceptable level of service, output, or performance that must be maintained or restored during disruption. |
| Critical Activity | An activity that must be maintained or recovered within a defined time period to avoid unacceptable impact. |
| Dependency | A resource, supplier, system, person, facility, data set, approval, or service required to perform a process or activity. |

## Executive Summary

The Business Impact Analysis confirms that the organisation’s highest-priority continuity requirements are concentrated in customer-facing service delivery, technology-enabled transaction processing, cashflow management, regulatory obligations, payroll, and crisis communications.

The assessment identified several activities where disruption would create unacceptable consequences within the first 24 hours, including [critical customer service / operational activity], [key transaction platform], [incident communications], and [time-sensitive regulatory or contractual activity]. These activities require clearly documented recovery strategies, tested workarounds, defined manual processing arrangements, and confirmed resource availability.

Overall, the organisation has a reasonable understanding of its operational dependencies; however, continuity requirements are not yet consistently translated into formal recovery capability. Several recovery expectations currently depend on informal knowledge, individual availability, supplier responsiveness, or untested manual workarounds. The most significant resilience gaps relate to technology recovery alignment, third-party recovery assurance, cross-training, dependency mapping, and recovery resource prioritisation.

### Overall BIA Conclusions

| Area | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| Critical processes identified | Yes. Critical and time-sensitive activities have been identified across business units. |
| Recovery priorities defined | Partially. Priority tiers are clear, but some RTOs require validation against actual recovery capability. |
| Minimum continuity levels defined | Yes for most critical activities; further refinement required for measurable service levels in some areas. |
| IT recovery alignment | Partially aligned. Some system recovery capabilities do not yet meet business expectations. |
| Supplier dependency visibility | Moderate. Key suppliers are known, but evidence of their recovery capability is inconsistent. |
| Manual workaround readiness | Limited. Workarounds exist for selected processes but are not consistently documented or tested. |
| Resource requirements | Partially defined. Staffing and technology requirements need consolidation into recovery plans. |
| Management action required | Yes. Priority actions are listed in this report. |

### Highest Priority Recovery Requirements

| Priority | Process / Activity | Required Recovery Time | Required Data Recovery | Minimum Continuity Level |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | Crisis management and executive decision-making | 1 hour | Not applicable | Crisis team convened, situation assessed, decisions recorded |
| 2 | Customer-facing critical service delivery | 4 hours | 15 minutes to 1 hour | Minimum [percentage]% of priority customer requests processed |
| 3 | Core transaction processing | 4 hours | 15 minutes | Priority transactions processed and reconciled |
| 4 | Regulatory / contractual notifications | 4-8 hours | 1 hour | Mandatory notifications assessed, approved, and submitted |
| 5 | IT incident response and service restoration coordination | 1 hour | Not applicable | Response bridge established, triage active, recovery tasks assigned |
| 6 | Payroll processing | 24-48 hours, depending on pay cycle | 24 hours | Payroll completed for active employees by statutory or contractual deadline |
| 7 | Billing and cash collection | 24-72 hours | 24 hours | Critical invoices issued, priority cash receipts allocated |
| 8 | Supplier coordination for critical services | 8-24 hours | 24 hours | Critical suppliers contacted and service status confirmed |

### Key Risks Identified

- Recovery expectations for some systems are more demanding than current technology recovery capability.
- Several critical activities depend on a small number of key individuals with limited documented backup coverage.
- Supplier continuity arrangements are not consistently evidenced for critical outsourced services.
- Manual workarounds are not sufficiently mature for extended technology outages.
- Process owners use different assumptions when estimating acceptable downtime and minimum service levels.
- Data recovery expectations require clearer alignment between business owners, system owners, and IT operations.
- Crisis communications dependencies require more robust contact data, approval paths, and alternative communication channels.

### Management Attention Required

Management should prioritise the following:

1. Approve the recovery priorities and minimum service levels set out in this report.
2. Resolve gaps between business recovery needs and technology recovery capability.
3. Confirm continuity strategies for activities with recovery requirements of 24 hours or less.
4. Require critical suppliers to provide evidence of continuity and recovery capability.
5. Ensure recovery plans are updated to reflect the BIA results.
6. Schedule exercises to validate recovery assumptions and manual workarounds.

## Methodology

### Approach

The BIA was conducted using a structured business continuity assessment approach. Information was gathered from process owners, service owners, system owners, supplier managers, and functional leaders. Each assessed process was evaluated for operational, financial, legal, regulatory, contractual, reputational, safety, and customer impacts over time.

The methodology included:

- Review of existing organisational structure, service catalogues, process documentation, technology inventories, supplier lists, incident history, and risk information.
- Structured BIA questionnaires completed by process owners.
- Facilitated workshops with business units and support functions.
- Interviews with owners of critical products, services, systems, and suppliers.
- Review of contractual, regulatory, payroll, billing, and service-level deadlines.
- Identification of upstream and downstream dependencies.
- Validation of preliminary recovery requirements with business and technology stakeholders.
- Consolidation of findings into recovery tiers, process-level requirements, and recommended actions.

### BIA Impact Categories

Each process was assessed against the following impact categories:

| Impact Category | Assessment Considerations |
|---|---|
| Operational impact | Service interruption, backlog creation, inability to process work, loss of productivity, failure of key workflows |
| Customer impact | Customer harm, missed service commitments, reduced trust, complaints, churn, inability to support priority customers |
| Financial impact | Lost revenue, delayed billing, penalties, additional costs, cashflow disruption, recovery expenditure |
| Legal and contractual impact | Breach of contract, failure to meet customer commitments, exposure to claims or penalties |
| Regulatory and compliance impact | Missed reporting deadlines, non-compliance, enforcement risk, audit findings |
| Reputational impact | Negative media, stakeholder concern, loss of market confidence, brand damage |
| Health, safety, and welfare impact | Risk to employees, customers, visitors, or the public |
| Strategic impact | Disruption to strategic objectives, market position, major initiatives, executive commitments |

### Impact Timeline

Process owners assessed expected impacts at the following disruption intervals:

| Time Since Disruption | Purpose of Assessment |
|---|---|
| 0-1 hour | Immediate safety, command, communication, and operational control impacts |
| 1-4 hours | Same-day customer, transaction, incident, and communication impacts |
| 4-8 hours | End-of-day processing, service degradation, backlog, and escalation impacts |
| 8-24 hours | Daily operational, financial, supplier, and regulatory impacts |
| 1-2 days | Payroll, billing, fulfilment, customer confidence, and accumulated backlog impacts |
| 3-5 days | Significant financial, contractual, operational, and reputational impacts |
| More than 5 days | Strategic, market, regulatory, and long-term customer impacts |

### Rating Scale

The following scale was used to assess business impact severity:

| Rating | Severity | Description |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Low | Manageable disruption with limited internal inconvenience and no material external consequence |
| 2 | Moderate | Noticeable disruption causing inefficiency, minor customer impact, or short-term operational delay |
| 3 | Significant | Material service degradation, financial cost, customer impact, compliance concern, or management escalation |
| 4 | Major | Serious disruption causing substantial loss, breach exposure, customer harm, regulatory concern, or reputational damage |
| 5 | Critical | Unacceptable impact threatening essential services, financial viability, safety, legal standing, or strategic commitments |

### Recovery Tiering Model

Recovery tiers were assigned based on the earliest point at which impact becomes unacceptable, adjusted for management judgement and dependency constraints.

| Recovery Tier | Required Recovery Time | Typical Characteristics |
|---|---:|---|
| Tier 0 | Immediate to 1 hour | Crisis command, safety, cyber response, urgent communications, executive decisions |
| Tier 1 | 1-4 hours | Essential customer services, critical operations, priority transactions, urgent regulatory actions |
| Tier 2 | 4-24 hours | High-priority operations, customer support, supplier coordination, daily financial activities |
| Tier 3 | 1-3 days | Important business processes that can tolerate short delay with controlled backlog |
| Tier 4 | 3-5 days | Processes with moderate tolerance for disruption and manageable manual alternatives |
| Tier 5 | More than 5 days | Non-critical or deferrable activities that can be suspended temporarily without unacceptable impact |

### Validation

Preliminary results were reviewed with business owners and selected support functions. Recovery time objectives, recovery point objectives, and minimum business continuity objectives were challenged for realism, consistency, and dependency alignment.

Validation focused on:

- Whether the impact timeline reflected actual business consequences.
- Whether the requested recovery time was shorter than the maximum tolerable disruption.
- Whether data recovery requirements were aligned to business transaction volume and legal retention needs.
- Whether minimum continuity levels were measurable and practical.
- Whether resource dependencies were identified sufficiently to support recovery planning.
- Whether critical suppliers and systems were appropriately reflected.

### 6. Minimum Business Continuity Objectives

The following minimum continuity objectives have been defined for critical and high-priority activities.

| Payroll | Partial | One pay cycle if source data available | Management approval, bank file controls, exception handling | Needs formal emergency payroll procedure. |

### 9. Recovery Resource Requirements

| Resource Type | Critical Requirement | Processes Supported | Current Status | Gap / Action Needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Staff | Trained alternates for critical process roles | Operations, finance, payroll, crisis management | Partial | Complete cross-training and delegate authorisation. |
| Technology | Recovery capability meeting approved RTO/RPO | Customer service, transaction processing, finance, communications | Partial | Align system recovery capabilities with business requirements. |
| Facilities | Remote access or alternate site capability | Crisis management, operations, support functions | Moderate | Validate capacity for simultaneous remote work. |
| Communications | Alternate communication channels | Crisis management, customer support, supplier coordination | Partial | Maintain offline contact lists and backup channels. |
| Supplier support | Confirmed escalation routes and continuity capability | Hosting, payroll, telecoms, payment processing | Partial | Obtain supplier evidence and escalation contacts. |
| Records | Offline or alternate access to critical documents and contacts | Legal, compliance, procurement, crisis management | Limited | Create controlled emergency document pack. |
| Equipment | Laptops, secure access tokens, headsets, mobile devices | Remote work, customer support, operations | Moderate | Confirm availability for critical recovery team. |

## Analysis

### Overall Business Continuity Implications

The BIA demonstrates that the organisation must be able to manage immediate command and control, recover priority customer and operational services within hours, and maintain essential support functions within defined daily or pay-cycle deadlines.

The most important continuity implication is that recovery capability must be planned around business outcomes rather than individual systems or departments. Several critical activities are dependent on combinations of people, systems, data, suppliers, communications, and approval pathways. A system recovery alone will not restore service if trained staff, supplier support, access rights, customer communication channels, or manual reconciliation controls are unavailable.

### Recovery Time Objective Analysis

The recovery time objectives identified by process owners are generally reasonable when compared with impact severity. However, some requested recovery times appear to reflect business need rather than proven capability. The most significant examples are:

- Core transaction processing requires recovery within 4 hours, but current technology recovery evidence may not support that requirement.
- Customer-facing service delivery depends on both system availability and trained staffing; recovery within 4 hours may be achievable only for priority services unless capacity planning is improved.
- Collaboration and communication platforms are relied upon for crisis coordination, but alternative communication methods are not yet sufficiently formalised.
- Payroll recovery is feasible within the required timeframe if disruption does not coincide with payroll cut-off; additional controls are required for payroll-period disruption.

Management should treat approved RTOs as business requirements that must drive continuity strategy, technology design, supplier assurance, and exercise planning.

### Recovery Point Objective Analysis

Data recovery expectations are most stringent for transaction records and customer service records. Loss of recent transactional data would create reconciliation effort, customer disputes, financial error, and potential compliance exposure.

The following data recovery themes require attention:

- Transactional systems require clear confirmation of backup frequency, replication, journaling, and restore testing.
- Customer case data should be protected with recovery capabilities that avoid material loss of service history.
- Offline access to crisis contacts, supplier contacts, regulatory contacts, and escalation details is necessary because these records may be needed during technology outages.
- Manual workarounds must include procedures for later re-entry, validation, reconciliation, and exception approval.

### Maximum Tolerable Disruption Analysis

The maximum tolerable period of disruption varies significantly by process:

- Crisis management, employee welfare, IT incident response, and executive decision-making have very low disruption tolerance.
- Customer-facing operations and core transaction processing become unacceptable within 24 hours.
- Regulatory or contractual notification activities may become unacceptable within the same day, depending on incident type and obligation.
- Payroll, billing, and supplier payments can tolerate short delays but become critical near statutory, contractual, or cashflow deadlines.
- Administrative and non-critical activities can be deferred if resources are redirected to critical recovery priorities.

This analysis supports a tiered recovery model where scarce people, systems, facilities, and supplier support are allocated first to activities with the shortest tolerable disruption.

### Minimum Continuity Level Analysis

Minimum business continuity objectives have been defined for the most important activities. The quality of those objectives varies by process. Stronger objectives are measurable, time-bound, and linked to customer or compliance outcomes. Weaker objectives use general terms such as “resume service” or “provide support” without specifying minimum volume, priority criteria, or acceptable backlog.

The organisation should refine continuity objectives to include:

- Minimum percentage of normal capacity required during disruption.
- Priority customer or transaction categories.
- Acceptable backlog volume and maximum backlog age.
- Required operating hours during disruption.
- Minimum staffing and approval roles.
- Required communication frequency to customers, executives, employees, suppliers, or regulators.

### Dependency Analysis

The dependency analysis shows that technology and people are the most significant continuity dependencies. Critical activities are heavily dependent on [Core Transaction System], [Customer Relationship Management Platform], identity and access services, network connectivity, and collaboration tools.

People dependency is also material. Several critical processes rely on specialist knowledge, named approvers, or small teams. During a widespread disruption, recovery may be constrained by staff availability, competing priorities, fatigue, or inability to access systems remotely.

Supplier dependency is significant for hosting, telecommunications, payroll, payment processing, and outsourced services. While suppliers are known, assurance evidence is inconsistent. Contractual availability commitments do not provide sufficient assurance unless supported by tested recovery arrangements, escalation contacts, and service restoration communications.

### Manual Workaround Analysis

Manual workarounds are available for some activities but are generally suitable only for short periods and reduced transaction volumes. They are most effective for decision-making, communications, regulatory notifications, and selected finance activities. They are less effective for high-volume customer service and transaction processing.

Manual workarounds should not be treated as a substitute for technology recovery where transaction volumes are high, data accuracy is critical, or customer response time is important. Where workarounds are required, they must include:

- Trigger conditions for activation.
- Authorised roles and approval thresholds.
- Standard forms, logs, and numbering controls.
- Data protection and confidentiality safeguards.
- Reconciliation and re-entry procedures.
- Backlog prioritisation rules.
- Criteria for returning to normal processing.

### Continuity Strategy Implications

The BIA findings indicate the need for continuity strategies in the following areas:

| Strategy Area | Required Direction |
|---|---|
| Crisis management | Maintain rapid activation, clear roles, alternate communications, decision logs, and escalation procedures. |
| Technology recovery | Align technical recovery capability to approved business RTOs and RPOs for priority systems. |
| Remote working | Ensure critical staff can work securely from alternate locations with adequate access and equipment. |
| Workforce resilience | Develop cross-training, deputies, shift coverage, and role-based recovery instructions. |
| Supplier resilience | Obtain supplier continuity assurance and define escalation arrangements for critical services. |
| Manual processing | Document and test manual workarounds for short-term critical processing. |
| Data availability | Ensure critical records, contact lists, and recovery documents are available during technology disruption. |
| Communications | Establish approved templates, stakeholder lists, backup channels, and authority for crisis messaging. |

### Key Gaps

| Gap ID | Gap Description | Impact | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| BIA-GAP-001 | Recovery capability for [Core Transaction System] may not meet business RTO/RPO requirements. | Core transaction processing and customer service may not recover quickly enough. | High |
| BIA-GAP-002 | Manual workaround for customer-facing critical service delivery is not fully documented or tested. | Reduced ability to maintain priority service during system outage. | High |
| BIA-GAP-003 | Critical supplier recovery evidence is incomplete. | Organisation may overestimate supplier restoration capability. | High |
| BIA-GAP-004 | Key-person dependency exists in payroll, operations exception handling, and technical recovery. | Recovery may be delayed if named individuals are unavailable. | Medium |
| BIA-GAP-005 | Crisis contact lists and supplier escalation details are not consistently maintained offline. | Activation and coordination may be delayed during technology outage. | Medium |
| BIA-GAP-006 | Minimum continuity levels are not quantified for all high-priority processes. | Recovery plans may lack measurable success criteria. | Medium |
| BIA-GAP-007 | Remote working capacity has not been validated for simultaneous use by all critical recovery staff. | Assumed alternate working capability may fail under widespread disruption. | Medium |
| BIA-GAP-008 | Workload transfer between [Site A] and [Site B] has not been tested recently. | Site loss could cause extended operational delay. | Medium |

## Recommendations & Actions

### Management Recommendations

Management should approve the recovery priorities and require business and support functions to update continuity arrangements accordingly. The organisation should focus first on the activities that must be restored within 24 hours, particularly crisis management, customer-facing service delivery, core transaction processing, regulatory notifications, IT incident response, and external communications.

Recommended management decisions are:

1. Approve the process-level MTPDs, RTOs, RPOs, MBCOs, and recovery tiers documented in this report.
2. Confirm that business continuity planning will prioritise Tier 0, Tier 1, and Tier 2 activities.
3. Require system owners to assess current technology recovery capabilities against business recovery requirements.
4. Require owners of critical suppliers to obtain and review continuity assurance evidence.
5. Require process owners to document and test manual workarounds for all critical activities where technology recovery may not be immediate.
6. Require continuity plans to be updated within [number] days of report approval.
7. Direct Internal Audit, Risk, or Compliance to review closure evidence for high-priority actions.

### Action Plan

| Action ID | Action | Owner | Priority | Target Date | Expected Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BIA-ACT-001 | Obtain management approval of BIA results, including process criticality, MTPDs, RTOs, RPOs, and MBCOs. | Business Continuity Manager | High | [DD Month YYYY] | Approved report, management meeting record |
| BIA-ACT-002 | Validate technology recovery capability for all systems supporting Tier 0, Tier 1, and Tier 2 processes. | Chief Information Officer | High | [DD Month YYYY] | Recovery capability assessment, test results, gap register |
| BIA-ACT-003 | Resolve recovery gap for [Core Transaction System] or revise continuity strategy with approved compensating measures. | Chief Information Officer / Operations Director | High | [DD Month YYYY] | Remediation plan, test evidence, approved residual risk if applicable |
| BIA-ACT-004 | Document manual workaround procedures for customer-facing critical service delivery and core transaction processing. | Operations Director | High | [DD Month YYYY] | Approved workaround procedures, manual logs, training record |

| 4 | Core transaction processing | Required to maintain financial, operational, and customer integrity. |
| 5 | Regulatory and contractual obligations | Failure may create legal, enforcement, or contractual consequences. |
| 6 | Payroll and employee welfare | Required to maintain workforce stability and meet employment obligations. |
| 7 | Supplier coordination | Required to restore outsourced and dependent services. |
| 8 | Finance operations | Required to manage cashflow, billing, payments, and financial control. |

### Review and Maintenance Requirements

This BIA report should be reviewed:

- At least annually.
- Following significant organisational restructuring.
- Following launch, retirement, or material change of a critical product or service.
- Following implementation or major change of a critical technology platform.
- Following material change to a critical supplier or outsourced service.
- Following a major incident, exercise, audit finding, or lessons-learned review.
- Following relocation, facility change, or major workforce model change.
- When process owners identify that impact assumptions or recovery requirements have changed.

Process owners are responsible for notifying the Business Continuity Manager of material changes that may affect BIA results. The Business Continuity Manager is responsible for coordinating updates, maintaining approved versions, and ensuring recovery plans remain aligned.

## Distribution & Confidentiality

### Confidentiality Requirements

This report is classified as Confidential - Internal Use Only. It contains sensitive information about operational dependencies, recovery capabilities, technology reliance, suppliers, staffing constraints, and potential continuity weaknesses.

Personnel receiving this report must:

### External Disclosure

External disclosure may be permitted only where there is a legitimate business requirement, such as customer assurance, supplier coordination, insurance assessment, external audit, or regulatory engagement. Before external disclosure:

## Purpose

This report documents the results of the organisation’s business continuity management risk assessment for the reporting period stated below. It identifies disruption risks that could affect the organisation’s ability to continue or recover prioritised products, services, processes, activities, resources and dependencies.

The report is intended to:

- Provide management with a clear view of material disruption risks.
- Assess the likelihood and impact of credible disruptive events.
- Evaluate the effectiveness of existing prevention, response and recovery controls.
- Identify residual risks requiring treatment, escalation or acceptance.
- Support business continuity strategies, plans, exercises and improvement actions.
- Align business continuity risk assessment outputs with the organisation’s enterprise risk methodology.

This report focuses on disruption scenarios relevant to continuity of operations. It is not a general information security, health and safety, financial, legal or enterprise risk report, although related risks are referenced where they create business continuity exposure.

## Reporting Period & Scope

### Reporting Period

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Assessment period | [Start Date] to [End Date] |
| Fieldwork conducted | [Date Range] |

### Organisational Scope

This assessment covers disruption risks affecting the following organisational areas:

| Area | Included in Scope | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Corporate functions | Yes | Finance, HR, Legal, Compliance, Procurement and Executive Management |
| Customer-facing services | Yes | Services delivered to external customers through [Service Channels] |
| Operational delivery teams | Yes | Teams responsible for processing, fulfilment, support and service delivery |
| Technology services | Yes | Core applications, infrastructure, networks, end-user services and support |
| Facilities and workplace | Yes | [Head Office], [Operational Site], remote working arrangements |
| Third-party dependencies | Yes | Critical suppliers, outsourced providers, utilities and professional services |
| Supply chain dependencies | Yes | Suppliers supporting priority activities and service commitments |
| People and key roles | Yes | Key-person dependency, specialist teams, crisis and continuity roles |

### Products, Services and Activities Considered

The assessment considered disruption risks to priority products, services and activities that support customer obligations, regulatory commitments, revenue generation, safety, contractual performance and reputation.

| Priority Product / Service / Activity | Primary Owner | Key Locations | Key Systems | Key Third Parties | Maximum Tolerable Disruption | Recovery Time Objective |

| [Priority Service 1] | [Owner] | [Location] | [System] | [Supplier] | [Duration] | [Duration] |
| [Priority Service 2] | [Owner] | [Location] | [System] | [Supplier] | [Duration] | [Duration] |
| [Priority Activity 1] | [Owner] | [Location] | [System] | [Supplier] | [Duration] | [Duration] |
| [Priority Activity 2] | [Owner] | [Location] | [System] | [Supplier] | [Duration] | [Duration] |

Where full business impact analysis outputs were available, they were used to validate impact ratings, recovery priorities and dependency criticality.

### Risk Categories Assessed

The following disruption risk categories were included:

- Loss of workplace or operating site.
- Loss or degradation of technology services.
- Cyber incident causing business interruption.
- Loss of critical supplier or outsourced service.
- Loss of key people or workforce availability.
- Failure of utilities, telecommunications or logistics.
- Severe weather or environmental disruption.
- Public health event or widespread absenteeism.
- Physical security incident affecting operations.
- Data loss or unavailability affecting recovery.
- Regulatory, legal or contractual disruption arising from service failure.
- Market, geopolitical or civil disruption affecting operations or supply chain.

### Exclusions and Limitations

The following were outside the scope of this report:

- Detailed occupational health and safety risk assessment.
- Detailed cyber threat modelling.
- Full financial risk modelling.
- Insurance valuation or claims analysis.
- Internal audit testing of control design and operating effectiveness.
- Disaster recovery technical testing, except where results were provided as evidence.

Limitations noted during the assessment:

- Some dependency information relies on business owner confirmation and has not yet been independently validated.
- Recovery capability for selected applications has been assessed based on documented recovery objectives and recent test outcomes where available.
- Supplier continuity capability has been assessed using available due diligence responses, contracts and service performance information.
- Quantified financial impact data remains incomplete for some lower-tier activities.

## Executive Summary

The assessment identified a moderate to high business continuity risk profile for the organisation. The organisation has established key continuity capabilities, including documented incident escalation paths, crisis management roles, technology recovery procedures for several core systems and partial remote working capability. However, several material disruption risks remain above the organisation’s target tolerance due to concentration of critical activities, dependency on a limited number of technology platforms and suppliers, incomplete recovery validation, and inconsistent local continuity planning across business units.

The most significant disruption risks are:

1. Prolonged outage of core technology platforms supporting customer-facing services.
2. Major cyber incident causing extended unavailability of systems, data or communications.
3. Failure or disruption of a critical third-party service provider.
4. Loss of access to the main operating site during a peak business period.
5. Workforce unavailability affecting specialist teams with limited cross-training.
6. Inability to recover priority activities within required timeframes due to untested dependencies.

Overall residual risk remains above target for several priority services. Immediate management attention is recommended for risks where recovery time objectives are not supported by tested capability, where single points of failure exist, or where third-party continuity arrangements are not contractually assured.

| Total disruption risks assessed | 18 |

| Risks requiring supplier action | 5 |

| Risks proposed for acceptance | 3 |

### Key Positive Findings

- The organisation has identified its priority services and has assigned business owners for most critical activities.
- Incident escalation and crisis management arrangements are documented and broadly understood by senior stakeholders.
- Remote working capability is available for a substantial proportion of corporate and support activities.
- Several core systems have documented backup and restoration procedures.
- Existing supplier management processes include basic resilience and continuity due diligence for new critical suppliers.
- Business continuity awareness has improved following recent exercises and incident debriefs.

### Key Areas of Concern

- Recovery objectives for some priority services are not fully aligned with tested technology recovery capability.
- Several key business processes depend on small teams or named individuals with limited alternates.
- Some critical suppliers have not provided current evidence of business continuity and recovery capability.
- Local business continuity plans vary in quality, completeness and currency.
- Manual workarounds exist for selected activities but have not been consistently tested at realistic volumes.
- Communication arrangements during technology outage scenarios require strengthening, particularly for customer and supplier communications.
- Dependency mapping remains incomplete for upstream and downstream process interconnections.

### Management Conclusion

The organisation has a workable foundation for business continuity management but must strengthen its ability to withstand and recover from high-impact disruption scenarios. Priority should be given to closing gaps that affect customer-facing services, regulated obligations, revenue-critical processes and time-sensitive operations.

## Methodology

### Assessment Approach

The assessment followed the organisation’s risk management approach and was adapted to focus on business continuity disruption scenarios. The process included:

1. Confirming the products, services, processes and activities in scope.
2. Reviewing business impact information and recovery priorities.
3. Identifying credible disruption scenarios and affected resources.
4. Assessing inherent risk based on likely impact before continuity controls.
5. Reviewing existing preventive, responsive and recovery controls.
6. Assessing residual risk after considering current capability.
7. Comparing residual risk against risk tolerance.
8. Identifying required treatment actions, owners and target dates.
9. Escalating material risks to management for decision and oversight.

### Information Sources

The following sources were used:

| Source | Description |
|---|---|
| Business impact analysis outputs | Recovery priorities, impact tolerances, critical activities and dependency information |
| Business continuity plans | Current departmental and site-level response and recovery plans |
| Crisis management documentation | Roles, escalation routes, decision-making arrangements and communications processes |
| Technology recovery documentation | Backup, restoration, failover and recovery information for core systems |
| Supplier records | Contracts, due diligence responses, service performance reports and continuity evidence |
| Incident records | Previous incidents, near misses, lessons learned and corrective actions |
| Exercise reports | Outcomes from scenario exercises, plan walkthroughs and technical recovery tests |
| Interviews and workshops | Input from process owners, system owners, facilities, procurement, HR, legal and management |
| Enterprise risk register | Existing risk definitions, scoring criteria, owners, tolerances and treatment statuses |
| Operational metrics | Service availability, incident volumes, staffing data and support performance information |

### Participants

| Function / Role | Participation |
|---|---|
| Executive Management | Risk appetite, business priorities and escalation decisions |
| Business Continuity Management | Assessment coordination, methodology, reporting and recommendations |
| Information Technology | System dependencies, recovery capability, backup and restoration information |
| Information Security | Cyber disruption scenarios and security incident dependencies |
| Facilities Management | Site access, building services, utilities and physical disruption scenarios |
| Human Resources | Workforce availability, key role resilience and people-related dependencies |
| Procurement / Supplier Management | Third-party dependencies, supplier continuity evidence and contractual arrangements |
| Legal / Compliance | Regulatory, contractual and customer obligation considerations |
| Business Process Owners | Process impact, manual workarounds, staffing and recovery procedures |
| Communications / Customer Support | Internal, customer and stakeholder communications during disruption |

### Risk Rating Method

Risks were assessed using the organisation’s standard likelihood and impact scoring model. Impact was considered across multiple dimensions relevant to business continuity.

#### Likelihood Scale

| Rating | Descriptor | Description |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | Not expected to occur except in exceptional circumstances |
| 2 | Unlikely | Could occur but has not occurred recently or would require unusual conditions |
| 3 | Possible | Could occur under normal operating conditions or has occurred in comparable organisations |
| 4 | Likely | Expected to occur periodically or has occurred internally or in the sector |
| 5 | Almost Certain | Expected to occur frequently or conditions indicate a high probability of occurrence |

#### Impact Scale

| Rating | Descriptor | Business Continuity Meaning |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Insignificant | Minor local disruption with no meaningful service impact |
| 2 | Minor | Short disruption manageable within normal operations; limited internal impact |
| 3 | Moderate | Disruption to important activities; customer, financial or operational impact manageable with recovery action |
| 4 | Major | Significant disruption to priority services; material customer, contractual, financial or reputational impact |
| 5 | Severe | Extended disruption to critical services; serious regulatory, financial, safety or reputational consequences |

#### Impact Dimensions Considered

| Impact Dimension | Considerations |
|---|---|
| Customer impact | Service availability, customer harm, service-level failure, complaints and churn |
| Operational impact | Process interruption, backlog, rework, missed deadlines and degraded capacity |
| Financial impact | Revenue loss, additional cost, penalties, recovery cost and cash flow impact |
| Regulatory and legal impact | Breach of obligations, reportable incidents, contractual exposure and litigation |
| Reputation impact | Media attention, stakeholder confidence, brand damage and market perception |
| People impact | Safety, welfare, workload, absenteeism and dependence on specialist staff |
| Recovery impact | Ability to meet recovery objectives and sustain operations during disruption |

### Risk Scoring

Risk score is calculated as:

**Likelihood x Impact = Risk Score**

| Score Range | Rating | Management Response |
|---:|---|---|
| 1-4 | Low | Manage through normal controls and periodic monitoring |
| 5-9 | Medium | Treat where cost-effective; monitor through business owner governance |
| 10-16 | High | Treatment plan required; monitor through management review |
| 17-25 | Extreme | Immediate escalation and urgent treatment required |

### Risk Tolerance

A risk is considered above target tolerance when one or more of the following apply:

- Residual risk is rated High or Extreme.
- The organisation cannot recover a priority activity within the required timeframe.
- A single point of failure exists for a priority service.
- A critical supplier cannot demonstrate adequate continuity capability.
- Workarounds are undocumented, untested or not viable at expected volumes.
- The disruption could create material customer, regulatory, contractual or financial exposure.
- Executive management has determined that the risk exceeds acceptable business tolerance.

### Treatment Options

The following treatment options were considered:

| Treatment Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Avoid | Stop or change the activity creating the exposure |
| Reduce | Implement controls, resilience measures or recovery improvements |
| Transfer | Use insurance, outsourcing, contractual provisions or risk-sharing mechanisms |
| Accept | Formally accept the residual risk within approved authority |
| Monitor | Track indicators and reassess periodically where no immediate treatment is required |

### Finding 1 - Core Technology Platform Outage

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Risk ID | BCM-R01 |
| Risk rating | High residual risk |
| Affected services | [Priority Service 1], [Priority Service 2] |
| Primary owner | [Chief Information Officer / Head of Operations] |
| Risk status | Above tolerance |

#### Description

A prolonged outage of the core customer platform would prevent staff and customers from completing time-sensitive transactions, accessing records, resolving service requests and meeting contractual commitments. Current reliance on a small number of integrated platforms means that disruption to one service can quickly affect multiple business processes.

#### Causes

- Application failure or infrastructure outage.
- Cloud or hosting provider disruption.
- Failed change implementation.
- Integration or database failure.
- Capacity issue during peak demand.
- Dependency failure in identity, network, storage or monitoring services.

#### Existing Controls

- Documented incident management process.
- Application support provided by internal IT and vendor support teams.
- Backups configured for production data.
- Monitoring and alerting for selected services.
- Some manual workarounds for customer service and operations.
- Change management and release approval process.

#### Control Gaps

- Recovery time objectives are not consistently supported by recent recovery test evidence.
- Manual workarounds are not proven at peak transaction volumes.
- Dependency mapping for integrations remains incomplete.
- Business communication triggers during extended outage are not consistently defined.
- Recovery sequence between applications, data services and integrations is not fully documented.

#### Consequences

- Missed customer service commitments.
- Backlog accumulation and operational rework.
- Revenue delay or loss.
- Contractual penalties or service credits.
- Increased complaint levels.
- Reputational damage.
- Potential regulatory attention if obligations are not met.

#### Residual Risk Rationale

Residual risk remains High because the potential impact is Major and current recovery capability has not been fully validated against business recovery requirements.

### Finding 2 - Cyber Incident Causing Business Interruption

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Risk ID | BCM-R02 |
| Risk rating | Extreme residual risk |
| Affected services | Enterprise-wide |
| Primary owner | [Chief Information Security Officer / Chief Information Officer] |
| Risk status | Executive escalation required |

#### Description

A ransomware attack, destructive malware event, credential compromise or targeted cyber incident could cause extended unavailability of systems, data, endpoints, communications channels and third-party connections. The incident could also affect trust in data integrity and delay recovery decisions.

#### Causes

- Phishing or credential theft.
- Exploitation of externally facing systems.
- Compromised third-party access.
- Malware propagation across endpoints or servers.
- Privileged account compromise.
- Inadequate segregation of recovery environments.

#### Existing Controls

- Information security monitoring and alerting.
- Security incident response process.
- Endpoint protection and access controls.
- Backup processes for key systems.
- User awareness training.
- Vulnerability management activities.
- Cyber insurance coverage where applicable.

#### Control Gaps

- Cyber recovery procedures are not fully integrated with business continuity plans.
- Isolation and restoration priorities for business-critical systems require confirmation.
- Offline or immutable backup coverage requires validation for all priority systems.
- Crisis communication arrangements for cyber-specific disruption require further testing.
- Dependencies between cyber incident response, legal, communications and business recovery teams require clearer operating rhythm.

#### Consequences

- Extended service interruption.
- Data loss or data integrity concerns.
- Customer harm and loss of confidence.
- Regulatory reporting and investigation.
- Legal and contractual exposure.
- High recovery cost.
- Management distraction and reputational impact.

#### Residual Risk Rationale

Residual risk is Extreme due to potentially Severe impact and the need for stronger evidence that the organisation can recover priority services within acceptable timeframes following a major cyber disruption.

### Finding 3 - Critical Supplier Service Failure

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Risk ID | BCM-R03 |
| Risk rating | High residual risk |
| Affected services | [Priority Service 1], [Finance Process], [Customer Support] |
| Primary owner | [Head of Procurement / Supplier Relationship Owner] |
| Risk status | Above tolerance |

#### Description

The organisation depends on several third parties to deliver priority services. Failure of a critical supplier could interrupt customer service, transaction processing, technology support, payment services, logistics or specialist operations.

#### Causes

- Supplier technology outage.
- Supplier financial distress or insolvency.
- Supplier cyber incident.
- Capacity failure or service degradation.
- Loss of supplier premises or staff.
- Contract termination or dispute.
- Subcontractor or fourth-party failure.

#### Existing Controls

- Contracts and service-level arrangements for selected suppliers.
- Supplier relationship management meetings.
- Basic onboarding due diligence.
- Incident escalation contacts.
- Some alternative supplier options for non-critical services.

#### Control Gaps

- Not all critical suppliers have provided current continuity evidence.
- Continuity requirements are inconsistently included in contracts.
- Exit and substitution plans are incomplete for high-dependency suppliers.
- Supplier recovery time commitments are not always aligned with internal recovery objectives.
- Fourth-party dependencies are not consistently visible.

#### Consequences

- Inability to deliver contracted services.
- Customer dissatisfaction and complaints.
- Regulatory and contractual exposure.
- Operational backlog.
- Emergency procurement and increased cost.
- Reduced management control during incidents.

#### Residual Risk Rationale

Residual risk remains High due to concentration of supplier dependency and insufficient assurance over supplier recovery capability.

### Finding 4 - Loss of Main Operating Site

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Risk ID | BCM-R04 |
| Risk rating | Medium residual risk |
| Affected services | Operations, Corporate Functions, Customer Support |
| Primary owner | [Facilities Manager / Business Continuity Manager] |
| Risk status | Within tolerance with improvement required |

#### Description

Loss of access to the main operating site due to fire, flood, building services failure, police cordon, transport disruption or landlord restriction could affect staff availability, specialist equipment use, paper-based records and team coordination.

#### Existing Controls

- Hybrid and remote working arrangements.
- Cloud-based productivity tools.
- Staff contact lists and emergency communications.
- Building evacuation procedures.
- Facilities management support.
- Some equipment can be relocated or accessed remotely.

#### Control Gaps

- Site loss scenario has not been tested recently with full business participation.
- Equipment and secure access needs for selected teams are not fully documented.
- Alternative workspace arrangements are informal for some functions.
- Dependencies on physical records and mail handling are not fully resolved.

#### Residual Risk Rationale

Residual risk is Medium because remote working reduces site dependency for many activities, but selected operational functions remain location-sensitive.

### Finding 5 - Specialist Workforce Unavailability

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Risk ID | BCM-R05 |
| Risk rating | High residual risk |
| Affected services | IT Operations, Finance, Specialist Operations |
| Primary owner | [Relevant Department Heads] |
| Risk status | Above tolerance |

#### Description

Several priority activities depend on small teams or individuals with specialist knowledge. Sustained absence, resignation, industrial action, travel restriction or competing incident response demands could reduce the organisation’s ability to maintain or recover priority services.

#### Existing Controls

- Role descriptions and departmental procedures.
- Some cross-training within operational teams.
- External support for selected technology and professional services.
- Remote working arrangements.
- Management escalation for resourcing issues.

#### Control Gaps

- Key-person dependencies are not consistently documented.
- Cross-training coverage is incomplete.
- Procedure documentation varies in quality and usability.
- Succession and deputisation arrangements are informal.
- Incident rosters for extended disruptions are not fully developed.

#### Consequences

- Delay in recovery decision-making.
- Inability to perform specialised tasks.
- Increased error rates and rework.
- Staff fatigue during prolonged incidents.
- Failure to meet recovery objectives.
- Increased reliance on external providers.

#### Residual Risk Rationale

Residual risk remains High due to limited depth in specialist roles and the potential for disruption to affect multiple priority services simultaneously.

### Finding 6 - Crisis Communications Failure

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Risk ID | BCM-R15 |
| Risk rating | High residual risk |
| Affected services | Enterprise-wide |
| Primary owner | [Head of Communications / Crisis Management Lead] |
| Risk status | Above tolerance |

#### Description

During a major disruption, delayed, inconsistent or inaccurate communications could worsen customer impact, reduce staff confidence, create regulatory exposure and damage reputation. This risk is heightened where technology channels are unavailable or where incident ownership is unclear.

#### Existing Controls

- Internal communication channels.
- Draft customer communication templates for some scenarios.
- Senior management escalation routes.
- Contact lists for key stakeholders.
- Customer support team procedures.

#### Control Gaps

- Communication approval paths are not clearly defined for all scenarios.
- Out-of-band communication methods require testing.
- Customer notification thresholds are not consistently documented.
- Supplier and regulator contact protocols require updating.
- Communication roles during a cyber disruption require greater clarity.

#### Consequences

- Conflicting messages to customers or staff.
- Delays in customer notification.
- Increased complaint levels.
- Reputational damage.
- Regulatory and legal risk.
- Reduced coordination during recovery.

#### Residual Risk Rationale

Residual risk remains High because communication failures can materially amplify the impact of operational disruption.

### Finding 7 - Manual Workaround Limitations

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Risk ID | BCM-R17 |
| Risk rating | High residual risk |
| Affected services | Operations, Customer Services, Finance |
| Primary owner | [Head of Operations] |
| Risk status | Above tolerance |

#### Description

Manual workarounds are documented for some activities but may not operate effectively under realistic volumes, extended outage duration or reduced staffing. Some workarounds also depend on access to data that may be unavailable during a system outage.

#### Existing Controls

- Documented workaround steps for selected processes.
- Spreadsheets and templates for temporary processing.
- Supervisor approval for exceptional processing.
- Customer prioritisation arrangements.
- Backlog monitoring by operational teams.

#### Control Gaps

- Workarounds have not been tested at expected peak volumes.
- Data extraction requirements are not consistently documented.
- Reconciliation procedures after system restoration are incomplete.
- Staff training on workarounds is inconsistent.
- Workaround ownership and activation triggers require clarification.

#### Consequences

- Processing errors.
- Unmanageable backlog.
- Missed service commitments.
- Data integrity issues.
- Customer dissatisfaction.
- Increased recovery and reconciliation effort.

#### Residual Risk Rationale

Residual risk remains High because workaround effectiveness is uncertain and could prevent the organisation from meeting recovery objectives during prolonged system disruption.

### Risk Heat Map

| Impact \ Likelihood | 1 - Rare | 2 - Unlikely | 3 - Possible | 4 - Likely | 5 - Almost Certain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 - Severe | Medium | High | High | Extreme | Extreme |
| 4 - Major | Medium | Medium | High | High | Extreme |
| 3 - Moderate | Low | Medium | Medium | High | High |
| 2 - Minor | Low | Low | Medium | Medium | High |
| 1 - Insignificant | Low | Low | Low | Medium | Medium |

### Residual Risk Distribution

| Risk Rating | Count | Percentage | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Extreme | 1 | 6% | Immediate executive attention required |
| High | 6 | 33% | Formal treatment and management oversight required |
| Medium | 8 | 44% | Monitor and improve through planned actions |
| Low | 3 | 17% | Accept or monitor through normal management |

### Risks Above Target Tolerance

| Risk ID | Risk | Reason Above Tolerance | Required Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| BCM-R01 | Core technology platform outage | Recovery capability not fully validated against business needs | Approve recovery validation and dependency remediation |
| BCM-R02 | Cyber incident causing business interruption | Severe potential impact and incomplete cyber recovery integration | Executive escalation and accelerated treatment |
| BCM-R03 | Critical supplier service failure | Supplier recovery evidence and contractual obligations incomplete | Mandate supplier assurance and contract remediation |
| BCM-R05 | Specialist workforce unavailability | Key-person dependency and limited cross-training | Approve cross-training and succession actions |
| BCM-R08 | Loss or corruption of critical operational data | Backup and recovery assurance incomplete for all priority data | Validate backup recoverability and restoration priorities |
| BCM-R15 | Crisis communication failure | Communication triggers, approvals and out-of-band methods incomplete | Approve crisis communications improvement plan |
| BCM-R17 | Manual workaround failure under peak volume | Workarounds not tested for volume, duration or data availability | Require operational workaround testing |

## Analysis

### Overall Business Continuity Risk Profile

The organisation’s continuity risk profile is shaped by three main factors:

1. **High dependency on technology platforms and digital data** 
 Priority services rely heavily on integrated applications, identity services, networks, cloud platforms, communications channels and data repositories. Technology outages therefore have immediate operational and customer impact.

2. **Dependency concentration** 
 Several critical activities rely on limited suppliers, specialist teams, named individuals or single systems. These dependencies increase the likelihood that a disruption in one area will create wider business interruption.

3. **Uneven maturity of recovery capability** 
 Crisis escalation and high-level response arrangements are in place, but detailed recovery capability varies across business units, systems and suppliers. The main gap is not the absence of plans, but the level of evidence that plans will work under realistic conditions.

### Alignment with Business Impact Expectations

The assessment indicates partial alignment between business impact expectations and actual recovery capability.

| Area | Alignment Status | Observations |
|---|---|---|
| Priority service identification | Mostly aligned | Priority services have been identified, but dependency details require refinement |
| Recovery time objectives | Partially aligned | Objectives are documented, but not always supported by tested recovery capability |
| Resource requirements | Partially aligned | People, system and supplier needs are known at a high level; detailed mapping is incomplete |
| Technology recovery | Partially aligned | Procedures exist for core systems, but integrated recovery sequencing requires improvement |
| Supplier recovery | Weak to partial | Supplier continuity evidence is inconsistent |
| Manual workarounds | Partial | Workarounds exist but require practical validation |
| Communications | Partial | Templates and channels exist, but triggers and approval paths need strengthening |

### Key Themes

#### Technology and Data Recovery

Technology and data recovery represent the highest continuity exposure. Recovery of systems alone may not be sufficient if data integrity, integration dependencies, identity services, communications tools and user access are not restored in the correct order. Business recovery planning should therefore include end-to-end recovery sequences for priority services, not only individual system restoration steps.

#### Supplier Resilience

Supplier resilience is a material risk due to reliance on external providers for technology, payment, customer support, logistics and specialist services. Supplier continuity assurance is currently not consistent enough for the organisation to rely on supplier claims without further validation. Critical suppliers should be subject to enhanced assurance, including evidence review, contractual requirements and incident notification expectations.

#### Workforce Resilience

Workforce resilience is generally acceptable for broad corporate activities but weaker for specialist operational and technology functions. Key-person dependencies create continuity exposure where recovery actions depend on a small number of individuals. Cross-training, documented procedures, deputy roles and extended incident rosters should be prioritised.

#### Workaround Capability

Manual workarounds are important to maintaining priority activities during technology disruption, but their effectiveness is not fully proven. Workarounds must be tested for volume, duration, required data access, approval controls, error handling and reconciliation after systems return.

#### Communications and Decision-Making

The organisation’s incident escalation routes are broadly defined, but communication thresholds and approval paths require improvement. Clear, timely and controlled communications are especially important during customer-impacting incidents and cyber events. Out-of-band communication channels should be tested to ensure the organisation can coordinate when normal tools are unavailable.

### Risk Interdependencies

Several risks are interdependent and could occur together:

| Primary Event | Likely Secondary Effects |
|---|---|
| Cyber incident | Technology outage, data integrity concerns, communications disruption, supplier escalation, regulatory exposure |
| Core platform outage | Manual workaround activation, customer communications, backlog creation, supplier support dependency |
| Main site loss | Remote working activation, telecommunications dependency, workforce availability issues |
| Supplier failure | Customer impact, process interruption, emergency procurement, contractual escalation |
| Workforce shortage | Delayed recovery, increased error rates, inability to maintain manual workarounds |
| Severe weather | Site access issues, staff availability reduction, logistics disruption and supplier delays |

Because of these interdependencies, treatment actions should prioritise end-to-end resilience of priority services rather than isolated control improvements.

### Residual Risk Acceptability

| Residual Risk Level | Acceptability Position |
|---|---|
| Extreme | Not acceptable without immediate executive review and urgent treatment plan |
| High | Not acceptable unless supported by approved treatment plan or time-bound risk acceptance |
| Medium | Acceptable where monitored and supported by proportionate improvement actions |
| Low | Acceptable with routine monitoring |

The current profile includes one Extreme risk and six High risks. These should be reported to the appropriate management forum and tracked until treatment is complete or residual exposure is formally accepted by authorised management.

### Maturity Observations

| Capability Area | Current Maturity | Target Direction |
|---|---|---|
| Risk identification | Developing | Improve scenario library and dependency mapping |
| Business impact alignment | Developing to established | Strengthen linkage between impacts, recovery objectives and risk assessment |
| Technology recovery assurance | Developing | Increase frequency and realism of recovery testing |
| Supplier continuity assurance | Developing | Introduce risk-based supplier assurance and contract controls |
| Crisis management | Established | Improve role clarity, decision logs and communication triggers |
| Business continuity plans | Developing to established | Standardise plan quality and ownership |
| Exercise and testing | Developing | Expand scenario testing for high-risk disruption events |
| Management reporting | Established | Continue risk-based reporting and action tracking |

## Recommendations & Actions

### Priority Recommendations

1. **Integrate cyber recovery and business continuity planning** 
 Develop and test a coordinated response model for cyber incidents that includes crisis management, technology recovery, business workarounds, legal, communications, supplier management and customer support.

2. **Validate recovery capability for priority services** 
 Conduct end-to-end recovery validation for priority services, including systems, data, integrations, people, suppliers, facilities and communications.

3. **Strengthen supplier continuity assurance** 
 Identify critical suppliers, confirm continuity requirements, obtain current evidence of supplier recovery capability and update contracts where necessary.

4. **Reduce key-person dependencies** 
 Document specialist activities, establish deputy arrangements, cross-train staff and maintain incident rosters for extended disruption.

5. **Test manual workarounds under realistic conditions** 
 Perform volume-based and duration-based workaround exercises, including data access, approval controls, reconciliation and backlog recovery.

6. **Improve crisis communications capability** 
 Define communication triggers, approval routes, stakeholder responsibilities, out-of-band channels and pre-approved templates for high-impact scenarios.

7. **Complete dependency mapping** 
 Map end-to-end dependencies for priority services, including technology, data, suppliers, people, premises, equipment, records and communications channels.

8. **Establish formal risk treatment tracking** 
 Track all continuity risk actions through management reporting, with owners, dates, status, evidence and residual risk reassessment.

### Action Plan

| Action ID | Related Risk ID | Action | Owner | Priority | Target Date | Success Criteria | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BCM-A01 | BCM-R02 | Develop integrated cyber business recovery playbook covering business continuity, technology recovery, communications, legal and supplier coordination | [CISO / BCM Manager] | Critical | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Playbook approved and exercised with executive participation | Not started |
| BCM-A02 | BCM-R01, BCM-R08 | Perform end-to-end recovery test for [Priority Service 1], including application, data, integrations and business validation | [CIO / Service Owner] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Test completed, recovery time measured, issues logged and remediated | Not started |
| BCM-A03 | BCM-R03 | Complete continuity assurance review for all critical suppliers | [Head of Procurement] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Supplier evidence received, reviewed and risk-rated | In progress |
| BCM-A04 | BCM-R03 | Update critical supplier contracts to include continuity, incident notification, recovery cooperation and exit support requirements | [Legal / Procurement] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Contract amendments completed or risk exceptions approved | Not started |
| BCM-A05 | BCM-R05 | Identify key-person dependencies for all priority activities and assign trained deputies | [Department Heads] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Deputy coverage documented for all priority activities | Not started |
| BCM-A06 | BCM-R17 | Conduct manual workaround test for [Priority Activity] at realistic transaction volume | [Head of Operations] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Test completed, throughput measured, reconciliation proven | Not started |
| BCM-A07 | BCM-R15 | Update crisis communication plan with triggers, approval paths and out-of-band communication channels | [Head of Communications] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Plan approved and contact channels tested | In progress |
| BCM-A08 | BCM-R16 | Complete dependency mapping for all priority services | [BCM Manager / Process Owners] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Dependency maps approved by service owners and linked to continuity plans | In progress |
| BCM-A09 | BCM-R04 | Conduct main site loss exercise involving facilities, operations, IT and HR | [Facilities Manager / BCM Manager] | Medium | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Exercise report completed and actions tracked | Not started |
| BCM-A10 | BCM-R06 | Validate telecommunications failover for key sites and remote workforce coordination | [Network Manager] | Medium | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Failover test completed and results documented | Not started |
| BCM-A11 | BCM-R10 | Review workforce availability assumptions for sustained absenteeism scenario | [HR Director] | Medium | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Minimum staffing thresholds and escalation actions documented | Not started |
| BCM-A12 | BCM-R11 | Confirm alternative arrangements for payment or banking disruption | [Finance Director] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Alternative process documented and tested | Not started |
| BCM-A13 | BCM-R14 | Validate recovery of key document repositories and access for priority teams | [IT Service Owner / Records Owner] | Medium | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Restoration and access test completed | Not started |
| BCM-A14 | BCM-R09 | Update severe weather and transport disruption guidance for staff and managers | [HR / Facilities] | Low | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Guidance approved and communicated | Not started |
| BCM-A15 | All High Risks | Add continuity risk treatment progress to monthly management reporting | [BCM Manager] | High | [YYYY-MM-DD] | Monthly reporting pack includes action status and overdue items | Not started |

### Management Decisions Required

| Decision ID | Decision Required | Recommended Decision Owner | Due Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| DEC-01 | Approve urgent treatment plan for cyber-related business interruption risk | [Executive Committee / Risk Committee] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| DEC-02 | Confirm acceptable target recovery times for priority services where current capability is uncertain | [Service Owners / Executive Sponsor] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| DEC-03 | Approve funding and resource allocation for recovery testing and dependency remediation | [CFO / COO / CIO] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| DEC-04 | Mandate enhanced continuity assurance for critical suppliers | [Procurement Governance Forum] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |
| DEC-05 | Approve formal acceptance or treatment of residual risks that remain above tolerance after planned actions | [Risk Committee] | [YYYY-MM-DD] |

### Proposed Review Schedule

| Activity | Frequency | Responsible Role | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuity risk register update | Monthly | [BCM Manager] | Updated risk status and action tracking |
| High-risk action review | Monthly | [Risk Committee / BCM Steering Group] | Decisions, escalations and overdue action review |
| Supplier continuity assurance refresh | Annually or on material change | [Procurement / Supplier Owners] | Updated supplier risk ratings |
| Priority service dependency review | Annually or on material change | [Service Owners / BCM Manager] | Updated dependency maps |
| Business continuity risk reassessment | Annually or after major incident | [BCM Manager] | Updated risk assessment report |
| Exercise and test programme review | Quarterly | [BCM Manager / CIO / Operations] | Updated exercise plan and results |
| Risk acceptance review | At least annually | [Authorised Risk Owner] | Confirmed, revised or expired acceptance decisions |

### Evidence to Retain

The following evidence should be retained to support governance, auditability and continual improvement:

- Approved risk assessment report.
- Risk assessment working papers and scoring rationale.
- Attendance records from workshops and interviews.
- Business impact analysis inputs used in the assessment.
- Current business continuity plans and recovery procedures.
- Technology recovery test reports.
- Supplier continuity evidence and assurance reviews.
- Exercise reports and lessons learned.
- Action tracking records and closure evidence.
- Management approvals, escalations and risk acceptance decisions.
- Updated risk register entries.

## Distribution & Confidentiality

### Distribution

This report is intended for controlled internal distribution to personnel with responsibility for governance, risk management, business continuity, technology recovery, operational resilience, supplier management and executive oversight.

| Recipient / Group | Purpose of Distribution |
|---|---|
| [Executive Committee] | Review material continuity risks and approve decisions |
| [Risk Committee] | Monitor risk profile, treatment actions and residual exposure |
| [Business Continuity Steering Group] | Coordinate improvement actions and plan updates |
| [Chief Operating Officer] | Oversee operational recovery capability and resource needs |
| [Chief Information Officer] | Oversee technology recovery, dependency and testing actions |
| [Chief Information Security Officer] | Coordinate cyber disruption and recovery improvements |
| [Head of Procurement] | Manage supplier resilience actions |
| [Business Unit Heads] | Own process-level continuity risks and treatment actions |
| [Internal Audit] | Use as evidence for independent assurance planning |
| [Compliance / Legal] | Consider regulatory, contractual and notification implications |

Distribution outside the listed recipients requires approval from [Business Continuity Manager] and [Information Security / Legal], unless required by law, contract or approved governance process.

### Confidentiality

This report is classified as **Confidential - Internal Use Only**.

It contains sensitive information relating to business disruption exposure, technology dependencies, supplier dependencies, operational weaknesses and recovery capability. Unauthorised disclosure could increase operational, security, commercial or reputational risk.

Recipients must:

- Store the report only in approved document repositories.
- Not forward the report to unauthorised recipients.
- Not share detailed risk information with suppliers unless approved and limited to relevant content.
- Protect printed copies from unauthorised access.
- Dispose of printed copies securely when no longer required.
- Report suspected unauthorised disclosure to [Information Security Contact] immediately.

| Approved report | Retain for [Retention Period] | [Business Continuity Manager] |
| Working papers | Retain for [Retention Period] | [Business Continuity Manager] |
